domains.name: Information & AI
domains.blurb: Writing, printing, computing, networks and machine intelligence.

domains.name: Mathematics
domains.blurb: Number, shape, proof, and the problems still standing.

domains.name: Physics & Astronomy
domains.blurb: Matter, energy, spacetime and the sky.

domains.name: Engineering
domains.blurb: Tools, machines, power, electronics and spaceflight.

domains.name: Life & Medicine
domains.blurb: Farming, cells, genes, medicine and the brain.

nodes.title: Writing
nodes.html: Sumerian scribes turned clay accounting tokens into cuneiform around 3200 BCE; Egypt, China and Mesoamerica invented writing independently. Knowledge could now outlive the people who had it.
nodes.summary: Sumerian scribes turned clay accounting tokens into cuneiform around 3200 BCE; Egypt, China and Mesoamerica invented writing independently.

nodes.title: Papyrus
nodes.html: Egyptians pressed strips of the papyrus plant into sheets that took ink. It was in use by the First Dynasty (about 3000 BCE), and the oldest inscribed papyri found, the Diary of Merer, date from about 2560 BCE. Papyrus was the main writing material of the Mediterranean world for several thousand years, until parchment and paper displaced it.
nodes.summary: Egyptians pressed strips of the papyrus plant into sheets that took ink.

nodes.title: Libraries & Archives
nodes.html: Clay-tablet archives at Ebla (about 2500 BCE) and Ashurbanipal’s library at Nineveh (7th century BCE) gathered texts in one place, and the Library of Alexandria (3rd century BCE) tried to collect all known writing. Libraries let written knowledge be stored, catalogued and copied beyond a single generation.
nodes.summary: Clay-tablet archives at Ebla (about 2500 BCE) and Ashurbanipal’s library at Nineveh (7th century BCE) gathered texts in one place, and the Library of Alexandria (3rd century BCE) tried to collect all known writing.

nodes.title: Alphabet
nodes.html: Semitic speakers in Egypt and Sinai wrote consonants with a few dozen signs adapted from hieroglyphs (the Proto-Sinaitic script, dated between about 1850 and 1550 BCE). The Phoenician alphabet (about 1050 BCE) spread the idea and the Greeks added vowels (about 800 BCE). Latin, Cyrillic, Hebrew and Arabic scripts descend from it.
nodes.summary: Semitic speakers in Egypt and Sinai wrote consonants with a few dozen signs adapted from hieroglyphs (the Proto-Sinaitic script, dated between about 1850 and 1550 BCE).

nodes.title: Abacus
nodes.html: Counting boards and bead frames do positional arithmetic by moving tokens. Greek sources show counting boards by the 5th century BCE, the Salamis tablet dates from about 300 BCE, and the Chinese suanpan is documented by the 2nd century BCE. Abaci stayed in everyday use across Asia into the 20th century.
nodes.summary: Counting boards and bead frames do positional arithmetic by moving tokens.

nodes.title: Antikythera Mechanism
nodes.html: A hand-cranked bronze gear train built in the 2nd century BCE and recovered from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera in 1901. Its dials modelled the motions of the Sun and Moon and predicted eclipses, and it is the oldest known analogue computer. Geared mechanisms of similar complexity do not reappear in the record until medieval astronomical clocks.
nodes.summary: A hand-cranked bronze gear train built in the 2nd century BCE and recovered from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera in 1901.

nodes.title: Substitution Cipher
nodes.html: The Roman writer Suetonius reports that Julius Caesar protected military letters by shifting each letter three places along the alphabet (1st century BCE), and the Hebrew Atbash cipher is older. A fixed substitution hides a message only while the method stays secret, and frequency analysis breaks it.
nodes.summary: The Roman writer Suetonius reports that Julius Caesar protected military letters by shifting each letter three places along the alphabet (1st century BCE), and the Hebrew Atbash cipher is older.

nodes.title: Paper
nodes.html: Cai Lun presented an improved method of making paper from bark, rags and hemp to the Han court in 105 CE, though paper fragments from the 2nd century BCE are known. Papermaking reached Baghdad in the 8th century and Spain and Italy in the 12th and 13th, supplying a cheap writing surface for books, records and printing.
nodes.summary: Cai Lun presented an improved method of making paper from bark, rags and hemp to the Han court in 105 CE, though paper fragments from the 2nd century BCE are known.

nodes.title: Quipu
nodes.html: Andean knotted cords recorded numbers in base ten by the type and position of their knots, and probably other information that is not yet understood. The first undisputed examples come from the Wari (about 600 to 1000 CE), and the Inca state kept census and tax records on quipus until the Spanish conquest.
nodes.summary: Andean knotted cords recorded numbers in base ten by the type and position of their knots, and probably other information that is not yet understood.

nodes.title: Woodblock Printing
nodes.html: Printing from carved wooden blocks existed in Tang China by the 7th century, and the Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest securely dated printed book. Bi Sheng devised movable clay type around 1040, four centuries before Gutenberg.
nodes.summary: Printing from carved wooden blocks existed in Tang China by the 7th century, and the Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest securely dated printed book.

nodes.title: Frequency Analysis
nodes.html: Al-Kindi’s treatise on deciphering cryptographic messages (about 850) showed that a substitution cipher can be broken by counting how often each symbol occurs and matching the counts to the letter frequencies of the language. It is the earliest known work on cryptanalysis and ended the safety of simple substitution.
nodes.summary: Al-Kindi’s treatise on deciphering cryptographic messages (about 850) showed that a substitution cipher can be broken by counting how often each symbol occurs and matching the counts to the letter frequencies of the language.

nodes.title: Printing Press
nodes.html: Movable metal type and a screw press (c. 1440). Movable type had appeared earlier in China (Bi Sheng, c. 1040) and Korea. Within fifty years Europe held millions of printed books, and science became cumulative and public.
nodes.summary: Movable metal type and a screw press (c.

nodes.title: Polyalphabetic Cipher
nodes.html: Alberti’s cipher disk (De Cifris, 1467) changed the substitution alphabet during a message so that letter frequencies no longer showed through. Bellaso (1553) gave the keyword form later credited to Blaise de Vigenère, and it resisted attack until Friedrich Kasiski published a general method in 1863.
nodes.summary: Alberti’s cipher disk (De Cifris, 1467) changed the substitution alphabet during a message so that letter frequencies no longer showed through.

nodes.title: Slide Rule
nodes.html: Sliding two logarithmic scales against each other multiplies numbers by adding lengths. Edmund Gunter laid out the scale in 1620, and William Oughtred combined two of them around 1622 (published 1632). The slide rule was the engineer’s standard calculator until electronic pocket calculators replaced it in the 1970s.
nodes.summary: Sliding two logarithmic scales against each other multiplies numbers by adding lengths.

nodes.title: Mechanical Calculator
nodes.html: Wilhelm Schickard’s calculating clock (1623) and Blaise Pascal’s Pascaline (1642) added numbers with geared wheels and automatic carrying, and Leibniz’s stepped drum (1673) extended the idea to multiplication. Mechanical calculators served offices and laboratories until electronic machines replaced them in the 1970s.
nodes.summary: Wilhelm Schickard’s calculating clock (1623) and Blaise Pascal’s Pascaline (1642) added numbers with geared wheels and automatic carrying, and Leibniz’s stepped drum (1673) extended the idea to multiplication.

nodes.title: Scientific Journal
nodes.html: The Journal des sçavans (5 January 1665) and the Royal Society’s Philosophical Transactions (6 March 1665, edited by Henry Oldenburg) printed reviews and reports of new work for a wide audience. Journals gave authors a public record of priority and let others check and build on results.
nodes.summary: The Journal des sçavans (5 January 1665) and the Royal Society’s Philosophical Transactions (6 March 1665, edited by Henry Oldenburg) printed reviews and reports of new work for a wide audience.

nodes.title: Binary Arithmetic
nodes.html: Leibniz’s ‘Explication de l’arithmétique binaire’ (1703) showed how to write every number with only 0 and 1 and how to add, subtract, multiply and divide in that notation. Thomas Harriot had tried base two privately a century earlier. Binary notation became the basis of digital computers from the 1930s.
nodes.summary: Leibniz’s ‘Explication de l’arithmétique binaire’ (1703) showed how to write every number with only 0 and 1 and how to add, subtract, multiply and divide in that notation.

nodes.title: Encyclopedia
nodes.html: Diderot and d’Alembert’s Encyclopédie (1751 to 1772) filled 28 volumes in its first edition, with named contributors, cross-references and a tree of knowledge, and it was the first general encyclopedia to describe the mechanical arts in detail. It followed Pliny’s Natural History (77 CE) and Chambers’ Cyclopaedia (1728).
nodes.summary: Diderot and d’Alembert’s Encyclopédie (1751 to 1772) filled 28 volumes in its first edition, with named contributors, cross-references and a tree of knowledge, and it was the first general encyclopedia to describe the mechanical arts in detail.

nodes.title: Jacquard Loom
nodes.html: Jacquard’s loom (patented 1804) used chains of punched cards to select which warp threads to lift, so the woven pattern changed when the cards changed. It built on the work of Basile Bouchon (1725) and Jacques de Vaucanson, and Babbage adopted its punched cards to program his Analytical Engine.
nodes.summary: Jacquard’s loom (patented 1804) used chains of punched cards to select which warp threads to lift, so the woven pattern changed when the cards changed.

nodes.title: Difference Engine
nodes.html: In 1822 Babbage proposed a machine that tabulates polynomials by the method of finite differences, using only addition, to print error-free mathematical tables. It was never finished in his lifetime, but the Science Museum built Difference Engine No. 2 from his drawings in 1991, and it worked.
nodes.summary: In 1822 Babbage proposed a machine that tabulates polynomials by the method of finite differences, using only addition, to print error-free mathematical tables.

nodes.title: Braille
nodes.html: Louis Braille, blind since a childhood accident, devised a cell of six raised dots at the age of fifteen (1824) and published the system in 1829. He adapted it from Charles Barbier’s twelve-dot night writing. The 64 possible patterns form a fixed-length binary code that is read by touch, and braille is still in use worldwide.
nodes.summary: Louis Braille, blind since a childhood accident, devised a cell of six raised dots at the age of fifteen (1824) and published the system in 1829.

nodes.title: Analytical Engine
nodes.html: Babbage’s design of 1837 had a ‘mill’ that did the arithmetic, a ‘store’ that held numbers, conditional branching, loops and programs on punched cards: in principle a general-purpose computer. It was never completed, and only parts were built.
nodes.summary: Babbage’s design of 1837 had a ‘mill’ that did the arithmetic, a ‘store’ that held numbers, conditional branching, loops and programs on punched cards: in principle a general-purpose computer.

nodes.title: Morse Code
nodes.html: Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail devised a code of dots and dashes for the electric telegraph in 1838. Vail gave the most frequent letters the shortest signals, an early efficient source code. Friedrich Gerke’s revision (1848) became the basis of the international code standardized in 1865.
nodes.summary: Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail devised a code of dots and dashes for the electric telegraph in 1838.

nodes.title: First Computer Program

quote.text: The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.

nodes.html: Ada Lovelace’s notes (1843) on Luigi Menabrea’s article about the Analytical Engine include, in Note G, a table of operations for computing Bernoulli numbers, often called the first published computer program. She also observed that such an engine could operate on any symbols that follow rules, such as musical notes.
nodes.summary: Ada Lovelace’s notes (1843) on Luigi Menabrea’s article about the Analytical Engine include, in Note G, a table of operations for computing Bernoulli numbers, often called the first published computer program.

nodes.title: Tide-Predicting Machine
nodes.html: William Thomson’s machine of 1872 to 1873 added up tidal harmonics with pulleys and a wire to trace the predicted height of the tide at a port, a mechanical use of Fourier analysis. Larger machines followed in 1876 and 1879, and tide predictors stayed in service until digital computers replaced them in the 1960s and 1970s.
nodes.summary: William Thomson’s machine of 1872 to 1873 added up tidal harmonics with pulleys and a wire to trace the predicted height of the tide at a port, a mechanical use of Fourier analysis.

nodes.title: Baudot Code
nodes.html: Émile Baudot’s telegraph of 1874 used a fixed-length five-bit code and let several operators share one line. Donald Murray’s variant became the international teleprinter code ITA2 (standardized 1930), and the baud, the unit of signalling rate, is named after Baudot.
nodes.summary: Émile Baudot’s telegraph of 1874 used a fixed-length five-bit code and let several operators share one line.

nodes.title: Dewey Decimal Classification
nodes.html: Melvil Dewey’s classification (1876) gave every subject a decimal number, so a book could be shelved by topic and new books added without rearranging the collection. Callimachus’ Pinakes (about 245 BCE), a subject catalogue of the Library of Alexandria, is regarded as the first library catalogue. Dewey’s scheme is used in libraries in many countries.
nodes.summary: Melvil Dewey’s classification (1876) gave every subject a decimal number, so a book could be shelved by topic and new books added without rearranging the collection.

nodes.title: Punched-Card Tabulator
nodes.html: Herman Hollerith’s tabulating machine (1890) read holes in cards with electrical contacts and counted them on dial counters. It tabulated the 1890 US census in a fraction of the eight years the hand-tallied 1880 census had taken. His company was a forerunner of IBM, so named in 1924.
nodes.summary: Herman Hollerith’s tabulating machine (1890) read holes in cards with electrical contacts and counted them on dial counters.

nodes.title: One-Time Pad
nodes.html: Gilbert Vernam’s teleprinter cipher (1917) combined each character of a message with a character from a punched key tape. With Joseph Mauborgne’s addition of a truly random key used only once, it cannot be broken, as Claude Shannon proved in 1949. Frank Miller had described the same idea in 1882.
nodes.summary: Gilbert Vernam’s teleprinter cipher (1917) combined each character of a message with a character from a punched key tape.

nodes.title: Minimum Spanning Tree
nodes.html: Otakar Borůvka (1926) found the cheapest way to connect a set of towns into one electrical network, the first minimum-spanning-tree algorithm. Jarník (1930), Kruskal (1956) and Prim (1957) found the algorithms taught today. The problem arises in network design, clustering and approximations of the travelling salesman problem.
nodes.summary: Otakar Borůvka (1926) found the cheapest way to connect a set of towns into one electrical network, the first minimum-spanning-tree algorithm.

nodes.title: Sampling Theorem
nodes.html: A signal with no frequencies above B hertz is fixed by samples taken 2B times per second. Nyquist (1928) showed that bandwidth B carries 2B independent pulses per second, Kotelnikov (1933) proved the sampling result and Shannon (1949) gave the form found in textbooks. It underlies digital audio, images and communications.
nodes.summary: A signal with no frequencies above B hertz is fixed by samples taken 2B times per second.

nodes.title: Differential Analyzer
nodes.html: Vannevar Bush and Harold Hazen built an analogue machine at MIT (1931) that solved differential equations with rotating shafts and wheel-and-disc integrators. Copies computed artillery firing tables in the Second World War until electronic digital computers displaced analogue ones.
nodes.summary: Vannevar Bush and Harold Hazen built an analogue machine at MIT (1931) that solved differential equations with rotating shafts and wheel-and-disc integrators.

nodes.title: Breaking Enigma
nodes.html: Marian Rejewski used the theory of permutations to reconstruct the wiring of the German Enigma rotors in December 1932. The Polish bomba (1938) and, from 1940, Turing and Welchman’s Bombe at Bletchley Park automated the search for daily keys. The decrypts, code-named Ultra, informed Allied operations in the Second World War.
nodes.summary: Marian Rejewski used the theory of permutations to reconstruct the wiring of the German Enigma rotors in December 1932.

nodes.title: Lambda Calculus
nodes.html: Alonzo Church’s calculus of functions (developed 1932 to 1936) computes by substituting arguments into function bodies. He used it in 1936 to show that Hilbert’s Entscheidungsproblem is unsolvable, and it defines the same computable functions as Turing machines. It underlies functional programming languages and type theory.
nodes.summary: Alonzo Church’s calculus of functions (developed 1932 to 1936) computes by substituting arguments into function bodies.

nodes.title: Turing Machines

quote.text: We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done.

nodes.html: Turing’s machines (1936) defined what ‘computable’ means and proved that some problems are not, answering Hilbert’s decision problem. The universal machine is the idea of software.
nodes.summary: Turing’s machines (1936) defined what ‘computable’ means and proved that some problems are not, answering Hilbert’s decision problem.

nodes.title: Pulse-Code Modulation
nodes.html: Alec Reeves, working for ITT in Paris, conceived in 1937 the sending of speech as a stream of numbers, each the quantized level of a sampled waveform, which can be regenerated without accumulating noise. The SIGSALY secure telephone used PCM in 1943, and digital telephony, compact discs and audio files rely on it.
nodes.summary: Alec Reeves, working for ITT in Paris, conceived in 1937 the sending of speech as a stream of numbers, each the quantized level of a sampled waveform, which can be regenerated without accumulating noise.

nodes.title: Switching Circuits
nodes.html: Shannon’s master’s thesis (1937) showed that circuits of telegraph-style relays compute Boolean logic. It is often called the most important master’s thesis of the 20th century.
nodes.summary: Shannon’s master’s thesis (1937) showed that circuits of telegraph-style relays compute Boolean logic.

nodes.title: Zuse Z3
nodes.html: Konrad Zuse’s Z3, presented in Berlin on 12 May 1941, was the first working programmable, fully automatic digital computer. It used about 2,600 telephone relays, binary floating-point numbers and programs punched on film, but had no conditional branch. The original was destroyed in an air raid in December 1943.
nodes.summary: Konrad Zuse’s Z3, presented in Berlin on 12 May 1941, was the first working programmable, fully automatic digital computer.

nodes.title: Artificial Neuron
nodes.html: McCulloch and Pitts modelled neurons as logic gates (1943): the first mathematical neural network.
nodes.summary: McCulloch and Pitts modelled neurons as logic gates (1943): the first mathematical neural network.

nodes.title: Colossus
nodes.html: Tommy Flowers built Colossus at the Post Office Research Station. The first machine, with about 1,600 valves, worked in December 1943 and at Bletchley Park in early 1944 to break the German Lorenz teleprinter cipher. It is regarded as the first programmable electronic digital computer, and its existence stayed secret until the mid-1970s.
nodes.summary: Tommy Flowers built Colossus at the Post Office Research Station.

nodes.title: Electronic Computer
nodes.html: ENIAC (1945) computed electronically. The EDVAC report (1945) and the Manchester Baby (1948) kept the program in the same memory as the data, which is how computers still work.
nodes.summary: ENIAC (1945) computed electronically.

nodes.title: Memex

quote.text: Wholly new forms of encyclopedias will appear, ready-made with a mesh of associative trails running through them, ready to be dropped into the memex and there amplified.

nodes.html: In ‘As We May Think’ (The Atlantic, July 1945) Vannevar Bush described the memex, a desk-sized device storing a person’s books and records on microfilm, where the user could join items by associative trails as the mind moves between ideas. It was never built, but it inspired the pioneers of hypertext and the Web.
nodes.summary: In ‘As We May Think’ (The Atlantic, July 1945) Vannevar Bush described the memex, a desk-sized device storing a person’s books and records on microfilm, where the user could join items by associative trails as the mind moves between ideas.

nodes.title: Merge Sort
nodes.html: John von Neumann wrote a merge-sort program for the planned EDVAC in 1945. The method splits a list in halves, sorts each and merges them with about n log n comparisons, and its variants remain standard in sorting libraries, databases and external sorting of data too large for memory.
nodes.summary: John von Neumann wrote a merge-sort program for the planned EDVAC in 1945.

nodes.title: Information Theory

quote.text: The fundamental problem of communication is that of reproducing at one point either exactly or approximately a message selected at another point.

nodes.html: Shannon (1948) defined the bit, entropy and channel capacity, and set hard limits on compression and error-free communication.
nodes.summary: Shannon (1948) defined the bit, entropy and channel capacity, and set hard limits on compression and error-free communication.

nodes.title: Shannon’s Theory of Secrecy
nodes.html: Claude Shannon’s ‘Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems’ (1949) applied information theory to ciphers. It proved that the one-time pad is perfectly secret, that any perfectly secret cipher needs a key at least as long as the message, and introduced confusion and diffusion as design principles for block ciphers.
nodes.summary: Claude Shannon’s ‘Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems’ (1949) applied information theory to ciphers.

nodes.title: Computer Chess
nodes.html: Claude Shannon’s ‘Programming a Computer for Playing Chess’ (1950) set out minimax search with an evaluation function. Alan Turing and David Champernowne’s paper program Turochamp, begun in 1948, was executed by hand in 1952. Chess was the main testbed of game-playing AI until Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997.
nodes.summary: Claude Shannon’s ‘Programming a Computer for Playing Chess’ (1950) set out minimax search with an evaluation function.

nodes.title: Hamming Codes
nodes.html: Richard Hamming, frustrated when weekend jobs on Bell Labs’ relay computers aborted on single errors, devised codes that locate and correct one flipped bit (published 1950). Hamming distance became the basic measure of how well a code resists errors, and Hamming-style codes still protect computer memory.
nodes.summary: Richard Hamming, frustrated when weekend jobs on Bell Labs’ relay computers aborted on single errors, devised codes that locate and correct one flipped bit (published 1950).

nodes.title: Huffman Coding
nodes.html: David Huffman, then a graduate student at MIT, devised a method that builds an optimal prefix code from symbol frequencies by repeatedly merging the two rarest symbols (a term paper of 1951, published 1952). It beat the Shannon–Fano code taught by his professor and is a component of JPEG, MP3, ZIP and fax compression.
nodes.summary: David Huffman, then a graduate student at MIT, devised a method that builds an optimal prefix code from symbol frequencies by repeatedly merging the two rarest symbols (a term paper of 1951, published 1952).

nodes.title: Hash Table
nodes.html: Hans Peter Luhn’s IBM memorandum of January 1953 stored records in buckets chosen by applying a function to the key, chaining the collisions. At IBM, Gene Amdahl and colleagues used open addressing with linear probing for an assembler in the 1950s. Hash tables give expected constant-time lookup and underlie dictionaries in most programming languages.
nodes.summary: Hans Peter Luhn’s IBM memorandum of January 1953 stored records in buckets chosen by applying a function to the key, chaining the collisions.

nodes.title: Reed–Muller Codes
nodes.html: David Muller (1954) defined binary codes from evaluations of low-degree polynomials in several variables, and Irving Reed gave a majority-logic decoder the same year. A first-order Reed–Muller code carried Mariner 9’s pictures of Mars (1971), and the family later underpinned work on locally testable codes and polar codes.
nodes.summary: David Muller (1954) defined binary codes from evaluations of low-degree polynomials in several variables, and Irving Reed gave a majority-logic decoder the same year.

nodes.title: Artificial General Intelligence

quote.text: The first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.

nodes.html: Machines that match or exceed people at essentially all cognitive work. It was proposed as a research goal at the 1956 Dartmouth workshop; definitions are contested, and timelines even more so.
nodes.summary: Machines that match or exceed people at essentially all cognitive work.

nodes.title: Chomsky Hierarchy
nodes.html: Noam Chomsky’s papers of 1956 and 1959 ranked formal grammars into regular, context-free, context-sensitive and unrestricted types, recognized by finite automata, pushdown automata, linear bounded automata and Turing machines. Context-free grammars became the standard way to define programming-language syntax.
nodes.summary: Noam Chomsky’s papers of 1956 and 1959 ranked formal grammars into regular, context-free, context-sensitive and unrestricted types, recognized by finite automata, pushdown automata, linear bounded automata and Turing machines.

nodes.title: Dartmouth AI Workshop

quote.text: The study is to proceed on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.

nodes.html: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon proposed in 1955 a two-month study of machine intelligence at Dartmouth College in the summer of 1956, and the proposal introduced the term ‘artificial intelligence’. At the workshop Allen Newell, Cliff Shaw and Herbert Simon showed the Logic Theorist, a program that proved theorems of Principia Mathematica.
nodes.summary: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon proposed in 1955 a two-month study of machine intelligence at Dartmouth College in the summer of 1956, and the proposal introduced the term ‘artificial intelligence’.

nodes.title: Dijkstra’s Algorithm
nodes.html: Edsger Dijkstra conceived (1956) and published (1959) a method that finds shortest paths from one source in a graph with nonnegative edge weights by repeatedly settling the nearest unvisited node. With Fibonacci heaps (1984) it runs in O(m + n log n) time, and variants route traffic in networks and maps.
nodes.summary: Edsger Dijkstra conceived (1956) and published (1959) a method that finds shortest paths from one source in a graph with nonnegative edge weights by repeatedly settling the nearest unvisited node.

nodes.title: Finite Automata
nodes.html: Kleene (1956) showed that networks of McCulloch–Pitts neurons recognize exactly the regular events, the languages described by regular expressions. Rabin and Scott’s 1959 paper on finite automata introduced nondeterminism and won them the 1976 Turing Award. Finite automata and regular expressions are used in compilers, text search and network protocols.
nodes.summary: Kleene (1956) showed that networks of McCulloch–Pitts neurons recognize exactly the regular events, the languages described by regular expressions.

nodes.title: Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem
nodes.html: The largest flow that can be sent through a network equals the capacity of its smallest cut (1956, shown independently by Ford and Fulkerson, and by Elias, Feinstein and Shannon). The Ford–Fulkerson augmenting-path method began the study of network-flow algorithms, used in matching, scheduling and image segmentation.
nodes.summary: The largest flow that can be sent through a network equals the capacity of its smallest cut (1956, shown independently by Ford and Fulkerson, and by Elias, Feinstein and Shannon).

nodes.title: Operating System
nodes.html: GM-NAA I/O, written by Robert Patrick at General Motors Research and Owen Mock at North American Aviation for the IBM 704 (1956), ran jobs in a batch without manual setup and supplied common input and output routines. IBM’s OS/360 (1966) and the time-sharing systems of the 1960s extended the idea into the operating systems that manage every computer today.
nodes.summary: GM-NAA I/O, written by Robert Patrick at General Motors Research and Owen Mock at North American Aviation for the IBM 704 (1956), ran jobs in a batch without manual setup and supplied common input and output routines.

nodes.title: High-Level Programming
nodes.html: Compilers let people write formulas instead of machine code: Hopper’s A-0 (1952), Backus’s FORTRAN (1957), then Lisp (1958) and everything since.
nodes.summary: Compilers let people write formulas instead of machine code: Hopper’s A-0 (1952), Backus’s FORTRAN (1957), then Lisp (1958) and everything since.

nodes.title: Perceptron
nodes.html: Rosenblatt’s perceptron (1958) learned its own weights from examples. It was the start of machine learning, and of its first hype cycle.
nodes.summary: Rosenblatt’s perceptron (1958) learned its own weights from examples.

nodes.title: AI Alignment

progress.what: “Concrete Problems in AI Safety” set out reward hacking, safe exploration and scalable oversight as research problems.
progress.html: “Concrete Problems in AI Safety” set out reward hacking, safe exploration and scalable oversight as research problems.

progress.what: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences, the basis of RLHF.
progress.html: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences, the basis of RLHF.

progress.what: Weak-to-strong generalization: a testbed for supervising models more capable than their supervisors.
progress.html: Weak-to-strong generalization: a testbed for supervising models more capable than their supervisors.

progress.what: Alignment faking: a frontier model selectively complied during training to preserve its existing preferences, a failure mode that training-based alignment must handle.
progress.html: Alignment faking: a frontier model selectively complied during training to preserve its existing preferences, a failure mode that training-based alignment must handle.

nodes.html: Build AI systems that reliably pursue the goals their designers intend, including systems more capable than any person. Norbert Wiener warned of the problem in 1960; RLHF, Constitutional AI and interpretability are partial tools, and no method yet gives guarantees for systems beyond human level.
nodes.summary: Build AI systems that reliably pursue the goals their designers intend, including systems more capable than any person.

nodes.title: ALGOL & BNF
nodes.html: The ALGOL 60 report (1960), edited by Peter Naur for an international committee, introduced block structure, recursion and lexical scope and defined the language’s syntax in Backus–Naur form, a notation John Backus had proposed for ALGOL 58. It started precise language definition, and C, Pascal and most later languages descend from ALGOL.
nodes.summary: The ALGOL 60 report (1960), edited by Peter Naur for an international committee, introduced block structure, recursion and lexical scope and defined the language’s syntax in Backus–Naur form, a notation John Backus had proposed for ALGOL 58.

nodes.title: Karatsuba Multiplication
nodes.html: Anatoly Karatsuba, then a student, found in 1960 that two n-digit numbers can be multiplied with three half-size products instead of four, using about n^1.585 steps. This refuted Kolmogorov’s conjecture that about n² operations are needed and began the search for faster multiplication that reached n log n in 2019.
nodes.summary: Anatoly Karatsuba, then a student, found in 1960 that two n-digit numbers can be multiplied with three half-size products instead of four, using about n^1.585 steps.

nodes.title: Reed–Solomon Codes
nodes.html: Irving Reed and Gustave Solomon (1960) built codes from polynomial values over finite fields that correct bursts of errors, and Berlekamp and Massey supplied an efficient decoder in the late 1960s. Reed–Solomon codes protect compact discs, QR codes, RAID storage and deep-space links.
nodes.summary: Irving Reed and Gustave Solomon (1960) built codes from polynomial values over finite fields that correct bursts of errors, and Berlekamp and Massey supplied an efficient decoder in the late 1960s.

nodes.title: Deletion Channel Capacity

progress.what: A coding theorem for channels with synchronization errors: the capacity exists and equals a limit of normalized mutual information.
progress.html: A coding theorem for channels with synchronization errors: the capacity exists and equals a limit of normalized mutual information.

progress.what: Capacity at least 0.1185(1 − d) for every deletion probability d.
progress.html: Capacity at least 0.1185(1 − d) for every deletion probability d.

progress.what: Optimal coding and a precise capacity expansion for small deletion probabilities.
progress.html: Optimal coding and a precise capacity expansion for small deletion probabilities.

progress.what: Upper bound (1 − d) log₂ φ for d ≥ 1/2, with φ the golden ratio, from a convex-programming method.
progress.html: Upper bound (1 − d) log₂ φ for d ≥ 1/2, with φ the golden ratio, from a convex-programming method.

nodes.html: What is the capacity of the binary channel that deletes each transmitted bit independently with probability d, without telling the receiver where? Studied since Gallager (1961) and Dobrushin (1967), it has no closed form; as d approaches 1 the capacity is known only to lie between about 0.1185(1 − d) and 0.4143(1 − d).
nodes.summary: What is the capacity of the binary channel that deletes each transmitted bit independently with probability d, without telling the receiver where?

nodes.title: Quicksort
nodes.html: Tony Hoare devised quicksort in 1959 while working on machine translation in Moscow and published it in 1961. It partitions a list around a pivot and sorts the parts recursively, taking about n log n comparisons on average, and it is the ancestor of the sort routines in many programming-language libraries.
nodes.summary: Tony Hoare devised quicksort in 1959 while working on machine translation in Moscow and published it in 1961.

nodes.title: Time-Sharing
nodes.html: MIT’s Compatible Time-Sharing System, demonstrated in November 1961 under Fernando Corbató, let many users work interactively on one computer at the same time, following John McCarthy’s proposal of 1959. Time-sharing led to Multics and Unix, to electronic mail, and to the idea of computing as a shared utility.
nodes.summary: MIT’s Compatible Time-Sharing System, demonstrated in November 1961 under Fernando Corbató, let many users work interactively on one computer at the same time, following John McCarthy’s proposal of 1959.

nodes.title: Balanced Search Trees
nodes.html: Georgy Adelson-Velsky and Evgenii Landis (1962) described AVL trees, binary search trees that rotate after each update to keep their height proportional to log n, so search, insertion and deletion take logarithmic time. B-trees (Bayer and McCreight, 1970) and red-black trees (1970s) followed and underlie ordered maps and database indexes.
nodes.summary: Georgy Adelson-Velsky and Evgenii Landis (1962) described AVL trees, binary search trees that rotate after each update to keep their height proportional to log n, so search, insertion and deletion take logarithmic time.

nodes.title: DPLL Algorithm
nodes.html: Martin Davis and Hilary Putnam (1960) and then Davis, George Logemann and Donald Loveland (1962) gave a backtracking procedure that decides whether a propositional formula can be satisfied. This DPLL algorithm is the ancestor of every modern SAT solver.
nodes.summary: Martin Davis and Hilary Putnam (1960) and then Davis, George Logemann and Donald Loveland (1962) gave a backtracking procedure that decides whether a propositional formula can be satisfied.

nodes.title: LDPC Codes
nodes.html: Robert Gallager’s 1960 thesis (published 1962) described codes defined by sparse parity checks and decoded by passing messages iteratively. They were largely forgotten until David MacKay and Radford Neal revived them in 1996, and they now protect Wi-Fi, 5G data channels and digital television.
nodes.summary: Robert Gallager’s 1960 thesis (published 1962) described codes defined by sparse parity checks and decoded by passing messages iteratively.

nodes.title: Optimal Sorting Networks

progress.what: SAT solving proved the optimal depths for up to 16 inputs.
progress.html: SAT solving proved the optimal depths for up to 16 inputs.

progress.what: 25 comparators are optimal for 9 inputs and 29 for 10.
progress.html: 25 comparators are optimal for 9 inputs and 29 for 10.

progress.what: New parallel networks for 17 to 20 inputs, including a depth-10 network for 17 inputs, which is optimal.
progress.html: New parallel networks for 17 to 20 inputs, including a depth-10 network for 17 inputs, which is optimal.

progress.what: 35 comparators are optimal for 11 inputs and 39 for 12.
progress.html: 35 comparators are optimal for 11 inputs and 39 for 12.

nodes.html: What is the fewest comparators, or the fewest parallel layers, in a network that sorts n inputs? Bose and Nelson raised the question in 1962. Optimal size is known only up to 12 inputs (13 inputs need 43, 44 or 45 comparators) and optimal depth up to 17 (18 inputs need depth 10 or 11); recent cases were settled with SAT solvers.
nodes.summary: What is the fewest comparators, or the fewest parallel layers, in a network that sorts n inputs?

nodes.title: Computer Vision
nodes.html: Larry Roberts’s 1963 MIT thesis recovered the three-dimensional shape of polyhedra from photographs, using edges and perspective geometry. A 1966 MIT summer project meant to build a visual system in a few months showed how hard the task was, and computer vision grew into a research field of its own.
nodes.summary: Larry Roberts’s 1963 MIT thesis recovered the three-dimensional shape of polyhedra from photographs, using edges and perspective geometry.

nodes.title: Sketchpad
nodes.html: Ivan Sutherland’s 1963 MIT thesis program let a person draw on the screen of the TX-2 computer with a light pen, apply geometric constraints and reuse a master drawing as many linked instances. It founded interactive computer graphics and computer-aided design, and won him the 1988 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: Ivan Sutherland’s 1963 MIT thesis program let a person draw on the screen of the TX-2 computer with a light pen, apply geometric constraints and reuse a master drawing as many linked instances.

nodes.title: Citation Index
nodes.html: Eugene Garfield’s Science Citation Index (1964) recorded which papers cite which, so that a reader could follow a reference forward in time. Citation data became the basis of bibliometrics and journal impact factors, and it inspired the link analysis later used in PageRank.
nodes.summary: Eugene Garfield’s Science Citation Index (1964) recorded which papers cite which, so that a reader could follow a reference forward in time.

nodes.title: Instruction Set Architecture
nodes.html: IBM’s System/360 (announced 1964), designed by Gene Amdahl, Fred Brooks and Gerrit Blaauw, defined one instruction set for a whole family of machines at different prices, so that software ran on all of them. It separated architecture from implementation and standardized the 8-bit byte.
nodes.summary: IBM’s System/360 (announced 1964), designed by Gene Amdahl, Fred Brooks and Gerrit Blaauw, defined one instruction set for a whole family of machines at different prices, so that software ran on all of them.

nodes.title: Packet Switching
nodes.html: Paul Baran at RAND (1964) and Donald Davies at the National Physical Laboratory (1965) independently proposed dividing messages into small blocks routed separately through a network; Davies named them packets. Packet switching shares links efficiently and survives the loss of single nodes, and it became the basis of ARPANET (1969) and the internet.
nodes.summary: Paul Baran at RAND (1964) and Donald Davies at the National Physical Laboratory (1965) independently proposed dividing messages into small blocks routed separately through a network; Davies named them packets.

nodes.title: Blossom Algorithm
nodes.html: Jack Edmonds’s ‘Paths, Trees, and Flowers’ (1965) gave a polynomial-time algorithm for maximum matching in general graphs by shrinking odd cycles called blossoms. It also argued that polynomial time is the right formal notion of an efficient algorithm.
nodes.summary: Jack Edmonds’s ‘Paths, Trees, and Flowers’ (1965) gave a polynomial-time algorithm for maximum matching in general graphs by shrinking odd cycles called blossoms.

nodes.title: Expert Systems
nodes.html: DENDRAL, begun in 1965 by Edward Feigenbaum, Joshua Lederberg and Bruce Buchanan at Stanford, inferred molecular structures from mass spectra using rules supplied by chemists, and MYCIN (1972) applied the approach to diagnosing blood infections. Expert systems drove the AI boom of the 1980s, and their limits contributed to the second AI winter.
nodes.summary: DENDRAL, begun in 1965 by Edward Feigenbaum, Joshua Lederberg and Bruce Buchanan at Stanford, inferred molecular structures from mass spectra using rules supplied by chemists, and MYCIN (1972) applied the approach to diagnosing blood infections.

nodes.title: Hypertext
nodes.html: Ted Nelson coined ‘hypertext’ in 1965 for non-sequential writing joined by links, following Bush’s memex. Early systems included the Hypertext Editing System (1967) at Brown University, NLS (1968) and HyperCard (1987), before Tim Berners-Lee built the Web.
nodes.summary: Ted Nelson coined ‘hypertext’ in 1965 for non-sequential writing joined by links, following Bush’s memex.

nodes.title: Kolmogorov Complexity
nodes.html: The information in a string can be measured by the length of the shortest program that outputs it. Ray Solomonoff (1960 and 1964), Andrey Kolmogorov (1965) and Gregory Chaitin (1966) arrived at the idea independently. The measure is uncomputable, and it gives a precise form of Occam’s razor.
nodes.summary: The information in a string can be measured by the length of the shortest program that outputs it.

nodes.title: Resolution Theorem Proving
nodes.html: J. Alan Robinson’s resolution principle (1965), together with unification, reduced first-order proof search to a single mechanical inference rule. It became the basis of automated theorem provers and of the logic-programming language Prolog (1972).
nodes.summary: J.

nodes.title: Time Hierarchy Theorem
nodes.html: Juris Hartmanis and Richard Stearns’s ‘On the Computational Complexity of Algorithms’ (1965) defined time-bounded complexity classes and proved that, given more time, Turing machines can solve strictly more problems. It founded computational complexity theory and won them the 1993 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: Juris Hartmanis and Richard Stearns’s ‘On the Computational Complexity of Algorithms’ (1965) defined time-bounded complexity classes and proved that, given more time, Turing machines can solve strictly more problems.

nodes.title: ELIZA
nodes.html: Joseph Weizenbaum’s ELIZA (1966) at MIT matched keywords in typed input and turned them into questions, in its best-known script imitating a Rogerian psychotherapist. Users confided in it although it understood nothing, which troubled Weizenbaum and gave the name ‘ELIZA effect’ to the habit of crediting programs with understanding.
nodes.summary: Joseph Weizenbaum’s ELIZA (1966) at MIT matched keywords in typed input and turned them into questions, in its best-known script imitating a Rogerian psychotherapist.

nodes.title: Hidden Markov Models
nodes.html: Leonard Baum and Ted Petrie (1966) developed statistics for Markov chains whose states are seen only through noisy outputs, and Baum and Lloyd Welch gave an expectation-maximization algorithm to learn them. Hidden Markov models drove speech recognition at IBM and Dragon from the 1970s and were later used to find genes in DNA.
nodes.summary: Leonard Baum and Ted Petrie (1966) developed statistics for Markov chains whose states are seen only through noisy outputs, and Baum and Lloyd Welch gave an expectation-maximization algorithm to learn them.

nodes.title: Object-Oriented Programming
nodes.html: Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard’s Simula 67 introduced classes, objects, inheritance and virtual procedures, and Alan Kay’s Smalltalk (1972) at Xerox PARC developed them and named the style ‘object-oriented’. C++ (1985) and Java (1995) carried the model into mainstream software. Dahl and Nygaard received the 2001 Turing Award and Kay the 2003 award.
nodes.summary: Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard’s Simula 67 introduced classes, objects, inheritance and virtual procedures, and Alan Kay’s Smalltalk (1972) at Xerox PARC developed them and named the style ‘object-oriented’.

nodes.title: Virtual Machines
nodes.html: IBM’s CP-40 and CP-67 (1964 to 1967), developed at the Cambridge Scientific Center, gave each user a complete virtual copy of an IBM 360 computer. Popek and Goldberg formalized the requirements for virtualization in 1974, and VMware (1999) and cloud computing later built on the idea.
nodes.summary: IBM’s CP-40 and CP-67 (1964 to 1967), developed at the Cambridge Scientific Center, gave each user a complete virtual copy of an IBM 360 computer.

nodes.title: Analysis of Algorithms
nodes.html: Donald Knuth’s The Art of Computer Programming (volume 1, 1968) made the exact and asymptotic analysis of algorithms a mathematical discipline, with careful counts of the steps programs take. Knuth won the 1974 Turing Award and popularized big-O notation in computer science.
nodes.summary: Donald Knuth’s The Art of Computer Programming (volume 1, 1968) made the exact and asymptotic analysis of algorithms a mathematical discipline, with careful counts of the steps programs take.

nodes.title: Mouse & the NLS Demo
nodes.html: On 9 December 1968 Douglas Engelbart and his team at SRI showed the oN-Line System to about a thousand computer professionals in San Francisco, with a mouse (built in 1964 with Bill English), windows, hypertext links, shared-screen editing and video conferencing. The event was later called the Mother of All Demos.
nodes.summary: On 9 December 1968 Douglas Engelbart and his team at SRI showed the oN-Line System to about a thousand computer professionals in San Francisco, with a mouse (built in 1964 with Bill English), windows, hypertext links, shared-screen editing and video conferencing.

nodes.title: Sorting Networks
nodes.html: Ken Batcher’s odd-even merge sort and bitonic sort (1968) are fixed networks of comparators that sort n numbers in O(log² n) parallel steps. They suit hardware and graphics processors, and Ajtai, Komlós and Szemerédi (1983) built networks of depth O(log n) whose constants are too large for practice.
nodes.summary: Ken Batcher’s odd-even merge sort and bitonic sort (1968) are fixed networks of comparators that sort n numbers in O(log² n) parallel steps.

nodes.title: Strassen’s Algorithm
nodes.html: Multiplying 2×2 matrices with 7 multiplications instead of 8 gives an O(n^2.81) algorithm (1969), the first to beat the obvious n³.
nodes.summary: Multiplying 2×2 matrices with 7 multiplications instead of 8 gives an O(n^2.81) algorithm (1969), the first to beat the obvious n³.

nodes.title: Hoare Logic
nodes.html: Robert Floyd (1967) and Tony Hoare (1969) gave rules for proving that a program meets its specification, written as triples {P} C {Q} of a precondition, a command and a postcondition. Their approach underlies program verification tools and the verified compilers and kernels built since.
nodes.summary: Robert Floyd (1967) and Tony Hoare (1969) gave rules for proving that a program meets its specification, written as triples {P} C {Q} of a precondition, a command and a postcondition.

nodes.title: Matrix Multiplication Exponent

progress.what: ω < 2.371339, by making the laser method asymmetric.
progress.html: ω < 2.371339, by making the laser method asymmetric.

progress.what: AlphaEvolve-assisted numerical optimization, combined with the asymmetric laser method, gives ω < 2.371177.
progress.html: AlphaEvolve-assisted numerical optimization, combined with the asymmetric laser method, gives ω < 2.371177.

progress.what: Claimed ω ≤ 9/4 over the complex numbers by a new approach, and ω < 2.371054886 over every field (family 107 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed ω ≤ 9/4 over the complex numbers by a new approach, and ω < 2.371054886 over every field (family 107 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Can two n × n matrices be multiplied in about n² steps? The exponent ω is known to be below 2.3712 and is conjectured to be exactly 2. A 2026 claim, formalized in Lean but not yet reviewed, would lower it to 9/4 over the complex numbers.
nodes.summary: Can two n × n matrices be multiplied in about n² steps?

nodes.title: Unix
nodes.html: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs began Unix in 1969 on a PDP-7, with a hierarchical file system, small tools combined by pipes and, from 1973, a kernel written in C. Its descendants and imitators include BSD, Linux, macOS, Android and iOS, which run most servers and phones.
nodes.summary: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs began Unix in 1969 on a PDP-7, with a hierarchical file system, small tools combined by pipes and, from 1973, a kernel written in C.

nodes.title: Deterministic Polynomial Factoring

progress.what: Berlekamp’s algorithm factors deterministically in time polynomial in the degree and in p, so it is fast only for small fields.
progress.html: Berlekamp’s algorithm factors deterministically in time polynomial in the degree and in p, so it is fast only for small fields.

progress.what: Assuming the generalized Riemann hypothesis, deterministic polynomial time for polynomials of bounded degree.
progress.html: Assuming the generalized Riemann hypothesis, deterministic polynomial time for polynomials of bounded degree.

progress.what: Assuming the generalized Riemann hypothesis, deterministic time (n^(log n) log p)^O(1).
progress.html: Assuming the generalized Riemann hypothesis, deterministic time (n^(log n) log p)^O(1).

progress.what: Claimed in OpenAI’s math release (manuscript dated 4 October 2026): a deterministic algorithm that completely factors any degree-n polynomial over F_p in time polynomial in n and log p, with no GRH assumption. Not formalized and not independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed in OpenAI’s math release (manuscript dated 4 October 2026): a deterministic algorithm that completely factors any degree-n polynomial over F_p in time polynomial in n and log p, with no GRH assumption. Not formalized and not independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Can every polynomial of degree n over a prime field F_p be factored by a deterministic algorithm in time polynomial in n and log p? Randomized algorithms have done it since Berlekamp (1970), but deterministic ones needed small p or the generalized Riemann hypothesis. OpenAI claimed an unconditional algorithm in October 2026, not yet reviewed.
nodes.summary: Can every polynomial of degree n over a prime field F_p be factored by a deterministic algorithm in time polynomial in n and log p?

nodes.title: Relational Database
nodes.html: Edgar Codd’s 1970 paper proposed storing data as relations, tables manipulated by a declarative algebra, so that programs need not know how the data is laid out. SQL (1974) and Oracle (1979) turned the model into the dominant database technology, and Codd received the 1981 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: Edgar Codd’s 1970 paper proposed storing data as relations, tables manipulated by a declarative algebra, so that programs need not know how the data is laid out.

nodes.title: NP-Completeness
nodes.html: Cook (1971) and Levin showed that SAT is as hard as any problem whose solutions can be checked quickly; Karp (1972) found 21 more such problems. Thousands are now known, and they stand or fall together.
nodes.summary: Cook (1971) and Levin showed that SAT is as hard as any problem whose solutions can be checked quickly; Karp (1972) found 21 more such problems.

nodes.title: Email
nodes.html: Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between computers on the ARPANET in 1971 and chose the @ sign to separate user and host. Message exchange within one computer had existed since CTSS MAIL (1965). Email became the main application of the early network and remains in daily use.
nodes.summary: Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between computers on the ARPANET in 1971 and chose the @ sign to separate user and host.

nodes.title: Microprocessor
nodes.html: A whole processor on one chip: the Intel 4004 (1971) had 2,300 transistors. Moore’s law took it from there.
nodes.summary: A whole processor on one chip: the Intel 4004 (1971) had 2,300 transistors.

nodes.title: Multiplication & FFT Below n log n

progress.what: An Ω(n log n) lower bound for FFT algorithms whose constants have bounded size.
progress.html: An Ω(n log n) lower bound for FFT algorithms whose constants have bounded size.

progress.what: Integer multiplication in O(n log n) time, matching the conjectured optimum.
progress.html: Integer multiplication in O(n log n) time, matching the conjectured optimum.

progress.what: If a central conjecture of network coding holds, constant-degree Boolean circuits for multiplication need Ω(n log n) size.
progress.html: If a central conjecture of network coding holds, constant-degree Boolean circuits for multiplication need Ω(n log n) size.

progress.what: Claimed multiplication of n-bit integers in O(n (log n)^(1−κ)) time on a multitape Turing machine, with κ = 2^(−182), which would refute the conjectured optimality of n log n in that model (family 109 of OpenAI’s math release, not formalized). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed multiplication of n-bit integers in O(n (log n)^(1−κ)) time on a multitape Turing machine, with κ = 2^(−182), which would refute the conjectured optimality of n log n in that model (family 109 of OpenAI’s math release, not formalized). Not yet independently reviewed.

progress.what: Claimed exact length-n discrete Fourier transform in O(n (log n)^(1−δ)) operations, with δ = 10^(−13) (family 130, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed exact length-n discrete Fourier transform in O(n (log n)^(1−δ)) operations, with δ = 10^(−13) (family 130, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Can two n-bit integers be multiplied, or a length-n discrete Fourier transform computed, with o(n log n) operations? Schönhage and Strassen (1971) conjectured that n log n is optimal, and Harvey and van der Hoeven reached O(n log n) in 2019. Matching lower bounds are known only in restricted models or under conjectures, so either a faster algorithm or a general lower bound would settle it. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims both.
nodes.summary: Can two n-bit integers be multiplied, or a length-n discrete Fourier transform computed, with o(n log n) operations?

nodes.title: P vs NP
nodes.html: If a solution can be checked quickly, can it also be found quickly? Most researchers believe not, and the known proof techniques provably cannot settle it. A Clay Millennium Prize problem.
nodes.summary: If a solution can be checked quickly, can it also be found quickly?

nodes.title: VC Dimension
nodes.html: Vladimir Vapnik and Alexey Chervonenkis (1971) showed when empirical frequencies converge uniformly to true probabilities, and introduced the VC dimension as a measure of the capacity of a class of models. Statistical learning theory and the support vector machine build on it.
nodes.summary: Vladimir Vapnik and Alexey Chervonenkis (1971) showed when empirical frequencies converge uniformly to true probabilities, and introduced the VC dimension as a measure of the capacity of a class of models.

nodes.title: C Programming Language
nodes.html: Dennis Ritchie created C at Bell Labs in 1972 for Unix, and Unix was rewritten in it in 1973. C is close to the hardware yet portable across machines, and it remains the main language of operating systems and embedded software; C++ and many other languages build on its syntax.
nodes.summary: Dennis Ritchie created C at Bell Labs in 1972 for Unix, and Unix was rewritten in it in 1973.

nodes.title: Graph Isomorphism in P

progress.what: Polynomial time for graphs of bounded degree, using group theory.
progress.html: Polynomial time for graphs of bounded degree, using group theory.

progress.what: 2^O(√(n log n)) time for general graphs.
progress.html: 2^O(√(n log n)) time for general graphs.

progress.what: Quasipolynomial time 2^O((log n)^c), announced in 2015 and repaired in January 2017 after Harald Helfgott found an error; Helfgott showed that c = 3 works.
progress.html: Quasipolynomial time 2^O((log n)^c), announced in 2015 and repaired in January 2017 after Harald Helfgott found an error; Helfgott showed that c = 3 works.

progress.what: Canonical forms for graphs in quasipolynomial time (preliminary report).
progress.html: Canonical forms for graphs in quasipolynomial time (preliminary report).

nodes.html: Can one decide in polynomial time whether two graphs are isomorphic? The problem is in NP but unlikely to be NP-complete, since that would collapse the polynomial hierarchy, and many special classes are easy. The best general algorithm is Babai’s quasipolynomial one, announced in 2015 and corrected in 2017.
nodes.summary: Can one decide in polynomial time whether two graphs are isomorphic?

nodes.title: Ethernet
nodes.html: Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs at Xerox PARC built a shared-cable network (memo of May 1973) in which stations listen before sending, detect collisions and retry after random delays. Ethernet was standardized in 1983 as IEEE 802.3 and is the dominant wired local network. Metcalfe received the 2022 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs at Xerox PARC built a shared-cable network (memo of May 1973) in which stations listen before sending, detect collisions and retry after random delays.

nodes.title: Evasiveness Conjecture

progress.what: Every nontrivial monotone graph property needs at least n²/16 queries, settling the weaker Aanderaa–Rosenberg conjecture.
progress.html: Every nontrivial monotone graph property needs at least n²/16 queries, settling the weaker Aanderaa–Rosenberg conjecture.

progress.what: Such properties are evasive whenever n is a prime power, by a topological argument.
progress.html: Such properties are evasive whenever n is a prime power, by a topological argument.

progress.what: All nontrivial monotone properties of bipartite graphs are evasive.
progress.html: All nontrivial monotone properties of bipartite graphs are evasive.

progress.what: The general lower bound reaches (1/3 − o(1))n² queries.
progress.html: The general lower bound reaches (1/3 − o(1))n² queries.

nodes.html: The Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture (1973): every nontrivial monotone graph property on n vertices is evasive, meaning some graph forces any deterministic algorithm to query all n(n − 1)/2 vertex pairs. It is proved when n is a prime power and for bipartite properties; in general only about n²/3 queries are known to be necessary.
nodes.summary: The Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture (1973): every nontrivial monotone graph property on n vertices is evasive, meaning some graph forces any deterministic algorithm to query all n(n − 1)/2 vertex pairs.

nodes.title: Graphical User Interface
nodes.html: Xerox PARC’s Alto (1973), designed by Chuck Thacker and Butler Lampson with Alan Kay’s vision of personal computing, had a bitmapped display, overlapping windows, icons, menus and a mouse. Xerox’s Star (1981), Apple’s Lisa (1983) and Macintosh (1984) and Microsoft Windows carried the interface to the public.
nodes.summary: Xerox PARC’s Alto (1973), designed by Chuck Thacker and Butler Lampson with Alan Kay’s vision of personal computing, had a bitmapped display, overlapping windows, icons, menus and a mouse.

nodes.title: Discrete Cosine Transform
nodes.html: Nasir Ahmed, T. Natarajan and K. R. Rao described the discrete cosine transform in 1974. It packs most of the energy of a block of an image into a few coefficients, and it is the core of JPEG, MPEG and most other lossy image and video codecs.
nodes.summary: Nasir Ahmed, T.

nodes.title: Internet
nodes.html: ARPANET (1969) and TCP/IP (Cerf and Kahn, 1974) created a network of networks with no central switch.
nodes.summary: ARPANET (1969) and TCP/IP (Cerf and Kahn, 1974) created a network of networks with no central switch.

nodes.title: Subset Sum Faster Than 2^(n/2)

progress.what: Meet-in-the-middle solves Subset Sum in O(2^(n/2)) time.
progress.html: Meet-in-the-middle solves Subset Sum in O(2^(n/2)) time.

progress.what: The same time bound with O(2^(n/4)) space.
progress.html: The same time bound with O(2^(n/4)) space.

progress.what: The first improvement on that space bound: O*(2^(n/2)) time with O*(2^(0.249999n)) space.
progress.html: The first improvement on that space bound: O*(2^(n/2)) time with O*(2^(0.249999n)) space.

progress.what: Worst-case time O(2^(n/2) n^(−0.5023)), the first improvement on meet-in-the-middle by a polynomial factor.
progress.html: Worst-case time O(2^(n/2) n^(−0.5023)), the first improvement on meet-in-the-middle by a polynomial factor.

progress.what: Claimed randomized algorithm that solves every Subset Sum instance in O(2^(0.49n)) time (family 138 of OpenAI’s math release, not formalized). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed randomized algorithm that solves every Subset Sum instance in O(2^(0.49n)) time (family 138 of OpenAI’s math release, not formalized). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Given n integers and a target, does some subset sum to the target? Meet-in-the-middle (Horowitz and Sahni, 1974) takes about 2^(n/2) steps, and solving every instance in 2^((1/2 − c)n) time for a constant c > 0 is a central open problem of exact algorithms; random instances are known to be easier. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a 2^(0.49n) algorithm.
nodes.summary: Given n integers and a target, does some subset sum to the target?

nodes.title: Z-Buffer & Texture Mapping
nodes.html: Edwin Catmull’s 1974 Utah thesis introduced the Z-buffer, which stores a depth value for each pixel so that the nearest surface is drawn, and texture mapping, which wraps images onto surfaces. Wolfgang Straßer described depth buffering in his own thesis the same year. Every GPU performs both operations, and Catmull shared the 2019 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: Edwin Catmull’s 1974 Utah thesis introduced the Z-buffer, which stores a depth value for each pixel so that the nearest surface is drawn, and texture mapping, which wraps images onto surfaces.

nodes.title: Personal Computer
nodes.html: The Altair 8800 kit (MITS, January 1975), built around the Intel 8080, started the personal computer market, and the Apple II, Commodore PET and TRS-80 (1977) brought computers to homes and schools. The IBM PC (1981) set the standard that later PCs followed.
nodes.summary: The Altair 8800 kit (MITS, January 1975), built around the Intel 8080, started the personal computer market, and the Apple II, Commodore PET and TRS-80 (1977) brought computers to homes and schools.

nodes.title: Relativization & Natural Proofs
nodes.html: Baker, Gill and Solovay (1975) built oracles relative to which P = NP and others relative to which P ≠ NP, so no proof technique that relativizes can settle the question. Razborov and Rudich’s natural proofs (1994) and Aaronson and Wigderson’s algebrization (2008) ruled out further techniques.
nodes.summary: Baker, Gill and Solovay (1975) built oracles relative to which P = NP and others relative to which P ≠ NP, so no proof technique that relativizes can settle the question.

nodes.title: Arithmetic Coding
nodes.html: Jorma Rissanen and Richard Pasco (1976) independently described coding a whole message as a single number inside a nested interval whose length is the probability of the message. It approaches the entropy bound more closely than Huffman coding and, with adaptive probability models, is used in modern image, video and text compressors.
nodes.summary: Jorma Rissanen and Richard Pasco (1976) independently described coding a whole message as a single number inside a nested interval whose length is the probability of the message.

nodes.title: Christofides Algorithm
nodes.html: Nicos Christofides (1976), and independently Anatoliy Serdyukov, combined a minimum spanning tree with a minimum matching of its odd-degree nodes to give a tour at most 3/2 times the optimum for the metric travelling salesman problem. No better guarantee was known until Karlin, Klein and Oveis Gharan found a slightly better ratio in 2020.
nodes.summary: Nicos Christofides (1976), and independently Anatoliy Serdyukov, combined a minimum spanning tree with a minimum matching of its odd-degree nodes to give a tour at most 3/2 times the optimum for the metric travelling salesman problem.

nodes.title: One-Way Functions

progress.what: An explicit universal one-way function, which is one-way if any one-way function exists.
progress.html: An explicit universal one-way function, which is one-way if any one-way function exists.

progress.what: One-way functions are necessary for private-key encryption, signatures and most other cryptography.
progress.html: One-way functions are necessary for private-key encryption, signatures and most other cryptography.

progress.what: Any one-way function yields a pseudorandom generator.
progress.html: Any one-way function yields a pseudorandom generator.

progress.what: One-way functions exist if and only if time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity is mildly hard on average.
progress.html: One-way functions exist if and only if time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity is mildly hard on average.

nodes.html: Do functions exist that are easy to compute but hard to invert on average? Nearly all cryptography assumes so, an assumption made central by Diffie and Hellman (1976). Existence would imply P ≠ NP, and Liu and Pass (2020) showed it is equivalent to the average-case hardness of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity.
nodes.summary: Do functions exist that are easy to compute but hard to invert on average?

nodes.title: Public-Key Cryptography
nodes.html: Diffie–Hellman key exchange (1976) and RSA (1977) let strangers communicate securely. Both rest on number-theoretic problems believed to be hard.
nodes.summary: Diffie–Hellman key exchange (1976) and RSA (1977) let strangers communicate securely.

nodes.title: Hardness of Colouring 3-Colourable Graphs

progress.what: Colouring a 3-colourable graph with 4 colours is NP-hard.
progress.html: Colouring a 3-colourable graph with 4 colours is NP-hard.

progress.what: Colouring a 3-colourable graph with 5 colours is NP-hard.
progress.html: Colouring a 3-colourable graph with 5 colours is NP-hard.

progress.what: Claimed proof that colouring a 3-colourable graph with any fixed number of colours is NP-hard, via a reduction from 3SAT (family 106 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that colouring a 3-colourable graph with any fixed number of colours is NP-hard, via a reduction from 3SAT (family 106 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Finding a 3-colouring of a 3-colourable graph is NP-hard, and the question is whether finding a colouring with any fixed larger number of colours is too. The study goes back to Michael Garey and David Johnson in 1976, and hardness was known only for 4 colours (1993) and 5 colours (2019). OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims NP-hardness for every fixed number, formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: Finding a 3-colouring of a 3-colourable graph is NP-hard, and the question is whether finding a colouring with any fixed larger number of colours is too.

nodes.title: Data Encryption Standard
nodes.html: IBM’s Lucifer cipher, designed by Horst Feistel’s group and modified in consultation with the NSA, became the Data Encryption Standard in 1977, the first publicly specified standard cipher. Its 56-bit key was broken by brute force by the EFF’s Deep Crack machine in 1998, and AES replaced it in 2001.
nodes.summary: IBM’s Lucifer cipher, designed by Horst Feistel’s group and modified in consultation with the NSA, became the Data Encryption Standard in 1977, the first publicly specified standard cipher.

nodes.title: Lempel–Ziv Compression
nodes.html: Abraham Lempel and Jacob Ziv’s LZ77 (1977) and LZ78 (1978) compress data by replacing repeated strings with references to earlier occurrences, and they approach the entropy of the source without knowing its statistics. Descendants sit inside ZIP, gzip, PNG and GIF.
nodes.summary: Abraham Lempel and Jacob Ziv’s LZ77 (1977) and LZ78 (1978) compress data by replacing repeated strings with references to earlier occurrences, and they approach the entropy of the source without knowing its statistics.

nodes.title: P vs BPP

progress.what: P = BPP if some problem in E requires circuits of exponential size.
progress.html: P = BPP if some problem in E requires circuits of exponential size.

progress.what: Primality testing, long the best-known problem in BPP not known to be in P, is in P.
progress.html: Primality testing, long the best-known problem in BPP not known to be in P, is in P.

progress.what: Derandomizing polynomial identity testing would itself prove new circuit lower bounds.
progress.html: Derandomizing polynomial identity testing would itself prove new circuit lower bounds.

nodes.html: Can every polynomial-time randomized algorithm with bounded error be made deterministic with only polynomial slowdown? Most theorists believe P = BPP, which follows from plausible circuit lower bounds (Impagliazzo and Wigderson, 1997), but a proof seems to need such lower bounds; polynomial identity testing is the main problem known to be in BPP and not known to be in P.
nodes.summary: Can every polynomial-time randomized algorithm with bounded error be made deterministic with only polynomial slowdown?

nodes.title: Randomized Primality Testing
nodes.html: Solovay and Strassen (1977), Miller (1976) and Rabin (1980) devised tests that use random witnesses to decide primality with a very small chance of error, far faster than factoring. The Miller–Rabin test remains the standard way to generate the large primes needed for RSA keys.
nodes.summary: Solovay and Strassen (1977), Miller (1976) and Rabin (1980) devised tests that use random witnesses to decide primality with a very small chance of error, far faster than factoring.

nodes.title: Logical Clocks
nodes.html: Leslie Lamport’s ‘Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System’ (1978) defined a happened-before order for events on separate machines and a counter-based clock that respects it, drawing on the ordering of events in special relativity. It became a foundation of distributed-systems theory, and Lamport received the 2013 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: Leslie Lamport’s ‘Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System’ (1978) defined a happened-before order for events on separate machines and a counter-based clock that respects it, drawing on the ordering of events in special relativity.

nodes.title: Sakoda–Sipser Problem

progress.what: If L = NL, every s-state two-way NFA has a two-way DFA with poly(s) states that agrees with it on all inputs of length up to s.
progress.html: If L = NL, every s-state two-way NFA has a two-way DFA with poly(s) states that agrees with it on all inputs of length up to s.

progress.what: An exponential lower bound for sweeping automata, which reverse direction only at the ends of the input.
progress.html: An exponential lower bound for sweeping automata, which reverse direction only at the ends of the input.

progress.what: NL ⊆ L/poly holds exactly when every s-state unary two-way NFA has an equivalent two-way DFA with poly(s) states.
progress.html: NL ⊆ L/poly holds exactly when every s-state unary two-way NFA has an equivalent two-way DFA with poly(s) states.

progress.what: Claimed exponential lower bounds for simulating one-way NFAs by two-way DFAs over growing alphabets, which would settle the Sakoda–Sipser conjecture in that form, and for complementing two-way NFAs (family 129 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed exponential lower bounds for simulating one-way NFAs by two-way DFAs over growing alphabets, which would settle the Sakoda–Sipser conjecture in that form, and for complementing two-way NFAs (family 129 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Sakoda and Sipser asked in 1978 whether every n-state two-way nondeterministic finite automaton, or one-way NFA, can be simulated by a two-way deterministic one with polynomially many states; they conjectured that exponentially many are needed. Exponential bounds are known for restricted machines, and the version for short inputs is tied to the L versus NL question. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims exponential lower bounds.
nodes.summary: Sakoda and Sipser asked in 1978 whether every n-state two-way nondeterministic finite automaton, or one-way NFA, can be simulated by a two-way deterministic one with polynomially many states; they conjectured that exponentially many are needed.

nodes.title: TeX Typesetting
nodes.html: Donald Knuth began TeX in 1977 and released it in 1978, after he was disappointed by the typesetting of the second edition of volume 2 of The Art of Computer Programming. Its mathematical typesetting and optimal paragraph breaking (Knuth and Plass, 1981) set a new standard, and Leslie Lamport’s LaTeX (1984) became the usual format of scientific papers.
nodes.summary: Donald Knuth began TeX in 1977 and released it in 1978, after he was disappointed by the typesetting of the second edition of volume 2 of The Art of Computer Programming.

nodes.title: Type Inference (Hindley–Milner)
nodes.html: Robin Milner’s algorithm W (1978) infers the most general type of every expression in the ML language without type annotations, rediscovering a result of Roger Hindley (1969). Hindley–Milner type systems and their descendants are used in Haskell, OCaml, Rust and other languages.
nodes.summary: Robin Milner’s algorithm W (1978) infers the most general type of every expression in the ML language without type annotations, rediscovering a result of Roger Hindley (1969).

nodes.title: Communication Complexity
nodes.html: Andrew Yao (1979) asked how many bits two parties who hold different parts of an input must exchange to compute a function of it. Lower bounds on communication give lower bounds for circuits, data structures and streaming algorithms, and the field is a standard tool of complexity theory.
nodes.summary: Andrew Yao (1979) asked how many bits two parties who hold different parts of an input must exchange to compute a function of it.

nodes.title: Linear Programming in P
nodes.html: Leonid Khachiyan’s ellipsoid method (1979) showed that linear programs can be solved in polynomial time, settling a question left open by the simplex method of 1947. It was too slow in practice, but Narendra Karmarkar’s interior-point method (1984) was both polynomial and fast.
nodes.summary: Leonid Khachiyan’s ellipsoid method (1979) showed that linear programs can be solved in polynomial time, settling a question left open by the simplex method of 1947.

nodes.title: Derandomizing Logspace (L = BPL)

progress.what: A pseudorandom generator for space-bounded computation; consequently BPL is in SC (polynomial time and polylogarithmic space).
progress.html: A pseudorandom generator for space-bounded computation; consequently BPL is in SC (polynomial time and polylogarithmic space).

progress.what: BPL ⊆ DSPACE(log^(3/2) n).
progress.html: BPL ⊆ DSPACE(log^(3/2) n).

progress.what: Undirected connectivity, the classic randomized logspace problem, is in deterministic logspace (SL = L).
progress.html: Undirected connectivity, the classic randomized logspace problem, is in deterministic logspace (SL = L).

progress.what: Improved Saks and Zhou to BPL ⊆ DSPACE(log^(3/2) n/√(log log n)).
progress.html: Improved Saks and Zhou to BPL ⊆ DSPACE(log^(3/2) n/√(log log n)).

progress.what: Claimed proof that L = RL = BPL: an explicit compiler turns any randomized logspace machine with one- or two-sided error into a deterministic logspace one (family 103 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that L = RL = BPL: an explicit compiler turns any randomized logspace machine with one- or two-sided error into a deterministic logspace one (family 103 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Can every problem solved by a bounded-error randomized algorithm in logarithmic space and polynomial time also be solved deterministically in logarithmic space? Asked since random walks put undirected connectivity in randomized logspace (1979); Reingold derandomized that case in 2005, and the best general simulation uses about log^(3/2) n space (Saks and Zhou, 1995). OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a proof that L = BPL.
nodes.summary: Can every problem solved by a bounded-error randomized algorithm in logarithmic space and polynomial time also be solved deterministically in logarithmic space?

nodes.title: Merkle Tree
nodes.html: Ralph Merkle’s hash trees (patented 1979) summarize a large dataset in one root hash, so that any piece can be verified with only about log n hashes. Merkle trees are used in Git, Bitcoin, peer-to-peer file sharing and certificate transparency logs.
nodes.summary: Ralph Merkle’s hash trees (patented 1979) summarize a large dataset in one root hash, so that any piece can be verified with only about log n hashes.
