nodes.title: #P and the Permanent
nodes.html: Leslie Valiant (1979) defined the class #P of counting problems and proved that computing the permanent of a 0-1 matrix, which counts perfect matchings, is #P-complete, although finding a single matching is easy. Toda’s theorem (1991) showed how hard #P is, and the hardness of the permanent underlies the argument for boson sampling.
nodes.summary: Leslie Valiant (1979) defined the class #P of counting problems and proved that computing the permanent of a 0-1 matrix, which counts perfect matchings, is #P-complete, although finding a single matching is easy.

nodes.title: Three-Machine Scheduling Problem

progress.what: A (1 + ε)-approximation for any fixed number of machines from LP hierarchies, in slightly superpolynomial time.
progress.html: A (1 + ε)-approximation for any fixed number of machines from LP hierarchies, in slightly superpolynomial time.

progress.what: The same approximation in quasipolynomial time.
progress.html: The same approximation in quasipolynomial time.

progress.what: An exact O(1.995^n) algorithm for any number of machines; before it, even three machines needed about 2^n time.
progress.html: An exact O(1.995^n) algorithm for any number of machines; before it, even three machines needed about 2^n time.

progress.what: Claimed polynomial-time algorithm that minimizes the makespan of unit jobs with precedence constraints on three identical machines (family 124 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed polynomial-time algorithm that minimizes the makespan of unit jobs with precedence constraints on three identical machines (family 124 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Schedule n unit-time jobs with precedence constraints on three identical machines so that the last one finishes as early as possible: is this NP-hard or polynomial? Two machines are easy (Coffman and Graham, 1972) and an unbounded number is NP-hard, but the three-machine case is one of the last open problems from Garey and Johnson’s 1979 book. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a polynomial-time algorithm.
nodes.summary: Schedule n unit-time jobs with precedence constraints on three identical machines so that the last one finishes as early as possible: is this NP-hard or polynomial?

nodes.title: Generalized Star-Height Problem

progress.what: Languages of generalized star height 0 (star-free) are exactly those with aperiodic syntactic monoids, so height 0 is decidable.
progress.html: Languages of generalized star height 0 (star-free) are exactly those with aperiodic syntactic monoids, so height 0 is decidable.

progress.what: Languages recognized by nilpotent groups of class 2 have height at most 1, and a long-standing candidate for height 2 has height 1.
progress.html: Languages recognized by nilpotent groups of class 2 have height at most 1, and a long-standing candidate for height 2 has height 1.

progress.what: Claimed proof that every regular language has generalized star height at most 3 (family 134 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that every regular language has generalized star height at most 3 (family 134 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: With complement allowed in regular expressions, is there a regular language that needs two or more nested Kleene stars? No language of generalized star height above 1 is known, and whether star height can be computed is open; the question is on Brzozowski’s 1980 list of open problems about regular languages.
nodes.summary: With complement allowed in regular expressions, is there a regular language that needs two or more nested Kleene stars?

nodes.title: Ray Tracing
nodes.html: Turner Whitted (1980) traced rays recursively from the eye to compute reflections, refractions and shadows, extending Arthur Appel’s ray casting of 1968. Ray tracing gives realistic images at a high computing cost, and consumer graphics cards began to do it in real time in 2018.
nodes.summary: Turner Whitted (1980) traced rays recursively from the eye to compute reflections, refractions and shadows, extending Arthur Appel’s ray casting of 1968.

nodes.title: RISC Architecture
nodes.html: John Cocke’s IBM 801 (1980), the Berkeley RISC project of David Patterson (1981) and Stanford’s MIPS of John Hennessy (1981) showed that a small set of simple, pipelined instructions runs faster than a large complex one. ARM and RISC-V descend from the approach, and Hennessy and Patterson received the 2017 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: John Cocke’s IBM 801 (1980), the Berkeley RISC project of David Patterson (1981) and Stanford’s MIPS of John Hennessy (1981) showed that a small set of simple, pipelined instructions runs faster than a large complex one.

nodes.title: ACID Transactions
nodes.html: Jim Gray’s ‘The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations’ (1981) described transactions that either happen completely or not at all, using locking and logging for isolation and recovery. The properties were named atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability (ACID) by Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter in 1983, and Gray received the 1998 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: Jim Gray’s ‘The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations’ (1981) described transactions that either happen completely or not at all, using locking and logging for isolation and recovery.

nodes.title: Model Checking
nodes.html: Edmund Clarke and E. Allen Emerson (1981) and, independently, Jean-Pierre Queille and Joseph Sifakis (1982) gave algorithms that check automatically whether a finite-state system satisfies a temporal-logic specification. Model checking is used to verify chips and protocols, and Clarke, Emerson and Sifakis received the 2007 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: Edmund Clarke and E.

nodes.title: Parity Is Not in AC⁰
nodes.html: Furst, Saxe and Sipser (1981) and Ajtai (1983) proved that circuits of constant depth and polynomial size, built from unbounded fan-in AND, OR and NOT gates, cannot compute the parity of n bits. Håstad’s switching lemma (1986) made the bound exponential, an early unconditional lower bound for circuits.
nodes.summary: Furst, Saxe and Sipser (1981) and Ajtai (1983) proved that circuits of constant depth and polynomial size, built from unbounded fan-in AND, OR and NOT gates, cannot compute the parity of n bits.

nodes.title: Byzantine Agreement
nodes.html: Lamport, Shostak and Pease (1980, 1982) showed in the ‘Byzantine generals’ problem that without digital signatures, n machines can agree despite f arbitrarily faulty or malicious members only if n is greater than 3f. Practical Byzantine fault tolerance (Castro and Liskov, 1999) and blockchain consensus protocols build on the result.
nodes.summary: Lamport, Shostak and Pease (1980, 1982) showed in the ‘Byzantine generals’ problem that without digital signatures, n machines can agree despite f arbitrarily faulty or malicious members only if n is greater than 3f.

nodes.title: Hopfield Network
nodes.html: John Hopfield (1982) described a network of binary neurons that stores patterns as minima of an energy function and recalls them from partial cues by descending that landscape, borrowing ideas from the physics of spin glasses. Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for foundational work on artificial neural networks.
nodes.summary: John Hopfield (1982) described a network of binary neurons that stores patterns as minima of an energy function and recalls them from partial cues by descending that landscape, borrowing ideas from the physics of spin glasses.

nodes.title: LLL Lattice Reduction
nodes.html: Arjen Lenstra, Hendrik Lenstra and László Lovász (1982) gave a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a reasonably short basis of a lattice. It was first used to factor polynomials with rational coefficients, and it breaks knapsack-based public-key systems and is the standard attack tool against lattice cryptography.
nodes.summary: Arjen Lenstra, Hendrik Lenstra and László Lovász (1982) gave a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a reasonably short basis of a lattice.

nodes.title: No-Cloning Theorem
nodes.html: William Wootters and Wojciech Zurek, and independently Dennis Dieks (1982), proved that no physical process can copy an unknown quantum state. The theorem protects quantum cryptography against eavesdroppers who try to copy photons, and it forces quantum error correction to protect information without copying it.
nodes.summary: William Wootters and Wojciech Zurek, and independently Dennis Dieks (1982), proved that no physical process can copy an unknown quantum state.

nodes.title: Useful Quantum Advantage

progress.what: Sycamore sampled random circuits faster than the classical methods it was compared with; the task has no practical use, and classical simulations later narrowed the gap.
progress.html: Sycamore sampled random circuits faster than the classical methods it was compared with; the task has no practical use, and classical simulations later narrowed the gap.

progress.what: A 127-qubit kicked-Ising simulation presented as evidence of utility before fault tolerance; tensor-network methods reproduced it classically within weeks.
progress.html: A 127-qubit kicked-Ising simulation presented as evidence of utility before fault tolerance; tensor-network methods reproduced it classically within weeks.

progress.what: Claimed beyond-classical simulation of spin-glass quench dynamics on a quantum annealer; tensor-network groups reported classical simulations of the same models.
progress.html: Claimed beyond-classical simulation of spin-glass quench dynamics on a quantum annealer; tensor-network groups reported classical simulations of the same models.

progress.what: Quantum Echoes: a verifiable beyond-classical measurement of out-of-time-order correlators on the Willow chip, with a proof-of-principle application to molecular structure.
progress.html: Quantum Echoes: a verifiable beyond-classical measurement of out-of-time-order correlators on the Willow chip, with a proof-of-principle application to molecular structure.

nodes.html: A quantum computer solving a problem people actually need, such as a chemistry or materials calculation, faster or more accurately than any classical method. Feynman proposed quantum simulation in 1982; beyond-classical demonstrations since 2019 have solved no practical problem, and several were matched by improved classical simulation.
nodes.summary: A quantum computer solving a problem people actually need, such as a chemistry or materials calculation, faster or more accurately than any classical method.

nodes.title: Free Software (GNU)
nodes.html: Richard Stallman announced the GNU project in September 1983 to write a complete Unix-compatible operating system whose users could run, study, change and share the code. He founded the Free Software Foundation in 1985 and wrote the GNU General Public License in 1989, whose copyleft terms keep derived works free.
nodes.summary: Richard Stallman announced the GNU project in September 1983 to write a complete Unix-compatible operating system whose users could run, study, change and share the code.

nodes.title: Learning DNF Formulas

progress.what: Polynomial-time learning with membership queries under the uniform distribution (the Harmonic Sieve).
progress.html: Polynomial-time learning with membership queries under the uniform distribution (the Harmonic Sieve).

progress.what: PAC learning from random examples in 2^Õ(n^(1/3)) time, via polynomial threshold functions.
progress.html: PAC learning from random examples in 2^Õ(n^(1/3)) time, via polynomial threshold functions.

progress.what: Learning DNF is hard if refuting random K-SAT formulas is hard.
progress.html: Learning DNF is hard if refuting random K-SAT formulas is hard.

nodes.html: Valiant asked in 1984 whether polynomial-size DNF formulas can be learned in polynomial time from random labeled examples. The fastest known algorithm takes 2^Õ(n^(1/3)) time (Klivans and Servedio, 2001); with membership queries under the uniform distribution it is polynomial (Jackson, 1997), and hardness is known only under average-case assumptions.
nodes.summary: Valiant asked in 1984 whether polynomial-size DNF formulas can be learned in polynomial time from random labeled examples.

nodes.title: PAC Learning
nodes.html: Leslie Valiant’s ‘A Theory of the Learnable’ (1984) defined learning as finding, from random examples and in polynomial time, a hypothesis that is probably approximately correct. The framework started computational learning theory, and Valiant received the 2010 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: Leslie Valiant’s ‘A Theory of the Learnable’ (1984) defined learning as finding, from random examples and in polynomial time, a hypothesis that is probably approximately correct.

nodes.title: Quantum Key Distribution
nodes.html: Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard’s BB84 protocol (1984) sends secret keys as single polarized photons, and any eavesdropper disturbs the states and leaves detectable errors. Artur Ekert’s entanglement-based protocol followed in 1991. Bennett and Brassard received the 2025 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard’s BB84 protocol (1984) sends secret keys as single polarized photons, and any eavesdropper disturbs the states and leaves detectable errors.

nodes.title: Bayesian Networks
nodes.html: Judea Pearl introduced Bayesian networks (1985; book 1988), directed graphs that encode a joint probability distribution compactly and support inference by message passing. His do-calculus (1995) gave a formal language for causal reasoning, and he received the 2011 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: Judea Pearl introduced Bayesian networks (1985; book 1988), directed graphs that encode a joint probability distribution compactly and support inference by message passing.

nodes.title: Boltzmann Machine
nodes.html: David Ackley, Geoffrey Hinton and Terrence Sejnowski (1985) described stochastic Hopfield networks with hidden units that learn the statistics of their inputs. Restricted Boltzmann machines trained layer by layer helped restart deep learning in 2006.
nodes.summary: David Ackley, Geoffrey Hinton and Terrence Sejnowski (1985) described stochastic Hopfield networks with hidden units that learn the statistics of their inputs.

nodes.title: Competitive Analysis
nodes.html: Daniel Sleator and Robert Tarjan (1985) analysed list update and paging by comparing an online algorithm, which sees requests one at a time, with the best offline algorithm that knows them all in advance. Competitive analysis became the standard way to study caching, scheduling and other decisions made under uncertainty.
nodes.summary: Daniel Sleator and Robert Tarjan (1985) analysed list update and paging by comparing an online algorithm, which sees requests one at a time, with the best offline algorithm that knows them all in advance.

nodes.title: Dynamic Optimality Conjecture

progress.what: Tango trees are O(log log n)-competitive, the first sublogarithmic ratio for any binary search tree.
progress.html: Tango trees are O(log log n)-competitive, the first sublogarithmic ratio for any binary search tree.

progress.what: A binary search tree algorithm that is dynamically optimal if any is.
progress.html: A binary search tree algorithm that is dynamically optimal if any is.

progress.what: Splaying is dynamically optimal if and only if it is approximately monotone, a proposed route to a proof.
progress.html: Splaying is dynamically optimal if and only if it is approximately monotone, a proposed route to a proof.

progress.what: Preprint: splay trees are O(log log n · (log log log n)²)-competitive, the first o(log n) bound for splaying.
progress.html: Preprint: splay trees are O(log log n · (log log log n)²)-competitive, the first o(log n) bound for splaying.

nodes.html: Do splay trees serve every sequence of accesses within a constant factor of the best binary search tree that may restructure itself with rotations? Sleator and Tarjan conjectured it in 1985. Tango trees (2004) are O(log log n)-competitive, and a July 2026 preprint claims the first sublogarithmic ratio, about log log n, for splay trees themselves.
nodes.summary: Do splay trees serve every sequence of accesses within a constant factor of the best binary search tree that may restructure itself with rotations?

nodes.title: Elliptic-Curve Cryptography
nodes.html: Neal Koblitz and Victor Miller independently proposed in 1985 the use of the group of points on an elliptic curve for discrete-logarithm cryptography. Keys of about 256 bits give security comparable to 3,072-bit RSA, and elliptic curves are used in TLS, Signal, Bitcoin and most mobile devices.
nodes.summary: Neal Koblitz and Victor Miller independently proposed in 1985 the use of the group of points on an elliptic curve for discrete-logarithm cryptography.

nodes.title: FLP Impossibility
nodes.html: Michael Fischer, Nancy Lynch and Michael Paterson (1985) proved that no deterministic protocol can guarantee consensus in an asynchronous system if even one process may crash. Practical systems escape the result with timeouts or randomness, and the paper won the 2001 Dijkstra Prize.
nodes.summary: Michael Fischer, Nancy Lynch and Michael Paterson (1985) proved that no deterministic protocol can guarantee consensus in an asynchronous system if even one process may crash.

nodes.title: Interactive & Zero-Knowledge Proofs
nodes.html: Shafi Goldwasser, Silvio Micali and Charles Rackoff, and independently László Babai (1985), defined proofs in which a randomized verifier questions a powerful prover. Zero-knowledge proofs let the prover convince the verifier without revealing anything else. The work won the 1993 Gödel Prize, and Goldwasser and Micali received the 2012 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: Shafi Goldwasser, Silvio Micali and Charles Rackoff, and independently László Babai (1985), defined proofs in which a randomized verifier questions a powerful prover.

nodes.title: Quantum Computation

quote.text: Nature isn’t classical, dammit, and if you want to make a simulation of nature, you’d better make it quantum mechanical.

nodes.html: Feynman proposed computers built from quantum systems (1981); Deutsch defined the universal quantum computer (1985).
nodes.summary: Feynman proposed computers built from quantum systems (1981); Deutsch defined the universal quantum computer (1985).

nodes.title: Splay Trees
nodes.html: Daniel Sleator and Robert Tarjan’s splay trees (1985) are binary search trees that move each accessed key to the root and need no balance information, yet take O(log n) amortized time per operation. Whether they are as fast as any binary search tree, the dynamic optimality conjecture, remains open.
nodes.summary: Daniel Sleator and Robert Tarjan’s splay trees (1985) are binary search trees that move each accessed key to the root and need no balance information, yet take O(log n) amortized time per operation.

nodes.title: Backpropagation
nodes.html: Train many-layer networks by running the chain rule backwards. Reverse-mode differentiation dates to Linnainmaa (1970); Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams (1986) made it the standard way networks learn.
nodes.summary: Train many-layer networks by running the chain rule backwards.

nodes.title: Rendering Equation
nodes.html: James Kajiya (1986) wrote light transport in a scene as one integral equation, the rendering equation, which Monte Carlo path tracing solves by sampling random light paths. Animation and film studios switched to path tracing in the 2010s, and it is now widely used to render photorealistic images.
nodes.summary: James Kajiya (1986) wrote light transport in a scene as one integral equation, the rendering equation, which Monte Carlo path tracing solves by sampling random light paths.

nodes.title: k-Server Conjecture

progress.what: The conjecture holds on tree metrics.
progress.html: The conjecture holds on tree metrics.

progress.what: The work function algorithm is (2k − 1)-competitive on every metric space.
progress.html: The work function algorithm is (2k − 1)-competitive on every metric space.

progress.what: The work function algorithm is k-competitive on the line, on weighted stars and on metrics with k + 2 points.
progress.html: The work function algorithm is k-competitive on the line, on weighted stars and on metrics with k + 2 points.

progress.what: Refuted the randomized analogue: some metric spaces force a randomized competitive ratio of Ω(log² k).
progress.html: Refuted the randomized analogue: some metric spaces force a randomized competitive ratio of Ω(log² k).

progress.what: Claimed a randomized algorithm that is O(log² k)-competitive on every metric space, matching the 2023 lower bound (family 110 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed a randomized algorithm that is O(log² k)-competitive on every metric space, matching the 2023 lower bound (family 110 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator conjectured in 1988 that k servers moving in any metric space can answer requests online at most k times as expensively as an optimal offline schedule. The best general ratio is 2k − 1, from the work function algorithm (Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou, 1995); the randomized O(log k) analogue was disproved in 2023.
nodes.summary: Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator conjectured in 1988 that k servers moving in any metric space can answer requests online at most k times as expensively as an optimal offline schedule.

nodes.title: Log-Rank Conjecture

progress.what: Communication complexity O(√rank · log rank).
progress.html: Communication complexity O(√rank · log rank).

progress.what: Functions whose communication complexity is about (log rank)², so the exponent must be at least 2.
progress.html: Functions whose communication complexity is about (log rank)², so the exponent must be at least 2.

progress.what: Disproved the log-approximate-rank conjecture, the analogous statement for randomized communication.
progress.html: Disproved the log-approximate-rank conjecture, the analogous statement for randomized communication.

progress.what: Communication complexity O(√rank), the best known upper bound.
progress.html: Communication complexity O(√rank), the best known upper bound.

nodes.html: Lovász and Saks conjectured in 1988 that the deterministic communication complexity of a Boolean function is bounded by a polynomial in the logarithm of the rank of its communication matrix. The best upper bound is O(√rank) (Sudakov and Tomon, 2023), and the polynomial must have degree at least 2 (Göös, Pitassi and Watson).
nodes.summary: Lovász and Saks conjectured in 1988 that the deterministic communication complexity of a Boolean function is bounded by a polynomial in the logarithm of the rank of its communication matrix.

nodes.title: Reinforcement Learning
nodes.html: Learning from reward by trial and error: Bellman’s dynamic programming (1957), temporal-difference learning (Sutton, 1988) and Q-learning (Watkins, 1989).
nodes.summary: Learning from reward by trial and error: Bellman’s dynamic programming (1957), temporal-difference learning (Sutton, 1988) and Q-learning (Watkins, 1989).

nodes.title: Convolutional Neural Network
nodes.html: Kunihiko Fukushima’s neocognitron (1980) and Yann LeCun’s convolutional networks trained by backpropagation (1989) used shared local filters, an idea taken from studies of the visual cortex. LeCun’s LeNet read handwritten ZIP codes and bank cheques in the 1990s, and convolutional networks won the ImageNet contest in 2012.
nodes.summary: Kunihiko Fukushima’s neocognitron (1980) and Yann LeCun’s convolutional networks trained by backpropagation (1989) used shared local filters, an idea taken from studies of the visual cortex.

nodes.title: Paxos Consensus
nodes.html: Leslie Lamport devised Paxos in 1989 and published it in 1998 as ‘The Part-Time Parliament’, a protocol by which a majority of unreliable machines agree on a sequence of values. Variants run in Google’s Chubby and Spanner, and Raft (2014) was designed as a more understandable alternative.
nodes.summary: Leslie Lamport devised Paxos in 1989 and published it in 1998 as ‘The Part-Time Parliament’, a protocol by which a majority of unreliable machines agree on a sequence of values.

nodes.title: World Wide Web
nodes.html: Hypertext over the internet, proposed at CERN in 1989: URLs, HTTP and HTML. It became the largest body of text ever written, and later the training data for language models.
nodes.summary: Hypertext over the internet, proposed at CERN in 1989: URLs, HTTP and HTML.

nodes.title: Differential Cryptanalysis
nodes.html: Eli Biham and Adi Shamir (1990) showed that tracing how chosen differences between plaintexts propagate through a cipher can recover keys faster than brute force. DES turned out to have been designed to resist the attack, which IBM had known since 1974, and Matsui’s linear cryptanalysis (1993) followed.
nodes.summary: Eli Biham and Adi Shamir (1990) showed that tracing how chosen differences between plaintexts propagate through a cipher can recover keys faster than brute force.

nodes.title: arXiv Preprint Server
nodes.html: Paul Ginsparg started an e-mail server for preprints in high-energy physics in August 1991, which became arXiv. Free and instant, it now carries preprints in physics, mathematics, computer science and other fields, and most AI research appears there before it is published elsewhere.
nodes.summary: Paul Ginsparg started an e-mail server for preprints in high-energy physics in August 1991, which became arXiv.

nodes.title: Linux

quote.text: Hello everybody out there using minix - I’m doing a (free) operating system (just a hobby, won’t be big and professional like gnu) for 386(486) AT clones.

nodes.html: Linus Torvalds announced a hobby kernel for 386 PCs in August 1991. Combined with GNU tools under the GPL, it grew into the operating system behind most servers, all of the TOP500 supercomputers since 2017 and Android phones.
nodes.summary: Linus Torvalds announced a hobby kernel for 386 PCs in August 1991.

nodes.title: Parity Games in Polynomial Time

progress.what: Memoryless determinacy of parity games, which puts deciding the winner in NP ∩ coNP.
progress.html: Memoryless determinacy of parity games, which puts deciding the winner in NP ∩ coNP.

progress.what: Deciding the winner is in UP ∩ coUP.
progress.html: Deciding the winner is in UP ∩ coUP.

progress.what: The first quasipolynomial-time algorithm.
progress.html: The first quasipolynomial-time algorithm.

progress.what: Quasipolynomial lower bounds for every separating-automaton approach, which covers the known quasipolynomial algorithms.
progress.html: Quasipolynomial lower bounds for every separating-automaton approach, which covers the known quasipolynomial algorithms.

nodes.html: Two players move a token around a graph whose vertices carry priorities, and the winner is decided by the parity of the highest priority seen infinitely often: can the winner be computed in polynomial time? The problem is equivalent to model checking the modal μ-calculus, lies in NP ∩ coNP (1991) and has quasipolynomial algorithms (2017).
nodes.summary: Two players move a token around a graph whose vertices carry priorities, and the winner is decided by the parity of the highest priority seen infinitely often: can the winner be computed in polynomial time?

nodes.title: JPEG
nodes.html: The JPEG standard (1992) compresses photographs about tenfold with little visible loss by applying the discrete cosine transform to image blocks, quantizing the coefficients and Huffman coding the result. It is still the most common format for photographs.
nodes.summary: The JPEG standard (1992) compresses photographs about tenfold with little visible loss by applying the discrete cosine transform to image blocks, quantizing the coefficients and Huffman coding the result.

nodes.title: PCP Theorem
nodes.html: Arora, Lund, Motwani, Sudan and Szegedy, and Arora and Safra (1992), proved that every NP proof can be rewritten so that a randomized verifier reads only a constant number of its bits. A consequence is that many optimization problems are NP-hard even to approximate. The result won the 2001 Gödel Prize.
nodes.summary: Arora, Lund, Motwani, Sudan and Szegedy, and Arora and Safra (1992), proved that every NP proof can be rewritten so that a randomized verifier reads only a constant number of its bits.

nodes.title: Policy Gradient Methods
nodes.html: Ronald Williams’s REINFORCE algorithm (1992) adjusts a policy’s parameters along an estimate of the gradient of expected reward obtained from sampled actions, and Sutton and colleagues proved the policy gradient theorem (1999). Proximal policy optimization (2017), a descendant, is widely used in reinforcement learning from human feedback.
nodes.summary: Ronald Williams’s REINFORCE algorithm (1992) adjusts a policy’s parameters along an estimate of the gradient of expected reward obtained from sampled actions, and Sutton and colleagues proved the policy gradient theorem (1999).

nodes.title: Support Vector Machine
nodes.html: Bernhard Boser, Isabelle Guyon and Vladimir Vapnik (1992) combined maximum-margin classifiers with the kernel trick, and Corinna Cortes and Vapnik added soft margins (1995). Support vector machines were among the leading methods for classification until deep learning overtook them around 2012.
nodes.summary: Bernhard Boser, Isabelle Guyon and Vladimir Vapnik (1992) combined maximum-margin classifiers with the kernel trick, and Corinna Cortes and Vapnik added soft margins (1995).

nodes.title: Barendregt–Geuvers–Klop Conjecture

progress.what: Weak normalization implies strong normalization for certain non-dependent typed lambda calculi, via a continuation-passing translation.
progress.html: Weak normalization implies strong normalization for certain non-dependent typed lambda calculi, via a continuation-passing translation.

progress.what: Extended this to a class of non-dependent pure type systems.
progress.html: Extended this to a class of non-dependent pure type systems.

progress.what: Claimed proof that weak normalization implies strong normalization in every pure type system (family 245 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that weak normalization implies strong normalization in every pure type system (family 245 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Is every weakly normalizing pure type system also strongly normalizing, so that if every typable term has a normal form then every reduction sequence terminates? Posed by Barendregt, Geuvers and Klop and stated in Geuvers’ 1993 thesis, it is open problem 9 of the TLCA list; it is proved only for a class of non-dependent systems. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a proof.
nodes.summary: Is every weakly normalizing pure type system also strongly normalizing, so that if every typable term has a normal form then every reduction sequence terminates?

nodes.title: Quantum Complexity (BQP)
nodes.html: Ethan Bernstein and Umesh Vazirani’s ‘Quantum complexity theory’ (1993) defined BQP, the problems a quantum computer solves efficiently with bounded error, constructed a universal quantum Turing machine, and gave an oracle problem separating BQP from classical randomized polynomial time. It founded quantum complexity theory.
nodes.summary: Ethan Bernstein and Umesh Vazirani’s ‘Quantum complexity theory’ (1993) defined BQP, the problems a quantum computer solves efficiently with bounded error, constructed a universal quantum Turing machine, and gave an oracle problem separating BQP from classical randomized polynomial time.

nodes.title: Quantum Teleportation
nodes.html: Bennett, Brassard, Crépeau, Jozsa, Peres and Wootters (1993) showed that an unknown quantum state can be transferred to a distant qubit using a shared entangled pair and two classical bits. It was demonstrated in 1997, and in 2017 from the ground to the Micius satellite, and it is a basic primitive of quantum networks.
nodes.summary: Bennett, Brassard, Crépeau, Jozsa, Peres and Wootters (1993) showed that an unknown quantum state can be transferred to a distant qubit using a shared entangled pair and two classical bits.

nodes.title: Graphical Web Browser
nodes.html: NCSA Mosaic (1993), written by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina, displayed images inline with text, ran on ordinary Unix, Windows and Macintosh computers, and had a simple point-and-click interface. Netscape Navigator (1994) followed, and use of the Web grew very quickly.
nodes.summary: NCSA Mosaic (1993), written by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina, displayed images inline with text, ran on ordinary Unix, Windows and Macintosh computers, and had a simple point-and-click interface.

nodes.title: Hardness vs Randomness
nodes.html: Noam Nisan and Avi Wigderson (1994) showed that functions that are hard for small circuits can be turned into pseudorandom generators that fool efficient algorithms. Impagliazzo and Wigderson (1997) proved that if some problem solvable in exponential time needs exponential-size circuits then P = BPP, and Wigderson received the 2023 Turing Award.
nodes.summary: Noam Nisan and Avi Wigderson (1994) showed that functions that are hard for small circuits can be turned into pseudorandom generators that fool efficient algorithms.

nodes.title: Shor’s Algorithm
nodes.html: Factor integers in polynomial time on a quantum computer (1994). That would break RSA, once someone builds a large enough machine.
nodes.summary: Factor integers in polynomial time on a quantum computer (1994).

nodes.title: Simon’s Algorithm
nodes.html: Daniel Simon (1994) found a problem, finding the hidden XOR period of a function, that quantum computers solve exponentially faster than classical ones with oracle access. Peter Shor said that this result inspired his factoring algorithm the same year.
nodes.summary: Daniel Simon (1994) found a problem, finding the hidden XOR period of a function, that quantum computers solve exponentially faster than classical ones with oracle access.

nodes.title: 4/3 Conjecture for Metric TSP

progress.what: Christofides’ tour costs at most 3/2 times the subtour LP value, so the integrality gap is at most 3/2.
progress.html: Christofides’ tour costs at most 3/2 times the subtour LP value, so the integrality gap is at most 3/2.

progress.what: A randomized (3/2 − ε)-approximation with ε > 10^(−36), the first improvement on Christofides for general metrics.
progress.html: A randomized (3/2 − ε)-approximation with ε > 10^(−36), the first improvement on Christofides for general metrics.

progress.what: The integrality gap of the subtour LP is at most 3/2 − 10^(−36).
progress.html: The integrality gap of the subtour LP is at most 3/2 − 10^(−36).

progress.what: New capacity bounds for strongly Rayleigh distributions slightly improve the approximation constant.
progress.html: New capacity bounds for strongly Rayleigh distributions slightly improve the approximation constant.

nodes.html: The subtour (Held–Karp) linear program is conjectured to come within a factor 4/3 of the shortest tour on every metric travelling salesman instance (Goemans, 1995). Proving it would point the way to a 4/3-approximation; the best proven ratio is 3/2 − 10^(−36) (Karlin, Klein and Oveis Gharan, 2020), and approximating below 123/122 is NP-hard.
nodes.summary: The subtour (Held–Karp) linear program is conjectured to come within a factor 4/3 of the shortest tour on every metric travelling salesman instance (Goemans, 1995).

nodes.title: Quantum Error Correction
nodes.html: Protect fragile quantum states by spreading one logical qubit across many physical ones: Shor’s code (1995), Steane’s code (1996) and Kitaev’s surface code (1997).
nodes.summary: Protect fragile quantum states by spreading one logical qubit across many physical ones: Shor’s code (1995), Steane’s code (1996) and Kitaev’s surface code (1997).

nodes.title: SSL/TLS
nodes.html: Netscape’s Secure Sockets Layer, released as version 2.0 in 1995 with Taher Elgamal as chief scientist, encrypts and authenticates connections between browsers and servers. Its successor TLS (1999) now protects most web traffic through HTTPS.
nodes.summary: Netscape’s Secure Sockets Layer, released as version 2.0 in 1995 with Taher Elgamal as chief scientist, encrypts and authenticates connections between browsers and servers.

nodes.title: 3SUM & APSP Hypotheses

progress.what: A deterministic 3SUM algorithm in n²/(log n/log log n)^(2/3) time, the first to beat n² by more than a constant factor; the polynomial version of the conjecture stood.
progress.html: A deterministic 3SUM algorithm in n²/(log n/log log n)^(2/3) time, the first to beat n² by more than a constant factor; the polynomial version of the conjecture stood.

progress.what: All-pairs shortest paths in n³/2^Ω(√log n) time via circuit complexity, still not truly subcubic.
progress.html: All-pairs shortest paths in n³/2^Ω(√log n) time via circuit complexity, still not truly subcubic.

progress.what: Claimed refutation (preprint, 5 October 2026): deterministic 3SUM in O(n^1.9992) time and APSP in O(n^2.9995) for polynomially bounded integers, from a new algorithm for thin matrix products. The paper credits an internal research model of Anthropic’s Claude with finding the core algorithm and reports a Lean 4 formalization of the main results; not yet peer reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed refutation (preprint, 5 October 2026): deterministic 3SUM in O(n^1.9992) time and APSP in O(n^2.9995) for polynomially bounded integers, from a new algorithm for thin matrix products. The paper credits an internal research model of Anthropic’s Claude with finding the core algorithm and reports a Lean 4 formalization of the main results; not yet peer reviewed.

nodes.html: Fine-grained complexity long assumed that 3SUM (do three of n integers sum to zero?) needs n^(2−o(1)) time and all-pairs shortest paths needs n^(3−o(1)); 3SUM-hardness dates from 1995 and many conditional lower bounds rest on the two hypotheses. A preprint of 5 October 2026 claims to refute both, with exponents 1.9992 and 2.9995.
nodes.summary: Fine-grained complexity long assumed that 3SUM (do three of n integers sum to zero?) needs n^(2−o(1)) time and all-pairs shortest paths needs n^(3−o(1)); 3SUM-hardness dates from 1995 and many conditional lower bounds rest on the two hypotheses.

nodes.title: CDCL SAT Solvers
nodes.html: João Marques-Silva and Karem Sakallah’s GRASP (1996) added conflict-driven clause learning to the DPLL procedure, and Chaff (Moskewicz, Madigan, Zhao, Zhang and Malik, 2001) made it fast with watched literals. Modern SAT solvers handle formulas with millions of variables, verify chips and have settled problems in combinatorics.
nodes.summary: João Marques-Silva and Karem Sakallah’s GRASP (1996) added conflict-driven clause learning to the DPLL procedure, and Chaff (Moskewicz, Madigan, Zhao, Zhang and Malik, 2001) made it fast with watched literals.

nodes.title: Grover’s Algorithm
nodes.html: Lov Grover (1996) showed that a quantum computer can search an unsorted list of N items in about the square root of N steps, which was later proved optimal. The speedup is only quadratic, so doubling the key length of a symmetric cipher restores its security against quantum attack.
nodes.summary: Lov Grover (1996) showed that a quantum computer can search an unsorted list of N items in about the square root of N steps, which was later proved optimal.

nodes.title: Lattice Cryptography
nodes.html: Miklós Ajtai (1996) showed how to build cryptographic functions whose security depends on the worst-case difficulty of lattice problems, and Hoffstein, Pipher and Silverman’s NTRU (1996) gave a practical encryption scheme. No efficient quantum attack on lattice problems is known, so lattice schemes became the basis of post-quantum standards.
nodes.summary: Miklós Ajtai (1996) showed how to build cryptographic functions whose security depends on the worst-case difficulty of lattice problems, and Hoffstein, Pipher and Silverman’s NTRU (1996) gave a practical encryption scheme.

nodes.title: Universal Quantum Simulation
nodes.html: Seth Lloyd (1996) proved Richard Feynman’s conjecture that a quantum computer can efficiently simulate any physical system with local interactions. Simulating chemistry and materials is regarded as one of the most likely first useful applications of quantum computers.
nodes.summary: Seth Lloyd (1996) proved Richard Feynman’s conjecture that a quantum computer can efficiently simulate any physical system with local interactions.

nodes.title: Deep Blue
nodes.html: IBM’s Deep Blue, a chess computer with custom search chips built by Feng-hsiung Hsu, Murray Campbell and A. Joseph Hoane, beat world champion Garry Kasparov 3.5 to 2.5 in a six-game match in May 1997. It searched about 200 million positions per second with a hand-tuned evaluation function.
nodes.summary: IBM’s Deep Blue, a chess computer with custom search chips built by Feng-hsiung Hsu, Murray Campbell and A.

nodes.title: Long Short-Term Memory
nodes.html: Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber (1997) added gated memory cells that let recurrent networks learn dependencies across hundreds of time steps, overcoming the vanishing gradient problem. LSTMs powered speech recognition and machine translation until transformers replaced them around 2018.
nodes.summary: Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber (1997) added gated memory cells that let recurrent networks learn dependencies across hundreds of time steps, overcoming the vanishing gradient problem.

nodes.title: Locality-Sensitive Hashing
nodes.html: Piotr Indyk and Rajeev Motwani (1998) showed that hash functions that collide more often for nearby points allow approximate nearest-neighbour search in time sublinear in the size of the data, even in high dimensions. Locality-sensitive hashing is used in near-duplicate detection and similarity search.
nodes.summary: Piotr Indyk and Rajeev Motwani (1998) showed that hash functions that collide more often for nearby points allow approximate nearest-neighbour search in time sublinear in the size of the data, even in high dimensions.

nodes.title: Open Source
nodes.html: The term ‘open source’ was proposed by Christine Peterson in February 1998, after Netscape released its browser code, and Bruce Perens and Eric Raymond founded the Open Source Initiative to promote it. Raymond’s essay ‘The Cathedral and the Bazaar’ (1997) had argued for open development.
nodes.summary: The term ‘open source’ was proposed by Christine Peterson in February 1998, after Netscape released its browser code, and Bruce Perens and Eric Raymond founded the Open Source Initiative to promote it.

nodes.title: PageRank
nodes.html: Larry Page and Sergey Brin (1998) ranked web pages by the stationary distribution of a random surfer who follows links, treating each link as a vote weighted by the rank of its source, as citations are for papers. PageRank was the core of Google’s search engine.
nodes.summary: Larry Page and Sergey Brin (1998) ranked web pages by the stationary distribution of a random surfer who follows links, treating each link as a vote weighted by the rank of its source, as citations are for papers.

nodes.title: Strongly Polynomial Linear Programming

progress.what: Linear programming in linear time when the dimension is fixed.
progress.html: Linear programming in linear time when the dimension is fixed.

progress.what: A strongly polynomial algorithm for linear programs whose constraint matrix has small integer entries, including network flow problems.
progress.html: A strongly polynomial algorithm for linear programs whose constraint matrix has small integer entries, including network flow problems.

progress.what: Primal-dual log-barrier interior point methods are not strongly polynomial, shown by tropicalizing the central path.
progress.html: Primal-dual log-barrier interior point methods are not strongly polynomial, shown by tropicalizing the central path.

progress.what: A strongly polynomial algorithm for linear programs with at most two nonzero entries per row or per column, via minimum-cost generalized flow.
progress.html: A strongly polynomial algorithm for linear programs with at most two nonzero entries per row or per column, via minimum-cost generalized flow.

nodes.html: Smale’s ninth problem (1998): decide whether a linear system Ax ≥ b has a solution using a number of arithmetic operations polynomial in the numbers of variables and constraints alone, independent of the size of the entries. Ellipsoid and interior-point methods are only weakly polynomial; strongly polynomial algorithms exist only for special classes such as combinatorial LPs (Tardos, 1986).
nodes.summary: Smale’s ninth problem (1998): decide whether a linear system Ax ≥ b has a solution using a number of arithmetic operations polynomial in the numbers of variables and constraints alone, independent of the size of the entries.

nodes.title: Mutually Unbiased Bases in Dimension 6

progress.what: Numerical searches find no set of four mutually unbiased bases in dimension 6.
progress.html: Numerical searches find no set of four mutually unbiased bases in dimension 6.

progress.what: The standard basis together with any member of the Fourier family F(a,b) of Hadamard matrices cannot be extended to four mutually unbiased bases.
progress.html: The standard basis together with any member of the Fourier family F(a,b) of Hadamard matrices cannot be extended to four mutually unbiased bases.

progress.what: Claimed proof that the maximum is three (manuscript dated 24 September 2026). The exclusion of a fourth basis is a computer-assisted floating-point certification, and the accompanying Lean formalization proves only a weaker bound of five bases. Not independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that the maximum is three (manuscript dated 24 September 2026). The exclusion of a fourth basis is a computer-assisted floating-point certification, and the accompanying Lean formalization proves only a weaker bound of five bases. Not independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Two orthonormal bases of ℂ^d are mutually unbiased if every vector of one has squared overlap 1/d with every vector of the other. Prime-power dimensions have d + 1 such bases (Wootters and Fields, 1989), but in dimension 6 only three were ever found, and Zauner conjectured in 1999 that three is the maximum. OpenAI claimed a computer-assisted proof in October 2026, not yet reviewed.
nodes.summary: Two orthonormal bases of ℂ^d are mutually unbiased if every vector of one has squared overlap 1/d with every vector of the other.

nodes.title: Non-Abelian Hidden Subgroup Problem

progress.what: Solving the dihedral hidden subgroup problem by coset sampling would solve the unique shortest vector problem on lattices.
progress.html: Solving the dihedral hidden subgroup problem by coset sampling would solve the unique shortest vector problem on lattices.

progress.what: A subexponential 2^O(√log N) quantum algorithm for the dihedral group.
progress.html: A subexponential 2^O(√log N) quantum algorithm for the dihedral group.

progress.what: Polynomially many oracle queries suffice for every finite group, though processing them may take exponential time.
progress.html: Polynomially many oracle queries suffice for every finite group, though processing them may take exponential time.

progress.what: Strong Fourier sampling cannot efficiently solve the symmetric-group case behind graph isomorphism.
progress.html: Strong Fourier sampling cannot efficiently solve the symmetric-group case behind graph isomorphism.

nodes.html: Shor’s algorithm efficiently finds hidden subgroups of abelian groups; can quantum computers do the same for non-abelian groups? An efficient algorithm for dihedral groups would solve lattice problems behind post-quantum cryptography (Regev, 2002), and one for symmetric groups would solve graph isomorphism; the best dihedral algorithm is subexponential (Kuperberg, 2003).
nodes.summary: Shor’s algorithm efficiently finds hidden subgroups of abelian groups; can quantum computers do the same for non-abelian groups?

nodes.title: Parity in QAC⁰

progress.what: Introduced the Pauli spectrum of QAC⁰ circuits and proved parity lower bounds for circuits with few ancilla qubits.
progress.html: Introduced the Pauli spectrum of QAC⁰ circuits and proved parity lower bounds for circuits with few ancilla qubits.

progress.what: Depth-d QAC⁰ circuits need n^(1+3^(−d)) ancillas to compute parity.
progress.html: Depth-d QAC⁰ circuits need n^(1+3^(−d)) ancillas to compute parity.

progress.what: Claimed proof (manuscripts dated 24 September 2026) that constant-depth circuits with polynomially many qubits cannot compute parity with any fixed advantage over guessing, in the measured-output model. The family carries a Lean formalization; not independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof (manuscripts dated 24 September 2026) that constant-depth circuits with polynomially many qubits cannot compute parity with any fixed advantage over guessing, in the measured-output model. The family carries a Lean formalization; not independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Can constant-depth quantum circuits of one-qubit gates and many-qubit Toffoli gates (QAC⁰) compute the parity of n bits? Moore defined QAC⁰ in 1999 and conjectured that they cannot, the quantum analogue of parity not being in AC⁰; he also showed parity is equivalent to quantum fan-out. OpenAI claimed a proof in October 2026, not yet reviewed.
nodes.summary: Can constant-depth quantum circuits of one-qubit gates and many-qubit Toffoli gates (QAC⁰) compute the parity of n bits?

nodes.title: Superconducting Qubits
nodes.html: Yasunobu Nakamura, Yuri Pashkin and Jaw-Shen Tsai (1999) made the first superconducting qubit from a Cooper-pair box, showing coherent control of a quantum state in an electrical circuit. The transmon (2007) became the basis of the quantum computers of Google and IBM, and the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis for the underlying circuit physics.
nodes.summary: Yasunobu Nakamura, Yuri Pashkin and Jaw-Shen Tsai (1999) made the first superconducting qubit from a Cooper-pair box, showing coherent control of a quantum state in an electrical circuit.

nodes.title: Zauner’s Conjecture (SIC-POVMs)

progress.what: Connected SICs to algebraic number theory and Hilbert’s twelfth problem.
progress.html: Connected SICs to algebraic number theory and Hilbert’s twelfth problem.

progress.what: A construction of SICs in every dimension from Stark units, proved valid assuming the abelian Stark conjecture for real quadratic fields and a special-value identity.
progress.html: A construction of SICs in every dimension from Stark units, proved valid assuming the abelian Stark conjecture for real quadratic fields and a special-value identity.

progress.what: Proved that Stark–Shintani invariants of real quadratic fields are algebraic and proved the quadratic Stark-unit identities conjectured by Appleby, Flammia and Kopp; they name one remaining obstacle, a Galois conjugate placing the relevant values on the unit circle.
progress.html: Proved that Stark–Shintani invariants of real quadratic fields are algebraic and proved the quadratic Stark-unit identities conjectured by Appleby, Flammia and Kopp; they name one remaining obstacle, a Galois conjugate placing the relevant values on the unit circle.

nodes.html: Zauner conjectured in his 1999 thesis that every dimension d has d² equiangular quantum states forming a SIC-POVM, obtainable as an orbit of the Weyl–Heisenberg group. Exact SICs are known for every d up to 53 and in 115 dimensions in all, numerical ones for every d up to 193; recent work ties the problem to Stark units and Hilbert’s twelfth problem.
nodes.summary: Zauner conjectured in his 1999 thesis that every dimension d has d² equiangular quantum states forming a SIC-POVM, obtainable as an orbit of the Weyl–Heisenberg group.

nodes.title: AES
nodes.html: Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen’s Rijndael won NIST’s open competition in 2000 and was published as the Advanced Encryption Standard (FIPS 197) in 2001. Built into processors, AES is the most widely used symmetric cipher.
nodes.summary: Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen’s Rijndael won NIST’s open competition in 2000 and was published as the Advanced Encryption Standard (FIPS 197) in 2001.

nodes.title: Smoothed Analysis
nodes.html: Daniel Spielman and Shang-Hua Teng (2001) explained why the simplex method is fast in practice although it can take exponential time in the worst case: on inputs slightly perturbed at random, its expected running time is polynomial. They shared the 2008 Gödel Prize.
nodes.summary: Daniel Spielman and Shang-Hua Teng (2001) explained why the simplex method is fast in practice although it can take exponential time in the worst case: on inputs slightly perturbed at random, its expected running time is polynomial.

nodes.title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis

progress.what: The PPSZ algorithm solves k-SAT in 2^((1 − Θ(1/k))n) time, still consistent with SETH.
progress.html: The PPSZ algorithm solves k-SAT in 2^((1 − Θ(1/k))n) time, still consistent with SETH.

progress.what: A substantially faster algorithm for orthogonal vectors would refute SETH, the first of many fine-grained reductions from it.
progress.html: A substantially faster algorithm for orthogonal vectors would refute SETH, the first of many fine-grained reductions from it.

progress.what: Edit distance in strongly subquadratic time would refute SETH.
progress.html: Edit distance in strongly subquadratic time would refute SETH.

nodes.html: Is it true that for every ε > 0 some k-SAT needs 2^((1−ε)n) time, so CNF satisfiability has no algorithm much faster than brute force? Impagliazzo and Paturi raised it around 2001; hundreds of tight conditional lower bounds assume it, and proving it would separate P from NP. The claimed October 2026 refutation of the 3SUM and APSP hypotheses leaves it untouched.
nodes.summary: Is it true that for every ε > 0 some k-SAT needs 2^((1−ε)n) time, so CNF satisfiability has no algorithm much faster than brute force?

nodes.title: Wikipedia
nodes.html: Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger launched Wikipedia on 15 January 2001 as an encyclopedia that anyone can edit. It now has editions in over 300 languages, with millions of articles in English alone, and it is widely used as a source of text for training language models.
nodes.summary: Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger launched Wikipedia on 15 January 2001 as an encyclopedia that anyone can edit.

nodes.title: Primes in P (AKS)
nodes.html: Manindra Agrawal, Neeraj Kayal and Nitin Saxena (2002) gave the first deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for testing whether a number is prime, without unproven assumptions. Kayal and Saxena were then students at IIT Kanpur. The paper won the 2006 Gödel Prize.
nodes.summary: Manindra Agrawal, Neeraj Kayal and Nitin Saxena (2002) gave the first deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for testing whether a number is prime, without unproven assumptions.

nodes.title: Quantum PCP Conjecture

progress.what: The detectability lemma and quantum gap amplification for Hamiltonians on expander interaction graphs.
progress.html: The detectability lemma and quantum gap amplification for Hamiltonians on expander interaction graphs.

progress.what: Games version under randomized reductions: approximating the entangled value of nonlocal games is QMA-hard.
progress.html: Games version under randomized reductions: approximating the entangled value of nonlocal games is QMA-hard.

progress.what: Proved the NLTS conjecture: local Hamiltonians whose low-energy states all need superconstant-depth circuits.
progress.html: Proved the NLTS conjecture: local Hamiltonians whose low-energy states all need superconstant-depth circuits.

progress.what: A derandomized tensor-product gap amplification for Hamiltonians, modeled on Dinur’s proof of the PCP theorem.
progress.html: A derandomized tensor-product gap amplification for Hamiltonians, modeled on Dinur’s proof of the PCP theorem.

nodes.html: Is it QMA-hard to approximate the ground energy of a local Hamiltonian to within a constant fraction of its number of terms? This quantum analogue of the PCP theorem, studied since the early 2000s, would mean even rough ground-state energies are hard for quantum computers; the NLTS theorem (2022) removed one obstacle, and a games version is known.
nodes.summary: Is it QMA-hard to approximate the ground energy of a local Hamiltonian to within a constant fraction of its number of terms?

nodes.title: Unique Games Conjecture

progress.what: A subexponential-time algorithm for unique games.
progress.html: A subexponential-time algorithm for unique games.

progress.what: Proved the 2-to-2 Games Conjecture, which implies that it is NP-hard to tell unique games of value at least 1/2 from those of value near 0.
progress.html: Proved the 2-to-2 Games Conjecture, which implies that it is NP-hard to tell unique games of value at least 1/2 from those of value near 0.

progress.what: Claimed proof in OpenAI’s math release of 6 October 2026 (manuscript dated 23 September): a deterministic polynomial-time reduction from 3SAT to unique games over a fixed alphabet with completeness 1 − ε and soundness δ. The reduction carries a Lean formalization; no independent expert review yet.
progress.html: Claimed proof in OpenAI’s math release of 6 October 2026 (manuscript dated 23 September): a deterministic polynomial-time reduction from 3SAT to unique games over a fixed alphabet with completeness 1 − ε and soundness δ. The reduction carries a Lean formalization; no independent expert review yet.

nodes.html: Khot’s 2002 conjecture: for every ε, δ > 0 it is NP-hard to tell unique games (labelings in which each edge constraint is a bijection) that are (1 − ε)-satisfiable from those at most δ-satisfiable. It would make the Goemans–Williamson Max-Cut ratio and factor 2 for Vertex Cover optimal. OpenAI claimed a proof on 6 October 2026, not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: Khot’s 2002 conjecture: for every ε, δ > 0 it is NP-hard to tell unique games (labelings in which each edge constraint is a bijection) that are (1 − ε)-satisfiable from those at most δ-satisfiable.

nodes.title: Neural Language Model
nodes.html: Yoshua Bengio, Réjean Ducharme, Pascal Vincent and Christian Jauvin’s ‘A Neural Probabilistic Language Model’ (2003) predicted the next word from learned vector representations of the preceding words, outperforming n-gram models. It is an ancestor of the language models used today.
nodes.summary: Yoshua Bengio, Réjean Ducharme, Pascal Vincent and Christian Jauvin’s ‘A Neural Probabilistic Language Model’ (2003) predicted the next word from learned vector representations of the preceding words, outperforming n-gram models.

nodes.title: Nearly-Linear Laplacian Solvers
nodes.html: Daniel Spielman and Shang-Hua Teng (2004) solved linear systems built from graph Laplacians in nearly linear time, using spectral sparsification. Electrical-flow methods based on such solvers led to faster algorithms for maximum flow and other graph problems, and the work won the 2015 Gödel Prize.
nodes.summary: Daniel Spielman and Shang-Hua Teng (2004) solved linear systems built from graph Laplacians in nearly linear time, using spectral sparsification.

nodes.title: Git
nodes.html: Linus Torvalds wrote Git in April 2005 for Linux kernel development, a distributed version-control system that identifies every file, directory and commit by a hash of its content. GitHub (2008) made it the usual home of open-source software.
nodes.summary: Linus Torvalds wrote Git in April 2005 for Linux kernel development, a distributed version-control system that identifies every file, directory and commit by a hash of its content.

nodes.title: Learning With Errors
nodes.html: Oded Regev (2005) showed, with a quantum reduction, that solving noisy linear equations modulo a number is as hard as worst-case lattice problems. Learning with errors is the basis of ML-KEM, the post-quantum key-exchange standard, and of fully homomorphic encryption. Regev received the 2018 Gödel Prize.
nodes.summary: Oded Regev (2005) showed, with a quantum reduction, that solving noisy linear equations modulo a number is as hard as worst-case lattice problems.

nodes.title: Undirected Connectivity in Logspace
nodes.html: Omer Reingold (2005) gave a deterministic algorithm that decides whether two vertices of an undirected graph are connected using only logarithmic memory, which showed that SL = L. It answered a question of Lewis and Papadimitriou from 1982 and used the zig-zag product of expander graphs.
nodes.summary: Omer Reingold (2005) gave a deterministic algorithm that decides whether two vertices of an undirected graph are connected using only logarithmic memory, which showed that SL = L.

nodes.title: Cloud Computing
nodes.html: Amazon Web Services launched its S3 storage service in March 2006 and EC2 virtual servers that August, renting computing by the hour to anyone with a credit card. Cloud platforms now host much of the internet and much of AI training.
nodes.summary: Amazon Web Services launched its S3 storage service in March 2006 and EC2 virtual servers that August, renting computing by the hour to anyone with a credit card.

nodes.title: Differential Privacy
nodes.html: Cynthia Dwork, Frank McSherry, Kobbi Nissim and Adam Smith (2006) defined differential privacy: adding calibrated random noise so that the output of an analysis barely depends on any one person’s data. It was used for the 2020 US Census and in products by Apple and Google, and the paper won the 2017 Gödel Prize.
nodes.summary: Cynthia Dwork, Frank McSherry, Kobbi Nissim and Adam Smith (2006) defined differential privacy: adding calibrated random noise so that the output of an analysis barely depends on any one person’s data.

nodes.title: Hutter Prize

progress.what: fx2-cmix: 110,793,128 bytes (September).
progress.html: fx2-cmix: 110,793,128 bytes (September).

progress.what: cmix-lex: 109,671,639 bytes (June).
progress.html: cmix-lex: 109,671,639 bytes (June).

progress.what: cmix-obias: 108,521,870 bytes (July).
progress.html: cmix-obias: 108,521,870 bytes (July).

progress.what: fx2-cmix-T: 100,424,672 bytes (24 July), a 7.46% improvement worth 37,300 euros.
progress.html: fx2-cmix-T: 100,424,672 bytes (24 July), a 7.46% improvement worth 37,300 euros.

nodes.html: Compress enwik9, the first gigabyte of an English Wikipedia dump, losslessly within about 50 hours on one CPU core with under 10 GB of RAM; each 1% gain over the record earns 5,000 euros from a 500,000-euro fund. Marcus Hutter launched it in 2006, arguing that compression measures intelligence. The record is 100,424,672 bytes (July 2026), so the next award needs under 99,420,425.
nodes.summary: Compress enwik9, the first gigabyte of an English Wikipedia dump, losslessly within about 50 hours on one CPU core with under 10 GB of RAM; each 1% gain over the record earns 5,000 euros from a 500,000-euro fund.

nodes.title: 2D Area Law

progress.what: An area law for gapped one-dimensional systems, implying matrix product state approximations.
progress.html: An area law for gapped one-dimensional systems, implying matrix product state approximations.

progress.what: An exponentially better one-dimensional bound, entropy O(log³ d/ε).
progress.html: An exponentially better one-dimensional bound, entropy O(log³ d/ε).

progress.what: A polynomial-time algorithm for ground states of gapped one-dimensional Hamiltonians.
progress.html: A polynomial-time algorithm for ground states of gapped one-dimensional Hamiltonians.

progress.what: An area law for locally gapped frustration-free 2D spin systems across vertical cuts.
progress.html: An area law for locally gapped frustration-free 2D spin systems across vertical cuts.

progress.what: Claimed area law for unique ground states of gapped finite-range Hamiltonians on finite square-lattice domains, assuming only a uniform spectral gap, plus PEPS approximations with polynomial bond dimension (family 265 of OpenAI’s math release, not formalized). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed area law for unique ground states of gapped finite-range Hamiltonians on finite square-lattice domains, assuming only a uniform spectral gap, plus PEPS approximations with polynomial bond dimension (family 265 of OpenAI’s math release, not formalized). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Do ground states of gapped local Hamiltonians on two-dimensional lattices obey an area law, with the entanglement entropy of a region bounded by the size of its boundary? Hastings proved the one-dimensional case in 2007, which makes 1D ground states classically tractable; in 2D it is known only for special classes such as frustration-free systems (2022). OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a proof for square-lattice domains.
nodes.summary: Do ground states of gapped local Hamiltonians on two-dimensional lattices obey an area law, with the entanglement entropy of a region bounded by the size of its boundary?

nodes.title: Checkers Solved
nodes.html: Jonathan Schaeffer’s team at the University of Alberta used the Chinook program, which won the world checkers title in 1994, to prove in 2007 that perfect play from the starting position leads to a draw. The computation ran for 18 years and weakly solved a game with about 5 × 10^20 positions.
nodes.summary: Jonathan Schaeffer’s team at the University of Alberta used the Chinook program, which won the world checkers title in 1994, to prove in 2007 that perfect play from the starting position leads to a draw.

nodes.title: GPU Computing
nodes.html: Graphics chips repurposed for general parallel computation (CUDA, 2007). This is the hardware that made deep learning practical.
nodes.summary: Graphics chips repurposed for general parallel computation (CUDA, 2007).

nodes.title: Unitary Synthesis Problem

progress.what: Any n-qubit unitary can be implemented approximately in Õ(2^(n/2)) time with queries to a suitable classical oracle.
progress.html: Any n-qubit unitary can be implemented approximately in Õ(2^(n/2)) time with queries to a suitable classical oracle.

progress.what: The state version is solved: one query to a classical oracle and polynomial time suffice to prepare any n-qubit state.
progress.html: The state version is solved: one query to a classical oracle and polynomial time suffice to prepare any n-qubit state.

progress.what: One query is not enough: some unitaries cannot be implemented by any efficient one-query oracle algorithm.
progress.html: One query is not enough: some unitaries cannot be implemented by any efficient one-query oracle algorithm.

progress.what: Claimed solution of the constant-error version: a polynomial-size quantum circuit with a suitably chosen Boolean oracle approximates every n-qubit unitary within diamond-norm error 1/2. Constructing that oracle efficiently is not claimed (family 283 of OpenAI’s math release). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed solution of the constant-error version: a polynomial-size quantum circuit with a suitably chosen Boolean oracle approximates every n-qubit unitary within diamond-norm error 1/2. Constructing that oracle efficiently is not claimed (family 283 of OpenAI’s math release). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Aaronson and Kuperberg asked in 2007 whether every n-qubit unitary can be implemented, at least approximately, by a polynomial-size quantum circuit with oracle access to a suitably chosen Boolean function. A yes would reduce all quantum transformations to classical oracles; one query is known to be insufficient (2023), while exponentially many suffice. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a yes for the constant-error version.
nodes.summary: Aaronson and Kuperberg asked in 2007 whether every n-qubit unitary can be implemented, at least approximately, by a polynomial-size quantum circuit with oracle access to a suitably chosen Boolean function.

nodes.title: Bitcoin

quote.text: The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks

nodes.html: A peer-to-peer ledger secured by proof-of-work: the whitepaper appeared in 2008 and the network launched in January 2009. It is the only node on this tree credited to a pseudonym.
nodes.summary: A peer-to-peer ledger secured by proof-of-work: the whitepaper appeared in 2008 and the network launched in January 2009.

nodes.title: Aaronson–Ambainis Conjecture
aliases: need for structure in quantum speedups

progress.what: Proved the influence statement for completely bounded block-multilinear forms.
progress.html: Proved the influence statement for completely bounded block-multilinear forms.

progress.what: The quantum-algorithm version holds for parallel algorithms: a t-query, d-round algorithm can be simulated on most inputs with t^O(d²) classical queries.
progress.html: The quantum-algorithm version holds for parallel algorithms: a t-query, d-round algorithm can be simulated on most inputs with t^O(d²) classical queries.

progress.what: Independently proved it for massively parallel quantum query algorithms and for constant rounds of adaptivity; the authors report that ChatGPT 5.5 Pro assisted with the proofs.
progress.html: Independently proved it for massively parallel quantum query algorithms and for constant rounds of adaptivity; the authors report that ChatGPT 5.5 Pro assisted with the proofs.

nodes.html: Aaronson and Ambainis conjectured in 2009 that every bounded low-degree polynomial on the Boolean cube has a variable whose influence is at least inverse-polynomial in the degree. It would imply that any quantum query algorithm can be simulated classically on most inputs with polynomially more queries, so exponential quantum speedups need structured inputs.
nodes.summary: Aaronson and Ambainis conjectured in 2009 that every bounded low-degree polynomial on the Boolean cube has a variable whose influence is at least inverse-polynomial in the degree.

nodes.title: Deterministic Prime Generation

progress.what: The parity of the number of primes in an interval of [N, 2N] can be computed in O(N^(1/2 − c)) time; finding a prime above N deterministically still takes Odlyzko’s O(N^(1/2 + o(1))).
progress.html: The parity of the number of primes in an interval of [N, 2N] can be computed in O(N^(1/2 − c)) time; finding a prime above N deterministically still takes Odlyzko’s O(N^(1/2 + o(1))).

progress.what: A pseudodeterministic construction of primes in subexponential time for infinitely many lengths.
progress.html: A pseudodeterministic construction of primes in subexponential time for infinitely many lengths.

progress.what: A pseudodeterministic polynomial-time construction of n-bit primes for infinitely many n.
progress.html: A pseudodeterministic polynomial-time construction of n-bit primes for infinitely many n.

nodes.html: Is there a deterministic algorithm that outputs a prime with n digits in time polynomial in n? Random search with a primality test does it easily, but the best deterministic method takes about 10^(n/2) steps; the Polymath4 project (2009–10) did not beat it, and a randomized algorithm that outputs one fixed prime with high probability exists for infinitely many n (2023).
nodes.summary: Is there a deterministic algorithm that outputs a prime with n digits in time polynomial in n?

nodes.title: Fully Homomorphic Encryption
nodes.html: Craig Gentry (2009) showed how to compute any function on encrypted data without decrypting it, constructing the first fully homomorphic encryption scheme from ideal lattices, with a bootstrapping step that refreshes noisy ciphertexts. Rivest, Adleman and Dertouzos had posed the question in 1978.
nodes.summary: Craig Gentry (2009) showed how to compute any function on encrypted data without decrypting it, constructing the first fully homomorphic encryption scheme from ideal lattices, with a bootstrapping step that refreshes noisy ciphertexts.

nodes.title: HHL Algorithm
nodes.html: Aram Harrow, Avinatan Hassidim and Seth Lloyd (2009) gave a quantum algorithm that estimates properties of the solution of a linear system in time polylogarithmic in its size, under strong assumptions about how the input is loaded and the output is read. It launched quantum machine learning, and later work by Ewin Tang showed that some related speedups disappear.
nodes.summary: Aram Harrow, Avinatan Hassidim and Seth Lloyd (2009) gave a quantum algorithm that estimates properties of the solution of a linear system in time polylogarithmic in its size, under strong assumptions about how the input is loaded and the output is read.

nodes.title: ImageNet
nodes.html: Fei-Fei Li, Jia Deng and colleagues built ImageNet (presented 2009), a database of millions of web images labelled by crowd workers into thousands of categories. The ImageNet challenge (2010 to 2017) was where deep convolutional networks overtook older methods in 2012.
nodes.summary: Fei-Fei Li, Jia Deng and colleagues built ImageNet (presented 2009), a database of millions of web images labelled by crowd workers into thousands of categories.

nodes.title: Polar Codes
nodes.html: Erdal Arıkan (2009) introduced channel polarization, which turns many noisy channels into some that are almost perfect and some that are useless, and used it to build the first explicit codes proved to achieve channel capacity with fast encoding and decoding. Polar codes are used for control channels in 5G.
nodes.summary: Erdal Arıkan (2009) introduced channel polarization, which turns many noisy channels into some that are almost perfect and some that are useless, and used it to build the first explicit codes proved to achieve channel capacity with fast encoding and decoding.

nodes.title: Verified OS Kernel (seL4)
nodes.html: Gerwin Klein, Gernot Heiser, June Andronick and colleagues (2009) completed a machine-checked proof in Isabelle/HOL that the C code of the seL4 microkernel implements its formal specification. Later proofs covered integrity and confidentiality, and seL4 is used in some high-assurance systems, including projects funded by DARPA.
nodes.summary: Gerwin Klein, Gernot Heiser, June Andronick and colleagues (2009) completed a machine-checked proof in Isabelle/HOL that the C code of the seL4 microkernel implements its formal specification.

nodes.title: Boson Sampling
nodes.html: Scott Aaronson and Alex Arkhipov (2011) showed that sampling the output of photons passing through a linear optical network would be hard for classical computers unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses, a route to quantum advantage with far simpler hardware than a universal quantum computer. The Jiuzhang photonic experiments (2020) followed.
nodes.summary: Scott Aaronson and Alex Arkhipov (2011) showed that sampling the output of photons passing through a linear optical network would be hard for classical computers unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses, a route to quantum advantage with far simpler hardware than a universal quantum computer.

nodes.title: Deep Learning
nodes.html: AlexNet (2012), a convolutional network trained on GPUs, won the ImageNet benchmark by a wide margin. Within a few years deep networks led in vision, speech and translation.
nodes.summary: AlexNet (2012), a convolutional network trained on GPUs, won the ImageNet benchmark by a wide margin.

nodes.title: Courtade–Kumar Conjecture

progress.what: An improved upper bound for balanced functions when 1/3 < α < 1/2.
progress.html: An improved upper bound for balanced functions when 1/3 < α < 1/2.

progress.what: Combined with the previous bound, the conjecture holds in the high-noise regime α ≥ 1/2 − δ for an absolute constant δ > 0.
progress.html: Combined with the previous bound, the conjecture holds in the high-noise regime α ≥ 1/2 − δ for an absolute constant δ > 0.

progress.what: The two-function version holds: I(f(X); g(Y)) ≤ I(X; Y) for all Boolean f and g, with equality only for dictators.
progress.html: The two-function version holds: I(f(X); g(Y)) ≤ I(X; Y) for all Boolean f and g, with equality only for dictators.

progress.what: Claimed proof of the Courtade–Kumar conjecture, together with the Hellinger conjecture for every output bias and noise level (family 119 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof of the Courtade–Kumar conjecture, together with the Hellinger conjecture for every output bias and noise level (family 119 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Let X be n uniform random bits and Y a copy with each bit flipped independently with probability α. Courtade and Kumar conjectured in 2013 that every Boolean function f satisfies I(f(X); Y) ≤ 1 − h(α), so a single coordinate is the most informative one-bit summary. It is proved for α close to 1/2 and open in general. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a proof.
nodes.summary: Let X be n uniform random bits and Y a copy with each bit flipped independently with probability α.

nodes.title: Deep Q-Network
nodes.html: A DeepMind team led by Volodymyr Mnih trained one deep convolutional network with Q-learning to play Atari 2600 games from raw pixels and the score alone (arXiv 2013, Nature 2015). The agent reached a level comparable to a professional human games tester across 49 games.
nodes.summary: A DeepMind team led by Volodymyr Mnih trained one deep convolutional network with Q-learning to play Atari 2600 games from raw pixels and the score alone (arXiv 2013, Nature 2015).

nodes.title: Succinct Proofs (SNARKs)
nodes.html: Gennaro, Gentry, Parno and Raykova (2013) and the Pinocchio system of Parno, Howell, Gentry and Raykova (2013) made succinct non-interactive arguments practical: short proofs that a computation was done correctly, checkable in milliseconds. Groth’s 2016 scheme is widely used, and SNARKs power private payments in Zcash (2016) and blockchain rollups.
nodes.summary: Gennaro, Gentry, Parno and Raykova (2013) and the Pinocchio system of Parno, Howell, Gentry and Raykova (2013) made succinct non-interactive arguments practical: short proofs that a computation was done correctly, checkable in milliseconds.

nodes.title: Word Embeddings
nodes.html: Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google (2013) released word2vec, which learns a vector for each word from the contexts it appears in, so that arithmetic on the vectors captures relations such as king minus man plus woman landing near queen. Word embeddings became the standard input layer of language models.
nodes.summary: Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google (2013) released word2vec, which learns a vector for each word from the contexts it appears in, so that arithmetic on the vectors captures relations such as king minus man plus woman landing near queen.

nodes.title: Generative Adversarial Networks
nodes.html: Ian Goodfellow and colleagues (2014) trained a generator network to fool a discriminator network in a two-player game, each improving against the other.
