Generative adversarial networks produced the first photorealistic synthetic faces (StyleGAN, 2018) before diffusion models largely replaced them for image generation.
nodes.summary: Ian Goodfellow and colleagues (2014) trained a generator network to fool a discriminator network in a two-player game, each improving against the other.

nodes.title: Sequence-to-Sequence & Attention
nodes.html: Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le (2014) mapped a sentence to a vector with one recurrent network and decoded a translation with another, and Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho and Yoshua Bengio (2014) added learned attention over the source words. Neural translation beat phrase-based systems, and Google adopted it in 2016.
nodes.summary: Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le (2014) mapped a sentence to a vector with one recurrent network and decoded a translation with another, and Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho and Yoshua Bengio (2014) added learned attention over the source words.

nodes.title: Diffusion Models
nodes.html: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues (2015) proposed generating data by learning to reverse a gradual noising process, a method inspired by nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Song and Ermon (2019) and Ho, Jain and Abbeel (2020) made it work at scale, and diffusion models underlie most image, video and audio generators.
nodes.summary: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues (2015) proposed generating data by learning to reverse a gradual noising process, a method inspired by nonequilibrium thermodynamics.

nodes.title: Quasipolynomial Graph Isomorphism
nodes.html: László Babai announced in November 2015 an algorithm that decides graph isomorphism in quasipolynomial time, 2^O((log n)^c). Harald Helfgott found a flaw in January 2017, and Babai restored the bound within days with a correction that Helfgott confirmed. A full journal version had not appeared as of 2025.
nodes.summary: László Babai announced in November 2015 an algorithm that decides graph isomorphism in quasipolynomial time, 2^O((log n)^c).

nodes.title: Residual Networks
nodes.html: Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren and Jian Sun (2015) added skip connections that let each layer learn a correction to its input, making networks of 152 and more layers trainable. Residual networks won the ImageNet 2015 contest, and the paper became one of the most cited in science; transformers also use residual connections.
nodes.summary: Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren and Jian Sun (2015) added skip connections that let each layer learn a correction to its input, making networks of 152 and more layers trainable.

nodes.title: Rust
nodes.html: Graydon Hoare began Rust as a personal project in 2006, Mozilla sponsored it from 2009, and version 1.0 appeared in May 2015. Its ownership and borrowing rules, checked at compile time, give memory safety without garbage collection, and Rust was accepted into the Linux kernel in 2022.
nodes.summary: Graydon Hoare began Rust as a personal project in 2006, Mozilla sponsored it from 2009, and version 1.0 appeared in May 2015.

nodes.title: AlphaGo
nodes.html: Beat Lee Sedol 4–1 at Go in March 2016, about a decade before most experts expected. Move 37 of game two, which almost no human would have played, became the symbol of machine creativity.
nodes.summary: Beat Lee Sedol 4–1 at Go in March 2016, about a decade before most experts expected.

nodes.title: EFX Allocations

progress.what: EFX allocations exist for two agents with any monotone valuations.
progress.html: EFX allocations exist for two agents with any monotone valuations.

progress.what: EFX allocations exist for three agents with additive valuations.
progress.html: EFX allocations exist for three agents with additive valuations.

progress.what: Four agents always admit an EFX allocation that leaves at most one good unallocated.
progress.html: Four agents always admit an EFX allocation that leaves at most one good unallocated.

progress.what: EFX exists when every agent has one of three additive valuation functions.
progress.html: EFX exists when every agent has one of three additive valuation functions.

nodes.html: Can indivisible goods always be divided so that no agent envies another’s bundle once any single good is removed from it (EFX, introduced in 2016)? Existence is proved for two agents and for three agents with additive valuations (Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn, 2020); the smallest open case is four agents with additive valuations.
nodes.summary: Can indivisible goods always be divided so that no agent envies another’s bundle once any single good is removed from it (EFX, introduced in 2016)?

nodes.title: AlphaZero
nodes.html: AlphaGo Zero (October 2017) learned Go from self-play alone, with no human games, and surpassed the version that beat Lee Sedol. AlphaZero (December 2017) used the same method to master chess and shogi as well, and MuZero (2019) did so without being told the rules.
nodes.summary: AlphaGo Zero (October 2017) learned Go from self-play alone, with no human games, and surpassed the version that beat Lee Sedol.

nodes.title: RLHF
nodes.html: Paul Christiano, Jan Leike and colleagues (2017) trained a reward model from human comparisons of pairs of behaviours and optimized an agent against it, so that people could specify goals they could not write as a reward function. Long Ouyang and colleagues applied it to language models in InstructGPT (2022), a basis of ChatGPT.
nodes.summary: Paul Christiano, Jan Leike and colleagues (2017) trained a reward model from human comparisons of pairs of behaviours and optimized an agent against it, so that people could specify goals they could not write as a reward function.

nodes.title: Superhuman Poker
nodes.html: Libratus (Noam Brown and Tuomas Sandholm, January 2017) beat four top professionals at two-player no-limit Texas hold’em over 120,000 hands, and Pluribus (2019) beat elite professionals at six-player poker. Both rely on counterfactual regret minimization, which copes with hidden information.
nodes.summary: Libratus (Noam Brown and Tuomas Sandholm, January 2017) beat four top professionals at two-player no-limit Texas hold’em over 120,000 hands, and Pluribus (2019) beat elite professionals at six-player poker.

nodes.title: Transformer
nodes.html: ‘Attention Is All You Need’ (2017) introduced an architecture built on self-attention that parallelizes well and kept improving with scale.
nodes.summary: ‘Attention Is All You Need’ (2017) introduced an architecture built on self-attention that parallelizes well and kept improving with scale.

nodes.title: BQP vs PH Oracle Separation
nodes.html: Ran Raz and Avishay Tal (2018) constructed an oracle relative to which BQP is not contained in the polynomial hierarchy, using the Forrelation problem of Aaronson and a new analysis of constant-depth circuits. This answered a question that Bernstein and Vazirani raised in 1993, and it was published at STOC 2019.
nodes.summary: Ran Raz and Avishay Tal (2018) constructed an oracle relative to which BQP is not contained in the polynomial hierarchy, using the Forrelation problem of Aaronson and a new analysis of constant-depth circuits.

nodes.title: Dequantization
nodes.html: Ewin Tang, then an 18-year-old undergraduate advised by Scott Aaronson, gave a classical algorithm (2018) for the recommendation-system problem that matches the exponential speedup of the quantum algorithm of Kerenidis and Prakash up to polynomial factors. Her dequantization technique was extended to other proposals in quantum machine learning.
nodes.summary: Ewin Tang, then an 18-year-old undergraduate advised by Scott Aaronson, gave a classical algorithm (2018) for the recommendation-system problem that matches the exponential speedup of the quantum algorithm of Kerenidis and Prakash up to polynomial factors.

nodes.title: Pretrained Transformers (GPT, BERT)
nodes.html: OpenAI’s GPT (Alec Radford and colleagues, June 2018) and Google’s BERT (Jacob Devlin and colleagues, October 2018) pretrained transformers on large amounts of unlabelled text and then fine-tuned them for specific tasks, setting records across language benchmarks. GPT-2 (2019) generated fluent paragraphs.
nodes.summary: OpenAI’s GPT (Alec Radford and colleagues, June 2018) and Google’s BERT (Jacob Devlin and colleagues, October 2018) pretrained transformers on large amounts of unlabelled text and then fine-tuned them for specific tasks, setting records across language benchmarks.

nodes.title: Spectre & Meltdown
nodes.html: Disclosed in January 2018, Spectre (Jann Horn; Paul Kocher and others) and Meltdown (Moritz Lipp, Daniel Gruss and others) showed that speculative execution in modern processors can leak secrets across security boundaries through cache timing. Most high-performance processors of the previous two decades were affected, and chip designs and operating systems were changed in response.
nodes.summary: Disclosed in January 2018, Spectre (Jann Horn; Paul Kocher and others) and Meltdown (Moritz Lipp, Daniel Gruss and others) showed that speculative execution in modern processors can leak secrets across security boundaries through cache timing.

nodes.title: ARC-AGI Grand Prize

progress.what: Top ARC Prize 2024 score: 53.5% on the private ARC-AGI-1 set within Kaggle limits; the 85% grand prize went unclaimed.
progress.html: Top ARC Prize 2024 score: 53.5% on the private ARC-AGI-1 set within Kaggle limits; the 85% grand prize went unclaimed.

progress.what: o3 scored 75.7% on the semi-private ARC-AGI-1 set within the public leaderboard compute limit, outside the prize rules.
progress.html: o3 scored 75.7% on the semi-private ARC-AGI-1 set within the public leaderboard compute limit, outside the prize rules.

progress.what: Top ARC Prize 2025 score: 24.0% on the private ARC-AGI-2 set; the grand prize again went unclaimed.
progress.html: Top ARC Prize 2025 score: 24.0% on the private ARC-AGI-2 set; the grand prize again went unclaimed.

nodes.html: Chollet’s Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (2019) tests whether a system can infer new rules from a few grid examples, tasks most people solve easily. ARC Prize 2026 offers $700,000 to the first open-source agent scoring 100% on the interactive ARC-AGI-3 evaluation and $150,000 for 85% on ARC-AGI-2’s private set, both run offline within Kaggle’s compute limits.
nodes.summary: Chollet’s Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (2019) tests whether a system can infer new rules from a few grid examples, tasks most people solve easily.

nodes.title: Integer Multiplication in O(n log n)
nodes.html: David Harvey and Joris van der Hoeven (2019) gave an algorithm that multiplies two n-bit integers in O(n log n) time, the bound that Schönhage and Strassen guessed in 1971 to be optimal. It pays off only for astronomically large numbers, and no matching lower bound is known.
nodes.summary: David Harvey and Joris van der Hoeven (2019) gave an algorithm that multiplies two n-bit integers in O(n log n) time, the bound that Schönhage and Strassen guessed in 1971 to be optimal.

nodes.title: Quantum Supremacy (Sycamore)
nodes.html: Google’s Sycamore chip, with 53 working superconducting qubits, sampled the output of a random quantum circuit in about 200 seconds (Arute et al., October 2019), a task Google estimated would take a supercomputer 10,000 years. IBM disputed the estimate, and later classical simulations reduced it sharply.
nodes.summary: Google’s Sycamore chip, with 53 working superconducting qubits, sampled the output of a random quantum circuit in about 200 seconds (Arute et al., October 2019), a task Google estimated would take a supercomputer 10,000 years.

nodes.title: Indistinguishability Obfuscation
nodes.html: Aayush Jain, Huijia Lin and Amit Sahai (2020) constructed indistinguishability obfuscation, which makes two programs with the same behaviour look identical, from assumptions that cryptographers had studied for other purposes. One of them is not secure against quantum computers. Obfuscation of this kind implies most other cryptographic primitives.
nodes.summary: Aayush Jain, Huijia Lin and Amit Sahai (2020) constructed indistinguishability obfuscation, which makes two programs with the same behaviour look identical, from assumptions that cryptographers had studied for other purposes.

nodes.title: Large Language Models
nodes.html: Train a transformer on web-scale text and it learns to write, translate and code. GPT-3 (2020) showed abilities emerging with scale, and ChatGPT (2022) put them in everyone’s hands.
nodes.summary: Train a transformer on web-scale text and it learns to write, translate and code.

nodes.title: Neural Radiance Fields
nodes.html: Ben Mildenhall and colleagues (2020) represented a 3D scene as a small neural network that maps a position and viewing direction to colour and density, rendered by integrating along camera rays. Trained on a set of photographs, a neural radiance field synthesizes new views of the scene and started a wave of neural 3D reconstruction.
nodes.summary: Ben Mildenhall and colleagues (2020) represented a 3D scene as a small neural network that maps a position and viewing direction to colour and density, rendered by integrating along camera rays.

nodes.title: AI Ascends in NetHack

progress.what: The NeurIPS 2021 NetHack Challenge: symbolic bots beat deep reinforcement learning by a wide margin, and no agent came close to ascending.
progress.html: The NeurIPS 2021 NetHack Challenge: symbolic bots beat deep reinforcement learning by a wide margin, and no agent came close to ascending.

progress.what: The BALROG benchmark found that frontier language and vision-language model agents make only minimal progress in NetHack.
progress.html: The BALROG benchmark found that frontier language and vision-language model agents make only minimal progress in NetHack.

nodes.html: Can an AI agent win NetHack, a 1987 roguelike with random dungeons, permadeath and hundreds of interacting items and monsters, by retrieving the Amulet of Yendor and ascending? The NetHack Learning Environment (2020) counts it solved when an agent ascends in ten consecutive games on unseen seeds with random characters; no verified AI ascension in the current game has been reported.
nodes.summary: Can an AI agent win NetHack, a 1987 roguelike with random dungeons, permadeath and hundreds of interacting items and monsters, by retrieving the Amulet of Yendor and ascending?

nodes.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
nodes.html: Patrick Lewis and colleagues (2020) combined a language model with a retriever that fetches relevant passages from a document collection and conditions the answer on them. Retrieval-augmented generation lets a system cite and update its sources without retraining, and it is widely used in search assistants and enterprise tools.
nodes.summary: Patrick Lewis and colleagues (2020) combined a language model with a retriever that fetches relevant passages from a document collection and conditions the answer on them.

nodes.title: AI Code Generation
nodes.html: OpenAI’s Codex (Chen and colleagues, 2021), a GPT model fine-tuned on public code, powered GitHub Copilot, which completed code from comments and context from June 2021. DeepMind’s AlphaCode (2022) reached roughly the median level of human participants in Codeforces programming contests.
nodes.summary: OpenAI’s Codex (Chen and colleagues, 2021), a GPT model fine-tuned on public code, powered GitHub Copilot, which completed code from comments and context from June 2021.

nodes.title: CLIP
nodes.html: Alec Radford and colleagues at OpenAI (2021) trained image and text encoders on 400 million image-caption pairs from the web so that matching pairs map to nearby vectors. CLIP classifies images into categories described in words with no task-specific training, and its text encoder guides many image generators.
nodes.summary: Alec Radford and colleagues at OpenAI (2021) trained image and text encoders on 400 million image-caption pairs from the web so that matching pairs map to nearby vectors.

nodes.title: Good Quantum LDPC Codes
nodes.html: Pavel Panteleev and Gleb Kalachev (2021) constructed quantum error-correcting codes with constant rate, linear distance and sparse parity checks, resolving a long-standing open problem. Such codes could sharply cut the number of physical qubits needed per logical qubit, and IBM’s fault-tolerance roadmap uses related qLDPC codes.
nodes.summary: Pavel Panteleev and Gleb Kalachev (2021) constructed quantum error-correcting codes with constant rate, linear distance and sparse parity checks, resolving a long-standing open problem.

nodes.title: Almost-Linear-Time Max Flow
nodes.html: Li Chen, Rasmus Kyng, Yang P. Liu, Richard Peng, Maximilian Probst Gutenberg and Sushant Sachdeva (2022) gave an algorithm for exact maximum flow and minimum-cost flow in m^(1+o(1)) time on graphs with m edges, using interior-point steps supported by dynamic data structures. It was a best paper at FOCS 2022.
nodes.summary: Li Chen, Rasmus Kyng, Yang P.

nodes.title: AlphaTensor
nodes.html: Framed matrix multiplication as a single-player game and found new algorithms, including 4×4 matrices in 47 multiplications over arithmetic mod 2 (Nature, 2022).
nodes.summary: Framed matrix multiplication as a single-player game and found new algorithms, including 4×4 matrices in 47 multiplications over arithmetic mod 2 (Nature, 2022).

nodes.title: Constitutional AI
nodes.html: Yuntao Bai and colleagues at Anthropic (December 2022) trained an assistant to critique and revise its own responses against a written list of principles, then trained a preference model from AI-generated comparisons, replacing most human labels of harmfulness. The method is also called reinforcement learning from AI feedback.
nodes.summary: Yuntao Bai and colleagues at Anthropic (December 2022) trained an assistant to critique and revise its own responses against a written list of principles, then trained a preference model from AI-generated comparisons, replacing most human labels of harmfulness.

nodes.title: LLM Agents & Tool Use
nodes.html: Shunyu Yao and colleagues’ ReAct (2022) prompted language models to alternate between reasoning steps and actions such as searching, and Timo Schick and colleagues’ Toolformer (2023) taught models to decide when to call external tools. This loop, in which a model acts step by step and reads the results, underlies assistants that browse, run code and operate software.
nodes.summary: Shunyu Yao and colleagues’ ReAct (2022) prompted language models to alternate between reasoning steps and actions such as searching, and Timo Schick and colleagues’ Toolformer (2023) taught models to decide when to call external tools.

nodes.title: NLTS Theorem
nodes.html: Anurag Anshu, Nikolas Breuckmann and Chinmay Nirkhe (2022) proved the NLTS conjecture of Freedman and Hastings: there are local Hamiltonians all of whose low-energy states need circuits of more than constant depth to prepare. The construction uses good quantum LDPC codes, and NLTS is a weaker consequence of the quantum PCP conjecture, which remains open.
nodes.summary: Anurag Anshu, Nikolas Breuckmann and Chinmay Nirkhe (2022) proved the NLTS conjecture of Freedman and Hastings: there are local Hamiltonians all of whose low-energy states need circuits of more than constant depth to prepare.

nodes.title: SIKE Broken
nodes.html: In July 2022 Wouter Castryck and Thomas Decru found a classical attack that recovers SIKE keys, using a 1997 theorem of Ernst Kani on glued elliptic curves. It broke the smallest NIST parameter set in about an hour on a single core, and SIKE, a post-quantum candidate in NIST’s process, was no longer viable.
nodes.summary: In July 2022 Wouter Castryck and Thomas Decru found a classical attack that recovers SIKE keys, using a 1997 theorem of Ernst Kani on glued elliptic curves.

nodes.title: Text-to-Image Generation
nodes.html: OpenAI’s DALL·E 2 (April 2022), Google’s Imagen (May 2022) and the open-weight Stable Diffusion (August 2022, from Stability AI with Robin Rombach and colleagues) generated detailed images from text prompts using diffusion models guided by language encoders. The first DALL·E (Aditya Ramesh and colleagues, 2021) had used a transformer.
nodes.summary: OpenAI’s DALL·E 2 (April 2022), Google’s Imagen (May 2022) and the open-weight Stable Diffusion (August 2022, from Stability AI with Robin Rombach and colleagues) generated detailed images from text prompts using diffusion models guided by language encoders.

nodes.title: AlphaDev
nodes.html: Daniel Mankowitz and colleagues at Google DeepMind (Nature, June 2023) trained a reinforcement learning agent, AlphaDev, to play a game of writing assembly instructions, and it found shorter routines for sorting three to five elements. They were merged into LLVM’s libc++ standard library, the first change to its sorting code in over a decade.
nodes.summary: Daniel Mankowitz and colleagues at Google DeepMind (Nature, June 2023) trained a reinforcement learning agent, AlphaDev, to play a game of writing assembly instructions, and it found shorter routines for sorting three to five elements.

nodes.title: Mechanistic Interpretability
nodes.html: Chris Olah and colleagues began reverse-engineering the circuits inside vision networks in 2020. In 2023 and 2024 Anthropic and other groups used sparse autoencoders to extract interpretable features from language models, and in 2025 Anthropic published attribution graphs that trace how a model reaches an answer.
nodes.summary: Chris Olah and colleagues began reverse-engineering the circuits inside vision networks in 2020.

nodes.title: Logical Qubits on Neutral Atoms
nodes.html: Dolev Bluvstein, Mikhail Lukin and colleagues at Harvard, MIT and QuEra (Nature, December 2023) ran error-detecting and error-correcting circuits on up to 48 logical qubits encoded in reconfigurable arrays of neutral atoms moved by optical tweezers. Arrays with thousands of atoms followed in 2025.
nodes.summary: Dolev Bluvstein, Mikhail Lukin and colleagues at Harvard, MIT and QuEra (Nature, December 2023) ran error-detecting and error-correcting circuits on up to 48 logical qubits encoded in reconfigurable arrays of neutral atoms moved by optical tweezers.

nodes.title: Open-Weight Language Models
nodes.html: Meta’s LLaMA (February 2023) went to researchers and was soon leaked, and Llama 2 (July 2023), Mistral 7B (September 2023), Alibaba’s Qwen and DeepSeek’s models were released with downloadable weights. DeepSeek-R1 (January 2025) reported reasoning performance comparable to OpenAI’s o1 on several benchmarks.
nodes.summary: Meta’s LLaMA (February 2023) went to researchers and was soon leaked, and Llama 2 (July 2023), Mistral 7B (September 2023), Alibaba’s Qwen and DeepSeek’s models were released with downloadable weights.

nodes.title: Othello Solved
nodes.html: A preprint by Hiroki Takizawa (October 2023, revised 2024) reports that perfect play in standard 8×8 Othello ends in a draw, a weak solution obtained by a large search with a modified Edax engine. The computed results have been shared publicly.
nodes.summary: A preprint by Hiroki Takizawa (October 2023, revised 2024) reports that perfect play in standard 8×8 Othello ends in a draw, a weak solution obtained by a large search with a modified Edax engine.

nodes.title: Reed–Muller Codes Achieve Capacity
nodes.html: Emmanuel Abbe and Colin Sandon (FOCS 2023) proved that Reed–Muller codes, introduced in 1954, achieve Shannon capacity on symmetric binary channels, and Galen Reeves and Henry Pfister (2024) proved vanishing bit error below capacity. Kudekar and coauthors had shown the result for the erasure channel in 2017.
nodes.summary: Emmanuel Abbe and Colin Sandon (FOCS 2023) proved that Reed–Muller codes, introduced in 1954, achieve Shannon capacity on symmetric binary channels, and Galen Reeves and Henry Pfister (2024) proved vanishing bit error below capacity.

nodes.title: Tree Evaluation in Small Space
nodes.html: James Cook and Ian Mertz (2023) showed that the tree evaluation problem can be solved in O(log n log log n) space, improving the earlier O(log² n / log log n) and using ideas from catalytic computing. It undercut the plan of using tree evaluation to separate L from P, and it led to Ryan Williams’s 2025 result.
nodes.summary: James Cook and Ian Mertz (2023) showed that the tree evaluation problem can be solved in O(log n log log n) space, improving the earlier O(log² n / log log n) and using ideas from catalytic computing.

nodes.title: Below-Threshold Error Correction
nodes.html: Google’s Willow chip (2024) showed logical error rates falling as the surface code grew. Operating below this threshold is the regime fault tolerance needs.
nodes.summary: Google’s Willow chip (2024) showed logical error rates falling as the surface code grew.

nodes.title: Busy Beaver BB(5)
nodes.html: Radó’s busy beaver function (1962) asks for the longest-running halting Turing machine with n states. An open online collaboration proved BB(5) = 47,176,870 in 2024, with the proof checked in Coq (now Rocq); the paper followed in 2025.
nodes.summary: Radó’s busy beaver function (1962) asks for the longest-running halting Turing machine with n states.

nodes.title: Automatic C-to-Rust Translation

progress.what: Launched the TRACTOR program to translate legacy C into Rust of the quality a skilled Rust developer would write.
progress.html: Launched the TRACTOR program to translate legacy C into Rust of the quality a skilled Rust developer would write.

progress.what: Released the TRACTOR benchmark: test batteries and milestone projects scored for correctness, safety, idiomaticity and performance.
progress.html: Released the TRACTOR benchmark: test batteries and milestone projects scored for correctness, safety, idiomaticity and performance.

nodes.html: Translate legacy C programs automatically into safe, idiomatic Rust that passes the original tests and performs comparably, removing memory-safety bugs at scale. DARPA’s TRACTOR program (2024) set this goal, with benchmarks from MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 2026; transpilers such as C2Rust still emit unsafe, unidiomatic Rust.
nodes.summary: Translate legacy C programs automatically into safe, idiomatic Rust that passes the original tests and performs comparably, removing memory-safety bugs at scale.

nodes.title: Autonomous Coding Agents
nodes.html: Coding agents combine a language model with tools to read and edit a code repository, run tests and iterate. SWE-bench (2023) measured them on real GitHub issues, SWE-agent and Devin (2024) and then Claude Code and OpenAI Codex (2025) were released as products, and METR (March 2025) found that the task length frontier agents complete had doubled about every seven months since 2019.
nodes.summary: Coding agents combine a language model with tools to read and edit a code repository, run tests and iterate.

nodes.title: Post-Quantum Standards
nodes.html: NIST published FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, from CRYSTALS-Kyber), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, from CRYSTALS-Dilithium) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, from SPHINCS+) on 13 August 2024, the first standards designed to resist attack by quantum computers, after an open competition begun in 2016. In March 2025 NIST selected the code-based HQC as a backup key-encapsulation method.
nodes.summary: NIST published FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, from CRYSTALS-Kyber), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, from CRYSTALS-Dilithium) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, from SPHINCS+) on 13 August 2024, the first standards designed to resist attack by quantum computers, after an open competition begun in 2016.

nodes.title: Reasoning Models
nodes.html: Language models trained with reinforcement learning to think before they answer: OpenAI’s o1 (September 2024) and DeepSeek-R1 (January 2025, open weights). They are why vibemathing became possible.
nodes.summary: Language models trained with reinforcement learning to think before they answer: OpenAI’s o1 (September 2024) and DeepSeek-R1 (January 2025, open weights).

nodes.title: Video Generation Models
nodes.html: Diffusion transformers trained on large video collections generate coherent clips from text prompts. OpenAI previewed Sora in February 2024 with videos up to one minute long, and Google DeepMind’s Veo 3 (May 2025) added synchronized sound.
nodes.summary: Diffusion transformers trained on large video collections generate coherent clips from text prompts.

nodes.title: AI Programming Olympiad Gold
nodes.html: In August 2025 OpenAI reported that an ensemble of general-purpose reasoning models scored at gold-medal level in the online AI track of the International Olympiad in Informatics, ahead of all but five of 330 human contestants. In September 2025 OpenAI reported 12 of 12 problems at the ICPC World Finals in Baku and Google DeepMind’s Gemini 2.5 Deep Think 10 of 12, while the best human team solved 11.
nodes.summary: In August 2025 OpenAI reported that an ensemble of general-purpose reasoning models scored at gold-medal level in the online AI track of the International Olympiad in Informatics, ahead of all but five of 330 human contestants.

nodes.title: Optimal Open Addressing
nodes.html: Andrew Krapivin, then an undergraduate at Rutgers, with Martín Farach-Colton and William Kuszmaul (arXiv, January 2025) built hash tables whose worst-case cost grows like (log x)² as the table fills, where x measures how full it is, contradicting a conjecture of Andrew Yao from 1985 that the cost must be of order x. They also proved matching lower bounds.
nodes.summary: Andrew Krapivin, then an undergraduate at Rutgers, with Martín Farach-Colton and William Kuszmaul (arXiv, January 2025) built hash tables whose worst-case cost grows like (log x)² as the table fills, where x measures how full it is, contradicting a conjecture of Andrew Yao from 1985 that the cost must be of order x.

nodes.title: Simulating Time in Square-Root Space
nodes.html: Ryan Williams (2025) proved that any computation running in t steps on a multitape Turing machine can be simulated in about the square root of t log t space, improving the t / log t space bound of Hopcroft, Paul and Valiant (1975). The proof builds on the tree evaluation algorithm of Cook and Mertz. The paper appeared at STOC 2025.
nodes.summary: Ryan Williams (2025) proved that any computation running in t steps on a multitape Turing machine can be simulated in about the square root of t log t space, improving the t / log t space bound of Hopcroft, Paul and Valiant (1975).

nodes.title: Shortest Paths Beyond Dijkstra
nodes.html: Ran Duan, Jiayi Mao, Xiao Mao, Xinkai Shu and Longhui Yin (arXiv April 2025, STOC 2025) gave a deterministic O(m log^(2/3) n) algorithm for single-source shortest paths on directed graphs with nonnegative real weights. It is the first to beat the O(m + n log n) bound of Dijkstra’s algorithm on sparse graphs, breaking the sorting barrier.
nodes.summary: Ran Duan, Jiayi Mao, Xiao Mao, Xinkai Shu and Longhui Yin (arXiv April 2025, STOC 2025) gave a deterministic O(m log^(2/3) n) algorithm for single-source shortest paths on directed graphs with nonnegative real weights.

nodes.title: Turing Test with GPT-4.5

quote.text: I propose to consider the question, ‘Can machines think?’

nodes.html: Cameron Jones and Benjamin Bergen (2025) ran a pre-registered three-party Turing test in which interrogators chatted for five minutes with a person and a model at once. GPT-4.5, given a humanlike persona, was judged to be the human in 73% of conversations, more often than the real participants, while ELIZA and GPT-4o scored well below chance. Critics say the result does not show general intelligence.
nodes.summary: Cameron Jones and Benjamin Bergen (2025) ran a pre-registered three-party Turing test in which interrogators chatted for five minutes with a person and a model at once.

nodes.title: Verifiable Quantum Advantage
nodes.html: Google Quantum AI’s Quantum Echoes experiment (Nature, 22 October 2025) measured an out-of-time-order correlator on the 105-qubit Willow chip, which Google estimates would take the Frontier supercomputer about 13,000 times longer to simulate. The result is a number that other quantum computers can reproduce, and like earlier advantage claims it may be challenged by better classical algorithms.
nodes.summary: Google Quantum AI’s Quantum Echoes experiment (Nature, 22 October 2025) measured an out-of-time-order correlator on the 105-qubit Willow chip, which Google estimates would take the Frontier supercomputer about 13,000 times longer to simulate.

nodes.title: Busy Beaver BB(6)

progress.what: A six-state machine shows BB(6) exceeds 2↑↑↑5, a tower of exponentials far beyond physical scale.
progress.html: A six-state machine shows BB(6) exceeds 2↑↑↑5, a tower of exponentials far beyond physical scale.

nodes.html: Six-state machines include ‘cryptids’ such as Antihydra, whose halting behaviour resembles open Collatz-type problems. BB(6) may be out of reach of current mathematics.
nodes.summary: Six-state machines include ‘cryptids’ such as Antihydra, whose halting behaviour resembles open Collatz-type problems.

nodes.title: Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computer
nodes.html: Thousands of error-corrected logical qubits running long algorithms, enough to run Shor’s algorithm on RSA-2048. Most of the remaining obstacles are engineering.
nodes.summary: Thousands of error-corrected logical qubits running long algorithms, enough to run Shor’s algorithm on RSA-2048.

nodes.title: Deterministic Linear-Time MST

progress.what: Randomized linear expected time.
progress.html: Randomized linear expected time.

progress.what: Deterministic O(m α(m, n)) time using soft heaps.
progress.html: Deterministic O(m α(m, n)) time using soft heaps.

progress.what: An optimal deterministic comparison-based algorithm, with running time somewhere between linear and Chazelle’s bound.
progress.html: An optimal deterministic comparison-based algorithm, with running time somewhere between linear and Chazelle’s bound.

nodes.html: Can a minimum spanning tree of a graph with m edges be found deterministically in O(m) time using only comparisons of edge weights? Randomized linear time is known (Karger, Klein and Tarjan, 1995) and Chazelle’s deterministic algorithm (2000) is within an inverse-Ackermann factor; Pettie and Ramachandran (2002) gave a provably optimal algorithm whose running time nobody can determine.
nodes.summary: Can a minimum spanning tree of a graph with m edges be found deterministically in O(m) time using only comparisons of edge weights?

nodes.title: Threshold of Transcendence

quote.text: Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.

nodes.html: In Sid Meier’s Alpha Centauri this is the last technology, the one that unlocks the Ascent to Transcendence. Here it marks the edge of the map, and its prerequisites are a guess.
nodes.summary: In Sid Meier’s Alpha Centauri this is the last technology, the one that unlocks the Ascent to Transcendence.

nodes.title: Counting
nodes.html: Tally marks on bones such as the Ishango bone, about 20,000 years old, suggest people were recording counts long before writing.
nodes.summary: Tally marks on bones such as the Ishango bone, about 20,000 years old, suggest people were recording counts long before writing.

nodes.title: Arithmetic
nodes.html: Babylonian scribes computed in base 60 with place value: multiplication tables, reciprocals, square roots, and the Pythagorean triples of the tablet Plimpton 322 (c. 1800 BCE).
nodes.summary: Babylonian scribes computed in base 60 with place value: multiplication tables, reciprocals, square roots, and the Pythagorean triples of the tablet Plimpton 322 (c.

nodes.title: Egyptian Fractions
nodes.html: The Rhind papyrus (c. 1550 BCE, copied by the scribe Ahmes from an older text) writes fractions as sums of distinct unit fractions and tabulates 2/n for odd n up to 101. Such decompositions are still studied, for example in the Erdős–Straus conjecture of 1948.
nodes.summary: The Rhind papyrus (c.

nodes.title: Pythagorean Theorem
nodes.html: In a right triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. Babylonian tablets of about 1800 BCE already use the relation; the Greek tradition credits Pythagoras (c. 530 BCE) with a proof, and Euclid’s Elements I.47 gives the classic one.
nodes.summary: In a right triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

nodes.title: Irrational Numbers
aliases: irrationality of the square root of 2
nodes.html: The diagonal of a square is incommensurable with its side: √2 is not a ratio of whole numbers. The discovery is traditionally credited to Hippasus (c. 450 BCE) and led Greek geometry to Eudoxus’s theory of proportion.
nodes.summary: The diagonal of a square is incommensurable with its side: √2 is not a ratio of whole numbers.

nodes.title: Method of Exhaustion
nodes.html: Areas and volumes are found by squeezing a figure between inscribed and circumscribed polygons or solids. Eudoxus devised the method (c. 370 BCE); Archimedes used it to bound π between 223/71 and 22/7, to square the parabola and to find the volume of the sphere.
nodes.summary: Areas and volumes are found by squeezing a figure between inscribed and circumscribed polygons or solids.

nodes.title: Aristotelian Logic
nodes.html: Aristotle’s Prior Analytics (c. 350 BCE) gave the first formal system of valid inference, the syllogism: from ‘all A are B’ and ‘all B are C’ conclude ‘all A are C’. It was the standard logic of Europe and the Islamic world for about two thousand years, until Boole and Frege.
nodes.summary: Aristotle’s Prior Analytics (c.

nodes.title: Euclidean Algorithm
nodes.html: Elements VII (c. 300 BCE) finds the greatest common divisor of two numbers by repeated subtraction, in modern form by repeated division with remainder. It is among the oldest algorithms still in use, and its extended form computes modular inverses in cryptography.
nodes.summary: Elements VII (c.

nodes.title: Euclidean Geometry
nodes.html: Euclid’s Elements derived hundreds of theorems from a handful of postulates. It became the model for every axiomatic theory since, and was a textbook for over two thousand years.
nodes.summary: Euclid’s Elements derived hundreds of theorems from a handful of postulates.

nodes.title: Infinitude of Primes
nodes.html: Elements, Book IX: multiply any finite list of primes and add one; the result has a prime factor missing from the list. It is the oldest proof still taught unchanged.
nodes.summary: Elements, Book IX: multiply any finite list of primes and add one; the result has a prime factor missing from the list.

nodes.title: Conic Sections
nodes.html: Menaechmus found the curves cut from a cone by a plane (c. 350 BCE), and Apollonius’s Conics (c. 200 BCE) developed their geometry and named the ellipse, parabola and hyperbola. Kepler’s elliptical orbits (1609) and Newton’s gravitation rest on it.
nodes.summary: Menaechmus found the curves cut from a cone by a plane (c.

nodes.title: Gaussian Elimination
nodes.html: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art (parts from about 150 BCE; Liu Hui’s commentary, 263 CE) solves systems of linear equations by row reduction on a counting board. Gauss used the method for least-squares problems around 1809, long before it carried his name.
nodes.summary: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art (parts from about 150 BCE; Liu Hui’s commentary, 263 CE) solves systems of linear equations by row reduction on a counting board.

nodes.title: Trigonometry
nodes.html: Hipparchus tabulated chords to predict eclipses (c. 140 BCE), and Aryabhata gave sine tables (499 CE). Tables of angles made astronomy, surveying and navigation computable.
nodes.summary: Hipparchus tabulated chords to predict eclipses (c.

nodes.title: Diophantine Equations
nodes.html: Diophantus’s Arithmetica (c. 250 CE) poses problems asking for rational or integer solutions of polynomial equations and uses symbolic shorthand for unknowns. Fermat’s famous marginal note of the 1630s was written in a copy of Bachet’s 1621 edition of the book.
nodes.summary: Diophantus’s Arithmetica (c.

nodes.title: Chinese Remainder Theorem
nodes.html: The Sunzi Suanjing (3rd to 5th century) solves simultaneous congruences, and Qin Jiushao’s Mathematical Treatise in Nine Sections (1247) gives a general method. The theorem is used in cryptography (RSA decryption) and in fast arithmetic.
nodes.summary: The Sunzi Suanjing (3rd to 5th century) solves simultaneous congruences, and Qin Jiushao’s Mathematical Treatise in Nine Sections (1247) gives a general method.

nodes.title: Zero & Place Value
nodes.html: Brahmagupta’s Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628) gave rules for computing with zero and negative numbers. Decimal place value reached Europe through al-Khwārizmī and Fibonacci’s Liber Abaci (1202).
nodes.summary: Brahmagupta’s Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628) gave rules for computing with zero and negative numbers.

nodes.title: Algebra
nodes.html: Al-Khwārizmī’s book on completion and balancing (al-jabr, c. 820) solved linear and quadratic equations systematically. The words ‘algebra’ and ‘algorithm’ come from the book and from its author.
nodes.summary: Al-Khwārizmī’s book on completion and balancing (al-jabr, c.

nodes.title: Binomial Coefficients
nodes.html: The triangle of binomial coefficients appears in Indian, Persian and Chinese works: al-Karaji (c. 1000), Jia Xian (c. 1050), Yang Hui (1261). Pascal’s treatise (written 1654, published 1665) proved its properties by induction, and Newton extended the binomial theorem to arbitrary exponents (c. 1665).
nodes.summary: The triangle of binomial coefficients appears in Indian, Persian and Chinese works: al-Karaji (c.

nodes.title: Pell’s Equation
nodes.html: The equation x² − Ny² = 1 has infinitely many integer solutions for every non-square N. Brahmagupta’s composition rule (628) and the chakravala method, completed by Bhāskara II (1150), solved it long before Fermat’s challenge of 1657; Lagrange proved that solutions always exist (1768).
nodes.summary: The equation x² − Ny² = 1 has infinitely many integer solutions for every non-square N.

nodes.title: Madhava’s Infinite Series
nodes.html: Madhava (c. 1340 to 1425) and the Kerala school found infinite series for sine, cosine and arctangent, including π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − …, centuries before Gregory (1671), Newton and Leibniz. Their results survive in later works such as Nilakantha’s Tantrasamgraha (1501).
nodes.summary: Madhava (c.

nodes.title: Cubic & Quartic Formulas
nodes.html: Cardano’s Ars Magna (1545) published the solution of the cubic by radicals, found by del Ferro (c. 1515) and rediscovered by Tartaglia (1535), together with Ferrari’s solution of the quartic. The general quintic then resisted until Abel and Galois showed in the 1820s and 1830s that no such formula exists.
nodes.summary: Cardano’s Ars Magna (1545) published the solution of the cubic by radicals, found by del Ferro (c.

nodes.title: Complex Numbers
nodes.html: Square roots of negative numbers forced their way into Cardano’s formula for cubics (1545). Bombelli’s Algebra (1572) gave the rules for computing with them.
nodes.summary: Square roots of negative numbers forced their way into Cardano’s formula for cubics (1545).

nodes.title: Logarithms
nodes.html: Napier’s Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio (1614) introduced logarithms, which turn multiplication into addition. Briggs’s base-10 tables (1617) and the slide rule (Oughtred, 1622) were the main tools of calculation in science and engineering for about 350 years.
nodes.summary: Napier’s Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio (1614) introduced logarithms, which turn multiplication into addition.

nodes.title: Analytic Geometry
nodes.html: Coordinates turn curves into equations and geometry into algebra. Descartes published La Géométrie in 1637; Fermat had the same idea independently.
nodes.summary: Coordinates turn curves into equations and geometry into algebra.

nodes.title: Projective Geometry
nodes.html: Geometry of perspective, in which parallel lines meet at a point at infinity. Desargues (1639) and Pascal’s hexagon theorem (1640) opened it, and Poncelet’s treatise (1822) made it a subject in its own right.
nodes.summary: Geometry of perspective, in which parallel lines meet at a point at infinity.

nodes.title: Fermat’s Little Theorem
nodes.html: If p is prime then a^p ≡ a (mod p) for every integer a, as Fermat stated in a letter of 1640. Euler gave the first published proof in 1736. The theorem underlies Fermat primality testing and the RSA cryptosystem.
nodes.summary: If p is prime then a^p ≡ a (mod p) for every integer a, as Fermat stated in a letter of 1640.

nodes.title: Probability
nodes.html: In 1654 Pascal and Fermat exchanged letters on how to divide the stakes of an unfinished game. The mathematics of chance grew from that correspondence.
nodes.summary: In 1654 Pascal and Fermat exchanged letters on how to divide the stakes of an unfinished game.

nodes.title: Calculus
nodes.html: Derivatives, integrals, and the fundamental theorem linking them. Newton had his method of fluxions by 1666; Leibniz published first, in 1684, with the notation still in use.
nodes.summary: Derivatives, integrals, and the fundamental theorem linking them.

nodes.title: Newton’s Method
nodes.html: Solve f(x) = 0 by replacing a guess with the root of the tangent line at that point; near a simple root the number of correct digits roughly doubles at each step. Newton described a version around 1669, Raphson published a simpler one in 1690, and Simpson gave the modern derivative form in 1740.
nodes.summary: Solve f(x) = 0 by replacing a guess with the root of the tangent line at that point; near a simple root the number of correct digits roughly doubles at each step.

nodes.title: Kissing Numbers

progress.what: Exact answers in dimensions 8 (240) and 24 (196,560).
progress.html: Exact answers in dimensions 8 (240) and 24 (196,560).

progress.what: Dimension 4: the answer is 24.
progress.html: Dimension 4: the answer is 24.

progress.what: A new lower bound in dimension 11: 593 spheres.
progress.html: A new lower bound in dimension 11: 593 spheres.

nodes.html: How many unit spheres can touch a central one? Newton and Gregory argued in 1694 over 12 or 13 in three dimensions (it is 12, proved in 1953). Exact answers are known only in dimensions 1–4, 8 and 24.
nodes.summary: How many unit spheres can touch a central one?

nodes.title: Ordinary Differential Equations
nodes.html: Equations relating a function to its derivatives. Newton classified first-order equations in 1671, Leibniz separated variables (1691), and Jacob Bernoulli posed the equation that bears his name (1695), solved by Leibniz and Johann Bernoulli. Newton’s laws, circuits and population models are all written in them.
nodes.summary: Equations relating a function to its derivatives.

nodes.title: Law of Large Numbers
nodes.html: Bernoulli’s Ars Conjectandi (published after his death in 1713) proved that observed frequencies converge to the underlying probability as the number of trials grows, the first limit theorem of probability. It justifies estimating chances from data.
nodes.summary: Bernoulli’s Ars Conjectandi (published after his death in 1713) proved that observed frequencies converge to the underlying probability as the number of trials grows, the first limit theorem of probability.

nodes.title: Taylor Series
nodes.html: A smooth function can be expanded as an infinite polynomial built from its derivatives at one point. Taylor published the general formula in 1715; Madhava, Gregory and Newton had special cases, and Maclaurin popularized the case at zero (1742). It is the basic tool of approximation.
nodes.summary: A smooth function can be expanded as an infinite polynomial built from its derivatives at one point.

nodes.title: Basel Problem
nodes.html: Euler showed that 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + … = π²/6 (1734), solving a problem posed by Mengoli in 1650 that had defeated Jacob Bernoulli and others. His comparison of the sine function with its infinite product led on to the zeta function and its values at even integers.
nodes.summary: Euler showed that 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + … = π²/6 (1734), solving a problem posed by Mengoli in 1650 that had defeated Jacob Bernoulli and others.

nodes.title: Graph Theory
nodes.html: Euler proved that no walk crosses each of Königsberg’s seven bridges exactly once (1736), by throwing away distances and keeping only connections.
nodes.summary: Euler proved that no walk crosses each of Königsberg’s seven bridges exactly once (1736), by throwing away distances and keeping only connections.

nodes.title: Euler Product Formula
aliases: divergence of the sum of prime reciprocals
nodes.html: Euler showed that the sum of 1/nˢ over all n equals the product of (1 − p⁻ˢ)⁻¹ over all primes p (1737). From it he deduced that the sum of 1/p diverges, a second proof that primes are infinite and the first link between primes and analysis.
nodes.summary: Euler showed that the sum of 1/nˢ over all n equals the product of (1 − p⁻ˢ)⁻¹ over all primes p (1737).

nodes.title: Goldbach’s Conjecture

progress.what: Proved the weak version: every odd number greater than 5 is a sum of three primes.
progress.html: Proved the weak version: every odd number greater than 5 is a sum of three primes.

nodes.html: Every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes. It has been checked by computer up to 4 × 10¹⁸ and remains unproved.
nodes.summary: Every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes.

nodes.title: Partial Differential Equations
nodes.html: D’Alembert’s solution of the vibrating string (1747) opened the theory of PDEs. Heat, waves, fluids and fields, nearly all of mathematical physics, are written in them.
nodes.summary: D’Alembert’s solution of the vibrating string (1747) opened the theory of PDEs.

nodes.title: Euler’s Formula
nodes.html: The identity e^{ix} = cos x + i sin x, presented in Euler’s Introductio in analysin infinitorum (1748), links the exponential function to trigonometry; at x = π it gives e^{iπ} + 1 = 0. It underlies complex analysis, Fourier analysis and the phasor methods of electrical engineering.
nodes.summary: The identity e^{ix} = cos x + i sin x, presented in Euler’s Introductio in analysin infinitorum (1748), links the exponential function to trigonometry; at x = π it gives e^{iπ} + 1 = 0.

nodes.title: Euler’s Polyhedron Formula
nodes.html: For a convex polyhedron the numbers of vertices, edges and faces satisfy V − E + F = 2 (Euler, 1752; Descartes had an equivalent statement earlier). The quantity V − E + F became the Euler characteristic, the first topological invariant.
nodes.summary: For a convex polyhedron the numbers of vertices, edges and faces satisfy V − E + F = 2 (Euler, 1752; Descartes had an equivalent statement earlier).

nodes.title: Calculus of Variations
nodes.html: Find the function that makes an integral as small or as large as possible. It began with Johann Bernoulli’s brachistochrone problem (1696) and acquired its general equation from Lagrange’s 1755 letter to Euler, now the Euler–Lagrange equation. It is the basis of Lagrangian mechanics and least-action principles.
nodes.summary: Find the function that makes an integral as small or as large as possible.

nodes.title: Bayes’ Theorem
nodes.html: A rule for updating a probability in the light of new evidence. Bayes’s essay was published after his death by Richard Price (1763), and Laplace developed and applied it independently (1774). It underlies Bayesian statistics, spam filtering and much of machine learning.
nodes.summary: A rule for updating a probability in the light of new evidence.

nodes.title: Lagrange’s Four-Square Theorem
nodes.html: Every natural number is a sum of four squares of integers. Bachet conjectured it in 1621, Fermat claimed a proof and Euler came close, and Lagrange proved it in 1770, the year Waring posed the corresponding problem for higher powers.
nodes.summary: Every natural number is a sum of four squares of integers.

nodes.title: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
nodes.html: Every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root, so a polynomial of degree n has n roots counted with multiplicity. Gauss’s 1799 thesis gave the first serious proof, which had a topological gap, and Argand published the first rigorous proof in 1806.
nodes.summary: Every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root, so a polynomial of degree n has n roots counted with multiplicity.

nodes.title: Modular Arithmetic
nodes.html: Gauss’s Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801) made congruences a calculus of their own and proved quadratic reciprocity. Public-key cryptography runs on it.
nodes.summary: Gauss’s Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801) made congruences a calculus of their own and proved quadratic reciprocity.

nodes.title: Central Limit Theorem
nodes.html: Sums of many small independent effects are approximately bell-shaped. De Moivre found the normal approximation to the binomial (1733), Laplace stated the general theorem (1810), and Lyapunov (1901) and Lindeberg (1922) gave rigorous conditions. It is the reason the normal distribution appears throughout statistics.
nodes.summary: Sums of many small independent effects are approximately bell-shaped.

nodes.title: Rigorous Analysis
nodes.html: Limits, continuity and the real numbers made precise: Cauchy’s Cours d’analyse (1821), Weierstrass’s ε–δ definitions, and Dedekind’s construction of the reals (1872).
nodes.summary: Limits, continuity and the real numbers made precise: Cauchy’s Cours d’analyse (1821), Weierstrass’s ε–δ definitions, and Dedekind’s construction of the reals (1872).

nodes.title: Fourier Analysis
nodes.html: Fourier claimed that any function is a sum of sines and cosines (1822). Making that precise drove much of 19th-century analysis; today it runs signal processing, JPEG and MRI.
nodes.summary: Fourier claimed that any function is a sum of sines and cosines (1822).

nodes.title: Complex Analysis
nodes.html: Calculus over the complex numbers, where differentiable functions turn out to be astonishingly rigid: Cauchy’s integral theorem (1825) and Riemann surfaces (1851).
nodes.summary: Calculus over the complex numbers, where differentiable functions turn out to be astonishingly rigid: Cauchy’s integral theorem (1825) and Riemann surfaces (1851).

nodes.title: Non-Euclidean Geometry
nodes.html: Drop Euclid’s parallel postulate and you still get a consistent geometry. Lobachevsky (1829) and Bolyai (1832) published it; Gauss had found it earlier and kept quiet.
nodes.summary: Drop Euclid’s parallel postulate and you still get a consistent geometry.

nodes.title: Group Theory
nodes.html: Galois linked the solvability of polynomial equations to their symmetry groups, explaining why the quintic has no general formula. He wrote it up the night before his fatal duel in 1832.
nodes.summary: Galois linked the solvability of polynomial equations to their symmetry groups, explaining why the quintic has no general formula.

nodes.title: Sturm–Liouville Theory
nodes.html: Boundary-value problems for second-order equations have a discrete sequence of eigenvalues, and their orthogonal eigenfunctions expand arbitrary functions (Sturm and Liouville, 1836 to 1837). The theory generalizes Fourier series and is the template for the discrete spectra of quantum mechanics.
nodes.summary: Boundary-value problems for second-order equations have a discrete sequence of eigenvalues, and their orthogonal eigenfunctions expand arbitrary functions (Sturm and Liouville, 1836 to 1837).

nodes.title: Primes in Arithmetic Progressions
nodes.html: Every arithmetic progression a, a + d, a + 2d, … with gcd(a, d) = 1 contains infinitely many primes (Dirichlet, 1837). The proof introduced Dirichlet characters and L-functions and founded analytic number theory.
nodes.summary: Every arithmetic progression a, a + d, a + 2d, … with gcd(a, d) = 1 contains infinitely many primes (Dirichlet, 1837).

nodes.title: Impossible Constructions
nodes.html: Wantzel proved in 1837 that a general angle cannot be trisected and a cube cannot be doubled with ruler and compass, because constructible lengths have degree a power of two over the rationals. Lindemann’s 1882 proof that π is transcendental showed that the circle cannot be squared.
nodes.summary: Wantzel proved in 1837 that a general angle cannot be trisected and a cube cannot be doubled with ruler and compass, because constructible lengths have degree a power of two over the rationals.

nodes.title: Quaternions
nodes.html: Hamilton carved i² = j² = k² = ijk = −1 into Broom Bridge in Dublin on 16 October 1843. Quaternions are the first number system in which multiplication does not commute, and they describe rotations in three dimensions, as used in graphics, aerospace and robotics.
nodes.summary: Hamilton carved i² = j² = k² = ijk = −1 into Broom Bridge in Dublin on 16 October 1843.

nodes.title: Combinatorial Designs
nodes.html: Kirkman (1847) studied arrangements of points in triples so that every pair lies in exactly one triple, later called Steiner triple systems, and posed the schoolgirl problem (1850): walk fifteen girls in rows of three for seven days with no pair repeated. Designs are used in experiment planning, coding theory and finite geometry.
nodes.summary: Kirkman (1847) studied arrangements of points in triples so that every pair lies in exactly one triple, later called Steiner triple systems, and posed the schoolgirl problem (1850): walk fifteen girls in rows of three for seven days with no pair repeated.

nodes.title: Gradient Descent
nodes.html: Cauchy proposed minimizing a function by repeatedly stepping against its gradient (1847). Its stochastic variants train most modern neural networks.
nodes.summary: Cauchy proposed minimizing a function by repeatedly stepping against its gradient (1847).

nodes.title: Twin Prime Conjecture

progress.what: Bounded gaps: infinitely many pairs of primes differ by at most 70,000,000.
progress.html: Bounded gaps: infinitely many pairs of primes differ by at most 70,000,000.

progress.what: A simpler sieve method brought the bound down to 600.
progress.html: A simpler sieve method brought the bound down to 600.

progress.what: A large online collaboration lowered the bound to 246.
progress.html: A large online collaboration lowered the bound to 246.

nodes.html: Are there infinitely many primes p for which p + 2 is also prime?
nodes.summary: Are there infinitely many primes p for which p + 2 is also prime?

nodes.title: Boolean Logic
nodes.html: Boole’s Laws of Thought (1854) turned logic into algebra over true and false. Eighty years later, Shannon used it to design circuits.
nodes.summary: Boole’s Laws of Thought (1854) turned logic into algebra over true and false.

nodes.title: Riemannian Geometry
nodes.html: Gauss showed that curvature can be measured from inside a surface (1827). Riemann’s 1854 lecture extended the idea to curved spaces of any dimension, the geometry Einstein would need sixty years later.
nodes.summary: Gauss showed that curvature can be measured from inside a surface (1827).

nodes.title: Linear Algebra
nodes.html: Vectors, matrices and linear maps, from Grassmann’s Ausdehnungslehre (1844) and Cayley’s memoir on matrices (1858). It is now the workhorse of physics, statistics and machine learning.
nodes.summary: Vectors, matrices and linear maps, from Grassmann’s Ausdehnungslehre (1844) and Cayley’s memoir on matrices (1858).

nodes.title: Riemann Hypothesis

progress.what: Infinitely many zeros lie on the critical line.
progress.html: Infinitely many zeros lie on the critical line.

progress.what: More than two-fifths of the zeros lie on the critical line.
progress.html: More than two-fifths of the zeros lie on the critical line.

progress.what: New large-value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials, the first substantial improvement on Ingham’s 1940 zero-density bound.
progress.html: New large-value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials, the first substantial improvement on Ingham’s 1940 zero-density bound.

progress.what: Claimed proof of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis: every Dirichlet L-function, including ζ(s), is zero-free for Re s > 7/8 (family 003 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis: every Dirichlet L-function, including ζ(s), is zero-free for Re s > 7/8 (family 003 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: All non-trivial zeros of ζ(s) have real part ½. It is equivalent to the best possible error term in the prime number theorem. A Clay Millennium Prize problem.
nodes.summary: All non-trivial zeros of ζ(s) have real part ½.

nodes.title: Riemann Zeta Function
nodes.html: Riemann’s only paper on number theory (1859) tied the distribution of the primes to the zeros of ζ(s) in the complex plane.
nodes.summary: Riemann’s only paper on number theory (1859) tied the distribution of the primes to the zeros of ζ(s) in the complex plane.

nodes.title: Irrationality of Catalan’s Constant

progress.what: Infinitely many of the values β(2n) of the Dirichlet beta function are irrational; Catalan’s constant is β(2).
progress.html: Infinitely many of the values β(2n) of the Dirichlet beta function are irrational; Catalan’s constant is β(2).

progress.what: At least one of β(2), β(4), β(6), β(8), β(10) and β(12) is irrational.
progress.html: At least one of β(2), β(4), β(6), β(8), β(10) and β(12) is irrational.

progress.what: Claimed proof that Catalan’s constant is irrational (family 005 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that Catalan’s constant is irrational (family 005 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Catalan’s constant G = 1 − 1/9 + 1/25 − 1/49 + … ≈ 0.916 appears throughout combinatorics and analysis; Eugène Catalan published a memoir on it in 1865. It has been called arguably the most basic constant whose irrationality is unproven, and only partial results were known. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a proof, formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: Catalan’s constant G = 1 − 1/9 + 1/25 − 1/49 + … ≈ 0.916 appears throughout combinatorics and analysis; Eugène Catalan published a memoir on it in 1865.

nodes.title: Riemann–Roch Theorem
nodes.html: For a compact Riemann surface the theorem computes the dimension of the space of meromorphic functions with prescribed poles from the genus and the degree of the pole divisor. Riemann proved an inequality (1857) and Roch completed it (1865); Hirzebruch and Grothendieck generalized it in the 1950s.
nodes.summary: For a compact Riemann surface the theorem computes the dimension of the space of meromorphic functions with prescribed poles from the genus and the degree of the pole divisor.

nodes.title: Algebraic Number Theory
nodes.html: Kummer’s ideal numbers (1847) restored unique factorization in cyclotomic integers and proved Fermat’s Last Theorem for all regular primes. Dedekind’s ideals (1871) made the idea general and gave number rings their modern theory.
nodes.summary: Kummer’s ideal numbers (1847) restored unique factorization in cyclotomic integers and proved Fermat’s Last Theorem for all regular primes.

nodes.title: Erlangen Program
nodes.html: Klein’s 1872 programme defined a geometry as the study of the properties left unchanged by a group of transformations. It unified Euclidean, affine, projective and non-Euclidean geometry and made group theory central to geometry and, later, to physics.
nodes.summary: Klein’s 1872 programme defined a geometry as the study of the properties left unchanged by a group of transformations.

nodes.title: Singular Value Decomposition
nodes.html: Every real matrix can be written as a rotation, a stretch along coordinate axes and another rotation. Beltrami (1873) and Jordan (1874) found it independently, and Golub and Kahan made it computable (1965). It is the basis of principal component analysis, low-rank compression and recommender systems.
nodes.summary: Every real matrix can be written as a rotation, a stretch along coordinate axes and another rotation.

nodes.title: Set Theory
nodes.html: Cantor proved that the real numbers outnumber the integers (1874) and built a theory of infinite sets. The Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms (1908–1922) now underpin most of mathematics.
nodes.summary: Cantor proved that the real numbers outnumber the integers (1874) and built a theory of infinite sets.

nodes.title: Cauchy–Kovalevskaya Theorem
nodes.html: A system of PDEs with analytic coefficients and analytic initial data has a unique analytic solution near the data surface. Cauchy proved special cases (1842), and Kovalevskaya proved the general theorem in her 1874 thesis, published in 1875. It is the first general existence theorem for PDEs.
nodes.summary: A system of PDEs with analytic coefficients and analytic initial data has a unique analytic solution near the data surface.

nodes.title: Predicate Logic
nodes.html: Frege’s Begriffsschrift (1879) introduced quantifiers and a fully formal language of proof. Every proof assistant descends from it.
nodes.summary: Frege’s Begriffsschrift (1879) introduced quantifiers and a fully formal language of proof.

nodes.title: Transcendental Numbers
nodes.html: Numbers that are not roots of any nonzero rational polynomial. Liouville constructed the first examples (1844), Hermite proved that e is transcendental (1873), and Lindemann proved the same for π (1882), which showed that the circle cannot be squared with ruler and compass.
nodes.summary: Numbers that are not roots of any nonzero rational polynomial.

nodes.title: Plane Jacobian Conjecture

progress.what: A computer-assisted argument verified the plane case for polynomials of degree at most 100.
progress.html: A computer-assisted argument verified the plane case for polynomials of degree at most 100.

progress.what: Raised the verified degree bound to 104.
progress.html: Raised the verified degree bound to 104.

progress.what: An explicit counterexample in three variables, which Alpöge credited to Claude Fable 5, refuted the conjecture in every dimension from 3 up, leaving the plane.
progress.html: An explicit counterexample in three variables, which Alpöge credited to Claude Fable 5, refuted the conjecture in every dimension from 3 up, leaving the plane.

nodes.html: If a polynomial map of the plane to itself has constant nonzero Jacobian determinant, must it have a polynomial inverse? Ludwig Kraus stated the question in 1884 and Keller posed it in n variables in 1939. Since a counterexample in three variables appeared in July 2026 (jacobian-3d), the plane is the only open case; it is verified for polynomials of degree up to 104.
nodes.summary: If a polynomial map of the plane to itself has constant nonzero Jacobian determinant, must it have a polynomial inverse?

nodes.title: Regression & Correlation
nodes.html: Galton described regression to the mean in inherited traits (1886), and Pearson formalized the correlation coefficient (1895 to 1896). Together they gave statistics its first methods for measuring how strongly one variable predicts another.
nodes.summary: Galton described regression to the mean in inherited traits (1886), and Pearson formalized the correlation coefficient (1895 to 1896).

nodes.title: Jordan Curve Theorem
nodes.html: Every simple closed curve in the plane separates it into exactly two regions, an inside and an outside. Jordan stated and gave a proof in 1887; Veblen’s 1905 proof became the standard rigorous one, and formal proofs were machine-checked in 2005 in HOL Light and Mizar.
nodes.summary: Every simple closed curve in the plane separates it into exactly two regions, an inside and an outside.

nodes.title: Lie Groups
nodes.html: Lie developed the theory of continuous groups of symmetries, first for differential equations in the 1870s and fully in his Theorie der Transformationsgruppen (1888 to 1893). Lie groups and their Lie algebras are the language of rotations, special relativity and the gauge symmetries of particle physics.
nodes.summary: Lie developed the theory of continuous groups of symmetries, first for differential equations in the 1870s and fully in his Theorie der Transformationsgruppen (1888 to 1893).

nodes.title: Peano Axioms
nodes.html: Five axioms define the natural numbers through zero, a successor operation and induction. Dedekind (1888) and Peano (1889) stated them; they are the basis of formal arithmetic and the setting of Gödel’s incompleteness theorems.
nodes.summary: Five axioms define the natural numbers through zero, a successor operation and induction.

nodes.title: Three-Body Problem & Chaos
nodes.html: Poincaré’s prize memoir (1890) showed that the three-body problem has no general closed-form solution and found homoclinic tangles, complicated orbits that depend sensitively on initial conditions. It founded the qualitative theory of dynamical systems and anticipated chaos.
nodes.summary: Poincaré’s prize memoir (1890) showed that the three-body problem has no general closed-form solution and found homoclinic tangles, complicated orbits that depend sensitively on initial conditions.

nodes.title: Simple Lie Algebras
nodes.html: Killing (1888 to 1890) and Cartan (thesis, 1894) classified the simple Lie algebras: four infinite families and five exceptional ones, including the 248-dimensional E₈. The classification is the basis of the root systems and Dynkin diagrams used throughout geometry and particle physics.
nodes.summary: Killing (1888 to 1890) and Cartan (thesis, 1894) classified the simple Lie algebras: four infinite families and five exceptional ones, including the 248-dimensional E₈.

nodes.title: Topology
nodes.html: The study of shape up to stretching. Poincaré’s Analysis Situs (1895) introduced homology and the fundamental group; Hausdorff axiomatized topological spaces (1914).
nodes.summary: The study of shape up to stretching.

nodes.title: Prime Number Theorem
nodes.html: The number of primes up to x is about x / ln x. Gauss and Legendre conjectured it; Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin proved it independently in 1896.
nodes.summary: The number of primes up to x is about x / ln x.

nodes.title: Representation Theory
nodes.html: Study a group through the ways it acts by matrices. Frobenius introduced group characters in 1896, and Burnside and Schur developed the theory in the following decade. It is used in number theory, quantum mechanics and chemistry, where it classifies molecular symmetries.
nodes.summary: Study a group through the ways it acts by matrices.

nodes.title: p-adic Numbers
nodes.html: Hensel (1897) completed the rational numbers with respect to divisibility by a prime p, giving a number system in which calculus-style methods work on number-theoretic problems. p-adic fields are central to modern number theory and arithmetic geometry.
nodes.summary: Hensel (1897) completed the rational numbers with respect to divisibility by a prime p, giving a number system in which calculus-style methods work on number-theoretic problems.

nodes.title: Chi-Squared Test
nodes.html: Pearson’s test (1900) compares observed counts with those a model predicts through a sum of squared deviations, whose distribution he derived. It was the first general significance test and is still used for goodness of fit and for contingency tables.
nodes.summary: Pearson’s test (1900) compares observed counts with those a model predicts through a sum of squared deviations, whose distribution he derived.

nodes.title: Hilbert’s Sixteenth Problem

progress.what: Quadratic vector fields with four limit cycles (Chen and Wang 1979, Shi 1980), so H(2) ≥ 4.
progress.html: Quadratic vector fields with four limit cycles (Chen and Wang 1979, Shi 1980), so H(2) ≥ 4.

progress.what: Independent proofs that every polynomial vector field has finitely many limit cycles, repairing Dulac’s 1923 argument.
progress.html: Independent proofs that every polynomial vector field has finitely many limit cycles, repairing Dulac’s 1923 argument.

progress.what: A cubic system with 13 limit cycles, so H(3) ≥ 13.
progress.html: A cubic system with 13 limit cycles, so H(3) ≥ 13.

progress.what: Claimed proof that the number of limit cycles of a planar polynomial vector field is bounded by a constant depending only on its degree (family 143 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that the number of limit cycles of a planar polynomial vector field is bounded by a constant depending only on its degree (family 143 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: How many limit cycles can a planar polynomial vector field of degree n have? The second part of Hilbert’s 16th problem (1900), also Smale’s 13th problem, asks for a bound H(n) that depends only on n. Each single field has finitely many (Ilyashenko and Écalle, around 1991), and quadratic fields can have at least four. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims that H(n) is always finite.
nodes.summary: How many limit cycles can a planar polynomial vector field of degree n have?

nodes.title: Principal Component Analysis
nodes.html: Find the orthogonal directions along which data vary most. Pearson gave the geometric idea in 1901 and Hotelling the statistical formulation in 1933. It is the standard first step for dimensionality reduction and exploratory data analysis.
nodes.summary: Find the orthogonal directions along which data vary most.

nodes.title: Runge–Kutta Methods
nodes.html: Runge (1895) and Kutta (1901) devised formulas that solve differential equations numerically with high accuracy by evaluating the slope several times per step. The fourth-order method, RK4, remains a default integrator in science and engineering.
nodes.summary: Runge (1895) and Kutta (1901) devised formulas that solve differential equations numerically with high accuracy by evaluating the slope several times per step.

nodes.title: Measure & Integration
nodes.html: Lebesgue’s integral (1902) handles functions and sets that defeat Riemann’s. It is the foundation of modern probability and of function spaces such as L².
nodes.summary: Lebesgue’s integral (1902) handles functions and sets that defeat Riemann’s.

nodes.title: Thomson Problem

progress.what: The regular icosahedron is optimal for 12 charges.
progress.html: The regular icosahedron is optimal for 12 charges.

progress.what: A computer-assisted proof that the triangular bipyramid is optimal for 5 charges.
progress.html: A computer-assisted proof that the triangular bipyramid is optimal for 5 charges.

progress.what: A computer-assisted proof, verified in Lean, that a square antiprism is the unique minimizer for 8 charges.
progress.html: A computer-assisted proof, verified in Lean, that a square antiprism is the unique minimizer for 8 charges.

progress.what: A Lean proof that the pentagonal bipyramid is the unique minimizer for 7 charges, written by ten Claude Sonnet 5.5 agents over about 15 hours and accepted by two independent Lean kernels.
progress.html: A Lean proof that the pentagonal bipyramid is the unique minimizer for 7 charges, written by ten Claude Sonnet 5.5 agents over about 15 hours and accepted by two independent Lean kernels.

nodes.html: How do n equal charges on a sphere arrange themselves to minimize their electrostatic energy? J. J. Thomson posed the problem in 1904 for his model of the atom. Proofs exist only for a handful of n: 2 to 6 and 12, plus 8 and 7, whose computer-assisted proofs, checked in Lean, appeared in September 2026.
nodes.summary: How do n equal charges on a sphere arrange themselves to minimize their electrostatic energy?

nodes.title: Markov Chains
nodes.html: Markov (1906) studied sequences in which the next state depends only on the present one, and proved that the law of large numbers holds for them. Markov chains underlie PageRank, queueing theory, hidden Markov models and sampling methods such as MCMC.
nodes.summary: Markov (1906) studied sequences in which the next state depends only on the present one, and proved that the law of large numbers holds for them.

nodes.title: Partition Principle and Choice

progress.what: Claimed construction, assuming ZF is consistent, of a model of ZF in which the Partition Principle holds but the axiom of choice fails (family 244 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed construction, assuming ZF is consistent, of a model of ZF in which the Partition Principle holds but the axiom of choice fails (family 244 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: The Partition Principle says that if a set A maps onto a set B, then B injects into A. It follows from the axiom of choice, and Bertrand Russell declared the two equivalent in 1906, but whether it implies choice stayed open for over a century. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a model where it holds and choice fails, formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: The Partition Principle says that if a set A maps onto a set B, then B injects into A.

nodes.title: Student’s t-Test
nodes.html: William Sealy Gosset, a Guinness brewer publishing as ‘Student’, derived the exact distribution of the standardized sample mean for small samples (1908). The t-test is among the most used procedures in experimental science.
nodes.summary: William Sealy Gosset, a Guinness brewer publishing as ‘Student’, derived the exact distribution of the standardized sample mean for small samples (1908).

nodes.title: Functional Analysis
nodes.html: Linear algebra in infinitely many dimensions: Hilbert and Banach spaces, operators and their spectra. It became the mathematical language of quantum mechanics (von Neumann, 1932).
nodes.summary: Linear algebra in infinitely many dimensions: Hilbert and Banach spaces, operators and their spectra.

nodes.title: Principia Mathematica
nodes.html: After Russell’s paradox (1901) undermined naive set theory, Whitehead and Russell derived mathematics from logic in a ramified theory of types (three volumes, 1910 to 1913). The work set the standard for formal proof and shaped logic and early computer science.
nodes.summary: After Russell’s paradox (1901) undermined naive set theory, Whitehead and Russell derived mathematics from logic in a ramified theory of types (three volumes, 1910 to 1913).

nodes.title: Brouwer Fixed-Point Theorem
nodes.html: Every continuous map of a closed ball to itself has a fixed point (Brouwer, 1911). It underlies existence proofs in analysis, game theory and economics, including Nash’s equilibrium theorem and general equilibrium.
nodes.summary: Every continuous map of a closed ball to itself has a fixed point (Brouwer, 1911).

nodes.title: Inscribed Square Problem

progress.what: Every smooth closed curve contains the corners of rectangles of every aspect ratio.
progress.html: Every smooth closed curve contains the corners of rectangles of every aspect ratio.

nodes.html: Does every closed curve in the plane pass through the four corners of some square? Yes for smooth curves and many others; open in general.
nodes.summary: Does every closed curve in the plane pass through the four corners of some square?

nodes.title: Sieve Methods
