nodes.html: Brun’s sieve (1915) bounds how many integers survive after the multiples of small primes are removed. With it Brun showed in 1919 that the sum of the reciprocals of the twin primes converges. Selberg’s sieve (1947) and its successors lead to modern results on gaps between primes.
nodes.summary: Brun’s sieve (1915) bounds how many integers survive after the multiples of small primes are removed.

nodes.title: Hardy–Littlewood Circle Method
nodes.html: Hardy and Ramanujan found an asymptotic formula for the number of partitions of an integer (1918). Hardy and Littlewood turned the idea into a general method for Waring’s problem and Goldbach-type questions, and Vinogradov used it to show that every large odd number is a sum of three primes (1937).
nodes.summary: Hardy and Ramanujan found an asymptotic formula for the number of partitions of an integer (1918).

nodes.title: Hausdorff Dimension
nodes.html: Hausdorff (1918) defined a dimension that can take fractional values: the Cantor set has dimension log 2 / log 3, about 0.63. It is the standard measure of roughness in fractal geometry and in problems such as Kakeya’s.
nodes.summary: Hausdorff (1918) defined a dimension that can take fractional values: the Cantor set has dimension log 2 / log 3, about 0.63.

nodes.title: Abstract Algebra
nodes.html: Noether’s ‘Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen’ (1921) recast algebra as the study of structures, such as rings, ideals and modules, rather than of equations.
nodes.summary: Noether’s ‘Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen’ (1921) recast algebra as the study of structures, such as rings, ideals and modules, rather than of equations.

nodes.title: Elliptic Curves
nodes.html: Cubic curves whose rational points form a group; Mordell proved that the group is finitely generated (1922). They are central to number theory and to modern cryptography.
nodes.summary: Cubic curves whose rational points form a group; Mordell proved that the group is finitely generated (1922).

nodes.title: Statistical Inference
nodes.html: From least squares (Legendre 1805, Gauss 1809) to Fisher’s maximum likelihood (1922): methods for learning from noisy data. Machine learning descends from them.
nodes.summary: From least squares (Legendre 1805, Gauss 1809) to Fisher’s maximum likelihood (1922): methods for learning from noisy data.

nodes.title: Wiener Process
nodes.html: Wiener (1923) constructed Brownian motion as a random continuous function that is nowhere differentiable. Bachelier had used it to model stock prices in 1900 and Einstein to describe diffusion in 1905. It is the basis of stochastic calculus and mathematical finance.
nodes.summary: Wiener (1923) constructed Brownian motion as a random continuous function that is nowhere differentiable.

nodes.title: Morse Theory
nodes.html: Morse (1925 to 1934) showed that the critical points of a smooth function on a manifold determine the topology of the manifold. It became a main tool in differential topology, used by Smale and Milnor in their work on high-dimensional manifolds.
nodes.summary: Morse (1925 to 1934) showed that the critical points of a smooth function on a manifold determine the topology of the manifold.

nodes.title: Class Field Theory
nodes.html: Describes all abelian extensions of a number field through its own arithmetic. Takagi proved the existence theorem (1920) and Artin the general reciprocity law (1927), completing a programme Hilbert had outlined. It is the abelian case of the Langlands programme.
nodes.summary: Describes all abelian extensions of a number field through its own arithmetic.

nodes.title: Game Theory
nodes.html: Von Neumann proved the minimax theorem for two-person zero-sum games (1928) and, with Morgenstern, wrote Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944). The mathematics of strategic choice now underlies economics, evolutionary biology and multi-agent AI.
nodes.summary: Von Neumann proved the minimax theorem for two-person zero-sum games (1928) and, with Morgenstern, wrote Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944).

nodes.title: Kakeya Needle Problem
nodes.html: Kakeya asked in 1917 for the smallest area in which a needle can be turned through a full circle. Besicovitch showed in 1928 that there is no minimum: regions of arbitrarily small area work. His sets containing a segment in every direction (1920) led to the Kakeya conjecture on their dimension.
nodes.summary: Kakeya asked in 1917 for the smallest area in which a needle can be turned through a full circle.

nodes.title: Knot Theory
nodes.html: Tait tabulated knots in the 1870s and 1880s, Reidemeister showed that three local moves relate any two diagrams of the same knot (1927), and Alexander gave the first knot polynomial (1928). Knot invariants now link topology with algebra and quantum physics.
nodes.summary: Tait tabulated knots in the 1870s and 1880s, Reidemeister showed that three local moves relate any two diagrams of the same knot (1927), and Alexander gave the first knot polynomial (1928).

nodes.title: Gödel’s Completeness Theorem
nodes.html: Every statement that is true in all models of a first-order theory can be derived from its axioms (Gödel’s doctoral thesis, 1929). Provability and truth therefore coincide for first-order logic, a result that underlies model theory and automated theorem proving.
nodes.summary: Every statement that is true in all models of a first-order theory can be derived from its axioms (Gödel’s doctoral thesis, 1929).

nodes.title: Intuitionistic Logic
nodes.html: Brouwer’s intuitionism (from 1907) requires a proof of existence to construct the object. Heyting formalized its logic in 1930, dropping the law of excluded middle. It is the logic of constructive mathematics and type theory.
nodes.summary: Brouwer’s intuitionism (from 1907) requires a proof of existence to construct the object.

nodes.title: Ramsey’s Theorem
nodes.html: In any large enough structure some orderly substructure must appear: colour the edges of a large complete graph with two colours and a single-coloured clique of any chosen size results. Ramsey proved the infinite and finite versions in 1930 and founded Ramsey theory.
nodes.summary: In any large enough structure some orderly substructure must appear: colour the edges of a large complete graph with two colours and a single-coloured clique of any chosen size results.

nodes.title: Ergodic Theorem
nodes.html: For ergodic systems the average over time along almost every trajectory equals the average over space. Von Neumann proved a mean version and Birkhoff the pointwise version in 1931 to 1932, giving a rigorous basis to Boltzmann’s ergodic hypothesis in statistical mechanics.
nodes.summary: For ergodic systems the average over time along almost every trajectory equals the average over space.

nodes.title: Incompleteness Theorems
nodes.html: Any consistent formal system that can express arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, and cannot prove its own consistency (1931).
nodes.summary: Any consistent formal system that can express arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, and cannot prove its own consistency (1931).

nodes.title: Borsuk’s Problem in Low Dimensions

progress.what: Proved the conjecture in three dimensions; H. G. Eggleston gave an independent proof in 1955.
progress.html: Proved the conjecture in three dimensions; H. G. Eggleston gave an independent proof in 1955.

progress.what: Counterexamples in every dimension from 65 on, built from two-distance sets.
progress.html: Counterexamples in every dimension from 65 on, built from two-distance sets.

progress.what: A 64-dimensional counterexample derived from Bondarenko’s construction.
progress.html: A 64-dimensional counterexample derived from Bondarenko’s construction.

progress.what: A 63-dimensional counterexample: a 321-point three-distance set that needs at least 65 pieces.
progress.html: A 63-dimensional counterexample: a 321-point three-distance set that needs at least 65 pieces.

progress.what: Claimed counterexample in dimension 9, built from rank-one projections onto lines in ℝ⁴ (family 156 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed counterexample in dimension 9, built from rank-one projections onto lines in ℝ⁴ (family 156 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Borsuk asked in 1933 whether every bounded set in ℝⁿ can be cut into n + 1 pieces of smaller diameter. The answer is yes for n ≤ 3 and no in high dimensions (Kahn and Kalai, 1993), and the smallest dimension with a known counterexample fell from 64 (2013) to 63 (May 2026), and OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims 9. Dimension 4 is the smallest open case.
nodes.summary: Borsuk asked in 1933 whether every bounded set in ℝⁿ can be cut into n + 1 pieces of smaller diameter.

nodes.title: Hadamard Conjecture

progress.what: Built Hadamard matrices from quadratic residues in finite fields, covering many orders at once.
progress.html: Built Hadamard matrices from quadratic residues in finite fields, covering many orders at once.

progress.what: Found a matrix of order 92 by computer at JPL, the smallest order that the Sylvester and Paley constructions cannot reach.
progress.html: Found a matrix of order 92 by computer at JPL, the smallest order that the Sylvester and Paley constructions cannot reach.

progress.what: Order 428, leaving 668 as the smallest order with no known Hadamard matrix.
progress.html: Order 428, leaving 668 as the smallest order with no known Hadamard matrix.

progress.what: Announced explicit Hadamard matrices for all twelve orders below 2000 that were still open, including 668. Each matrix can be checked by direct multiplication.
progress.html: Announced explicit Hadamard matrices for all twelve orders below 2000 that were still open, including 668. Each matrix can be checked by direct multiplication.

nodes.html: A Hadamard matrix is a square matrix of entries ±1 whose rows are mutually orthogonal; its order must be 1, 2 or a multiple of 4. The conjecture, usually credited to Paley (1933), says every multiple of 4 is the order of one. In August 2026 constructions were announced for all twelve orders below 2000 that were still open, so the smallest open order now lies above 2000.
nodes.summary: A Hadamard matrix is a square matrix of entries ±1 whose rows are mutually orthogonal; its order must be 1, 2 or a multiple of 4.

nodes.title: Kolmogorov’s Axioms
nodes.html: Kolmogorov’s Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung (1933) defined probability as a measure of total mass one on a space of outcomes. Almost all modern probability theory and mathematical statistics start from these axioms.
nodes.summary: Kolmogorov’s Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung (1933) defined probability as a measure of total mass one on a space of outcomes.

nodes.title: Hypothesis Testing
aliases: type I and type II errors
nodes.html: The Neyman–Pearson lemma (1933) identified the most powerful test of one hypothesis against another and introduced type I and type II errors; Neyman added confidence intervals in 1937. With Fisher’s methods it forms the framework of classical statistical testing.
nodes.summary: The Neyman–Pearson lemma (1933) identified the most powerful test of one hypothesis against another and introduced type I and type II errors; Neyman added confidence intervals in 1937.

nodes.title: Navier–Stokes Regularity

progress.what: Weak solutions exist for all time.
progress.html: Weak solutions exist for all time.

progress.what: Partial regularity: any singular set must be very small.
progress.html: Partial regularity: any singular set must be very small.

progress.what: Claimed finite-time blow-up with a smooth external force, which would settle the Clay problem through its breakdown alternatives (C) and (D). The 166-page proof, with a Lean formalization, came from an internal system of at least 10,000 agents running for 88 hours. On 11 September 2026 the Clay Institute said the problem has apparently been settled, but it has not finished verifying the proof or assigning credit. Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge dispute priority.
progress.html: Claimed finite-time blow-up with a smooth external force, which would settle the Clay problem through its breakdown alternatives (C) and (D). The 166-page proof, with a Lean formalization, came from an internal system of at least 10,000 agents running for 88 hours. On 11 September 2026 the Clay Institute said the problem has apparently been settled, but it has not finished verifying the proof or assigning credit. Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge dispute priority.

nodes.html: Do smooth solutions of the 3D Navier–Stokes equations stay smooth forever, or can they blow up in finite time? A Clay Millennium Prize problem. The Clay statement allows a smooth external force in its blow-up alternatives; without any force, the question stays open either way.
nodes.summary: Do smooth solutions of the 3D Navier–Stokes equations stay smooth forever, or can they blow up in finite time?

nodes.title: Navier–Stokes Without Forcing
nodes.html: Can a smooth solution of the 3D Navier–Stokes equations with no external force blow up in finite time? The 2026 blow-up claim relies on a carefully chosen force. Without one, regularity versus blow-up is still open.
nodes.summary: Can a smooth solution of the 3D Navier–Stokes equations with no external force blow up in finite time?

nodes.title: Randomized Experiments
nodes.html: Fisher developed analysis of variance in the 1920s at the Rothamsted Experimental Station and set out randomization, replication and blocking in The Design of Experiments (1935). Randomized controlled trials in medicine follow the same logic.
nodes.summary: Fisher developed analysis of variance in the 1920s at the Rothamsted Experimental Station and set out randomization, replication and blocking in The Design of Experiments (1935).

nodes.title: Erdős–Szekeres Theorem
nodes.html: Any sequence of n² + 1 distinct numbers contains a monotone subsequence of length n + 1, and any sufficiently large set of points in general position contains a convex n-gon (1935). The second result, the ‘happy ending problem’, was an early landmark of discrete geometry.
nodes.summary: Any sequence of n² + 1 distinct numbers contains a monotone subsequence of length n + 1, and any sufficiently large set of points in general position contains a convex n-gon (1935).

nodes.title: Erdős–Szekeres Conjecture

progress.what: Constructed 2ⁿ⁻² points in general position with no n in convex position, so the conjectured value cannot be lowered.
progress.html: Constructed 2ⁿ⁻² points in general position with no n in convex position, so the conjectured value cannot be lowered.

progress.what: A computer search showed that every 17 points in general position contain a convex hexagon, settling n = 6.
progress.html: A computer search showed that every 17 points in general position contain a convex hexagon, settling n = 6.

progress.what: Proved that 2^(n+o(n)) points suffice, matching the conjecture up to lower-order terms in the exponent.
progress.html: Proved that 2^(n+o(n)) points suffice, matching the conjecture up to lower-order terms in the exponent.

progress.what: Sharpened the error term to 2^(n+O(√(n log n))).
progress.html: Sharpened the error term to 2^(n+O(√(n log n))).

nodes.html: Erdős and Szekeres proved in 1935 that every large enough set of points in general position in the plane contains n points in convex position, and conjectured that 2ⁿ⁻² + 1 points always suffice, which would be sharp. It is confirmed for n ≤ 6, and Suk (2016) proved that 2^(n+o(n)) points suffice. The next case asks whether every 33 points in general position contain a convex heptagon.
nodes.summary: Erdős and Szekeres proved in 1935 that every large enough set of points in general position in the plane contains n points in convex position, and conjectured that 2ⁿ⁻² + 1 points always suffice, which would be sharp.

nodes.title: Landau–Siegel Zeros

progress.what: L(1, χ) ≥ C(ε) q^(−ε) for every ε > 0, with a constant that cannot be computed because a Siegel zero cannot be excluded.
progress.html: L(1, χ) ≥ C(ε) q^(−ε) for every ε > 0, with a constant that cannot be computed because a Siegel zero cannot be excluded.

progress.what: An effective lower bound for class numbers of imaginary quadratic fields that sidesteps Siegel zeros.
progress.html: An effective lower bound for class numbers of imaginary quadratic fields that sidesteps Siegel zeros.

progress.what: Posted a claimed effective bound L(1, χ) ≫ (log q)^(−2022), a weak form of excluding Siegel zeros; it has not been confirmed.
progress.html: Posted a claimed effective bound L(1, χ) ≫ (log q)^(−2022), a weak form of excluding Siegel zeros; it has not been confirmed.

progress.what: Claimed proof that every Dirichlet L-function is zero-free in Re s > 7/8, which would rule out Siegel zeros (family 003 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that every Dirichlet L-function is zero-free in Re s > 7/8, which would rule out Siegel zeros (family 003 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Can the L-function of a real Dirichlet character mod q have a real zero within about c/log q of s = 1? Such Siegel zeros are believed not to exist, but they have never been ruled out, which is why Siegel’s theorem (1935) and the many results that depend on it give no computable constants. A claim in OpenAI’s October 2026 math release (quasi-riemann-hypothesis) would exclude them.
nodes.summary: Can the L-function of a real Dirichlet character mod q have a real zero within about c/log q of s = 1?

nodes.title: Operator Algebras
nodes.html: Murray and von Neumann’s ‘rings of operators’ (1936) and Gelfand and Naimark’s C*-algebras (1943) give the algebra of quantum observables. Operator algebras grew into noncommutative geometry and have deep links to knot theory and quantum information.
nodes.summary: Murray and von Neumann’s ‘rings of operators’ (1936) and Gelfand and Naimark’s C*-algebras (1943) give the algebra of quantum observables.

nodes.title: Collatz Conjecture

progress.what: Almost all orbits attain almost bounded values.
progress.html: Almost all orbits attain almost bounded values.

nodes.html: Halve n if it is even; otherwise replace it with 3n + 1. Does every starting number eventually reach 1? Computers have checked enormous ranges, and Erdős is said to have remarked that mathematics may not be ready for such problems.
nodes.summary: Halve n if it is even; otherwise replace it with 3n + 1.

nodes.title: Modular Forms
nodes.html: Highly symmetric complex functions on the upper half-plane. Klein and Poincaré studied them in the 1880s, Ramanujan’s τ-function (1916) revealed their arithmetic, and Hecke’s operators (1937) gave the theory its structure. They link partitions, elliptic curves and sphere packing, and were central to the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem.
nodes.summary: Highly symmetric complex functions on the upper half-plane.

nodes.title: Mahler Conjecture

progress.what: Proved the conjecture up to a factor cⁿ for an absolute constant c.
progress.html: Proved the conjecture up to a factor cⁿ for an absolute constant c.

progress.what: Proved the symmetric case in dimension 3.
progress.html: Proved the symmetric case in dimension 3.

progress.what: Claimed proofs of the symmetric and general conjectures in every dimension, with Hanner polytopes and simplices as the minimizers and all equality cases classified (family 087 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proofs of the symmetric and general conjectures in every dimension, with Hanner polytopes and simplices as the minimizers and all equality cases classified (family 087 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Kurt Mahler conjectured in 1939 that the product of the volumes of a convex body and its polar is smallest for the cube among symmetric bodies and for the simplex in general. It is a central problem of convex geometry, tied to Banach space theory and symplectic geometry. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims both versions in every dimension, formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: Kurt Mahler conjectured in 1939 that the product of the volumes of a convex body and its polar is smallest for the cube among symmetric bodies and for the simplex in general.

nodes.title: Hilbert–Smith Conjecture

progress.what: Solved Hilbert’s fifth problem: a locally compact group that is a topological manifold is a Lie group.
progress.html: Solved Hilbert’s fifth problem: a locally compact group that is a topological manifold is a Lie group.

progress.what: Proved the conjecture for 3-manifolds.
progress.html: Proved the conjecture for 3-manifolds.

progress.what: Claimed proof in every dimension: a locally compact group acting faithfully on a connected finite-dimensional manifold is a Lie group (family 304 of OpenAI’s math release, not formalized). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof in every dimension: a locally compact group acting faithfully on a connected finite-dimensional manifold is a Lie group (family 304 of OpenAI’s math release, not formalized). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: The Hilbert–Smith conjecture says that a locally compact group acting faithfully on a connected manifold must be a Lie group. It grew out of Hilbert’s fifth problem (1900) and Paul Smith’s 1941 work, and was known only up to dimension three (John Pardon, 2013). OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a proof in every dimension; it is not formalized and not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: The Hilbert–Smith conjecture says that a locally compact group acting faithfully on a connected manifold must be a Lie group.

nodes.title: Hodge Theory
nodes.html: De Rham’s theorem (1931) identified the cohomology of a manifold with that of its differential forms, and Hodge’s harmonic integrals (1941) showed that each class has a unique harmonic representative on a compact Riemannian manifold. It is the setting of the Hodge conjecture.
nodes.summary: De Rham’s theorem (1931) identified the cohomology of a manifold with that of its differential forms, and Hodge’s harmonic integrals (1941) showed that each class has a unique harmonic representative on a compact Riemannian manifold.

nodes.title: Turán’s Theorem
nodes.html: A graph on n vertices with no complete subgraph on r + 1 vertices has at most (1 − 1/r)n²/2 edges, and the extremal graphs are complete r-partite (Turán, 1941; Mantel had proved the case r = 2 in 1907). It founded extremal graph theory.
nodes.summary: A graph on n vertices with no complete subgraph on r + 1 vertices has at most (1 − 1/r)n²/2 edges, and the extremal graphs are complete r-partite (Turán, 1941; Mantel had proved the case r = 2 in 1907).

nodes.title: Optimal Transport
nodes.html: Monge posed the problem of moving a pile of earth to fill a hole at least cost (1781). Kantorovich’s relaxation and duality (1942) made it tractable, and he shared the 1975 Nobel Prize in economics for related work. Wasserstein distances are now used in PDE, statistics and machine learning.
nodes.summary: Monge posed the problem of moving a pile of earth to fill a hole at least cost (1781).

nodes.title: Free Group Factor Isomorphism Problem

progress.what: Independently showed that the interpolated free group factors are either all isomorphic or pairwise non-isomorphic.
progress.html: Independently showed that the interpolated free group factors are either all isomorphic or pairwise non-isomorphic.

progress.what: Claimed proof that L(F₂) ≅ L(F₃), so that all interpolated free group factors, including L(F∞), are isomorphic (family 287 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that L(F₂) ≅ L(F₃), so that all interpolated free group factors, including L(F∞), are isomorphic (family 287 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: The free group factors L(Fₙ) are von Neumann algebras built from free groups, introduced by Francis Murray and John von Neumann in 1943. Whether L(F₂) and L(F₃) are isomorphic is a central problem of operator algebras, and Dan Voiculescu created free probability around 1986 to attack it. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims that all of them are isomorphic, formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: The free group factors L(Fₙ) are von Neumann algebras built from free groups, introduced by Francis Murray and John von Neumann in 1943.

nodes.title: Hadwiger’s Conjecture

progress.what: Proved the case k = 6, using the four colour theorem.
progress.html: Proved the case k = 6, using the four colour theorem.

progress.what: Graphs with no Kₖ minor are O(k log log k)-colourable.
progress.html: Graphs with no Kₖ minor are O(k log log k)-colourable.

progress.what: Claimed that graphs with no Kₖ minor are O(k)-colourable (the linear Hadwiger conjecture); the paper says the proof was found by GPT-6 Astra following the authors’ directions.
progress.html: Claimed that graphs with no Kₖ minor are O(k)-colourable (the linear Hadwiger conjecture); the paper says the proof was found by GPT-6 Astra following the authors’ directions.

progress.what: Claimed disproof, even for fractional colouring (family 157 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed disproof, even for fractional colouring (family 157 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Hadwiger conjectured in 1943 that every graph with no Kₖ minor can be coloured with k − 1 colours, a far-reaching generalization of the four colour theorem. It is proved for k ≤ 6. In October 2026 OpenAI claimed counterexamples, and separately Norin and Steiner claimed that a constant multiple of k colours always suffices. Both claims await review.
nodes.summary: Hadwiger conjectured in 1943 that every graph with no Kₖ minor can be coloured with k − 1 colours, a far-reaching generalization of the four colour theorem.

nodes.title: Itô Calculus
nodes.html: Itô (1944) defined integrals with respect to Brownian motion and later a chain rule for them (Itô’s lemma, 1951). Stochastic calculus is the language of stochastic differential equations, filtering and the Black–Scholes option-pricing model (1973).
nodes.summary: Itô (1944) defined integrals with respect to Brownian motion and later a chain rule for them (Itô’s lemma, 1951).

nodes.title: Category Theory
nodes.html: Eilenberg and Mac Lane (1945) introduced categories, functors and natural transformations to study mathematical structures through the maps between them. Category theory became the organizing language of algebraic geometry, topology and type theory.
nodes.summary: Eilenberg and Mac Lane (1945) introduced categories, functors and natural transformations to study mathematical structures through the maps between them.

nodes.title: Monte Carlo Method
nodes.html: Estimate hard quantities by random sampling on a computer. Ulam conceived the idea at Los Alamos in 1946, von Neumann and Metropolis developed it on early computers, and the first paper appeared in 1949. It is used in physics, finance, graphics and AI.
nodes.summary: Estimate hard quantities by random sampling on a computer.

nodes.title: Linear Programming
nodes.html: Maximize a linear function subject to linear constraints. Kantorovich formulated such problems in 1939, Dantzig devised the simplex method in 1947 and von Neumann supplied duality. It became the core of operations research, planning and logistics.
nodes.summary: Maximize a linear function subject to linear constraints.

nodes.title: Probabilistic Method

quote.text: My brain is open!
quote.by: Paul Erdős, arriving at a colleague’s door

nodes.html: Show that an object exists by proving that a random one works with positive probability. Erdős’s 1947 lower bound for Ramsey numbers launched a style of proof now used throughout combinatorics and computer science.
nodes.summary: Show that an object exists by proving that a random one works with positive probability.

nodes.title: Erdős–Straus Conjecture

progress.what: Polynomial identities settle every n outside six residue classes mod 840.
progress.html: Polynomial identities settle every n outside six residue classes mod 840.

progress.what: At most N/exp(c(log N)^(2/3)) exceptions up to N, so they have density zero.
progress.html: At most N/exp(c(log N)^(2/3)) exceptions up to N, so they have density zero.

progress.what: Bounds for the number of solutions: averaged over primes up to N, it grows only polylogarithmically.
progress.html: Bounds for the number of solutions: averaged over primes up to N, it grows only polylogarithmically.

progress.what: Verified the conjecture for every n up to 10¹⁸.
progress.html: Verified the conjecture for every n up to 10¹⁸.

nodes.html: Can 4/n be written as 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with positive integers x, y, z for every n ≥ 2? Erdős and Straus conjectured so in 1948. It suffices to treat prime n, the possible exceptions have density zero (Vaughan, 1970), and computers have checked every n up to 10¹⁸ (2025).
nodes.summary: Can 4/n be written as 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with positive integers x, y, z for every n ≥ 2?

nodes.title: Distributions & Sobolev Spaces
nodes.html: Generalized functions such as the Dirac delta can be differentiated any number of times. Sobolev introduced weak derivatives and the spaces that bear his name in the 1930s, and Schwartz’s theory of distributions (1945 to 1950) made the idea systematic and won him the 1950 Fields Medal. It is the standard framework for linear PDEs.
nodes.summary: Generalized functions such as the Dirac delta can be differentiated any number of times.

nodes.title: Chromatic Number of the Plane

progress.what: Ruled out 4 colours with a 1,581-vertex unit-distance graph. De Grey is a biologist by training; the Polymath16 project then shrank such graphs.
progress.html: Ruled out 4 colours with a 1,581-vertex unit-distance graph. De Grey is a biologist by training; the Polymath16 project then shrank such graphs.

progress.what: Claimed proof that the plane cannot be coloured with five colours, which would leave 6 or 7 (family 158 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that the plane cannot be coloured with five colours, which would leave 6 or 7 (family 158 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: How many colours are needed so that no two points at distance exactly 1 share a colour? It is proved to be 5, 6 or 7, and a 2026 claim, formalized in Lean, would rule out 5.
nodes.summary: How many colours are needed so that no two points at distance exactly 1 share a colour?

nodes.title: Hodge Conjecture

progress.what: Claimed proof of the rational Hodge conjecture for abelian varieties with complex multiplication (family 032 of OpenAI’s math release). Not formalized and not yet independently reviewed; three other Hodge-related manuscripts in the release were withdrawn on 7 October 2026 after a sign error.
progress.html: Claimed proof of the rational Hodge conjecture for abelian varieties with complex multiplication (family 032 of OpenAI’s math release). Not formalized and not yet independently reviewed; three other Hodge-related manuscripts in the release were withdrawn on 7 October 2026 after a sign error.

nodes.html: On a smooth projective complex variety, every Hodge class is a rational combination of classes of algebraic subvarieties. A Clay Millennium Prize problem.
nodes.summary: On a smooth projective complex variety, every Hodge class is a rational combination of classes of algebraic subvarieties.

nodes.title: Nash Equilibrium
nodes.html: A strategy profile from which no player gains by changing strategy alone. Nash proved in 1950 that every finite game has one in mixed strategies. The concept is central to economics (Nash shared the 1994 Nobel Prize in economics) and to multi-agent AI.
nodes.summary: A strategy profile from which no player gains by changing strategy alone.

nodes.title: Homotopy Groups of Spheres
nodes.html: How spheres of one dimension can wrap around spheres of another. Hopf’s map from the 3-sphere to the 2-sphere (1931) showed that the groups are nontrivial, and Serre (1951) proved that they are finite with a known pattern of exceptions. Their full computation remains out of reach.
nodes.summary: How spheres of one dimension can wrap around spheres of another.

nodes.title: Stochastic Approximation
nodes.html: Robbins and Monro (1951) found roots of functions from noisy measurements by taking steps that shrink at a suitable rate. Stochastic gradient descent, the method that trains neural networks, is a descendant.
nodes.summary: Robbins and Monro (1951) found roots of functions from noisy measurements by taking steps that shrink at a suitable rate.

nodes.title: Calderón–Zygmund Theory
nodes.html: Calderón and Zygmund (1952) proved boundedness of a broad class of singular integral operators, such as higher-dimensional analogues of the Hilbert transform, using a decomposition of functions across scales. The method is a cornerstone of harmonic analysis and elliptic PDE.
nodes.summary: Calderón and Zygmund (1952) proved boundedness of a broad class of singular integral operators, such as higher-dimensional analogues of the Hilbert transform, using a decomposition of functions across scales.

nodes.title: Dynamic Programming
nodes.html: Bellman’s principle of optimality (1953 papers, book 1957) solves multistage decision problems by working backward through a value function. It is the basis of optimal control, sequence alignment and reinforcement learning.
nodes.summary: Bellman’s principle of optimality (1953 papers, book 1957) solves multistage decision problems by working backward through a value function.

nodes.title: Markov Chain Monte Carlo
nodes.html: Metropolis, the Rosenbluths and the Tellers (1953) sampled from complicated distributions by running a Markov chain, and Hastings generalized the method (1970). It is the engine of Bayesian computation and statistical physics.
nodes.summary: Metropolis, the Rosenbluths and the Tellers (1953) sampled from complicated distributions by running a Markov chain, and Hastings generalized the method (1970).

nodes.title: Irrationality Measure of π

progress.what: First effective bound: the irrationality measure of π is at most 42.
progress.html: First effective bound: the irrationality measure of π is at most 42.

progress.what: Lowered the bound to about 7.103.
progress.html: Lowered the bound to about 7.103.

progress.what: Claimed proof that the irrationality measure of π is exactly 2, which also gives convergence of the Flint Hills series ∑ 1/(n³ sin² n) (family 017 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that the irrationality measure of π is exactly 2, which also gives convergence of the Flint Hills series ∑ 1/(n³ sin² n) (family 017 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: The irrationality measure of π says how closely fractions p/q can approach π. Almost every real number has measure 2, and π was expected to as well, but the proven bounds only went from 42 (Kurt Mahler, 1953) down to about 7.10. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims the value 2, which would also make the Flint Hills series converge; it is formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: The irrationality measure of π says how closely fractions p/q can approach π.

nodes.title: Sums of Three Cubes

progress.what: Found a representation of 74.
progress.html: Found a representation of 74.

progress.what: Settled 33 with a search whose running time depends on the smallest of the three cubes.
progress.html: Settled 33 with a search whose running time depends on the smallest of the three cubes.

progress.what: Settled 42 with about 1.3 million hours on the Charity Engine volunteer grid, and found a third representation of 3, answering Mordell’s 1953 question.
progress.html: Settled 42 with about 1.3 million hours on the Charity Engine volunteer grid, and found a third representation of 3, answering Mordell’s 1953 question.

nodes.html: Which integers are sums of three cubes of integers, positive or negative? Numbers congruent to ±4 mod 9 never are, and Heath-Brown conjectured (1992) that all others are, in infinitely many ways. After 33 and 42 fell to large computer searches in 2019, the unsolved cases below 1000 are 114, 390, 627, 633, 732, 921 and 975.
nodes.summary: Which integers are sums of three cubes of integers, positive or negative?

nodes.title: KAM Theorem
nodes.html: Most quasi-periodic motions of an integrable system survive a small perturbation: Kolmogorov announced the theorem in 1954, and Moser (1962) and Arnold (1963) proved it in full. It bears on the stability of planetary systems.
nodes.summary: Most quasi-periodic motions of an integrable system survive a small perturbation: Kolmogorov announced the theorem in 1954, and Moser (1962) and Arnold (1963) proved it in full.

nodes.title: Model Theory
nodes.html: The study of mathematical structures as models of formal theories. Löwenheim and Skolem (1915 to 1920), Gödel’s compactness theorem (1930) and Maltsev’s applications to algebra (1936) preceded Tarski’s naming of the subject in 1954.
nodes.summary: The study of mathematical structures as models of formal theories.

nodes.title: Tutte’s 5-Flow Conjecture

progress.what: Every bridgeless graph has a nowhere-zero 8-flow.
progress.html: Every bridgeless graph has a nowhere-zero 8-flow.

progress.what: Every bridgeless graph has a nowhere-zero 6-flow.
progress.html: Every bridgeless graph has a nowhere-zero 6-flow.

nodes.html: A nowhere-zero k-flow orients every edge of a graph and gives it a value from 1 to k − 1 so that inflow equals outflow at each vertex. Tutte conjectured in 1954 that every bridgeless graph has a nowhere-zero 5-flow; for planar graphs this is the dual of the five colour theorem. The Petersen graph shows that 5 would be best possible, and Seymour proved that 6 suffices (1981).
nodes.summary: A nowhere-zero k-flow orients every edge of a graph and gives it a value from 1 to k − 1 so that inflow equals outflow at each vertex.

nodes.title: Kadison Similarity Problem

progress.what: Solved the problem for homomorphisms with a cyclic vector.
progress.html: Solved the problem for homomorphisms with a cyclic vector.

progress.what: Showed the similarity problem is equivalent to the derivation problem for C*-algebras.
progress.html: Showed the similarity problem is equivalent to the derivation problem for C*-algebras.

progress.what: Claimed proof that every bounded unital homomorphism from a C*-algebra into the bounded operators on a Hilbert space is similar to a *-homomorphism (family 288 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that every bounded unital homomorphism from a C*-algebra into the bounded operators on a Hilbert space is similar to a *-homomorphism (family 288 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Richard Kadison asked in 1955 whether every bounded homomorphism from a C-algebra into the operators on a Hilbert space is similar to a -homomorphism. It is a central problem of operator algebras, solved for cyclic representations by Uffe Haagerup in 1983 and shown equivalent to the derivation problem. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a proof, formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: Richard Kadison asked in 1955 whether every bounded homomorphism from a C-algebra into the operators on a Hilbert space is similar to a -homomorphism.

nodes.title: Ramsey Number R(5,5)

progress.what: Lower bound 43, by an explicit colouring.
progress.html: Lower bound 43, by an explicit colouring.

progress.what: Upper bound 46, combining linear programming with a large computer search.
progress.html: Upper bound 46, combining linear programming with a large computer search.

nodes.html: The smallest n such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of the complete graph on n vertices contains five vertices joined in a single colour. Known: 43 ≤ R(5,5) ≤ 46.
nodes.summary: The smallest n such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of the complete graph on n vertices contains five vertices joined in a single colour.

nodes.title: Random Matrix Theory
nodes.html: Wigner (1955) modelled the energy levels of heavy nuclei by eigenvalues of large random matrices, and Dyson classified the ensembles (1962). The same eigenvalue statistics appear in number theory (zeros of ζ), quantum chaos and data science.
nodes.summary: Wigner (1955) modelled the energy levels of heavy nuclei by eigenvalues of large random matrices, and Dyson classified the ensembles (1962).

nodes.title: Exotic Spheres
nodes.html: Milnor (1956) found a smooth 7-manifold that is homeomorphic to the 7-sphere yet has a different smooth structure. Kervaire and Milnor later showed that the 7-sphere has exactly 28 smooth structures (1963). The discovery showed that topology and smooth structure can differ.
nodes.summary: Milnor (1956) found a smooth 7-manifold that is homeomorphic to the 7-sphere yet has a different smooth structure.

nodes.title: Finite Element Method
nodes.html: Divide a domain into small elements and approximate the solution of a PDE by simple functions on each. Courant described the idea in 1943, Turner, Clough and colleagues developed it for aircraft structures in 1956, and Zienkiewicz’s textbook (1967) spread it. It is the standard tool of structural and fluid simulation.
nodes.summary: Divide a domain into small elements and approximate the solution of a PDE by simple functions on each.

nodes.title: Homological Algebra
nodes.html: Cartan and Eilenberg’s book (1956) organized homology into a general algebraic machine of derived functors such as Tor and Ext. Its methods run through topology, algebraic geometry and number theory.
nodes.summary: Cartan and Eilenberg’s book (1956) organized homology into a general algebraic machine of derived functors such as Tor and Ext.

nodes.title: Kaplansky’s Zero-Divisor Conjecture

progress.what: The conjecture holds for every torsion-free elementary amenable group.
progress.html: The conjecture holds for every torsion-free elementary amenable group.

progress.what: Refuted the stronger unit conjecture in characteristic 2 with a group from the Hantzsche–Wendt manifold; the zero-divisor conjecture survives.
progress.html: Refuted the stronger unit conjecture in characteristic 2 with a group from the Hantzsche–Wendt manifold; the zero-divisor conjecture survives.

progress.what: Claimed counterexample: a finitely presented torsion-free group whose group algebra over 𝔽₂ has nonzero zero divisors (family 196 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed counterexample: a finitely presented torsion-free group whose group algebra over 𝔽₂ has nonzero zero divisors (family 196 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: If G is a torsion-free group and K a field, can the group ring K[G] have zero divisors? Kaplansky conjectured in 1956 that it cannot. The conjecture holds for large classes of groups, including the elementary amenable ones (1988), while its stronger relative, the unit conjecture, was disproved in 2021 (unit-conjecture). OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a counterexample over 𝔽₂.
nodes.summary: If G is a torsion-free group and K a field, can the group ring K[G] have zero divisors?

nodes.title: Nash Embedding Theorems
nodes.html: Every Riemannian manifold can be embedded isometrically in some Euclidean space. Nash proved the C¹ case (1954; Kuiper extended it in 1955) and the smooth case (1956). The C¹ construction is the origin of convex integration.
nodes.summary: Every Riemannian manifold can be embedded isometrically in some Euclidean space.

nodes.title: Shannon Capacity of the 7-Cycle

progress.what: The theta function proved that the 5-cycle has capacity √5 and bounds the 7-cycle’s capacity above by about 3.3177.
progress.html: The theta function proved that the 5-cycle has capacity √5 and bounds the 7-cycle’s capacity above by about 3.3177.

progress.what: An independent set of 367 words in the fifth strong power of the 7-cycle gives a lower bound of 367^(1/5) > 3.2578.
progress.html: An independent set of 367 words in the fifth strong power of the 7-cycle gives a lower bound of 367^(1/5) > 3.2578.

progress.what: An independent set of size 134,753 in the tenth power, found by working iteratively with a large language model, gives a lower bound above 3.258020.
progress.html: An independent set of size 134,753 in the tenth power, found by working iteratively with a large language model, gives a lower bound above 3.258020.

progress.what: Recursive product constructions built on these sets (Gao), extended by Buys, Polak and Zuiddam with bounds checked in Lean and refined by Tandon, raised the lower bound to about 3.2588.
progress.html: Recursive product constructions built on these sets (Gao), extended by Buys, Polak and Zuiddam with bounds checked in Lean and refined by Tandon, raised the lower bound to about 3.2588.

nodes.html: Shannon (1956) defined the zero-error capacity of a noisy channel, which depends only on the graph recording which symbols can be confused. For the 5-cycle Lovász proved it is √5 (1979), but for the 7-cycle it is unknown: computer constructions in 2026 raised the lower bound to about 3.2588, while the Lovász theta function caps it at 3.3177.
nodes.summary: Shannon (1956) defined the zero-error capacity of a noisy channel, which depends only on the graph recording which symbols can be confused.

nodes.title: De Giorgi–Nash Theorem
nodes.html: Solutions of elliptic and parabolic equations with merely bounded measurable coefficients are Hölder continuous (De Giorgi, 1957; Nash, 1958; Moser’s Harnack inequality, 1960). The theorem solved Hilbert’s nineteenth problem on the regularity of solutions of variational problems.
nodes.summary: Solutions of elliptic and parabolic equations with merely bounded measurable coefficients are Hölder continuous (De Giorgi, 1957; Nash, 1958; Moser’s Harnack inequality, 1960).

nodes.title: Percolation Theory
nodes.html: Broadbent and Hammersley (1957) asked when a randomly porous medium lets fluid through, and found that connectivity appears at a sharp critical probability. Kesten (1980) proved that the critical probability for bond percolation on the square lattice is exactly 1/2.
nodes.summary: Broadbent and Hammersley (1957) asked when a randomly porous medium lets fluid through, and found that connectivity appears at a sharp critical probability.

nodes.title: Graph Reconstruction Conjecture

progress.what: Every tree is determined by its vertex-deleted subgraphs.
progress.html: Every tree is determined by its vertex-deleted subgraphs.

progress.what: Infinite families of tournaments that cannot be reconstructed, so the analogue for directed graphs is false.
progress.html: Infinite families of tournaments that cannot be reconstructed, so the analogue for directed graphs is false.

progress.what: Almost every graph is determined by just three of its vertex-deleted subgraphs.
progress.html: Almost every graph is determined by just three of its vertex-deleted subgraphs.

progress.what: Computer verification for all graphs with at most 13 vertices.
progress.html: Computer verification for all graphs with at most 13 vertices.

nodes.html: Is every graph with at least three vertices determined, up to isomorphism, by the collection of subgraphs obtained by deleting one vertex at a time? Kelly (1957) and Ulam (1960) conjectured yes. It is proved for trees, regular graphs and disconnected graphs and for almost all graphs, and checked by computer for every graph with at most 13 vertices; for directed graphs it fails.
nodes.summary: Is every graph with at least three vertices determined, up to isomorphism, by the collection of subgraphs obtained by deleting one vertex at a time?

nodes.title: K-Theory & Bott Periodicity
nodes.html: Grothendieck’s K-group of vector bundles (1957), Bott’s periodicity theorem (1957 to 1959) and Atiyah and Hirzebruch’s topological K-theory (1959) turned vector bundles into algebra. K-theory became a tool in topology, operator algebras and number theory.
nodes.summary: Grothendieck’s K-group of vector bundles (1957), Bott’s periodicity theorem (1957 to 1959) and Atiyah and Hirzebruch’s topological K-theory (1959) turned vector bundles into algebra.

nodes.title: Nagata’s Conjecture on Curves

progress.what: Proved the case where the number of points is a perfect square at least 16, and used it in his counterexample to Hilbert’s fourteenth problem.
progress.html: Proved the case where the number of points is a perfect square at least 16, and used it in his counterexample to Hilbert’s fourteenth problem.

progress.what: Claimed proof of Nagata’s strict inequality for every r ≥ 10 and arbitrary multiplicities, together with maximal multipoint Seshadri constants on any polarized variety for enough points (family 039 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof of Nagata’s strict inequality for every r ≥ 10 and arbitrary multiplicities, together with maximal multipoint Seshadri constants on any polarized variety for enough points (family 039 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Masayoshi Nagata conjectured in 1959 that a plane curve of degree d through r ≥ 10 very general points with multiplicities m₁, …, mᵣ satisfies m₁ + … + mᵣ < d√r. He proved it for square r and used that case to answer Hilbert’s fourteenth problem, and it governs Seshadri constants. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a proof, formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: Masayoshi Nagata conjectured in 1959 that a plane curve of degree d through r ≥ 10 very general points with multiplicities m₁, …, mᵣ satisfies m₁ + … + mᵣ < d√r.

nodes.title: Random Graphs
nodes.html: Erdős and Rényi (1959 to 1960) studied graphs whose edges appear independently at random and found sharp thresholds, such as the sudden appearance of a giant connected component. The model is the starting point of probabilistic combinatorics and network science.
nodes.summary: Erdős and Rényi (1959 to 1960) studied graphs whose edges appear independently at random and found sharp thresholds, such as the sudden appearance of a giant connected component.

nodes.title: Scheme Theory
nodes.html: From 1960 Grothendieck rebuilt algebraic geometry on schemes, unifying it with number theory. It is the framework behind Deligne’s proof of the Weil conjectures (1974) and Wiles’s proof of Fermat.
nodes.summary: From 1960 Grothendieck rebuilt algebraic geometry on schemes, unifying it with number theory.

nodes.title: Sunflower Conjecture

progress.what: The sunflower lemma: more than k!(r − 1)ᵏ sets of size k always contain a sunflower with r sets.
progress.html: The sunflower lemma: more than k!(r − 1)ᵏ sets of size k always contain a sunflower with r sets.

progress.what: Cut the bound to roughly (log k)ᵏ for each fixed r, by proving a statement about robust sunflowers.
progress.html: Cut the bound to roughly (log k)ᵏ for each fixed r, by proving a statement about robust sunflowers.

progress.what: A simpler proof with the bound (O(r log(rk)))ᵏ.
progress.html: A simpler proof with the bound (O(r log(rk)))ᵏ.

progress.what: Improved the bound to (O(r log k))ᵏ, the best known.
progress.html: Improved the bound to (O(r log k))ᵏ, the best known.

nodes.html: A sunflower is a collection of sets whose pairwise intersections are all the same. Erdős and Rado (1960) conjectured that for each r there is a constant C such that any family of more than Cᵏ sets of size k contains a sunflower of r sets. It is open even for r = 3; the best bound, of order (r log k)ᵏ, comes from a 2019 breakthrough and its refinements.
nodes.summary: A sunflower is a collection of sets whose pairwise intersections are all the same.

nodes.title: Erdős–Ko–Rado Theorem
nodes.html: If every two sets in a family of k-element subsets of an n-element set intersect and n ≥ 2k, the family has at most C(n−1, k−1) members (proved in 1938, published 1961). With Sperner’s theorem (1928) it founded extremal set theory.
nodes.summary: If every two sets in a family of k-element subsets of an n-element set intersect and n ≥ 2k, the family has at most C(n−1, k−1) members (proved in 1938, published 1961).

nodes.title: Poincaré Conjecture in High Dimensions
nodes.html: Smale proved the Poincaré conjecture for spheres of dimension 5 and higher (1961) through the h-cobordism theorem, and Stallings and Zeeman gave other proofs. The higher-dimensional case was thus settled decades before the 4-dimensional (Freedman, 1982) and 3-dimensional (Perelman, 2003) cases.
nodes.summary: Smale proved the Poincaré conjecture for spheres of dimension 5 and higher (1961) through the h-cobordism theorem, and Stallings and Zeeman gave other proofs.

nodes.title: Atiyah–Singer Index Theorem
nodes.html: The index of an elliptic differential operator, the number of solutions minus the number of constraints, equals a topological quantity computed from the manifold (1963). The theorem unified Riemann–Roch and Gauss–Bonnet and became central to geometry and mathematical physics.
nodes.summary: The index of an elliptic differential operator, the number of solutions minus the number of constraints, equals a topological quantity computed from the manifold (1963).

nodes.title: Continuum Hypothesis Independence
nodes.html: Cantor conjectured in 1878 that no set is larger than the integers and smaller than the real numbers. Gödel showed in 1940 that the continuum hypothesis cannot be disproved from the ZFC axioms, and Cohen showed in 1963, with his method of forcing, that it cannot be proved. It was the first of Hilbert’s problems of 1900.
nodes.summary: Cantor conjectured in 1878 that no set is larger than the integers and smaller than the real numbers.

nodes.title: Deterministic Chaos
nodes.html: Lorenz’s simplified model of atmospheric convection (1963) showed that deterministic equations can be unpredictable because tiny differences in the starting state grow exponentially, the ‘butterfly effect’; its trajectories settle on a strange attractor. It set a limit on long-range weather forecasting.
nodes.summary: Lorenz’s simplified model of atmospheric convection (1963) showed that deterministic equations can be unpredictable because tiny differences in the starting state grow exponentially, the ‘butterfly effect’; its trajectories settle on a strange attractor.

nodes.title: Feit–Thompson Theorem
aliases: Burnside's conjecture on odd order groups
nodes.html: Every finite group of odd order is solvable (Feit and Thompson, 1963; 255 pages), as Burnside conjectured in 1911. It opened the classification of finite simple groups. Gonthier’s team machine-checked the proof in Coq in 2012.
nodes.summary: Every finite group of odd order is solvable (Feit and Thompson, 1963; 255 pages), as Burnside conjectured in 1911.

nodes.title: Golod–Shafarevich Theorem
nodes.html: Golod and Shafarevich (1964) proved an inequality that yields infinite class field towers, and, with Golod’s construction, infinite finitely generated torsion groups, answering the general Burnside problem. The same criterion supplied the number fields in the 2026 disproof of Erdős’s unit distance conjecture.
nodes.summary: Golod and Shafarevich (1964) proved an inequality that yields infinite class field towers, and, with Golod’s construction, infinite finitely generated torsion groups, answering the general Burnside problem.

nodes.title: Graceful Tree Conjecture

progress.what: Introduced graceful labellings (as β-valuations), showed that paths and caterpillars have them, and showed that a graceful tree with n edges tiles the complete graph on 2n + 1 vertices.
progress.html: Introduced graceful labellings (as β-valuations), showed that paths and caterpillars have them, and showed that a graceful tree with n edges tiles the complete graph on 2n + 1 vertices.

progress.what: Every tree with at most 27 vertices is graceful.
progress.html: Every tree with at most 27 vertices is graceful.

progress.what: Almost all trees are almost graceful: labels from 1 to (1 + ε)n suffice for trees whose maximum degree is O(n/log n).
progress.html: Almost all trees are almost graceful: labels from 1 to (1 + ε)n suffice for trees whose maximum degree is O(n/log n).

progress.what: Proved Ringel’s 1963 conjecture for large n: copies of any tree with n edges tile the complete graph on 2n + 1 vertices.
progress.html: Proved Ringel’s 1963 conjecture for large n: copies of any tree with n edges tile the complete graph on 2n + 1 vertices.

nodes.html: Can the vertices of every tree with n edges be labelled with distinct numbers from 0 to n so that the n edge differences are exactly 1, 2, …, n? The Ringel–Kotzig conjecture (1964) says yes. It is known for paths, caterpillars and other families and checked by computer for small trees; it would imply Ringel’s decomposition conjecture, proved for large trees in 2020.
nodes.summary: Can the vertices of every tree with n edges be labelled with distinct numbers from 0 to n so that the n edge differences are exactly 1, 2, …, n?

nodes.title: Andrews–Curtis Conjecture

progress.what: Gave balanced presentations of the trivial group, coming from a potential exotic 4-sphere, as potential counterexamples.
progress.html: Gave balanced presentations of the trivial group, coming from a potential exotic 4-sphere, as potential counterexamples.

progress.what: Some balanced presentations of the trivial group need enormous numbers of Andrews–Curtis moves to trivialize, so failed searches are weak evidence.
progress.html: Some balanced presentations of the trivial group need enormous numbers of Andrews–Curtis moves to trivialize, so failed searches are weak evidence.

progress.what: Resolved potential counterexamples in the Miller–Schupp series, including three infinite subfamilies, and showed that AK(3) is stably trivial, combining search with reinforcement learning.
progress.html: Resolved potential counterexamples in the Miller–Schupp series, including three infinite subfamilies, and showed that AK(3) is stably trivial, combining search with reinforcement learning.

nodes.html: Andrews and Curtis conjectured in 1965 that every balanced presentation of the trivial group, with as many relators as generators, can be reduced to the trivial presentation by Nielsen moves and conjugations. The conjecture is tied to questions in 4-dimensional topology and is widely believed to be false. The shortest potential counterexample is the Akbulut–Kirby presentation AK(3), which no computer search has trivialized.
nodes.summary: Andrews and Curtis conjectured in 1965 that every balanced presentation of the trivial group, with as many relators as generators, can be reduced to the trivial presentation by Nielsen moves and conjugations.

nodes.title: Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture

progress.what: Claimed proof of the full Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer leading-term formula for every elliptic curve over ℚ of low Selmer corank (family 002 of OpenAI’s math release). Not formalized and not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof of the full Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer leading-term formula for every elliptic curve over ℚ of low Selmer corank (family 002 of OpenAI’s math release). Not formalized and not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: The rank of an elliptic curve equals the order of vanishing of its L-function at s = 1. It came out of computer experiments on Cambridge’s EDSAC 2. A Clay Millennium Prize problem.
nodes.summary: The rank of an elliptic curve equals the order of vanishing of its L-function at s = 1.

nodes.title: Fast Fourier Transform
nodes.html: Cooley and Tukey (1965) computed the discrete Fourier transform of n points in about n log n operations, against n² for the direct method, an idea Gauss had used around 1805. It underlies digital signal processing, image and audio compression and fast multiplication of large numbers.
nodes.summary: Cooley and Tukey (1965) computed the discrete Fourier transform of n points in about n log n operations, against n² for the direct method, an idea Gauss had used around 1805.

nodes.title: Leech Lattice
nodes.html: A lattice in 24 dimensions in which each sphere touches 196,560 others, found by Leech in 1965 (published 1967). Its symmetry group led Conway in 1968 to three new sporadic simple groups, and the lattice gives the densest sphere packing in 24 dimensions (proved in 2016).
nodes.summary: A lattice in 24 dimensions in which each sphere touches 196,560 others, found by Leech in 1965 (published 1967).

nodes.title: Aperiodic Tilings
nodes.html: Wang asked in 1961 whether tilings by square tiles can be decided algorithmically. Berger (1966) proved they cannot, using a set of 20,426 tiles that tile the plane only aperiodically. Penrose found aperiodic sets of just two shapes in the 1970s, and quasicrystals were discovered in 1982.
nodes.summary: Wang asked in 1961 whether tilings by square tiles can be decided algorithmically.

nodes.title: Carleson’s Theorem
aliases: almost everywhere convergence of Fourier series
nodes.html: The Fourier series of every square-integrable function converges almost everywhere (Carleson, 1966), settling a question that Luzin raised in 1915. Hunt extended the result to L^p for p > 1 (1968).
nodes.summary: The Fourier series of every square-integrable function converges almost everywhere (Carleson, 1966), settling a question that Luzin raised in 1915.

nodes.title: Moving Sofa Problem

progress.what: Posted a long proof that Gerver’s sofa is optimal and submitted it to the Annals of Mathematics. As of mid-2026 it was still in peer review, though widely expected to hold.
progress.html: Posted a long proof that Gerver’s sofa is optimal and submitted it to the Annals of Mathematics. As of mid-2026 it was still in peer review, though widely expected to hold.

nodes.html: What is the largest shape that can be carried around a right-angled corner in a hallway of width 1? Gerver’s 1992 sofa, with area about 2.2195, was conjectured to be optimal.
nodes.summary: What is the largest shape that can be carried around a right-angled corner in a hallway of width 1?

nodes.title: Solitons & Inverse Scattering
nodes.html: Zabusky and Kruskal’s computer experiments (1965) found solitary waves that pass through each other unchanged and named them solitons. Gardner, Greene, Kruskal and Miura (1967) solved the Korteweg–de Vries equation exactly by the inverse scattering transform.
nodes.summary: Zabusky and Kruskal’s computer experiments (1965) found solitary waves that pass through each other unchanged and named them solitons.

nodes.title: Langlands Program
nodes.html: In a 1967 letter to André Weil, Langlands proposed a web of conjectures linking Galois representations with automorphic forms. Much of modern number theory works toward it, and the modularity of elliptic curves used in the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem is a special case.
nodes.summary: In a 1967 letter to André Weil, Langlands proposed a web of conjectures linking Galois representations with automorphic forms.

nodes.title: Lonely Runner Conjecture

progress.what: Proved the case of seven runners.
progress.html: Proved the case of seven runners.

progress.what: Eight runners, by a computer verification combined with recent bounds on the size of a minimal counterexample.
progress.html: Eight runners, by a computer verification combined with recent bounds on the size of a minimal counterexample.

progress.what: Nine and ten runners, refining Rosenfeld’s method with a sieve. Rosenfeld settled nine independently.
progress.html: Nine and ten runners, refining Rosenfeld’s method with a sieve. Rosenfeld settled nine independently.

progress.what: Eleven, twelve and thirteen runners, with new sieving techniques and a polynomial-method argument for special speed patterns.
progress.html: Eleven, twelve and thirteen runners, with new sieving techniques and a polynomial-method argument for special speed patterns.

nodes.html: Runners with distinct constant speeds circle a track of length 1. The conjecture, posed by Jörg Wills in 1967 and independently by Thomas Cusick, says that with n runners each one is at some moment at distance at least 1/n from all the others. Computer-assisted proofs in 2025–2026 extended the known cases from 7 runners to 13.
nodes.summary: Runners with distinct constant speeds circle a track of length 1.

nodes.title: Proof Assistants
nodes.html: Programs that check every step of a proof: de Bruijn’s Automath (1967), then Mizar, HOL, Coq and Isabelle. A proof becomes code that a small trusted kernel verifies.
nodes.summary: Programs that check every step of a proof: de Bruijn’s Automath (1967), then Mizar, HOL, Coq and Isabelle.

nodes.title: Rigidity of the Turing Degrees

progress.what: Claimed proof that every automorphism of the Turing degrees is the identity (family 241 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that every automorphism of the Turing degrees is the identity (family 241 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: The Turing degrees order sets of natural numbers by relative computability. Hartley Rogers asked in 1967 whether this order has any symmetry other than the identity, and Theodore Slaman and Hugh Woodin showed that rigidity is equivalent to their bi-interpretability conjecture. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims every automorphism is the identity, formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: The Turing degrees order sets of natural numbers by relative computability.

nodes.title: Barnette’s Conjecture

progress.what: Proved the case where every face has four or six edges.
progress.html: Proved the case where every face has four or six edges.

progress.what: A computer search found no counterexample with up to 64 vertices.
progress.html: A computer search found no counterexample with up to 64 vertices.

progress.what: Claimed proof that every cubic, bipartite, 3-connected planar graph has a Hamiltonian cycle (family 180 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that every cubic, bipartite, 3-connected planar graph has a Hamiltonian cycle (family 180 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: David Barnette conjectured in 1969 that every cubic, bipartite, 3-connected planar graph has a Hamiltonian cycle, a cycle through every vertex. Without bipartiteness this fails, as Tutte showed in 1946, and computer searches found no counterexample with fewer than 86 vertices. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a proof, formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: David Barnette conjectured in 1969 that every cubic, bipartite, 3-connected planar graph has a Hamiltonian cycle, a cycle through every vertex.

nodes.title: Černý Conjecture

progress.what: Every synchronizing automaton with n states has a reset word of length at most (n³ − n)/6. The bound stood for about 35 years.
progress.html: Every synchronizing automaton with n states has a reset word of length at most (n³ − n)/6. The bound stood for about 35 years.

progress.what: The first improvement of the leading constant, to about 0.1664 n³.
progress.html: The first improvement of the leading constant, to about 0.1664 n³.

progress.what: About 0.1654 n³, the best general bound.
progress.html: About 0.1654 n³, the best general bound.

nodes.html: An automaton is synchronizing if some input word, a reset word, sends every state to the same state. Černý found n-state automata whose shortest reset word has length (n − 1)² (1964) and conjectured in 1969 that no synchronizing automaton needs more. The best general bound is about 0.1654 n³ (Shitov, 2019); the conjecture is known for special classes, such as automata whose transitions preserve a cyclic order (Eppstein).
nodes.summary: An automaton is synchronizing if some input word, a reset word, sends every state to the same state.

nodes.title: Curry–Howard Correspondence
nodes.html: Propositions correspond to types and proofs to programs. Curry noticed the correspondence for combinatory logic (1934) and Howard for natural deduction (circulated 1969, published 1980). The principle underlies proof assistants such as Coq, Agda and Lean.
nodes.summary: Propositions correspond to types and proofs to programs.

nodes.title: Hilbert’s Tenth Problem
nodes.html: No algorithm can decide whether a polynomial equation with integer coefficients has an integer solution, so Hilbert’s tenth problem (1900) has a negative answer. Davis, Putnam and Julia Robinson reduced it in 1961, and Matiyasevich completed the proof in 1970 using Fibonacci numbers.
nodes.summary: No algorithm can decide whether a polynomial equation with integer coefficients has an integer solution, so Hilbert’s tenth problem (1900) has a negative answer.

nodes.title: Martin-Löf Type Theory
nodes.html: Martin-Löf’s intuitionistic type theory (1972, revised 1975 and 1984) is a constructive foundation for mathematics built on dependent types, in which proofs are programs. It is an ancestor of the type theories of Agda, Coq and Lean.
nodes.summary: Martin-Löf’s intuitionistic type theory (1972, revised 1975 and 1984) is a constructive foundation for mathematics built on dependent types, in which proofs are programs.

nodes.title: Expander Graphs
nodes.html: Sparse graphs that are nonetheless highly connected. Pinsker (1973) proved by counting that they exist, Margulis (1973) gave the first explicit construction, and Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak and Margulis built optimal ‘Ramanujan graphs’ (1988). They are used in error-correcting codes, derandomization and network design.
nodes.summary: Sparse graphs that are nonetheless highly connected.

nodes.title: Montgomery’s Pair Correlation
nodes.html: Montgomery found in 1973 that spacings between zeros of the Riemann zeta function follow the pair-correlation law of eigenvalues of random Hermitian matrices, a link Dyson recognized in conversation at Princeton. Odlyzko’s computations (1987) supported it.
nodes.summary: Montgomery found in 1973 that spacings between zeros of the Riemann zeta function follow the pair-correlation law of eigenvalues of random Hermitian matrices, a link Dyson recognized in conversation at Princeton.

nodes.title: Causal Inference
nodes.html: Methods to infer cause from data. Rubin’s potential-outcomes framework (1974, after Neyman 1923) and Pearl’s causal graphs and do-calculus (1995 to 2000) underlie modern epidemiology, economics and machine learning.
nodes.summary: Methods to infer cause from data.

nodes.title: Planar Hot Spots Conjecture

progress.what: Found a planar domain with holes where the conjecture fails.
progress.html: Found a planar domain with holes where the conjecture fails.

progress.what: Proved it for every triangle.
progress.html: Proved it for every triangle.

progress.what: Claimed proof of a strict form for every smooth bounded simply connected planar domain: the first nonconstant Neumann eigenfunction has no interior critical point (family 369 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof of a strict form for every smooth bounded simply connected planar domain: the first nonconstant Neumann eigenfunction has no interior critical point (family 369 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Jeffrey Rauch conjectured in 1974 that the hottest and coldest points of an insulated plate eventually lie on its boundary, a claim about the first nonconstant Neumann eigenfunction. It fails for some domains with holes, and Krzysztof Burdzy conjectured it for simply connected planar domains. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims that case for smooth domains, formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: Jeffrey Rauch conjectured in 1974 that the hottest and coldest points of an insulated plate eventually lie on its boundary, a claim about the first nonconstant Neumann eigenfunction.

nodes.title: Weil Conjectures
nodes.html: Weil (1949) conjectured that counting points on varieties over finite fields obeys a Riemann hypothesis. Dwork proved rationality (1960), Grothendieck and his school built étale cohomology to attack the rest, and Deligne proved the Riemann hypothesis part (1974).
nodes.summary: Weil (1949) conjectured that counting points on varieties over finite fields obeys a Riemann hypothesis.

nodes.title: Additive Combinatorics
nodes.html: Structure versus randomness in sets of numbers: Szemerédi’s theorem (1975), arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions in the primes (Green and Tao, 2004), and the cap set bound (Ellenberg and Gijswijt, 2016).
nodes.summary: Structure versus randomness in sets of numbers: Szemerédi’s theorem (1975), arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions in the primes (Green and Tao, 2004), and the cap set bound (Ellenberg and Gijswijt, 2016).

nodes.title: Fractal Geometry
nodes.html: Mandelbrot coined ‘fractal’ in 1975 and argued that coastlines, clouds and market prices share a self-similar roughness measured by a fractional dimension. His book The Fractal Geometry of Nature appeared in 1982.
nodes.summary: Mandelbrot coined ‘fractal’ in 1975 and argued that coastlines, clouds and market prices share a self-similar roughness measured by a fractional dimension.

nodes.title: Erdős Conjecture on Arithmetic Progressions

progress.what: The primes, whose reciprocals diverge, contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.
progress.html: The primes, whose reciprocals diverge, contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.

progress.what: The first nontrivial case: every set with divergent reciprocal sum contains a 3-term progression.
progress.html: The first nontrivial case: every set with divergent reciprocal sum contains a 3-term progression.

progress.what: Much stronger bounds for sets without 3-term progressions.
progress.html: Much stronger bounds for sets without 3-term progressions.

progress.what: Claimed proof of the full conjecture, with quasipolynomial bounds for Szemerédi’s theorem (family 159 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof of the full conjecture, with quasipolynomial bounds for Szemerédi’s theorem (family 159 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: If the reciprocals of a set of positive integers have a divergent sum, must the set contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions? Erdős offered $3,000 for it in 1976, later $5,000. The primes are the Green–Tao case (2004) and the 3-term case was settled in 2020; in October 2026 OpenAI claimed a full proof, formalized in Lean but not yet reviewed.
nodes.summary: If the reciprocals of a set of positive integers have a divergent sum, must the set contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions?

nodes.title: Four Color Theorem
nodes.html: Every map can be coloured with four colours so that neighbouring regions differ. It was the first major theorem whose proof needed a computer (1976); Gonthier’s formal proof in Coq (2005) settled the remaining doubts.
nodes.summary: Every map can be coloured with four colours so that neighbouring regions differ.

nodes.title: EM Algorithm
nodes.html: A general method for maximum-likelihood estimation with missing or hidden variables that alternates an expectation step and a maximization step (Dempster, Laird and Rubin, 1977). It is used in clustering, genetics, speech recognition and many machine-learning models.
nodes.summary: A general method for maximum-likelihood estimation with missing or hidden variables that alternates an expectation step and a maximization step (Dempster, Laird and Rubin, 1977).

nodes.title: Apéry’s Theorem
nodes.html: ζ(3) = 1 + 1/8 + 1/27 + … is irrational. Apéry announced the proof in 1978 with an unmotivated recurrence for rational approximations, and van der Poorten explained it in ‘A proof that Euler missed’ (1979). Rivoal (2000) showed that infinitely many odd zeta values are irrational.
nodes.summary: ζ(3) = 1 + 1/8 + 1/27 + … is irrational.

nodes.title: Calabi–Yau Manifolds
nodes.html: Yau proved in 1977 to 1978 Calabi’s 1954 conjecture: every compact Kähler manifold with vanishing first Chern class carries a Ricci-flat metric. Calabi–Yau manifolds provide the extra dimensions of string theory, and Yau received the Fields Medal in 1982.
nodes.summary: Yau proved in 1977 to 1978 Calabi’s 1954 conjecture: every compact Kähler manifold with vanishing first Chern class carries a Ricci-flat metric.

nodes.title: De Giorgi’s Conjecture

progress.what: Proved the conjecture in dimension 3, after Ghoussoub and Gui did dimension 2 in 1998.
progress.html: Proved the conjecture in dimension 3, after Ghoussoub and Gui did dimension 2 in 1998.

progress.what: Proved it in dimensions up to 8 under an extra limit condition; del Pino, Kowalczyk and Wei showed in 2011 that it fails from dimension 9.
progress.html: Proved it in dimensions up to 8 under an extra limit condition; del Pino, Kowalczyk and Wei showed in 2011 that it fails from dimension 9.

progress.what: Claimed proof in dimension 8, which implies all lower dimensions, together with a classification of stable solutions in dimension 7 (family 375 of OpenAI’s math release, not formalized). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof in dimension 8, which implies all lower dimensions, together with a classification of stable solutions in dimension 7 (family 375 of OpenAI’s math release, not formalized). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Ennio De Giorgi conjectured in 1978 that bounded solutions of the Allen–Cahn equation Δu = u³ − u that increase in one direction are one-dimensional in dimensions up to 8, an analogue of the Bernstein problem for minimal surfaces. It was known in dimensions 2 and 3. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims dimension 8, which covers all lower ones; it is not formalized and not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: Ennio De Giorgi conjectured in 1978 that bounded solutions of the Allen–Cahn equation Δu = u³ − u that increase in one direction are one-dimensional in dimensions up to 8, an analogue of the Bernstein problem for minimal surfaces.

nodes.title: Bootstrap
nodes.html: Efron (1979) estimated the uncertainty of almost any statistic by resampling the data with replacement, replacing formulas with computation. The bootstrap is routine in statistics and machine learning.
