nodes.summary: The Oxford Calculators of Merton College (about 1335) proved that a body accelerating uniformly covers the same distance as one moving at a constant speed equal to the average of its initial and final speeds.

nodes.title: Heliocentrism
nodes.html: Copernicus put the Sun at the centre (De revolutionibus, 1543). Galileo’s telescopic observations from 1610 made the idea hard to deny.
nodes.summary: Copernicus put the Sun at the centre (De revolutionibus, 1543).

nodes.title: Earth Is a Magnet
nodes.html: William Gilbert’s De Magnete (1600) reported experiments on a spherical lodestone, which showed that a compass needle dips toward its poles just as it does toward the Earth’s. He concluded that Earth itself is a giant magnet and separated magnetic attraction from the static electricity of rubbed amber. The book is an early model of experimental method.
nodes.summary: William Gilbert’s De Magnete (1600) reported experiments on a spherical lodestone, which showed that a compass needle dips toward its poles just as it does toward the Earth’s.

nodes.title: Kepler’s Laws
nodes.html: Elliptical orbits, equal areas in equal times, and the period–distance law (1609–1619), extracted from Tycho Brahe’s naked-eye observations.
nodes.summary: Elliptical orbits, equal areas in equal times, and the period–distance law (1609–1619), extracted from Tycho Brahe’s naked-eye observations.

nodes.title: Galileo’s Telescopic Discoveries
nodes.html: Galileo’s Sidereus Nuncius (1610) reported mountains on the Moon, four moons orbiting Jupiter and many stars too faint to see with the naked eye; the phases of Venus followed later that year. These observations contradicted the Ptolemaic picture of perfect heavens circling Earth and gave strong evidence for the Copernican system.
nodes.summary: Galileo’s Sidereus Nuncius (1610) reported mountains on the Moon, four moons orbiting Jupiter and many stars too faint to see with the naked eye; the phases of Venus followed later that year.

nodes.title: Scientific Method
nodes.html: Experiment, measurement and open publication: Galileo’s inclined planes, Bacon’s Novum Organum (1620), the Royal Society (1660) and the first scientific journals (1665).
nodes.summary: Experiment, measurement and open publication: Galileo’s inclined planes, Bacon’s Novum Organum (1620), the Royal Society (1660) and the first scientific journals (1665).

nodes.title: Law of Falling Bodies
nodes.html: In Two New Sciences (1638) Galileo showed that a body falling from rest covers distances proportional to the square of the elapsed time, and that a projectile follows a parabola, the result of steady horizontal motion combined with uniform downward acceleration. His inclined-plane experiments replaced Aristotle’s account of motion and prepared the ground for Newton’s laws.
nodes.summary: In Two New Sciences (1638) Galileo showed that a body falling from rest covers distances proportional to the square of the elapsed time, and that a projectile follows a parabola, the result of steady horizontal motion combined with uniform downward acceleration.

nodes.title: Atmospheric Pressure & Vacuum
nodes.html: Torricelli’s mercury barometer (1643) showed that air has weight and that a vacuum can exist above a liquid column. In 1648 Pascal’s brother-in-law carried a barometer up the Puy de Dôme and found that the column fell with height, and Otto von Guericke built air pumps in the 1650s. Boyle’s gas law followed in 1662.
nodes.summary: Torricelli’s mercury barometer (1643) showed that air has weight and that a vacuum can exist above a liquid column.

nodes.title: Fermat’s Principle
nodes.html: Fermat stated in 1662 that light travels between two points along the path that takes the least time, and showed that this gives the law of refraction already found by Snell and Descartes. It was an early variational principle in physics and a forerunner of the principle of least action.
nodes.summary: Fermat stated in 1662 that light travels between two points along the path that takes the least time, and showed that this gives the law of refraction already found by Snell and Descartes.

nodes.title: Principles of Stratigraphy
nodes.html: Nicolas Steno’s De solido (1669) set out three rules for reading rock layers: sediments are deposited in order with the oldest at the bottom, they start out horizontal, and they extend sideways until they thin out or meet a barrier. He had also shown that tongue stones are fossil shark teeth. The rules let geologists reconstruct the sequence of past events from rocks.
nodes.summary: Nicolas Steno’s De solido (1669) set out three rules for reading rock layers: sediments are deposited in order with the oldest at the bottom, they start out horizontal, and they extend sideways until they thin out or meet a barrier.

nodes.title: Spectrum of White Light
nodes.html: Newton’s prism experiments (1666, published 1672) showed that white sunlight is a mixture of colours, which a prism separates and a second prism recombines, and that each colour is refracted by its own amount. He concluded that lenses cannot bring all colours to one focus and built a reflecting telescope. His Opticks (1704) gave the full account.
nodes.summary: Newton’s prism experiments (1666, published 1672) showed that white sunlight is a mixture of colours, which a prism separates and a second prism recombines, and that each colour is refracted by its own amount.

nodes.title: Water Cycle
nodes.html: Pierre Perrault published in 1674 several years of rainfall and flow measurements for the upper Seine, showing that the rain falling on the catchment was about six times what the river carried away, so rain alone can feed rivers. Edme Mariotte’s Seine measurements agreed, and Edmond Halley estimated evaporation from the sea (1687). Quantitative hydrology began here.
nodes.summary: Pierre Perrault published in 1674 several years of rainfall and flow measurements for the upper Seine, showing that the rain falling on the catchment was about six times what the river carried away, so rain alone can feed rivers.

nodes.title: Finite Speed of Light
aliases: Rømer's determination of the speed of light
nodes.html: Ole Rømer noticed in 1676 that eclipses of Jupiter’s moon Io came later than predicted when Jupiter was farther from Earth, and concluded that light takes time to cross space. The delay implies a speed of roughly 220,000 km/s, about a quarter below the true value. Fizeau (1849) and Foucault (1862) later measured the speed on Earth.
nodes.summary: Ole Rømer noticed in 1676 that eclipses of Jupiter’s moon Io came later than predicted when Jupiter was farther from Earth, and concluded that light takes time to cross space.

nodes.title: Hooke’s Law
nodes.html: Robert Hooke published in 1678 the law that the extension of a spring is proportional to the force applied, in the Latin phrase ut tensio, sic vis. The linear relation holds for small deformations of most solids and became the starting point of the theory of elasticity and of the harmonic oscillator.
nodes.summary: Robert Hooke published in 1678 the law that the extension of a spring is proportional to the force applied, in the Latin phrase ut tensio, sic vis.

nodes.title: Newtonian Mechanics

quote.text: If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of Giants.
quote.by: Isaac Newton, letter to Robert Hooke, 1675

nodes.html: Three laws of motion and universal gravitation (Principia, 1687): the same law for a falling apple and the orbiting Moon.
nodes.summary: Three laws of motion and universal gravitation (Principia, 1687): the same law for a falling apple and the orbiting Moon.

nodes.title: Wave Theory of Light
nodes.html: Christiaan Huygens, in a treatise written in 1678 and published in 1690, proposed that light is a pulse travelling through an ether and that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets. The construction explained reflection, refraction and the double refraction of Iceland spar. Young and Fresnel revived the wave theory in the early 1800s.
nodes.summary: Christiaan Huygens, in a treatise written in 1678 and published in 1690, proposed that light is a pulse travelling through an ether and that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets.

nodes.title: Trade Winds & Hadley Circulation
nodes.html: Edmond Halley mapped the trade winds in 1686 and attributed them to the Sun heating the tropics. George Hadley (1735) argued that air moving toward the equator is deflected westward by Earth’s rotation, which gives the easterly trades, in one circulation cell in each hemisphere. William Ferrel’s three-cell picture (1856) later gave the tropical cell ending near 30 degrees.
nodes.summary: Edmond Halley mapped the trade winds in 1686 and attributed them to the Sun heating the tropics.

nodes.title: Return of Halley’s Comet
nodes.html: Edmond Halley noticed in 1705 that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 had similar orbits and predicted that one comet would return in 1758. After Alexis Clairaut calculated the delay caused by Jupiter and Saturn, it was sighted on Christmas Day 1758. The return confirmed that comets orbit the Sun under Newtonian gravity.
nodes.summary: Edmond Halley noticed in 1705 that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 had similar orbits and predicted that one comet would return in 1758.

nodes.title: Electrostatics
nodes.html: Franklin’s theory of positive and negative charge (1747) and Coulomb’s inverse-square law of electric force (1785).
nodes.summary: Franklin’s theory of positive and negative charge (1747) and Coulomb’s inverse-square law of electric force (1785).

nodes.title: Deep Time
nodes.html: James Hutton’s Theory of the Earth (1788) read the layers, folds and unconformities of rocks in Scotland as the product of slow, repeated cycles of erosion, deposition and uplift with no sign of a beginning. Charles Lyell’s Principles of Geology (1830-33) made this uniformitarian view standard. It gave geology, and later evolutionary biology, the immense timescales they needed.
nodes.summary: James Hutton’s Theory of the Earth (1788) read the layers, folds and unconformities of rocks in Scotland as the product of slow, repeated cycles of erosion, deposition and uplift with no sign of a beginning.

nodes.title: Lagrangian Mechanics
nodes.html: Joseph-Louis Lagrange’s Mécanique analytique (1788) rebuilt Newtonian mechanics on the principle of virtual work and d’Alembert’s principle, with equations of motion written in any convenient coordinates, extending the variational methods of Euler. The method handles constraints easily and became the standard language of theoretical physics, from field theory to general relativity.
nodes.summary: Joseph-Louis Lagrange’s Mécanique analytique (1788) rebuilt Newtonian mechanics on the principle of virtual work and d’Alembert’s principle, with equations of motion written in any convenient coordinates, extending the variational methods of Euler.

nodes.title: Nebular Hypothesis
nodes.html: Immanuel Kant (1755) and Pierre-Simon Laplace (1796) proposed that the Sun and planets formed from a rotating cloud of gas that flattened into a disk as it contracted. This accounts for the planets’ nearly circular, coplanar orbits and common direction of motion. Images of protoplanetary disks around young stars since the 1990s support the picture.
nodes.summary: Immanuel Kant (1755) and Pierre-Simon Laplace (1796) proposed that the Sun and planets formed from a rotating cloud of gas that flattened into a disk as it contracted.

nodes.title: Weighing the Earth
nodes.html: In 1798 Henry Cavendish used a torsion balance designed by John Michell to measure the tiny attraction between lead spheres. He deduced that Earth’s mean density is about 5.4 times that of water, which means a dense interior, and the result is now read as the first measurement of the gravitational constant.
nodes.summary: In 1798 Henry Cavendish used a torsion balance designed by John Michell to measure the tiny attraction between lead spheres.

nodes.title: Laplace’s Celestial Mechanics
nodes.html: Laplace’s Traité de mécanique céleste (five volumes, 1799-1825) used perturbation theory to show that the long-term irregularities in the motions of Jupiter, Saturn and the Moon follow from Newtonian gravity. It gathered the mathematics of the solar system into one work and established the standard methods of celestial mechanics.
nodes.summary: Laplace’s Traité de mécanique céleste (five volumes, 1799-1825) used perturbation theory to show that the long-term irregularities in the motions of Jupiter, Saturn and the Moon follow from Newtonian gravity.

nodes.title: Infrared Radiation
nodes.html: William Herschel passed sunlight through a prism in 1800 and placed thermometers along the spectrum. The one just beyond the red end showed the largest rise in temperature, revealing an invisible form of radiant heat. It was the first discovery of radiation outside the visible range, and Johann Ritter found ultraviolet beyond the violet end in 1801.
nodes.summary: William Herschel passed sunlight through a prism in 1800 and placed thermometers along the spectrum.

nodes.title: Interference of Light
nodes.html: Thomas Young showed in 1801-03 that two beams of light split from one source overlap in bands of bright and dark fringes, as water waves do, and used the fringe spacing to estimate the wavelengths of colours. The two-slit form of the experiment became the standard evidence for the wave nature of light and later for the quantum behaviour of matter.
nodes.summary: Thomas Young showed in 1801-03 that two beams of light split from one source overlap in bands of bright and dark fringes, as water waves do, and used the fringe spacing to estimate the wavelengths of colours.

nodes.title: Meteorites Fall from Space
nodes.html: Ernst Chladni argued in 1794 that stones and iron masses found on the ground had fallen from space. Jean-Baptiste Biot’s report on the thousands of stones that fell at L’Aigle in France in April 1803 convinced the French Academy of Sciences. Accepting that rocks reach Earth from space opened the study of the solar system’s raw material.
nodes.summary: Ernst Chladni argued in 1794 that stones and iron masses found on the ground had fallen from space.

nodes.title: Fresnel’s Wave Optics
nodes.html: Augustin-Jean Fresnel’s 1818 memoir on diffraction gave a wave theory that predicted the patterns of light around obstacles. Poisson objected that it implied a bright spot at the centre of a round shadow, and Arago found it. Fresnel’s proposal in 1821 that light waves are transverse explained polarization, which Étienne-Louis Malus had discovered in 1808.
nodes.summary: Augustin-Jean Fresnel’s 1818 memoir on diffraction gave a wave theory that predicted the patterns of light around obstacles.

nodes.title: Theory of Elasticity
nodes.html: Augustin-Louis Cauchy introduced the stress tensor and the equations of elastic equilibrium in 1822, building on Claude-Louis Navier’s general theory of 1821. Siméon Denis Poisson (1829) showed that elastic solids carry two kinds of waves, which seismologists later identified as P and S waves. The theory underlies structural engineering and continuum mechanics.
nodes.summary: Augustin-Louis Cauchy introduced the stress tensor and the equations of elastic equilibrium in 1822, building on Claude-Louis Navier’s general theory of 1821.

nodes.title: Thermodynamics

quote.text: The law that entropy always increases holds, I think, the supreme position among the laws of Nature.

nodes.html: Carnot’s analysis of heat engines (1824) led to conservation of energy and to entropy (Clausius, 1865): laws that no machine can break.
nodes.summary: Carnot’s analysis of heat engines (1824) led to conservation of energy and to entropy (Clausius, 1865): laws that no machine can break.

nodes.title: Ohm’s Law
nodes.html: In 1827 Georg Ohm showed that the current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage across it and inversely proportional to its resistance. He used a thermocouple as a steady source and measured the current by its magnetic effect on a needle. The law is the basis of circuit analysis and electrical design.
nodes.summary: In 1827 Georg Ohm showed that the current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage across it and inversely proportional to its resistance.

nodes.title: Electromagnetism
nodes.html: Electric currents make magnetic fields (Ørsted, 1820), and changing magnetic fields make currents (Faraday, 1831). Every motor and generator runs on these two facts.
nodes.summary: Electric currents make magnetic fields (Ørsted, 1820), and changing magnetic fields make currents (Faraday, 1831).

nodes.title: Hamiltonian Mechanics
nodes.html: William Rowan Hamilton (1834-35) recast mechanics as first-order equations for positions and momenta, with a single energy function, the Hamiltonian, generating the motion. Carl Jacobi added the Hamilton-Jacobi theory. The phase-space picture became the framework of statistical mechanics, and its Poisson brackets are the classical model for quantum commutators.
nodes.summary: William Rowan Hamilton (1834-35) recast mechanics as first-order equations for positions and momenta, with a single energy function, the Hamiltonian, generating the motion.

nodes.title: Coriolis Effect
nodes.html: Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis showed in 1835 that Newton’s laws in a rotating frame need an extra term that makes a moving body appear to curve sideways. On Earth it steers large-scale winds and ocean currents and sets the spin of cyclones, and Foucault’s pendulum displayed it directly in 1851.
nodes.summary: Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis showed in 1835 that Newton’s laws in a rotating frame need an extra term that makes a moving body appear to curve sideways.

nodes.title: Ice Ages
nodes.html: Louis Agassiz announced in 1837 that boulders, polished rock and moraines across northern Europe were left by ice sheets that once covered the land, and developed the case in Études sur les glaciers (1840). Karl Schimper coined the term Eiszeit, ice age, and Jean de Charpentier had argued for former glaciers in the Alps. It showed that Earth’s climate has changed greatly.
nodes.summary: Louis Agassiz announced in 1837 that boulders, polished rock and moraines across northern Europe were left by ice sheets that once covered the land, and developed the case in Études sur les glaciers (1840).

nodes.title: Stellar Parallax
nodes.html: In 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured the yearly shift of 61 Cygni against more distant stars, about 0.3 arcseconds, which puts it near 10 light-years away. Thomas Henderson (Alpha Centauri) and Friedrich Struve (Vega) had results at about the same time. It was the first generally accepted distance to a star and ended the long search for parallax, the missing proof of Earth’s motion.
nodes.summary: In 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured the yearly shift of 61 Cygni against more distant stars, about 0.3 arcseconds, which puts it near 10 light-years away.

nodes.title: Doppler Effect
nodes.html: Christian Doppler argued in 1842 that the observed frequency of a wave depends on the relative motion of source and observer. Buys Ballot confirmed it for sound in 1845 using trumpeters on a moving train, and Hippolyte Fizeau pointed out the same shift for light in 1848. It underlies radar speed measurement, medical flow imaging and stellar radial velocities.
nodes.summary: Christian Doppler argued in 1842 that the observed frequency of a wave depends on the relative motion of source and observer.

nodes.title: Faraday Rotation
nodes.html: Michael Faraday found in 1845 that a magnetic field along the path of polarized light rotates the plane of polarization as the light passes through glass. It was the first experimental evidence that light and magnetism are related, twenty years before Maxwell showed light to be an electromagnetic wave. The effect is used in optical isolators and magnetic sensing.
nodes.summary: Michael Faraday found in 1845 that a magnetic field along the path of polarized light rotates the plane of polarization as the light passes through glass.

nodes.title: Fluid Dynamics
nodes.html: From Bernoulli’s principle (1738) to the Navier–Stokes equations for viscous flow (1822–1845): the physics of wings, weather and blood.
nodes.summary: From Bernoulli’s principle (1738) to the Navier–Stokes equations for viscous flow (1822–1845): the physics of wings, weather and blood.

nodes.title: Discovery of Neptune
nodes.html: Urbain Le Verrier and John Couch Adams independently calculated, from irregularities in the motion of Uranus, where an unseen planet should be. Johann Galle at the Berlin Observatory found Neptune on 23 September 1846, within about one degree of Le Verrier’s predicted position. It was a major success of Newtonian gravity and of mathematical prediction in astronomy.
nodes.summary: Urbain Le Verrier and John Couch Adams independently calculated, from irregularities in the motion of Uranus, where an unseen planet should be.

nodes.title: Conservation of Energy
nodes.html: In the 1840s Julius Robert Mayer, James Joule and Hermann von Helmholtz established that heat, motion, electricity and chemical change are forms of one conserved quantity, energy. Joule measured the mechanical equivalent of heat in 1843-47, most famously with a paddle wheel, and Helmholtz stated the general law in 1847. It is the first law of thermodynamics and a pillar of physics.
nodes.summary: In the 1840s Julius Robert Mayer, James Joule and Hermann von Helmholtz established that heat, motion, electricity and chemical change are forms of one conserved quantity, energy.

nodes.title: Greenhouse Effect
nodes.html: Joseph Fourier argued in 1824 that the atmosphere keeps Earth warmer than it would be without one. Eunice Foote (1856) found that carbon dioxide and water vapour heat most in sunlight, and John Tyndall (1859) measured how strongly they absorb infrared radiation while oxygen and nitrogen do not. This is the physical basis of climate science and of the warming caused by added CO2.
nodes.summary: Joseph Fourier argued in 1824 that the atmosphere keeps Earth warmer than it would be without one.

nodes.title: Spectral Analysis
nodes.html: Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen showed in 1859 that each element emits and absorbs light at its own set of wavelengths, so spectra identify substances. They explained the dark Fraunhofer lines in sunlight as absorption in the Sun’s atmosphere and discovered caesium and rubidium this way. Spectral analysis revealed what stars are made of and later led to quantum theory.
nodes.summary: Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen showed in 1859 that each element emits and absorbs light at its own set of wavelengths, so spectra identify substances.

nodes.title: Weather Maps & Forecasts
nodes.html: Telegraphed observations made it possible to draw weather maps within hours of measurement. Urbain Le Verrier organized a storm-warning service in France in the 1850s, and in Britain Robert FitzRoy issued storm warnings and the first public forecasts, which appeared in The Times from 1861. Forecasting became a routine government service.
nodes.summary: Telegraphed observations made it possible to draw weather maps within hours of measurement.

nodes.title: Stellar Spectroscopy
nodes.html: William Huggins reported in 1864 that some nebulae have bright emission lines, so they are clouds of glowing gas, and that stars contain familiar elements such as hydrogen, sodium and iron. Angelo Secchi classified stellar spectra into types, and helium was identified in the Sun’s spectrum in 1868, 27 years before it was found on Earth. Astrophysics began here.
nodes.summary: William Huggins reported in 1864 that some nebulae have bright emission lines, so they are clouds of glowing gas, and that stars contain familiar elements such as hydrogen, sodium and iron.

nodes.title: Maxwell’s Equations

quote.text: From a long view of the history of mankind, seen from, say, ten thousand years from now, there can be little doubt that the most significant event of the 19th century will be judged as Maxwell’s discovery of the laws of electrodynamics.

nodes.html: Maxwell’s field equations (1865) predict waves travelling at the speed of light, so light turned out to be electromagnetism. Heaviside later condensed them into the four vector equations taught today (1884).
nodes.summary: Maxwell’s field equations (1865) predict waves travelling at the speed of light, so light turned out to be electromagnetism.

nodes.title: Statistical Mechanics
nodes.html: Heat as the statistics of countless molecules: Maxwell’s velocity distribution (1860), Boltzmann’s S = k log W (1877), Gibbs’s ensembles (1902).
nodes.summary: Heat as the statistics of countless molecules: Maxwell’s velocity distribution (1860), Boltzmann’s S = k log W (1877), Gibbs’s ensembles (1902).

nodes.title: Hall Effect
nodes.html: Edwin Hall found in 1879 that a magnetic field perpendicular to a current-carrying conductor produces a voltage across the conductor, at right angles to both. The sign and size of the voltage reveal whether the charge carriers are positive or negative and how many there are. Hall probes measure magnetic fields in many devices, and a quantum version of the effect was found in 1980.
nodes.summary: Edwin Hall found in 1879 that a magnetic field perpendicular to a current-carrying conductor produces a voltage across the conductor, at right angles to both.

nodes.title: Stefan–Boltzmann Law
nodes.html: Josef Stefan inferred from experimental data in 1879 that the total power radiated by a hot body grows as the fourth power of its absolute temperature, and Ludwig Boltzmann derived the law for an ideal black body from thermodynamics in 1884. It sets the equilibrium temperatures of planets and stars and was an early step toward Planck’s quantum theory.
nodes.summary: Josef Stefan inferred from experimental data in 1879 that the total power radiated by a hot body grows as the fourth power of its absolute temperature, and Ludwig Boltzmann derived the law for an ideal black body from thermodynamics in 1884.

nodes.title: Reynolds Number
nodes.html: In 1883 Osborne Reynolds injected dye into water flowing in a glass pipe and showed that the flow turns turbulent when one dimensionless number, speed times diameter over kinematic viscosity, passes a threshold, near 2,000 with disturbances and up to 13,000 in very quiet water. The number shows when flows of different sizes behave alike, which allows scale-model testing.
nodes.summary: In 1883 Osborne Reynolds injected dye into water flowing in a glass pipe and showed that the flow turns turbulent when one dimensionless number, speed times diameter over kinematic viscosity, passes a threshold, near 2,000 with disturbances and up to 13,000 in very quiet water.

nodes.title: Hertz’s Electromagnetic Waves
nodes.html: Heinrich Hertz generated radio waves with a spark-gap oscillator and detected them across a room in 1886-88. He showed that they travel at the speed of light and can be reflected, refracted and polarized like light. This confirmed Maxwell’s theory of electromagnetism and led directly to radio communication.
nodes.summary: Heinrich Hertz generated radio waves with a spark-gap oscillator and detected them across a room in 1886-88.

nodes.title: Michelson–Morley Experiment
nodes.html: In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley compared the travel time of light along two perpendicular arms of an interferometer and found no difference, whichever way the apparatus pointed relative to Earth’s motion. The null result ruled out a detectable ether wind and set the stage for special relativity. Descendants of the interferometer detect gravitational waves.
nodes.summary: In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley compared the travel time of light along two perpendicular arms of an interferometer and found no difference, whichever way the apparatus pointed relative to Earth’s motion.

nodes.title: Shock Waves
nodes.html: In 1887 Ernst Mach and Peter Salcher photographed the shock waves around a supersonic bullet and showed that the cone angle gives the speed relative to sound, the ratio now called the Mach number. William Rankine (1870) and Pierre-Henri Hugoniot (1887) derived the conservation laws that relate the gas on the two sides of a shock.
nodes.summary: In 1887 Ernst Mach and Peter Salcher photographed the shock waves around a supersonic bullet and showed that the cone angle gives the speed relative to sound, the ratio now called the Mach number.

nodes.title: X-rays
nodes.html: Röntgen’s mysterious rays (1895) passed through flesh but not bone. Doctors were using them within months.
nodes.summary: Röntgen’s mysterious rays (1895) passed through flesh but not bone.

nodes.title: Arrhenius’s CO₂ Calculation
nodes.html: In 1896 Svante Arrhenius calculated by hand how Earth’s surface temperature would change if the carbon dioxide in the air were halved or doubled, using measurements of infrared absorption. He found about 5 to 6 degrees Celsius of warming for a doubling, a larger figure than the roughly 3 degrees of modern estimates. Guy Callendar (1938) linked measured warming to rising CO2.
nodes.summary: In 1896 Svante Arrhenius calculated by hand how Earth’s surface temperature would change if the carbon dioxide in the air were halved or doubled, using measurements of infrared absorption.

nodes.title: Zeeman Effect
nodes.html: Pieter Zeeman observed in 1896 that spectral lines of sodium broaden when the light source is placed in a magnetic field. Hendrik Lorentz explained the effect with charged particles oscillating inside atoms, and the charge-to-mass ratio inferred for them was close to the value Thomson found for cathode rays in 1897. Zeeman and Lorentz shared the 1902 Nobel Prize in Physics.
nodes.summary: Pieter Zeeman observed in 1896 that spectral lines of sodium broaden when the light source is placed in a magnetic field.

nodes.title: The Electron
nodes.html: Cathode rays are streams of charged particles far lighter than any atom (1897). The electron was the first subatomic particle to be found.
nodes.summary: Cathode rays are streams of charged particles far lighter than any atom (1897).

nodes.title: Hilbert’s Sixth Problem (Kinetic Theory)

progress.what: Derived the Boltzmann equation from the dynamics of many hard spheres, but only for a short time, a fraction of the mean time between collisions.
progress.html: Derived the Boltzmann equation from the dynamics of many hard spheres, but only for a short time, a fraction of the mean time between collisions.

progress.what: Showed that renormalized solutions of the Boltzmann equation converge to Leray solutions of the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, the kinetic-to-fluid half of the programme.
progress.html: Showed that renormalized solutions of the Boltzmann equation converge to Leray solutions of the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, the kinetic-to-fluid half of the programme.

progress.what: Derived the Boltzmann equation from hard-sphere dynamics for as long as its solution stays regular, removing Lanford’s short-time limit. Accepted by Annals of Mathematics in 2025 and cited for Deng’s 2026 Fields Medal.
progress.html: Derived the Boltzmann equation from hard-sphere dynamics for as long as its solution stays regular, removing Lanford’s short-time limit. Accepted by Annals of Mathematics in 2025 and cited for Deng’s 2026 Fields Medal.

progress.what: Claimed derivation of the compressible Euler and incompressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier equations from hard-sphere dynamics through the Boltzmann equation. Not yet refereed as of October 2026.
progress.html: Claimed derivation of the compressible Euler and incompressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier equations from hard-sphere dynamics through the Boltzmann equation. Not yet refereed as of October 2026.

nodes.html: Hilbert’s sixth problem (1900) asked for an axiomatic treatment of physics, including a rigorous passage from the mechanics of atoms to the laws of fluids through Boltzmann’s kinetic theory. Deng, Hani and Ma derived the Boltzmann equation from hard-sphere dynamics for long times (2024), then the compressible Euler and incompressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier equations (2025); the second paper is not yet refereed.
nodes.summary: Hilbert’s sixth problem (1900) asked for an axiomatic treatment of physics, including a rigorous passage from the mechanics of atoms to the laws of fluids through Boltzmann’s kinetic theory.

nodes.title: Energy Quanta
nodes.html: Planck fitted black-body radiation by assuming energy comes in packets (1900). Einstein took the packets literally to explain the photoelectric effect (1905).
nodes.summary: Planck fitted black-body radiation by assuming energy comes in packets (1900).

nodes.title: Brownian Motion Explained
nodes.html: Albert Einstein showed in 1905 that the zigzag motion of small particles in a liquid comes from molecular impacts, and gave a formula linking their spread to temperature, viscosity, particle size and Avogadro’s number. Marian Smoluchowski found the result independently in 1906, and Jean Perrin’s measurements (1908) convinced most remaining sceptics that atoms exist.
nodes.summary: Albert Einstein showed in 1905 that the zigzag motion of small particles in a liquid comes from molecular impacts, and gave a formula linking their spread to temperature, viscosity, particle size and Avogadro’s number.

nodes.title: Special Relativity
nodes.html: The speed of light is the same for every observer, so space and time mix (1905). As a consequence, E = mc².
nodes.summary: The speed of light is the same for every observer, so space and time mix (1905).

nodes.title: Earth’s Core
nodes.html: Richard Oldham showed in 1906 from earthquake records that Earth has a distinct central core, where compressional waves slow down. Beno Gutenberg fixed its boundary at a depth of about 2,900 km (1913), and Harold Jeffreys concluded in 1926 that the outer core is liquid because shear waves do not pass through it.
nodes.summary: Richard Oldham showed in 1906 from earthquake records that Earth has a distinct central core, where compressional waves slow down.

nodes.title: Radiometric Dating
nodes.html: Bertram Boltwood showed in 1907 that the ratio of lead to uranium in rocks grows with age, and his dates ran from hundreds of millions to over two billion years. Arthur Holmes built the first geological time scale from radioactive decay in 1913. Radiometric dating gives absolute ages for rocks, meteorites and fossils, and it showed that Earth is billions of years old.
nodes.summary: Bertram Boltwood showed in 1907 that the ratio of lead to uranium in rocks grows with age, and his dates ran from hundreds of millions to over two billion years.

nodes.title: Liquefaction of Helium
nodes.html: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes liquefied helium at Leiden on 10 July 1908, reaching 4.2 K, the last of the permanent gases to give way. This opened low-temperature physics, and with the new cold he discovered superconductivity in mercury in 1911.
nodes.summary: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes liquefied helium at Leiden on 10 July 1908, reaching 4.2 K, the last of the permanent gases to give way.

nodes.title: Elastic Rebound Theory
nodes.html: After the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, Harry Fielding Reid studied the ground displacements on either side of the San Andreas Fault and proposed in 1910 that faults slowly accumulate elastic strain until the rock slips suddenly and releases it. The theory explains why earthquakes recur and remains the basic model of the earthquake cycle.
nodes.summary: After the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, Harry Fielding Reid studied the ground displacements on either side of the San Andreas Fault and proposed in 1910 that faults slowly accumulate elastic strain until the rock slips suddenly and releases it.

nodes.title: Hertzsprung–Russell Diagram
nodes.html: Ejnar Hertzsprung (1911) and Henry Norris Russell (1913) plotted the brightness of stars against their colour or spectral type and found that most lie on a diagonal band, the main sequence, with a separate group of giants above it. Annie Jump Cannon’s spectral classes (OBAFGKM) supplied the spectral types. The diagram became the basic tool of stellar astrophysics.
nodes.summary: Ejnar Hertzsprung (1911) and Henry Norris Russell (1913) plotted the brightness of stars against their colour or spectral type and found that most lie on a diagonal band, the main sequence, with a separate group of giants above it.

nodes.title: Radioactivity & the Nucleus
nodes.html: Radioactivity (Becquerel 1896; the Curies 1898) and Rutherford’s gold-foil experiment (1911) showed that atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus.
nodes.summary: Radioactivity (Becquerel 1896; the Curies 1898) and Rutherford’s gold-foil experiment (1911) showed that atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus.

nodes.title: Superconductivity
nodes.html: Below about 4.2 K, mercury loses all electrical resistance (1911). The explanation, Cooper pairs in BCS theory (1957), took another 46 years.
nodes.summary: Below about 4.2 K, mercury loses all electrical resistance (1911).

nodes.title: Cepheid Period–Luminosity Law
nodes.html: Henrietta Swan Leavitt, studying variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds at Harvard, reported in 1912 that brighter Cepheids pulse more slowly. Because the stars in each cloud are at nearly the same distance, the period tells the true brightness and so the distance, once calibrated. The relation became the first reliable standard candle for measuring distances to other galaxies.
nodes.summary: Henrietta Swan Leavitt, studying variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds at Harvard, reported in 1912 that brighter Cepheids pulse more slowly.

nodes.title: Continental Drift
nodes.html: Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents were once joined in a single supercontinent, later called Pangaea, and have drifted apart. He cited the fit of the coastlines, matching fossils and rock formations on both sides of the Atlantic, and ancient glacial traces. Most geologists rejected it for lack of a mechanism, and plate tectonics vindicated it in the 1960s.
nodes.summary: Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents were once joined in a single supercontinent, later called Pangaea, and have drifted apart.

nodes.title: Cosmic Rays
nodes.html: Victor Hess flew in balloons up to 5.3 km in 1912 and found that ionizing radiation increases with altitude, so it must come from space. Cosmic rays are mostly high-energy protons and nuclei, and they led to the discovery of the positron, the muon and the pion before high-energy accelerators were built.
nodes.summary: Victor Hess flew in balloons up to 5.3 km in 1912 and found that ionizing radiation increases with altitude, so it must come from space.

nodes.title: Bohr Model of the Atom
nodes.html: Niels Bohr proposed in 1913 that electrons in an atom move in fixed orbits with quantized angular momentum and emit or absorb light only when they jump between orbits. The model reproduced the hydrogen spectrum, including the Balmer series known since 1885, and gave the correct Rydberg constant in terms of fundamental constants.
nodes.summary: Niels Bohr proposed in 1913 that electrons in an atom move in fixed orbits with quantized angular momentum and emit or absorb light only when they jump between orbits.

nodes.title: General Relativity

quote.text: Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve.

nodes.html: Gravity is the curvature of spacetime (1915). Riemann’s geometry, sixty years old by then, turned out to be exactly the right tool.
nodes.summary: Gravity is the curvature of spacetime (1915).

nodes.title: Mercury’s Perihelion Explained
nodes.html: Urbain Le Verrier found in 1859 that Mercury’s orbit turns forward by about 38 arcseconds per century more than Newtonian gravity with the known planets allows (43 in modern values). In November 1915 Einstein showed that general relativity accounts for the difference exactly, his first quantitative test of the theory.
nodes.summary: Urbain Le Verrier found in 1859 that Mercury’s orbit turns forward by about 38 arcseconds per century more than Newtonian gravity with the known planets allows (43 in modern values).

nodes.title: Rayleigh–Bénard Convection
nodes.html: A fluid layer heated from below stays still until the temperature difference passes a threshold, then breaks into convection cells. Henri Bénard photographed cells in 1900 (later shown to be driven by surface tension), and Lord Rayleigh (1916) analysed the buoyancy-driven case, where onset depends on the dimensionless Rayleigh number. It models convection in atmospheres and mantles.
nodes.summary: A fluid layer heated from below stays still until the temperature difference passes a threshold, then breaks into convection cells.

nodes.title: Schwarzschild Solution
nodes.html: Karl Schwarzschild found, within weeks of the publication of general relativity and while serving on the Russian front, the exact gravitational field outside a spherical mass, published in 1916. It was the first exact solution of Einstein’s equations, and it contains the radius that later became understood as the event horizon of a black hole.
nodes.summary: Karl Schwarzschild found, within weeks of the publication of general relativity and while serving on the Russian front, the exact gravitational field outside a spherical mass, published in 1916.

nodes.title: Cosmological Constant
nodes.html: Einstein added a constant term to his field equations in 1917 so that they would allow a static universe. Willem de Sitter found a matter-free solution the same year, which was later understood to expand. Einstein dropped the term after the expansion of the universe was found, and it returned as a candidate for dark energy after 1998.
nodes.summary: Einstein added a constant term to his field equations in 1917 so that they would allow a static universe.

nodes.title: Stimulated Emission
nodes.html: In 1917 Einstein showed from the thermodynamics of radiation that an excited atom can be triggered by a passing photon to emit a second photon of the same frequency and direction. Stimulated emission is the principle behind masers and lasers, which were built in 1954 and 1960.
nodes.summary: In 1917 Einstein showed from the thermodynamics of radiation that an excited atom can be triggered by a passing photon to emit a second photon of the same frequency and direction.

nodes.title: Finiteness of Central Configurations
aliases: relative equilibria of the n-body problem

progress.what: Four bodies: for any positive masses there are finitely many central configurations, between 32 and 8,472, by symbolic and exact integer computation.
progress.html: Four bodies: for any positive masses there are finitely many central configurations, between 32 and 8,472, by symbolic and exact integer computation.

progress.what: Five bodies in the plane: finitely many central configurations except possibly for masses in a codimension-2 subvariety.
progress.html: Five bodies in the plane: finitely many central configurations except possibly for masses in a codimension-2 subvariety.

progress.what: Carried the Albouy–Kaloshin method toward the planar six-body problem by symbolic computation, determining the mass relations that possible infinite families must satisfy.
progress.html: Carried the Albouy–Kaloshin method toward the planar six-body problem by symbolic computation, determining the mass relations that possible infinite families must satisfy.

progress.what: Computer-assisted exact counts of five-body central configurations for several mass values left open by the planar and spatial finiteness theorems.
progress.html: Computer-assisted exact counts of five-body central configurations for several mass values left open by the planar and spatial finiteness theorems.

nodes.html: For given masses, are there only finitely many central configurations, arrangements of n gravitating bodies whose accelerations all point to the centre of mass in proportion to distance, so the shape can spin rigidly? Asked by Chazy (1918) and Wintner (1941) and listed as Smale’s sixth problem (1998), it is proved for four bodies (2006) and for five bodies in the plane outside a thin set of masses (2012).
nodes.summary: For given masses, are there only finitely many central configurations, arrangements of n gravitating bodies whose accelerations all point to the centre of mass in proportion to distance, so the shape can spin rigidly?

nodes.title: Noether’s Theorem
nodes.html: Emmy Noether’s 1918 paper, which grew out of work begun in 1915, proved that every continuous symmetry of a physical system’s action corresponds to a conserved quantity: symmetry under shifts in time gives conservation of energy, under shifts in space momentum, and under rotations angular momentum. The theorem ties symmetry to conservation laws throughout modern physics.
nodes.summary: Emmy Noether’s 1918 paper, which grew out of work begun in 1915, proved that every continuous symmetry of a physical system’s action corresponds to a conserved quantity: symmetry under shifts in time gives conservation of energy, under shifts in space momentum, and under rotations angular momentum.

nodes.title: Starlight Bent by the Sun
nodes.html: Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson organized expeditions to Príncipe and Sobral to photograph stars near the Sun during the total eclipse of 29 May 1919. The stars appeared displaced by about the amount general relativity predicts, twice the Newtonian value, and the result brought Einstein public attention worldwide.
nodes.summary: Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson organized expeditions to Príncipe and Sobral to photograph stars near the Sun during the total eclipse of 29 May 1919.

nodes.title: Proton & Nuclear Transmutation
nodes.html: Ernest Rutherford found in experiments of 1917, reported in 1919, that alpha particles striking nitrogen gas knock out hydrogen nuclei, the first artificial disintegration of a nucleus. Patrick Blackett showed in 1925 that the nitrogen captures the alpha and becomes oxygen-17, so one element had been turned into another. Rutherford named the proton in 1920.
nodes.summary: Ernest Rutherford found in experiments of 1917, reported in 1919, that alpha particles striking nitrogen gas knock out hydrogen nuclei, the first artificial disintegration of a nucleus.

nodes.title: Milankovitch Cycles
nodes.html: Milutin Milanković calculated from 1920 on how the wobble of Earth’s axis, the changing tilt and the shape of its orbit alter the sunlight reaching high northern latitudes, and proposed that these cycles pace the ice ages. His Canon of Insolation appeared in 1941, and deep-sea sediments studied by Hays, Imbrie and Shackleton in 1976 showed climate cycles at the predicted periods.
nodes.summary: Milutin Milanković calculated from 1920 on how the wobble of Earth’s axis, the changing tilt and the shape of its orbit alter the sunlight reaching high northern latitudes, and proposed that these cycles pace the ice ages.

nodes.title: Bose–Einstein Statistics
nodes.html: In 1924 Satyendra Nath Bose derived Planck’s law by counting photons as indistinguishable particles, and Einstein extended the method to atoms. The resulting Bose-Einstein statistics describes particles of integer spin and predicts that they can pile into a single lowest state at low temperature, as in the condensate observed in 1995.
nodes.summary: In 1924 Satyendra Nath Bose derived Planck’s law by counting photons as indistinguishable particles, and Einstein extended the method to atoms.

nodes.title: Matter Waves
nodes.html: Louis de Broglie proposed in 1924 that particles have a wavelength h/p, where h is Planck’s constant and p the momentum. Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer observed electrons diffracting from a nickel crystal in 1927, and George Paget Thomson saw the same effect independently. The idea led Schrödinger to wave mechanics.
nodes.summary: Louis de Broglie proposed in 1924 that particles have a wavelength h/p, where h is Planck’s constant and p the momentum.

nodes.title: Electron Spin
nodes.html: In 1925 George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit proposed that the electron has an intrinsic angular momentum, spin, with two possible orientations, to explain the doublets seen in atomic spectra. The two beams of silver atoms that Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach saw in 1922 were later understood as its effect. Spin underlies magnetism, the periodic table, MRI and spintronics.
nodes.summary: In 1925 George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit proposed that the electron has an intrinsic angular momentum, spin, with two possible orientations, to explain the doublets seen in atomic spectra.

nodes.title: Galaxies Beyond the Milky Way
nodes.html: Edwin Hubble identified Cepheid variable stars in the Andromeda nebula and showed, in a result announced on 1 January 1925, that it lies far outside the Milky Way. This settled the 1920 Shapley-Curtis debate in favour of island universes and showed that the Milky Way is one galaxy among very many, building on Harlow Shapley’s 1918 measurement of its size.
nodes.summary: Edwin Hubble identified Cepheid variable stars in the Andromeda nebula and showed, in a result announced on 1 January 1925, that it lies far outside the Milky Way.

nodes.title: Ising Model
nodes.html: Wilhelm Lenz proposed in 1920 a model of spins on a lattice that prefer to align with their neighbours, and his student Ernst Ising showed in 1925 that the one-dimensional chain has no phase transition. Onsager solved the two-dimensional case exactly in 1944, and the model became the standard test case for phase transitions and critical phenomena.
nodes.summary: Wilhelm Lenz proposed in 1920 a model of spins on a lattice that prefer to align with their neighbours, and his student Ernst Ising showed in 1925 that the one-dimensional chain has no phase transition.

nodes.title: Pauli Exclusion Principle
nodes.html: Wolfgang Pauli proposed in 1925 that no two electrons in an atom can occupy the same quantum state. The rule accounts for the shell structure of atoms and so for the periodic table and chemistry. The same principle keeps ordinary matter from collapsing and supports white dwarfs and neutron stars against gravity.
nodes.summary: Wolfgang Pauli proposed in 1925 that no two electrons in an atom can occupy the same quantum state.

nodes.title: Quantum Mechanics
nodes.html: Matrix mechanics (Heisenberg, 1925) and wave mechanics (Schrödinger, 1926): states are vectors, observables are operators, and outcomes are probabilities.
nodes.summary: Matrix mechanics (Heisenberg, 1925) and wave mechanics (Schrödinger, 1926): states are vectors, observables are operators, and outcomes are probabilities.

nodes.title: Stars Are Mostly Hydrogen
nodes.html: In her 1925 Harvard thesis Cecilia Payne used Meghnad Saha’s ionization equation (1920) to turn the spectral classes of stars into temperatures and abundances. Her results made stars mostly hydrogen and helium, far from Earth-like, which she called almost certainly not real, deferring to Henry Norris Russell, who confirmed them himself in 1929.
nodes.summary: In her 1925 Harvard thesis Cecilia Payne used Meghnad Saha’s ionization equation (1920) to turn the spectral classes of stars into temperatures and abundances.

nodes.title: Fermi–Dirac Statistics
nodes.html: Enrico Fermi and Paul Dirac independently derived in 1926 the statistics of identical particles that obey the exclusion principle. Fermi-Dirac statistics govern electrons in metals and semiconductors and explain the degeneracy pressure that holds up white dwarfs and neutron stars. Particles that follow it are called fermions.
nodes.summary: Enrico Fermi and Paul Dirac independently derived in 1926 the statistics of identical particles that obey the exclusion principle.

nodes.title: Internal Constitution of the Stars
nodes.html: Arthur Eddington’s The Internal Constitution of the Stars (1926) set out how gas pressure and radiation pressure balance gravity inside a star and how energy flows outward. It predicted a relation between a star’s mass and luminosity that observations confirmed, and it framed the question of the stellar energy source that fusion later answered.
nodes.summary: Arthur Eddington’s The Internal Constitution of the Stars (1926) set out how gas pressure and radiation pressure balance gravity inside a star and how energy flows outward.

nodes.title: Uncertainty Principle
nodes.html: Werner Heisenberg argued in 1927 that the position and momentum of a particle cannot both be sharply defined, and Earle Kennard soon proved the exact bound: the product of the two uncertainties is at least half the reduced Planck constant. The principle follows from the wave nature of matter and, with Bohr’s complementarity, shaped the Copenhagen interpretation.
nodes.summary: Werner Heisenberg argued in 1927 that the position and momentum of a particle cannot both be sharply defined, and Earle Kennard soon proved the exact bound: the product of the two uncertainties is at least half the reduced Planck constant.

nodes.title: Band Theory of Solids
nodes.html: Electrons in a crystal occupy energy bands (Bloch, 1928). The gaps between bands explain metals, insulators and semiconductors (Wilson, 1931).
nodes.summary: Electrons in a crystal occupy energy bands (Bloch, 1928).

nodes.title: Deep-Focus Earthquake Mechanism

progress.what: Laboratory experiments showed transformational faulting: metastable olivine turning into spinel along thin shear zones can produce sudden slip under high pressure.
progress.html: Laboratory experiments showed transformational faulting: metastable olivine turning into spinel along thin shear zones can produce sudden slip under high pressure.

progress.what: The energy budget of the 1994 Bolivia deep earthquake implies frictional melting on the fault, evidence for thermal runaway during rupture.
progress.html: The energy budget of the 1994 Bolivia deep earthquake implies frictional melting on the fault, evidence for thermal runaway during rupture.

progress.what: Analysed the 2013 Sea of Okhotsk earthquake, at magnitude 8.3 the largest deep event recorded, whose rupture properties differ from the 1994 Bolivia event.
progress.html: Analysed the 2013 Sea of Okhotsk earthquake, at magnitude 8.3 the largest deep event recorded, whose rupture properties differ from the 1994 Bolivia event.

progress.what: A review concluded that each proposed mechanism, transformational faulting, dehydration embrittlement and thermal runaway, fails to explain some observations.
progress.html: A review concluded that each proposed mechanism, transformational faulting, dehydration embrittlement and thermal runaway, fails to explain some observations.

nodes.html: Earthquakes occur as deep as about 700 km (Wadati, 1928), where pressure should suppress ordinary brittle faulting. Proposed mechanisms include transformational faulting in metastable olivine, dehydration embrittlement and thermal runaway, and each fails to explain some observations. A mechanism that matches laboratory experiments and the rupture properties of large deep earthquakes would settle it.
nodes.summary: Earthquakes occur as deep as about 700 km (Wadati, 1928), where pressure should suppress ordinary brittle faulting.

nodes.title: Dirac Equation
nodes.html: Paul Dirac wrote down in 1928 a relativistic wave equation for the electron. It gives the electron’s spin and magnetic moment automatically, accounts for the fine structure of hydrogen, and has negative-energy solutions that Dirac interpreted in 1931 as antielectrons, which predicted the positron (found in 1932).
nodes.summary: Paul Dirac wrote down in 1928 a relativistic wave equation for the electron.

nodes.title: Exchange Interaction & Ferromagnetism
nodes.html: Werner Heisenberg showed in 1928 that ferromagnetism arises from the quantum mechanical exchange interaction, an electrostatic energy that depends on whether the spins of two electrons are parallel or antiparallel. This explained why iron and nickel can be permanently magnetized, which classical physics cannot, and gave the Heisenberg model of interacting spins.
nodes.summary: Werner Heisenberg showed in 1928 that ferromagnetism arises from the quantum mechanical exchange interaction, an electrostatic energy that depends on whether the spins of two electrons are parallel or antiparallel.

nodes.title: Plasma
nodes.html: Irving Langmuir named the ionized state of gas plasma in 1928 and, with Lewi Tonks, studied its collective oscillations, now called Langmuir waves. Debye shielding (1923) shows how a plasma screens electric fields over short distances. Plasma physics is the basis of research on fusion, the Sun and stars, and the space environment.
nodes.summary: Irving Langmuir named the ionized state of gas plasma in 1928 and, with Lewi Tonks, studied its collective oscillations, now called Langmuir waves.

nodes.title: Quantum Tunnelling
nodes.html: George Gamow, and independently Ronald Gurney and Edward Condon, showed in 1928 that a quantum particle has a finite chance of passing through an energy barrier that classical physics forbids. This explained alpha decay and its widely varying lifetimes. Tunnelling also lets the Sun fuse hydrogen and underlies the scanning tunnelling microscope and flash memory.
nodes.summary: George Gamow, and independently Ronald Gurney and Edward Condon, showed in 1928 that a quantum particle has a finite chance of passing through an energy barrier that classical physics forbids.

nodes.title: Expanding Universe
nodes.html: Galaxies recede faster the farther away they are (Lemaître 1927, Hubble 1929). The cosmic microwave background (1965) confirmed a hot Big Bang.
nodes.summary: Galaxies recede faster the farther away they are (Lemaître 1927, Hubble 1929).

nodes.title: Geomagnetic Reversals
nodes.html: Bernard Brunhes found in 1906 that some volcanic rocks in France are magnetized opposite to today’s field, and Motonori Matuyama showed in 1929 from basalts in Japan and Manchuria that the field had reversed in the early Pleistocene. Earth’s field has reversed polarity many times at irregular intervals; the last reversal was about 780,000 years ago.
nodes.summary: Bernard Brunhes found in 1906 that some volcanic rocks in France are magnetized opposite to today’s field, and Motonori Matuyama showed in 1929 from basalts in Japan and Manchuria that the field had reversed in the early Pleistocene.

nodes.title: Chandrasekhar Limit
nodes.html: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar showed in 1930-31, combining special relativity with Fermi-Dirac statistics, that a white dwarf has a maximum mass because degenerate electrons cannot support more; the limit is about 1.4 solar masses for a carbon or oxygen star. Heavier stellar cores must collapse further, and white dwarfs reaching it are a leading model for Type Ia supernovae.
nodes.summary: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar showed in 1930-31, combining special relativity with Fermi-Dirac statistics, that a white dwarf has a maximum mass because degenerate electrons cannot support more; the limit is about 1.4 solar masses for a carbon or oxygen star.

nodes.title: Neutron
nodes.html: James Chadwick showed in 1932 that a neutral radiation produced when alpha particles hit beryllium consists of particles about as heavy as the proton. The neutron completed the picture of the nucleus as protons and neutrons, explained isotopes, and, because it carries no charge, became the key to inducing nuclear reactions, including fission.
nodes.summary: James Chadwick showed in 1932 that a neutral radiation produced when alpha particles hit beryllium consists of particles about as heavy as the proton.

nodes.title: Antimatter
nodes.html: Carl Anderson photographed in 1932, in a cloud chamber exposed to cosmic rays, the track of a particle with the mass of an electron and a positive charge. It was the antiparticle that Dirac’s equation had demanded and the first antimatter observed. Positron emission tomography now uses positrons for medical imaging.
nodes.summary: Carl Anderson photographed in 1932, in a cloud chamber exposed to cosmic rays, the track of a particle with the mass of an electron and a positive charge.

nodes.title: Cosmic Radio Waves
nodes.html: Karl Jansky, studying static for Bell Labs in 1932-33, found a steady radio hiss that rose and fell once per sidereal day and came from the direction of the centre of the Milky Way. Grote Reber built a dish telescope in 1937 and mapped the radio sky. Radio astronomy went on to reveal pulsars, quasars and the cosmic microwave background.
nodes.summary: Karl Jansky, studying static for Bell Labs in 1932-33, found a steady radio hiss that rose and fell once per sidereal day and came from the direction of the centre of the Milky Way.

nodes.title: Nature of Dark Matter
nodes.html: About 85% of the matter in the universe does not shine. Zwicky (1933) and Vera Rubin (1970s) measured its pull; nobody has detected what it is made of.
nodes.summary: About 85% of the matter in the universe does not shine.

nodes.title: Fermi Theory of Beta Decay
nodes.html: Wolfgang Pauli proposed in 1930 that an undetected neutral particle carries off part of the energy in beta decay, and Enrico Fermi’s theory of 1933-34 treated the decay as a neutron turning into a proton, an electron and a neutrino. It was the first theory of the weak interaction and it described the neutrino’s role long before the particle was detected in 1956.
nodes.summary: Wolfgang Pauli proposed in 1930 that an undetected neutral particle carries off part of the energy in beta decay, and Enrico Fermi’s theory of 1933-34 treated the decay as a neutron turning into a proton, an electron and a neutrino.

nodes.title: Cherenkov Radiation
nodes.html: Pavel Cherenkov studied in 1934 a faint blue glow from liquids exposed to gamma rays. In 1937 Ilya Frank and Igor Tamm explained that a charged particle moving faster than light does in a medium emits a cone of light, the optical counterpart of a sonic boom. Cherenkov detectors identify particles and detect neutrinos in water and ice.
nodes.summary: Pavel Cherenkov studied in 1934 a faint blue glow from liquids exposed to gamma rays.

nodes.title: Supernovae & Neutron Stars
nodes.html: Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky proposed in 1934 that supernovae are a distinct class of stellar explosion, far brighter than novae, in which an ordinary star collapses into a neutron star. They also suggested that supernovae are a source of cosmic rays. Pulsars, discovered in 1967, are such neutron stars.
nodes.summary: Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky proposed in 1934 that supernovae are a distinct class of stellar explosion, far brighter than novae, in which an ordinary star collapses into a neutron star.

nodes.title: Quantum Entanglement (EPR)
nodes.html: Albert Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen argued in 1935 that quantum mechanics is incomplete: measuring one of two correlated particles lets one predict the other’s position or momentum without disturbing it, so both must have definite values the theory omits. Schrödinger named such correlations entanglement, and Bell’s theorem (1964) made the question testable.
nodes.summary: Albert Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen argued in 1935 that quantum mechanics is incomplete: measuring one of two correlated particles lets one predict the other’s position or momentum without disturbing it, so both must have definite values the theory omits.

nodes.title: Earthquake Magnitude Scale
nodes.html: Charles Richter, working with Beno Gutenberg at Caltech in 1935, defined a logarithmic magnitude scale for earthquakes from the amplitude of seismograph traces, so that each unit is a tenfold increase in amplitude. Gutenberg and Richter later gave the frequency law of earthquake sizes (1944), and the moment magnitude scale (1979) replaced the original for large events.
nodes.summary: Charles Richter, working with Beno Gutenberg at Caltech in 1935, defined a logarithmic magnitude scale for earthquakes from the amplitude of seismograph traces, so that each unit is a tenfold increase in amplitude.

nodes.title: Earth’s Inner Core
nodes.html: Inge Lehmann found faint P waves from distant earthquakes arriving inside the shadow zone of the liquid core, and concluded in 1936 that the core has a distinct inner sphere that refracts waves into the shadow. It was later shown to be solid, is mostly iron and nickel, about 1,200 km in radius, and grows slowly as the Earth cools.
nodes.summary: Inge Lehmann found faint P waves from distant earthquakes arriving inside the shadow zone of the liquid core, and concluded in 1936 that the core has a distinct inner sphere that refracts waves into the shadow.

nodes.title: Muon
nodes.html: Carl Anderson and Seth Neddermeyer found in 1936, in cosmic-ray tracks in a cloud chamber, a particle with the electron’s charge and a mass between those of the electron and proton, now known to be 207 electron masses. First taken for Yukawa’s nuclear-force particle, it is a heavy, unstable cousin of the electron, the first sign that matter comes in repeated families.
nodes.summary: Carl Anderson and Seth Neddermeyer found in 1936, in cosmic-ray tracks in a cloud chamber, a particle with the electron’s charge and a mass between those of the electron and proton, now known to be 207 electron masses.

nodes.title: Landau Theory of Phase Transitions
nodes.html: Lev Landau proposed in 1937 that a phase transition can be described by an order parameter, zero in the symmetric phase and nonzero in the ordered one, with the free energy expanded in powers of it. The theory ties transitions to broken symmetry and gives universal behaviour near the critical point, which the renormalization group later corrected where fluctuations matter.
nodes.summary: Lev Landau proposed in 1937 that a phase transition can be described by an order parameter, zero in the symmetric phase and nonzero in the ordered one, with the free energy expanded in powers of it.

nodes.title: Nuclear Fission
nodes.html: Uranium nuclei split when struck by neutrons (Hahn and Strassmann, 1938). Meitner and Frisch explained the energy released using E = mc² (1939).
nodes.summary: Uranium nuclei split when struck by neutrons (Hahn and Strassmann, 1938).

nodes.title: Superfluidity
nodes.html: Pyotr Kapitsa, and independently John Allen and Don Misener, found in 1937-38 that liquid helium cooled below 2.17 K flows through narrow channels with no measurable viscosity. Fritz London linked the effect to Bose-Einstein condensation (1938), and Lev Landau’s two-fluid theory (1941) described its behaviour. It showed quantum mechanics at the scale of a visible liquid.
nodes.summary: Pyotr Kapitsa, and independently John Allen and Don Misener, found in 1937-38 that liquid helium cooled below 2.17 K flows through narrow channels with no measurable viscosity.

nodes.title: Coronal Heating Problem

progress.what: Proposed that the corona is heated by countless small reconnection events, nanoflares, in magnetic field lines braided by surface motions.
progress.html: Proposed that the corona is heated by countless small reconnection events, nanoflares, in magnetic field lines braided by surface motions.

progress.what: Solar Orbiter’s extreme-ultraviolet imager found ‘campfires’, tiny brightenings all over the quiet Sun that may be the smallest flares.
progress.html: Solar Orbiter’s extreme-ultraviolet imager found ‘campfires’, tiny brightenings all over the quiet Sun that may be the smallest flares.

progress.what: Parker Solar Probe crossed the Alfvén critical surface in April 2021, the first spacecraft to fly through the magnetically dominated corona.
progress.html: Parker Solar Probe crossed the Alfvén critical surface in April 2021, the first spacecraft to fly through the magnetically dominated corona.

progress.what: The Inouye Solar Telescope detected small-scale torsional Alfvén waves in the quiet corona, a candidate carrier of much of the heating energy.
progress.html: The Inouye Solar Telescope detected small-scale torsional Alfvén waves in the quiet corona, a candidate carrier of much of the heating energy.

nodes.html: The Sun’s corona is above a million degrees, hundreds of times hotter than the visible surface, as spectroscopy showed in 1939–1943. Is it heated by magnetic waves or by countless small reconnection events called nanoflares? Solar Orbiter, Parker Solar Probe and the Inouye telescope now see evidence for both, and an energy budget that closes for the quiet Sun and active regions would settle it.
nodes.summary: The Sun’s corona is above a million degrees, hundreds of times hotter than the visible surface, as spectroscopy showed in 1939–1943.

nodes.title: Gravitational Collapse
nodes.html: In 1939 Richard Tolman, Robert Oppenheimer and George Volkoff calculated that a neutron star cannot exceed a maximum mass, then put at about 0.7 solar masses (modern estimates are 2 to 3). Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder showed that a sufficiently massive star collapses without limit and seals itself off behind a horizon, the first picture of black hole formation.
nodes.summary: In 1939 Richard Tolman, Robert Oppenheimer and George Volkoff calculated that a neutron star cannot exceed a maximum mass, then put at about 0.7 solar masses (modern estimates are 2 to 3).

nodes.title: Million-Degree Solar Corona
nodes.html: Walter Grotrian (1939) and Bengt Edlén (about 1940) showed that the mysterious emission lines of the solar corona, once attributed to an element called coronium, come from iron, calcium and nickel stripped of many electrons. Such ionization needs temperatures above a million kelvin, far hotter than the Sun’s surface at about 5,800 K, which poses the coronal heating problem.
nodes.summary: Walter Grotrian (1939) and Bengt Edlén (about 1940) showed that the mysterious emission lines of the solar corona, once attributed to an element called coronium, come from iron, calcium and nickel stripped of many electrons.

nodes.title: Fusion in Stars
nodes.html: Bethe worked out how stars fuse hydrogen into helium (1939). Fusion is what powers the Sun.
nodes.summary: Bethe worked out how stars fuse hydrogen into helium (1939).

nodes.title: Kolmogorov’s Theory of Turbulence
nodes.html: Andrey Kolmogorov proposed in 1941 that in fully developed turbulence energy cascades from large eddies to ever smaller ones until viscosity dissipates it, with statistically universal small scales. The theory predicts an energy spectrum falling with wavenumber as a power of minus five thirds, which experiments confirm. Lewis Fry Richardson described the cascade in 1922.
nodes.summary: Andrey Kolmogorov proposed in 1941 that in fully developed turbulence energy cascades from large eddies to ever smaller ones until viscosity dissipates it, with statistically universal small scales.

nodes.title: Magnetohydrodynamics
nodes.html: Hannes Alfvén showed in 1942 that a magnetic field threading a conducting fluid is carried along with it and acts like elastic strings that support transverse waves, now called Alfvén waves. Magnetohydrodynamics became the theory of the Sun, the solar wind, planetary dynamos and fusion plasmas, and Alfvén received the 1970 Nobel Prize in Physics.
nodes.summary: Hannes Alfvén showed in 1942 that a magnetic field threading a conducting fluid is carried along with it and acts like elastic strings that support transverse waves, now called Alfvén waves.

nodes.title: Exact Solution of the 3D Ising Model

progress.what: The numerical conformal bootstrap placed the 3D Ising critical point at a kink of the allowed region of operator dimensions, a route to its exponents without simulating the lattice.
progress.html: The numerical conformal bootstrap placed the 3D Ising critical point at a kink of the allowed region of operator dimensions, a route to its exponents without simulating the lattice.

progress.what: Proved that the spontaneous magnetization of the 3D Ising model vanishes at the critical temperature, so the transition is continuous.
progress.html: Proved that the spontaneous magnetization of the 3D Ising model vanishes at the critical temperature, so the transition is continuous.

progress.what: A fuzzy-sphere regularization displayed the conformal symmetry of the 3D Ising critical point directly in a microscopic quantum model (PRX 2023).
progress.html: A fuzzy-sphere regularization displayed the conformal symmetry of the 3D Ising critical point directly in a microscopic quantum model (PRX 2023).

progress.what: Bootstrapping the stress tensor gave Δσ = 0.518148806(24) and Δε = 1.41262528(29), the critical exponents to about nine digits (JHEP 2025).
progress.html: Bootstrapping the stress tensor gave Δσ = 0.518148806(24) and Δε = 1.41262528(29), the critical exponents to about nine digits (JHEP 2025).

nodes.html: Onsager solved the two-dimensional Ising model exactly in 1944, but no exact solution is known in three dimensions, where the model describes uniaxial magnets and the liquid–gas critical point. The conformal bootstrap now fixes its critical exponents to about nine digits (2024); an exact solution, or a proof that the critical point is a conformal field theory with these data, would settle it.
nodes.summary: Onsager solved the two-dimensional Ising model exactly in 1944, but no exact solution is known in three dimensions, where the model describes uniaxial magnets and the liquid–gas critical point.

nodes.title: Onsager’s Solution of the 2D Ising Model
nodes.html: Lars Onsager found in 1944 the exact free energy of the two-dimensional Ising model, showing that a lattice of interacting spins has a sharp phase transition with a logarithmic divergence of the specific heat. It was the first exact solution of an interacting model with a phase transition, and its critical behaviour became a benchmark for later theories.
nodes.summary: Lars Onsager found in 1944 the exact free energy of the two-dimensional Ising model, showing that a lattice of interacting spins has a sharp phase transition with a logarithmic divergence of the specific heat.

nodes.title: Landau Damping
nodes.html: Lev Landau showed in 1946 that a wave in a collisionless plasma can die away without any energy lost to collisions, because particles moving at nearly the wave’s speed exchange energy with it. The effect is a basic part of kinetic plasma theory, was confirmed in laboratory experiments in 1964, and has analogues in galactic dynamics.
nodes.summary: Lev Landau showed in 1946 that a wave in a collisionless plasma can die away without any energy lost to collisions, because particles moving at nearly the wave’s speed exchange energy with it.

nodes.title: Lamb Shift
nodes.html: Willis Lamb and Robert Retherford found in 1947, with microwaves, that two hydrogen levels that Dirac’s theory makes equal differ by about 1,000 MHz, later refined to 1,058 MHz. Hans Bethe explained the shift as the electron’s interaction with the quantum vacuum, with a high-energy cutoff, which showed how to handle infinities and launched renormalized quantum electrodynamics.
nodes.summary: Willis Lamb and Robert Retherford found in 1947, with microwaves, that two hydrogen levels that Dirac’s theory makes equal differ by about 1,000 MHz, later refined to 1,058 MHz.

nodes.title: Pion
nodes.html: Hideki Yukawa predicted in 1935 that the nuclear force is carried by a particle about 200 times heavier than the electron. In 1947 Cecil Powell, César Lattes, Giuseppe Occhialini and Hugh Muirhead found it, the pion, in cosmic-ray tracks in photographic emulsions exposed on mountains. Yukawa’s link between a force’s range and the exchanged particle’s mass became a standard tool.
nodes.summary: Hideki Yukawa predicted in 1935 that the nuclear force is carried by a particle about 200 times heavier than the electron.

nodes.title: Big Bang Nucleosynthesis
nodes.html: Ralph Alpher and George Gamow proposed in 1948 that nuclei formed by neutron capture in a hot, expanding early universe. This works for the lightest elements: Chushiro Hayashi (1950) and Alpher, Follin and Herman (1953) worked out the neutron-proton balance that leaves about a quarter of the mass as helium, and calculations in 1966-67 added deuterium, helium-3 and lithium-7.
nodes.summary: Ralph Alpher and George Gamow proposed in 1948 that nuclei formed by neutron capture in a hot, expanding early universe.

nodes.title: Nature of the Glass Transition

progress.what: Random first-order transition theory tied the glass transition to an ideal thermodynamic transition at which the configurational entropy vanishes, Kauzmann’s entropy crisis.
progress.html: Random first-order transition theory tied the glass transition to an ideal thermodynamic transition at which the configurational entropy vanishes, Kauzmann’s entropy crisis.

progress.what: Solved the glass transition of hard spheres exactly in the limit of infinite dimensions, finding a further Gardner transition inside the glass.
progress.html: Solved the glass transition of hard spheres exactly in the limit of infinite dimensions, finding a further Gardner transition inside the glass.

progress.what: Equilibrated model liquids below the laboratory glass temperature and found the configurational entropy still falling, consistent with but not proving an entropy crisis.
progress.html: Equilibrated model liquids below the laboratory glass temperature and found the configurational entropy still falling, consistent with but not proving an entropy crisis.

progress.what: In two dimensions the configurational entropy extrapolates to zero only at zero temperature, so any ideal glass transition there sits at T = 0.
progress.html: In two dimensions the configurational entropy extrapolates to zero only at zero temperature, so any ideal glass transition there sits at T = 0.

nodes.html: Why does a supercooled liquid become rigid without crystallizing, and is there an ideal glass transition with vanishing configurational entropy beneath the laboratory one (Kauzmann, 1948)? Philip Anderson called it the deepest unsolved problem in solid-state theory (1995). Mean-field theory is exact in infinite dimensions (2014), but simulations reaching far lower temperatures have not settled three dimensions.
nodes.summary: Why does a supercooled liquid become rigid without crystallizing, and is there an ideal glass transition with vanishing configurational entropy beneath the laboratory one (Kauzmann, 1948)?

nodes.title: Path Integral Formulation
nodes.html: Richard Feynman formulated quantum mechanics in 1948 as a sum over all paths between two points, each weighted by a phase given by the classical action divided by the reduced Planck constant. The idea built on Dirac’s 1933 observation that the action governs quantum evolution. It leads to Feynman diagrams and is used throughout particle physics and statistical mechanics.
nodes.summary: Richard Feynman formulated quantum mechanics in 1948 as a sum over all paths between two points, each weighted by a phase given by the classical action divided by the reduced Planck constant.

nodes.title: Quantum Field Theory
nodes.html: Quantum electrodynamics (1946–49), with Feynman diagrams and renormalization, predicts the electron’s magnetic moment to better than one part in a billion.
nodes.summary: Quantum electrodynamics (1946–49), with Feynman diagrams and renormalization, predicts the electron’s magnetic moment to better than one part in a billion.

nodes.title: Mott Insulator
