nodes.html: Nevill Mott pointed out in 1949 that a material with a half-filled electron band, which band theory says should be a metal, becomes an insulator when the electrons repel each other strongly enough to stay on their atoms. Nickel oxide is the classic example. Mott insulators are the parent materials of the high-temperature cuprate superconductors.
nodes.summary: Nevill Mott pointed out in 1949 that a material with a half-filled electron band, which band theory says should be a metal, becomes an insulator when the electrons repel each other strongly enough to stay on their atoms.

nodes.title: Nuclear Shell Model
nodes.html: Maria Goeppert Mayer and, independently, Hans Jensen with Otto Haxel and Hans Suess showed in 1949 that nuclei have proton and neutron shells that fill at the magic numbers 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82 and 126 once strong spin-orbit coupling is included. The model explains the stability of magic nuclei and the spins of ground states. Mayer and Jensen shared the 1963 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Maria Goeppert Mayer and, independently, Hans Jensen with Otto Haxel and Hans Suess showed in 1949 that nuclei have proton and neutron shells that fill at the magic numbers 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82 and 126 once strong spin-orbit coupling is included.

nodes.title: Numerical Weather Prediction
nodes.html: Lewis Fry Richardson worked out a forecast by hand during the First World War and published it in 1922, with an unrealistic result. In 1950 Jule Charney, Ragnar Fjørtoft and John von Neumann made the first successful computer forecast on ENIAC, using a simplified equation for the large-scale flow. Computer models of the atmosphere became the basis of modern weather prediction.
nodes.summary: Lewis Fry Richardson worked out a forecast by hand during the First World War and published it in 1922, with an unrealistic result.

nodes.title: Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou Problem
nodes.html: In 1953 Enrico Fermi, John Pasta, Stanisław Ulam and Mary Tsingou simulated on the MANIAC computer a chain of masses joined by slightly nonlinear springs, expecting energy put into one mode to spread among all. Instead it nearly returned to the start (report, 1955). The result led to solitons and the study of chaos and is one of the first computer experiments in physics.
nodes.summary: In 1953 Enrico Fermi, John Pasta, Stanisław Ulam and Mary Tsingou simulated on the MANIAC computer a chain of masses joined by slightly nonlinear springs, expecting energy put into one mode to spread among all.

nodes.title: Yang–Mills Gauge Theory
nodes.html: Chen-Ning Yang and Robert Mills proposed in 1954 a field theory in which a symmetry group acts differently at each point of spacetime, which requires massless vector fields that interact with themselves. Their non-abelian gauge theory generalizes electromagnetism and underlies the electroweak theory and quantum chromodynamics, so it is the framework of the Standard Model.
nodes.summary: Chen-Ning Yang and Robert Mills proposed in 1954 a field theory in which a symmetry group acts differently at each point of spacetime, which requires massless vector fields that interact with themselves.

nodes.title: Oxygen-Isotope Paleoclimate
nodes.html: Harold Urey calculated in 1947 that the ratio of oxygen isotopes in carbonate depends on the water temperature, and his group measured shell temperatures in 1951. Cesare Emiliani applied the method to deep-sea cores in 1955 and found many glacial cycles, and Willi Dansgaard and others read ice cores the same way, extending climate records back hundreds of thousands of years.
nodes.summary: Harold Urey calculated in 1947 that the ratio of oxygen isotopes in carbonate depends on the water temperature, and his group measured shell temperatures in 1951.

nodes.title: Age of the Earth
nodes.html: Clair Patterson measured lead isotopes in the Canyon Diablo iron meteorite and in Earth samples, and in 1956 reported an age of 4.55 billion years for Earth and the meteorites, a figure that has stood since. The ultra-clean laboratory methods he developed also showed that leaded petrol had contaminated the environment with lead, which contributed to its phase-out.
nodes.summary: Clair Patterson measured lead isotopes in the Canyon Diablo iron meteorite and in Earth samples, and in 1956 reported an age of 4.55 billion years for Earth and the meteorites, a figure that has stood since.

nodes.title: BEC in an Interacting Bose Gas

progress.what: Proved complete condensation in the ground state of a dilute trapped gas in the Gross–Pitaevskii limit.
progress.html: Proved complete condensation in the ground state of a dilute trapped gas in the Gross–Pitaevskii limit.

progress.what: Extended this to positive temperature in the same dilute trapped limit.
progress.html: Extended this to positive temperature in the same dilute trapped limit.

progress.what: Claimed proof of condensation at a positive, volume-independent temperature for the dilute three-dimensional hard-sphere gas in the thermodynamic limit, plus Bogoliubov’s depletion law at zero temperature (family 267 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof of condensation at a positive, volume-independent temperature for the dilute three-dimensional hard-sphere gas in the thermodynamic limit, plus Bogoliubov’s depletion law at zero temperature (family 267 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Einstein predicted Bose–Einstein condensation for an ideal gas in 1925, and Oliver Penrose and Lars Onsager defined it for interacting systems in 1956, but no proof showed it for an interacting gas in the thermodynamic limit outside special scaling limits. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims it for a dilute hard-sphere gas at positive temperature, formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: Einstein predicted Bose–Einstein condensation for an ideal gas in 1925, and Oliver Penrose and Lars Onsager defined it for interacting systems in 1956, but no proof showed it for an interacting gas in the thermodynamic limit outside special scaling limits.

nodes.title: Neutrino Detection
nodes.html: Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines detected antineutrinos from the Savannah River nuclear reactor in 1956 through inverse beta decay, in which an antineutrino turns a proton into a neutron and a positron. The particle Pauli had proposed in 1930 was seen 26 years later, and Reines received the 1995 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.
nodes.summary: Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines detected antineutrinos from the Savannah River nuclear reactor in 1956 through inverse beta decay, in which an antineutrino turns a proton into a neutron and a positron.

nodes.title: Stellar Nucleosynthesis (B²FH)
nodes.html: Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle showed in 1957 how nuclear reactions in stars build the elements from carbon to uranium, through helium burning and the slow (s) and rapid (r) neutron-capture processes. Alastair Cameron reached similar conclusions independently. Most heavy elements were thus made in stars and supernovae.
nodes.summary: Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle showed in 1957 how nuclear reactions in stars build the elements from carbon to uranium, through helium burning and the slow (s) and rapid (r) neutron-capture processes.

nodes.title: Magnetic Reconnection
nodes.html: Peter Sweet and Eugene Parker described in 1957-58 how oppositely directed magnetic field lines in a conducting plasma can break and rejoin in a thin current sheet, turning magnetic energy into heat and fast particles. James Dungey applied the idea to Earth’s magnetosphere in 1961. Reconnection powers solar flares and geomagnetic substorms and causes disruptions in tokamaks.
nodes.summary: Peter Sweet and Eugene Parker described in 1957-58 how oppositely directed magnetic field lines in a conducting plasma can break and rejoin in a thin current sheet, turning magnetic energy into heat and fast particles.

nodes.title: Mapping the Ocean Floor
nodes.html: Marie Tharp turned echo-sounding profiles of the North Atlantic into maps, and in 1952 noticed a rift valley running down the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. With Bruce Heezen and Maurice Ewing she showed by 1957 that the ridge is part of a mountain system encircling the globe. The rift valley supported the idea that the ocean floor is spreading apart.
nodes.summary: Marie Tharp turned echo-sounding profiles of the North Atlantic into maps, and in 1952 noticed a rift valley running down the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

nodes.title: Parity Violation
nodes.html: Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang proposed in 1956 that the weak interaction might not respect mirror symmetry. In 1957 Chien-Shiung Wu and colleagues showed it: electrons from the beta decay of cobalt-60 nuclei, polarized in a magnetic field at low temperature, were emitted preferentially in one direction. This overturned the assumption that physics looks the same in a mirror.
nodes.summary: Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang proposed in 1956 that the weak interaction might not respect mirror symmetry.

nodes.title: Fast Magnetic Reconnection Problem

progress.what: In the GEM reconnection challenge, every code that included the Hall effect reconnected at a similar fast rate, much faster than resistive MHD.
progress.html: In the GEM reconnection challenge, every code that included the Hall effect reconnected at a similar fast rate, much faster than resistive MHD.

progress.what: Simulations showed that the plasmoid instability shatters long current sheets, making even resistive MHD reconnection fast and nearly independent of resistivity.
progress.html: Simulations showed that the plasmoid instability shatters long current sheets, making even resistive MHD reconnection fast and nearly independent of resistivity.

progress.what: NASA’s Magnetospheric Multiscale mission flew through an electron diffusion region at Earth’s magnetopause and measured reconnection at electron scales.
progress.html: NASA’s Magnetospheric Multiscale mission flew through an electron diffusion region at Earth’s magnetopause and measured reconnection at electron scales.

progress.what: A geometric force-balance argument showed why steady reconnection has a maximum local rate of order 0.1, whatever the dissipation mechanism.
progress.html: A geometric force-balance argument showed why steady reconnection has a maximum local rate of order 0.1, whatever the dissipation mechanism.

nodes.html: Solar flares and magnetospheric substorms release magnetic energy far faster than the Sweet–Parker theory of reconnection (1957) allows. Simulations and spacecraft show a normalized rate of about 0.1 across many plasmas, and plasmoid instabilities and geometric arguments explain parts of it. A first-principles theory of the rate and of how reconnection switches on, tested against spacecraft data, would settle it.
nodes.summary: Solar flares and magnetospheric substorms release magnetic energy far faster than the Sweet–Parker theory of reconnection (1957) allows.

nodes.title: Anderson Localization
nodes.html: Philip Anderson showed in 1958 that in a sufficiently disordered medium, quantum waves such as electrons can be trapped in a small region and stop diffusing, so that a conductor can become an insulator at zero temperature. The effect applies to any wave and has been observed with light, sound and cold atoms.
nodes.summary: Philip Anderson showed in 1958 that in a sufficiently disordered medium, quantum waves such as electrons can be trapped in a small region and stop diffusing, so that a conductor can become an insulator at zero temperature.

nodes.title: Keeling Curve
nodes.html: Charles David Keeling began measuring carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa Observatory in March 1958, with an infrared gas analyzer, supported by Roger Revelle at Scripps. The record shows a seasonal cycle from plant growth and a steady rise from about 313 parts per million in 1958 to over 420 today, the clearest evidence that fossil fuel burning is raising atmospheric CO2.
nodes.summary: Charles David Keeling began measuring carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa Observatory in March 1958, with an infrared gas analyzer, supported by Roger Revelle at Scripps.

nodes.title: Solar Wind
nodes.html: Eugene Parker argued in 1958 that the Sun’s hot corona cannot stay in static equilibrium and must expand into space as a supersonic flow, the solar wind, which drags the Sun’s magnetic field into a spiral. Ludwig Biermann had inferred a continuous outflow from comet tails in 1951. Mariner 2 measured the wind directly in 1962.
nodes.summary: Eugene Parker argued in 1958 that the Sun’s hot corona cannot stay in static equilibrium and must expand into space as a supersonic flow, the solar wind, which drags the Sun’s magnetic field into a spiral.

nodes.title: Aharonov–Bohm Effect
nodes.html: Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm showed in 1959 that a charged particle’s quantum phase is shifted by electromagnetic potentials even where the fields vanish, so interference fringes move when magnetic flux is enclosed between the paths. Akira Tonomura’s electron holography confirmed it in 1986. The effect shows that potentials are physically meaningful in quantum theory.
nodes.summary: Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm showed in 1959 that a charged particle’s quantum phase is shifted by electromagnetic potentials even where the fields vanish, so interference fringes move when magnetic flux is enclosed between the paths.

nodes.title: Impact Craters
nodes.html: Eugene Shoemaker and Edward Chao showed in 1960 that Meteor Crater in Arizona was made by an impact, using the high-pressure mineral coesite found in its rocks and the structure of its rim. This established impact as a geological process and supported the view that most craters on the Moon are impact scars.
nodes.summary: Eugene Shoemaker and Edward Chao showed in 1960 that Meteor Crater in Arizona was made by an impact, using the high-pressure mineral coesite found in its rocks and the structure of its rim.

nodes.title: Nonlinear Optics
nodes.html: Peter Franken and colleagues sent a ruby laser beam through a quartz crystal in 1961 and saw light come out at exactly twice the frequency, the first observation of second-harmonic generation. Nicolaas Bloembergen then built the theory of nonlinear interactions of light with matter. Nonlinear optics underlies laser frequency conversion, ultrafast pulses and optical communications.
nodes.summary: Peter Franken and colleagues sent a ruby laser beam through a quartz crystal in 1961 and saw light come out at exactly twice the frequency, the first observation of second-harmonic generation.

nodes.title: Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking
nodes.html: Yoichiro Nambu, with Giovanni Jona-Lasinio, and independently Jeffrey Goldstone showed in 1960-61 that the laws of a system can have a symmetry that its lowest-energy state lacks, as in a superconductor, and that breaking a continuous symmetry produces massless Goldstone bosons. The idea led to the Higgs mechanism of 1964 and to the origin of particle masses in the Standard Model.
nodes.summary: Yoichiro Nambu, with Giovanni Jona-Lasinio, and independently Jeffrey Goldstone showed in 1960-61 that the laws of a system can have a symmetry that its lowest-energy state lacks, as in a superconductor, and that breaking a continuous symmetry produces massless Goldstone bosons.

nodes.title: Thermohaline Circulation
nodes.html: Henry Stommel showed in 1961 with a two-box model that the density-driven overturning of the ocean, set by temperature and salinity, can have two stable states, so ocean circulation can switch abruptly. Wallace Broecker’s picture of a global conveyor belt (1987) linked deep-water formation in the North Atlantic to rapid climate shifts recorded in ice cores.
nodes.summary: Henry Stommel showed in 1961 with a two-box model that the density-driven overturning of the ocean, set by temperature and salinity, can have two stable states, so ocean circulation can switch abruptly.

nodes.title: Josephson Effect
nodes.html: Brian Josephson predicted in 1962 that a supercurrent can flow between two superconductors separated by a thin insulating barrier, and that a voltage across the junction makes it oscillate at a frequency proportional to the voltage. Anderson and Rowell observed the current in 1963. Josephson junctions underlie SQUIDs, the voltage standard and superconducting qubits.
nodes.summary: Brian Josephson predicted in 1962 that a supercurrent can flow between two superconductors separated by a thin insulating barrier, and that a voltage across the junction makes it oscillate at a frequency proportional to the voltage.

nodes.title: Seafloor Spreading
nodes.html: Robert Dietz (1961) and Harry Hess (1962) proposed that new ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges and moves away on both sides, to be consumed in deep trenches, driven by mantle convection as Arthur Holmes had suggested in 1931. The idea explained why the ocean floor is young and gave continental drift a mechanism.
nodes.summary: Robert Dietz (1961) and Harry Hess (1962) proposed that new ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges and moves away on both sides, to be consumed in deep trenches, driven by mantle convection as Arthur Holmes had suggested in 1931.

nodes.title: Hubbard Model
nodes.html: John Hubbard, Martin Gutzwiller and Junjiro Kanamori each proposed in 1963 a model of electrons hopping between sites of a lattice and repelling each other when two occupy the same site. It is the simplest model of strongly correlated electrons, describes the Mott transition and magnetism, and is a standard test case for numerical methods and quantum simulators.
nodes.summary: John Hubbard, Martin Gutzwiller and Junjiro Kanamori each proposed in 1963 a model of electrons hopping between sites of a lattice and repelling each other when two occupy the same site.

nodes.title: Kerr Rotating Black Hole
nodes.html: Roy Kerr found in 1963 the exact solution of Einstein’s equations for the spacetime around a rotating mass. It has an event horizon, an ergosphere in which nothing can stay at rest, and a ring singularity. By the uniqueness theorems an uncharged black hole settles into a Kerr black hole, so the solution describes the black holes now observed.
nodes.summary: Roy Kerr found in 1963 the exact solution of Einstein’s equations for the spacetime around a rotating mass.

nodes.title: Quasars
nodes.html: Maarten Schmidt recognized in 1963 that the spectrum of the radio source 3C 273, whose position Cyril Hazard had fixed from lunar occultations, has hydrogen lines at a redshift of 0.158, which puts it roughly two billion light-years away. Quasars shine with the power of whole galaxies and are now understood to be fed by gas falling into supermassive black holes.
nodes.summary: Maarten Schmidt recognized in 1963 that the spectrum of the radio source 3C 273, whose position Cyril Hazard had fixed from lunar occultations, has hydrogen lines at a redshift of 0.158, which puts it roughly two billion light-years away.

nodes.title: Magnetic Stripes on the Seafloor
nodes.html: Frederick Vine and Drummond Matthews (1963), and independently Lawrence Morley, proposed that the magnetic stripes measured across mid-ocean ridges record reversals of Earth’s field in new crust as it forms and spreads symmetrically. The pattern gave direct, testable evidence for seafloor spreading and a way of dating the ocean floor.
nodes.summary: Frederick Vine and Drummond Matthews (1963), and independently Lawrence Morley, proposed that the magnetic stripes measured across mid-ocean ridges record reversals of Earth’s field in new crust as it forms and spreads symmetrically.

nodes.title: Bell’s Theorem
nodes.html: John Stewart Bell proved in 1964 that no theory with local hidden variables can reproduce all the predictions of quantum mechanics: correlations between measurements on entangled particles can exceed a bound, the Bell inequality. This turned the debate between Einstein and Bohr over hidden variables into a question that experiments can decide.
nodes.summary: John Stewart Bell proved in 1964 that no theory with local hidden variables can reproduce all the predictions of quantum mechanics: correlations between measurements on entangled particles can exceed a bound, the Bell inequality.

nodes.title: CP Violation
nodes.html: James Cronin, Val Fitch, James Christenson and René Turlay found in 1964 that neutral kaons, which should decay in a way symmetric under combined charge conjugation and parity (CP), sometimes violate it, in about 2 of every 1,000 decays. Matter and antimatter therefore behave slightly differently, a necessary condition for a universe with more matter than antimatter.
nodes.summary: James Cronin, Val Fitch, James Christenson and René Turlay found in 1964 that neutral kaons, which should decay in a way symmetric under combined charge conjugation and parity (CP), sometimes violate it, in about 2 of every 1,000 decays.

nodes.title: Quark Model
nodes.html: After the Eightfold Way of Murray Gell-Mann and Yuval Ne’eman (1961) sorted the known hadrons into patterns, Gell-Mann and, independently, George Zweig proposed in 1964 that hadrons are made of three kinds of fractionally charged constituents, the quarks. The model accounted for the hadron spectrum and, after deep inelastic scattering in 1968, was accepted as real.
nodes.summary: After the Eightfold Way of Murray Gell-Mann and Yuval Ne’eman (1961) sorted the known hadrons into patterns, Gell-Mann and, independently, George Zweig proposed in 1964 that hadrons are made of three kinds of fractionally charged constituents, the quarks.

nodes.title: Singularity Theorems
nodes.html: Roger Penrose proved in 1965 that once a star has collapsed far enough to form a trapped surface, general relativity requires a singularity, a place where spacetime ends. Stephen Hawking applied the argument to the expanding universe, and the Hawking-Penrose theorem of 1970 covered both cases. The theorems showed that singularities are generic predictions of general relativity.
nodes.summary: Roger Penrose proved in 1965 that once a star has collapsed far enough to form a trapped surface, general relativity requires a singularity, a place where spacetime ends.

nodes.title: Matter–Antimatter Asymmetry

progress.what: Showed that anomalous electroweak processes violate baryon number rapidly in the hot early universe, opening electroweak baryogenesis.
progress.html: Showed that anomalous electroweak processes violate baryon number rapidly in the hot early universe, opening electroweak baryogenesis.

progress.what: Leptogenesis: decays of heavy neutrinos create a lepton excess that electroweak processes convert into baryons.
progress.html: Leptogenesis: decays of heavy neutrinos create a lepton excess that electroweak processes convert into baryons.

progress.what: For a Higgs as heavy as the W boson or heavier, the Standard Model has no electroweak phase transition, which rules out electroweak baryogenesis within it.
progress.html: For a Higgs as heavy as the W boson or heavier, the Standard Model has no electroweak phase transition, which rules out electroweak baryogenesis within it.

progress.what: First observation of CP violation in baryon decays, in Λb decays to pK⁻π⁺π⁻, consistent with the Standard Model.
progress.html: First observation of CP violation in baryon decays, in Λb decays to pK⁻π⁺π⁻, consistent with the Standard Model.

nodes.html: Why does the universe contain matter but almost no antimatter, about six baryons for every ten billion photons? Sakharov (1967) listed the conditions any explanation must meet, but Standard Model CP violation is far too weak and its electroweak transition is a smooth crossover. Leptogenesis and electroweak baryogenesis with new particles remain the leading candidates; none is confirmed.
nodes.summary: Why does the universe contain matter but almost no antimatter, about six baryons for every ten billion photons?

nodes.title: First Climate Model
nodes.html: Syukuro Manabe and Richard Wetherald published in 1967 a one-dimensional model of the atmosphere that treated radiation, convection and water vapour feedback together. It found that doubling carbon dioxide would warm the surface by about 2 degrees Celsius and cool the stratosphere, as later observed. Manabe shared the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics.
nodes.summary: Syukuro Manabe and Richard Wetherald published in 1967 a one-dimensional model of the atmosphere that treated radiation, convection and water vapour feedback together.

nodes.title: Plate Tectonics
nodes.html: Dan McKenzie and Robert Parker (1967), Jason Morgan (1968) and Xavier Le Pichon (1968) described Earth’s surface as rigid plates moving over the globe and meeting at ridges, trenches and transform faults, building on Tuzo Wilson’s transform faults (1965). The theory explains earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain building and organizes the earth sciences.
nodes.summary: Dan McKenzie and Robert Parker (1967), Jason Morgan (1968) and Xavier Le Pichon (1968) described Earth’s surface as rigid plates moving over the globe and meeting at ridges, trenches and transform faults, building on Tuzo Wilson’s transform faults (1965).

nodes.title: Pulsars
nodes.html: Jocelyn Bell Burnell, a graduate student working with Antony Hewish, noticed in 1967 a radio source in the Cambridge survey that pulsed with a period of 1.337 seconds. The pulses come from a rapidly rotating neutron star whose radio beam sweeps past Earth. Pulsars were the first observational evidence for neutron stars, and Hewish shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics.
nodes.summary: Jocelyn Bell Burnell, a graduate student working with Antony Hewish, noticed in 1967 a radio source in the Cambridge survey that pulsed with a period of 1.337 seconds.

nodes.title: Sakharov Conditions
nodes.html: Andrei Sakharov listed in 1967 three conditions for a universe that starts with equal matter and antimatter to end up with more matter: baryon number must be violated, charge conjugation and CP symmetry must both be violated, and there must be a departure from thermal equilibrium. The conditions frame most theories of the origin of the matter-antimatter asymmetry.
nodes.summary: Andrei Sakharov listed in 1967 three conditions for a universe that starts with equal matter and antimatter to end up with more matter: baryon number must be violated, charge conjugation and CP symmetry must both be violated, and there must be a departure from thermal equilibrium.

nodes.title: Stability of Matter
nodes.html: Freeman Dyson and Andrew Lenard proved in 1967-68 that the energy of ordinary matter made of electrons and nuclei is bounded below by a multiple of the number of particles, so matter does not collapse or release unlimited energy. The proof relies on the exclusion principle, and Elliott Lieb and Walter Thirring gave a much shorter proof in 1975.
nodes.summary: Freeman Dyson and Andrew Lenard proved in 1967-68 that the energy of ordinary matter made of electrons and nuclei is bounded below by a multiple of the number of particles, so matter does not collapse or release unlimited energy.

nodes.title: Quarks Seen Inside the Proton
nodes.html: Experiments at SLAC led by Jerome Friedman, Henry Kendall and Richard Taylor scattered high-energy electrons from protons in 1968-69 and found that they bounce off small, hard constituents, as James Bjorken had predicted and Richard Feynman interpreted in terms of point-like partons. The partons were identified with quarks, the first direct evidence that quarks are real.
nodes.summary: Experiments at SLAC led by Jerome Friedman, Henry Kendall and Richard Taylor scattered high-energy electrons from protons in 1968-69 and found that they bounce off small, hard constituents, as James Bjorken had predicted and Richard Feynman interpreted in terms of point-like partons.

nodes.title: Chiral Anomaly
nodes.html: Stephen Adler, and independently John Bell and Roman Jackiw, showed in 1969 that chiral symmetry, a symmetry of the classical theory of massless fermions, is broken by quantum effects when the particles are coupled to gauge fields. The anomaly explains the decay of the neutral pion into two photons and constrains which gauge theories are consistent.
nodes.summary: Stephen Adler, and independently John Bell and Roman Jackiw, showed in 1969 that chiral symmetry, a symmetry of the classical theory of massless fermions, is broken by quantum effects when the particles are coupled to gauge fields.

nodes.title: Cosmic Censorship Conjecture

progress.what: For spherical collapse of a scalar field, the naked singularities he had constructed are unstable: weak censorship holds for generic data in this model.
progress.html: For spherical collapse of a scalar field, the naked singularities he had constructed are unstable: weak censorship holds for generic data in this model.

progress.what: The Cauchy horizon inside a rotating Kerr black hole is stable in the C0 sense, so the C0 form of strong censorship is false; Christodoulou’s weaker formulation survives. Published in Annals of Mathematics in 2025.
progress.html: The Cauchy horizon inside a rotating Kerr black hole is stable in the C0 sense, so the C0 form of strong censorship is false; Christodoulou’s weaker formulation survives. Published in Annals of Mathematics in 2025.

progress.what: Strong censorship in the C2 sense for generic two-ended data in spherical symmetry with a scalar field.
progress.html: Strong censorship in the C2 sense for generic two-ended data in spherical symmetry with a scalar field.

progress.what: Claimed proof of strong censorship in Christodoulou’s formulation near two-ended Kerr data: generic nearby vacuum data admit no continuous extension with locally square-integrable connection (family 264 of OpenAI’s math release). Not formalized and not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof of strong censorship in Christodoulou’s formulation near two-ended Kerr data: generic nearby vacuum data admit no continuous extension with locally square-integrable connection (family 264 of OpenAI’s math release). Not formalized and not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Penrose (1969) conjectured that singularities formed by realistic gravitational collapse are hidden inside black holes (weak censorship); a strong version says Einstein’s equations are generically deterministic, with no continuation past a Cauchy horizon. Both are open beyond symmetric models, and Dafermos and Luk (2017) showed that the C0 form of strong censorship fails. It is problem 15 on Barry Simon’s 1984 list.
nodes.summary: Penrose (1969) conjectured that singularities formed by realistic gravitational collapse are hidden inside black holes (weak censorship); a strong version says Einstein’s equations are generically deterministic, with no continuation past a Cauchy horizon.

nodes.title: Energy-Balance Climate Models
nodes.html: Mikhail Budyko and William Sellers published in 1969 simple climate models in which the temperature at each latitude balances absorbed sunlight against emitted heat, with ice reflecting sunlight. The ice-albedo feedback allows more than one climate for the same sunlight and makes a runaway to a fully frozen Earth possible. Such models are still used for conceptual studies.
nodes.summary: Mikhail Budyko and William Sellers published in 1969 simple climate models in which the temperature at each latitude balances absorbed sunlight against emitted heat, with ice reflecting sunlight.

nodes.title: El Niño–Southern Oscillation
nodes.html: Gilbert Walker found in the 1920s that surface pressure over the Pacific and Indian Oceans rises and falls in opposition, the Southern Oscillation. In 1969 Jacob Bjerknes explained that it is coupled to El Niño warming of the eastern Pacific by a feedback between trade winds and sea surface temperature. ENSO is the largest natural source of year-to-year climate variability.
nodes.summary: Gilbert Walker found in the 1920s that surface pressure over the Pacific and Indian Oceans rises and falls in opposition, the Southern Oscillation.

nodes.title: Renormalization Group
nodes.html: Kenneth Wilson showed in 1971 how to describe a system by averaging out its short-distance details step by step, so that physics at different scales is linked by flows in the space of theories. Building on Leo Kadanoff’s block-spin idea, it explained why very different systems share the same critical behaviour and became central to field theory and condensed matter physics.
nodes.summary: Kenneth Wilson showed in 1971 how to describe a system by averaging out its short-distance details step by step, so that physics at different scales is linked by flows in the space of theories.

nodes.title: Faint Young Sun Paradox

progress.what: Argued that a lower albedo, from less continental area and fewer clouds, could keep early Earth warm with modest CO2.
progress.html: Argued that a lower albedo, from less continental area and fewer clouds, could keep early Earth warm with modest CO2.

progress.what: Three-dimensional general circulation models found temperate Archean climates with moderate amounts of CO2 and methane.
progress.html: Three-dimensional general circulation models found temperate Archean climates with moderate amounts of CO2 and methane.

progress.what: A review concluded that enough CO2, possibly with methane, can solve the paradox in 3D models, while the actual Archean CO2 level remains poorly constrained.
progress.html: A review concluded that enough CO2, possibly with methane, can solve the paradox in 3D models, while the actual Archean CO2 level remains poorly constrained.

nodes.html: Early in Earth’s history the Sun was 20–30% dimmer, yet geology shows liquid water on the young Earth (Sagan and Mullen, 1972). Which mix of greenhouse gases, clouds and surface albedo kept it warm? Three-dimensional climate models show that more CO2, possibly with methane, can do it, so the open question is what the Archean atmosphere contained; proxies that pin down Archean CO2 would settle it.
nodes.summary: Early in Earth’s history the Sun was 20–30% dimmer, yet geology shows liquid water on the young Earth (Sagan and Mullen, 1972).

nodes.title: Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless Transition
nodes.html: Vadim Berezinskii (1970-71) and, independently, Michael Kosterlitz and David Thouless (1972-73) showed that two-dimensional systems such as superfluid films have a phase transition in which vortices and antivortices bind in pairs below a critical temperature and unbind above it. It was the first topological phase transition, and Kosterlitz and Thouless shared the 2016 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Vadim Berezinskii (1970-71) and, independently, Michael Kosterlitz and David Thouless (1972-73) showed that two-dimensional systems such as superfluid films have a phase transition in which vortices and antivortices bind in pairs below a critical temperature and unbind above it.

nodes.title: Black Hole Thermodynamics
nodes.html: Jacob Bekenstein proposed in 1972-73 that a black hole has an entropy proportional to the area of its event horizon. In 1973 James Bardeen, Brandon Carter and Stephen Hawking derived four laws of black hole mechanics that parallel the laws of thermodynamics. Hawking’s discovery of black hole radiation in 1974 showed that the analogy is physical.
nodes.summary: Jacob Bekenstein proposed in 1972-73 that a black hole has an entropy proportional to the area of its event horizon.

nodes.title: Kobayashi–Maskawa Matrix
nodes.html: Makoto Kobayashi and Toshihide Maskawa showed in 1973 that CP violation in the Standard Model needs at least three generations of quarks, when only three quarks were known. The bottom (1977) and top (1995) quarks were then found, and their mixing matrix, with a complex phase, describes how quarks change flavour in weak decays. They shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physics.
nodes.summary: Makoto Kobayashi and Toshihide Maskawa showed in 1973 that CP violation in the Standard Model needs at least three generations of quarks, when only three quarks were known.

nodes.title: Penrose Inequality

progress.what: Proved the time-symmetric (Riemannian) inequality for the area of a connected horizon, using weak inverse mean curvature flow.
progress.html: Proved the time-symmetric (Riemannian) inequality for the area of a connected horizon, using weak inverse mean curvature flow.

progress.what: Proved the Riemannian inequality for horizons with any number of components, using a conformal flow of metrics and the positive mass theorem.
progress.html: Proved the Riemannian inequality for horizons with any number of components, using a conformal flow of metrics and the positive mass theorem.

progress.what: Proved a spacetime Penrose inequality with a suboptimal constant, for asymptotically flat and asymptotically hyperboloidal data.
progress.html: Proved a spacetime Penrose inequality with a suboptimal constant, for asymptotically flat and asymptotically hyperboloidal data.

progress.what: Claimed proof of the sharp spacetime Penrose inequality, with minimal enclosing area, for one-ended asymptotically flat data obeying the dominant energy condition in every dimension n ≥ 3 (family 260 of OpenAI’s math release). The main inequality is not formalized in Lean and has not been independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof of the sharp spacetime Penrose inequality, with minimal enclosing area, for one-ended asymptotically flat data obeying the dominant energy condition in every dimension n ≥ 3 (family 260 of OpenAI’s math release). The main inequality is not formalized in Lean and has not been independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Penrose (1973) argued that a spacetime containing black holes has total mass at least √(A/16π), where A is the horizon area. The time-symmetric (Riemannian) case was proved by Huisken and Ilmanen (1997) and Bray (1999); the general case with momentum, the spacetime Penrose conjecture, stayed open until a 2026 claim of the sharp inequality, which awaits independent review.
nodes.summary: Penrose (1973) argued that a spacetime containing black holes has total mass at least √(A/16π), where A is the horizon area.

nodes.title: Quantum Spin Liquids
nodes.html: Philip Anderson proposed in 1973 the resonating valence bond state, in which the spins of a frustrated magnet pair into singlets that fluctuate between arrangements, so that the system never orders even at zero temperature. He revived the idea in 1987 as a possible origin of high-temperature superconductivity. Candidate materials are still debated.
nodes.summary: Philip Anderson proposed in 1973 the resonating valence bond state, in which the spins of a frustrated magnet pair into singlets that fluctuate between arrangements, so that the system never orders even at zero temperature.

nodes.title: Standard Model
nodes.html: Electroweak unification (1961–68) plus quantum chromodynamics (1973) account for every known particle and every force except gravity.
nodes.summary: Electroweak unification (1961–68) plus quantum chromodynamics (1973) account for every known particle and every force except gravity.

nodes.title: Hulse–Taylor Binary Pulsar
nodes.html: Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found in 1974 a pulsar, PSR B1913+16, in a tight eight-hour orbit with another neutron star. The orbit shrinks by about 3.5 metres a year, within a fraction of a percent of the loss general relativity predicts from gravitational waves. It was the first, indirect, evidence for gravitational waves and earned the 1993 Nobel Prize in Physics.
nodes.summary: Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found in 1974 a pulsar, PSR B1913+16, in a tight eight-hour orbit with another neutron star.

nodes.title: Hawking Radiation
nodes.html: Stephen Hawking showed in 1974 that quantum effects near the event horizon make a black hole emit thermal radiation, with a temperature inversely proportional to its mass. A black hole therefore slowly evaporates, which gave physical meaning to its entropy and raised the black hole information paradox. The radiation from astrophysical black holes is far too faint to observe.
nodes.summary: Stephen Hawking showed in 1974 that quantum effects near the event horizon make a black hole emit thermal radiation, with a temperature inversely proportional to its mass.

nodes.title: Lattice Gauge Theory
nodes.html: Kenneth Wilson formulated gauge theory on a spacetime lattice in 1974. The lattice makes strongly coupled theories computable and gave a picture of how quarks are confined. Lattice QCD computed the masses of protons and other hadrons from first principles (Budapest-Marseille-Wuppertal, 2008) and supplies inputs for precision tests of the Standard Model.
nodes.summary: Kenneth Wilson formulated gauge theory on a spacetime lattice in 1974.

nodes.title: Giant-Impact Hypothesis
nodes.html: William Hartmann and Donald Davis (1975), and independently Alastair Cameron and William Ward (1976), proposed that the Moon formed from debris thrown out when a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth. The idea explains the Moon’s small iron core and the large angular momentum of the Earth-Moon system, and it is now the leading theory of lunar origin.
nodes.summary: William Hartmann and Donald Davis (1975), and independently Alastair Cameron and William Ward (1976), proposed that the Moon formed from debris thrown out when a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth.

nodes.title: Black Hole Information Paradox

progress.what: If evaporation is unitary, the entanglement entropy of the radiation must rise and then fall, turning over about halfway through: the Page curve.
progress.html: If evaporation is unitary, the entanglement entropy of the radiation must rise and then fall, turning over about halfway through: the Page curve.

progress.what: Argued that unitarity, effective field theory and a smooth horizon cannot all hold for an old black hole, suggesting a ‘firewall’ at the horizon (JHEP 2013).
progress.html: Argued that unitarity, effective field theory and a smooth horizon cannot all hold for an old black hole, suggesting a ‘firewall’ at the horizon (JHEP 2013).

progress.what: Quantum extremal surfaces that jump after the Page time reproduce the Page curve for evaporating black holes in holographic models.
progress.html: Quantum extremal surfaces that jump after the Page time reproduce the Page curve for evaporating black holes in holographic models.

progress.what: Two groups derived the same ‘island’ rule from the gravitational path integral, where replica wormholes give the Page curve.
progress.html: Two groups derived the same ‘island’ rule from the gravitational path integral, where replica wormholes give the Page curve.

nodes.html: If a black hole evaporates into purely thermal Hawking radiation, the information about what fell in seems destroyed, contradicting quantum mechanics (Hawking, 1976). Calculations since 2019 with quantum extremal surfaces and replica wormholes reproduce the Page curve that unitarity requires, mostly in simplified models; how the information gets out of a realistic black hole, and what an infalling observer meets, remain open.
nodes.summary: If a black hole evaporates into purely thermal Hawking radiation, the information about what fell in seems destroyed, contradicting quantum mechanics (Hawking, 1976).

nodes.title: Lieb–Thirring Conjecture

progress.what: Sharp constant in one dimension for γ = 1/2: it equals 1/2, the one-bound-state value.
progress.html: Sharp constant in one dimension for γ = 1/2: it equals 1/2, the one-bound-state value.

progress.what: The semiclassical constant is sharp for every γ ≥ 3/2 in every dimension.
progress.html: The semiclassical constant is sharp for every γ ≥ 3/2 in every dimension.

progress.what: Best bound for the key case: the constant for γ = 1 in three dimensions is at most 1.456 times the semiclassical value.
progress.html: Best bound for the key case: the constant for γ = 1 in three dimensions is at most 1.456 times the semiclassical value.

progress.what: Claimed proof of the one-dimensional conjecture for 1/2 < γ < 3/2: the sharp constant is the one-bound-state value, also for matrix-valued potentials (family 262 of OpenAI’s math release, main theorem formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed; the three-dimensional case is untouched.
progress.html: Claimed proof of the one-dimensional conjecture for 1/2 < γ < 3/2: the sharp constant is the one-bound-state value, also for matrix-valued potentials (family 262 of OpenAI’s math release, main theorem formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed; the three-dimensional case is untouched.

nodes.html: Lieb and Thirring (1976) conjectured the sharp constants in their inequality, which bounds the kinetic energy of many fermions and underlies the stability of matter. The key case, three dimensions with γ = 1, should have the semiclassical constant of Thomas–Fermi theory; the best proven bound is 1.456 times that value (2018), and sharp constants are known only for γ ≥ 3/2 and a few one-dimensional cases.
nodes.summary: Lieb and Thirring (1976) conjectured the sharp constants in their inequality, which bounds the kinetic energy of many fermions and underlies the stability of matter.

nodes.title: Mid-Pleistocene Transition

progress.what: Proposed that glaciers gradually scraped away soft regolith, so ice sheets could rest on bedrock, grow thicker and last longer.
progress.html: Proposed that glaciers gradually scraped away soft regolith, so ice sheets could rest on bedrock, grow thicker and last longer.

progress.what: Showed that late Pleistocene deglaciations are paced by obliquity and precession together, not by the 100,000-year eccentricity cycle itself.
progress.html: Showed that late Pleistocene deglaciations are paced by obliquity and precession together, not by the 100,000-year eccentricity cycle itself.

progress.what: An Earth-system model reproduced the transition when CO2 declined slowly and regolith was removed.
progress.html: An Earth-system model reproduced the transition when CO2 declined slowly and regolith was removed.

progress.what: Showed distinct roles for precession, obliquity and eccentricity, making the timing of the last 900,000 years of terminations largely predictable.
progress.html: Showed distinct roles for precession, obliquity and eccentricity, making the timing of the last 900,000 years of terminations largely predictable.

nodes.html: Between about 1.2 and 0.8 million years ago, ice-age cycles switched from a 41,000-year rhythm to longer, stronger cycles averaging 100,000 years, with no matching change in orbital forcing; the 100,000-year cycle was identified in 1976. Was it declining CO2, erosion of regolith under ice sheets or internal dynamics? A model that reproduces the switch and its timing from physical drivers would settle it.
nodes.summary: Between about 1.2 and 0.8 million years ago, ice-age cycles switched from a 41,000-year rhythm to longer, stronger cycles averaging 100,000 years, with no matching change in orbital forcing; the 100,000-year cycle was identified in 1976.

nodes.title: Strong CP Problem

progress.what: Proposed a new symmetry that dynamically sets the CP-violating angle θ to zero.
progress.html: Proposed a new symmetry that dynamically sets the CP-violating angle θ to zero.

progress.what: Independently showed that the Peccei–Quinn mechanism implies a new light particle, the axion.
progress.html: Independently showed that the Peccei–Quinn mechanism implies a new light particle, the axion.

progress.what: The Axion Dark Matter Experiment became the first search sensitive to the most plausible (DFSZ) axion couplings, over a narrow mass range.
progress.html: The Axion Dark Matter Experiment became the first search sensitive to the most plausible (DFSZ) axion couplings, over a narrow mass range.

progress.what: The neutron’s electric dipole moment is below 1.8 × 10⁻²⁶ e·cm (90% confidence), so θ must be below about 10⁻¹⁰.
progress.html: The neutron’s electric dipole moment is below 1.8 × 10⁻²⁶ e·cm (90% confidence), so θ must be below about 10⁻¹⁰.

nodes.html: Quantum chromodynamics allows a CP-violating parameter θ, yet the neutron’s electric dipole moment, measured below 1.8 × 10⁻²⁶ e·cm (2020), forces θ below about 10⁻¹⁰. Why is it so small? The leading answer, the Peccei–Quinn mechanism (1977) with its axion, also supplies a dark-matter candidate; detecting the axion, or another mechanism that explains the tiny θ, would settle it.
nodes.summary: Quantum chromodynamics allows a CP-violating parameter θ, yet the neutron’s electric dipole moment, measured below 1.8 × 10⁻²⁶ e·cm (2020), forces θ below about 10⁻¹⁰.

nodes.title: Meter-Size Barrier

progress.what: Discovered the streaming instability: drag between gas and drifting solids makes particles clump spontaneously.
progress.html: Discovered the streaming instability: drag between gas and drifting solids makes particles clump spontaneously.

progress.what: Simulations showed boulders concentrated in turbulent disks collapse gravitationally into planetesimals within a few orbits.
progress.html: Simulations showed boulders concentrated in turbulent disks collapse gravitationally into planetesimals within a few orbits.

progress.what: The orbital orientations of Kuiper-belt binaries match those predicted for planetesimals formed by the streaming instability and collapse.
progress.html: The orbital orientations of Kuiper-belt binaries match those predicted for planetesimals formed by the streaming instability and collapse.

progress.what: Turbulence can raise the dust-to-gas ratio needed for the streaming instability to form planetesimals by up to an order of magnitude.
progress.html: Turbulence can raise the dust-to-gas ratio needed for the streaming instability to form planetesimals by up to an order of magnitude.

nodes.html: Dust in a planet-forming disk sticks into pebbles, but bodies around a metre across should bounce, fragment or drift into the star faster than they can grow (Weidenschilling, 1977). How do kilometre-sized planetesimals form? The streaming instability followed by gravitational collapse is the leading answer and fits Kuiper-belt binaries, but whether it works under realistic disk turbulence is open.
nodes.summary: Dust in a planet-forming disk sticks into pebbles, but bodies around a metre across should bounce, fragment or drift into the star faster than they can grow (Weidenschilling, 1977).

nodes.title: Flat Galaxy Rotation Curves
nodes.html: Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured from 1970 the speeds of stars and gas at different distances from the centres of spiral galaxies, and Albert Bosma traced hydrogen gas in outer disks with radio telescopes (1978). The rotation speeds stay flat far beyond the visible edge, so galaxies hold much more mass than their stars and gas show, a main piece of evidence for dark matter.
nodes.summary: Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured from 1970 the speeds of stars and gas at different distances from the centres of spiral galaxies, and Albert Bosma traced hydrogen gas in outer disks with radio telescopes (1978).

nodes.title: Extended States in the Anderson Model

progress.what: Proved absence of diffusion at strong disorder or extreme energies in any dimension, with multiscale analysis.
progress.html: Proved absence of diffusion at strong disorder or extreme energies in any dimension, with multiscale analysis.

progress.what: Proved extended states at weak disorder on the Bethe lattice, an infinite tree.
progress.html: Proved extended states at weak disorder on the Bethe lattice, an infinite tree.

progress.what: Claimed proofs for uniform disorder: purely absolutely continuous spectrum on an energy interval at weak disorder in every dimension d ≥ 3, and pure-point spectrum at every disorder in two dimensions (family 261 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proofs for uniform disorder: purely absolutely continuous spectrum on an energy interval at weak disorder in every dimension d ≥ 3, and pure-point spectrum at every disorder in two dimensions (family 261 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: The 1979 scaling theory of localization predicted that weak disorder leaves extended, conducting electron states in three or more dimensions, while in two dimensions every state localizes. Barry Simon listed proving both for the lattice Anderson model among his problems of 1984 and 2000. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims both, formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: The 1979 scaling theory of localization predicted that weak disorder leaves extended, conducting electron states in three or more dimensions, while in two dimensions every state localizes.

nodes.title: Charney Report
nodes.html: A US National Academy of Sciences panel chaired by Jule Charney reviewed in 1979 the climate models of Syukuro Manabe and James Hansen and estimated that doubling carbon dioxide would warm the world by 3 degrees Celsius, with an uncertainty of 1.5 degrees either way. The range of 1.5 to 4.5 degrees stood as the standard estimate of climate sensitivity for about four decades.
nodes.summary: A US National Academy of Sciences panel chaired by Jule Charney reviewed in 1979 the climate models of Syukuro Manabe and James Hansen and estimated that doubling carbon dioxide would warm the world by 3 degrees Celsius, with an uncertainty of 1.5 degrees either way.

nodes.title: Equilibrium Climate Sensitivity

progress.what: Combining process understanding, the historical record and paleoclimate gave a likely range of 2.6–3.9 K, the first major narrowing since 1979.
progress.html: Combining process understanding, the historical record and paleoclimate gave a likely range of 2.6–3.9 K, the first major narrowing since 1979.

progress.what: The Sixth Assessment Report gave a best estimate of 3 °C, likely 2.5–4 °C and very likely 2–5 °C.
progress.html: The Sixth Assessment Report gave a best estimate of 3 °C, likely 2.5–4 °C and very likely 2–5 °C.

progress.what: Argued that the 2020 assessment’s probability distributions are still approximately valid, and that narrowing them needs better understanding of key climate processes and paleoclimate proxies.
progress.html: Argued that the 2020 assessment’s probability distributions are still approximately valid, and that narrowing them needs better understanding of key climate processes and paleoclimate proxies.

progress.what: Low-sensitivity climate models fail to reproduce the observed growth of Earth’s energy imbalance, evidence against the low end of the range.
progress.html: Low-sensitivity climate models fail to reproduce the observed growth of Earth’s energy imbalance, evidence against the low end of the range.

nodes.html: How much will Earth eventually warm if atmospheric CO2 doubles? The 1979 Charney report estimated 1.5–4.5 °C; multiple lines of evidence have narrowed it to a likely 2.5–4 °C (IPCC, 2021), with cloud feedbacks the main uncertainty. Narrowing the range to about half a degree, which would sharpen every carbon budget, is the goal.
nodes.summary: How much will Earth eventually warm if atmospheric CO2 doubles?

nodes.title: Spin Glasses
nodes.html: Sam Edwards and Philip Anderson proposed in 1975 a model of magnets with random interactions, the spin glass. Giorgio Parisi solved its mean-field version in 1979 with replica symmetry breaking; Francesco Guerra and Michel Talagrand proved his free-energy formula in 2003-06. The methods are used in optimization and neural networks, and Parisi shared the 2021 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Sam Edwards and Philip Anderson proposed in 1975 a model of magnets with random interactions, the spin glass.

nodes.title: Final Parsec Problem

progress.what: In any triaxial galaxy, stars on centrophilic orbits drive the binary to coalescence within about a billion years, even without collisional relaxation.
progress.html: In any triaxial galaxy, stars on centrophilic orbits drive the binary to coalescence within about a billion years, even without collisional relaxation.

progress.what: Simulations of merger remnants found collisionless refilling of the loss cone keeps binaries hardening, arguing there is no final parsec problem (MNRAS 2017).
progress.html: Simulations of merger remnants found collisionless refilling of the loss cone keeps binaries hardening, arguing there is no final parsec problem (MNRAS 2017).

progress.what: Evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background, consistent with a population of supermassive black-hole binaries at sub-parsec separations.
progress.html: Evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background, consistent with a population of supermassive black-hole binaries at sub-parsec separations.

progress.what: Showed that self-interacting dark matter could absorb the binary’s orbital energy at parsec separations while matching the observed background spectrum (PRL 2024).
progress.html: Showed that self-interacting dark matter could absorb the binary’s orbital energy at parsec separations while matching the observed background spectrum (PRL 2024).

nodes.html: When galaxies merge, their central black holes sink to within about a parsec of each other, where stellar encounters seem too few and gravitational waves too weak to finish the merger (Begelman, Blandford and Rees, 1980). Triaxial galaxy shapes, gas or dark matter may close the gap; the nanohertz gravitational-wave background found in 2023 suggests binaries do get closer, but which mechanism operates is unsettled.
nodes.summary: When galaxies merge, their central black holes sink to within about a parsec of each other, where stellar encounters seem too few and gravitational waves too weak to finish the merger (Begelman, Blandford and Rees, 1980).

nodes.title: Quantum Hall Effect
nodes.html: In 1980 Klaus von Klitzing found that in a two-dimensional electron gas in a silicon transistor at low temperature and high magnetic field, the Hall resistance sits on plateaus at exactly h/e² divided by an integer, whatever the sample’s size or purity. The effect gives a reproducible resistance standard and was later understood as a topological property of electron bands.
nodes.summary: In 1980 Klaus von Klitzing found that in a two-dimensional electron gas in a silicon transistor at low temperature and high magnetic field, the Hall resistance sits on plateaus at exactly h/e² divided by an integer, whatever the sample’s size or purity.

nodes.title: Cosmic Inflation
nodes.html: Alan Guth proposed in 1981 that the early universe went through a brief period of exponential expansion; Alexei Starobinsky (1980), Andrei Linde, Andreas Albrecht and Paul Steinhardt (1982) developed related versions. Inflation explains the universe’s uniformity and flatness and seeds galaxies with quantum fluctuations. It fits the cosmic microwave background but remains unproven.
nodes.summary: Alan Guth proposed in 1981 that the early universe went through a brief period of exponential expansion; Alexei Starobinsky (1980), Andrei Linde, Andreas Albrecht and Paul Steinhardt (1982) developed related versions.

nodes.title: Chiral Gauge Theories on a Lattice

progress.what: Domain-wall fermions: chiral fermions appear bound to a defect in one extra dimension, now standard for lattice QCD with chiral symmetry.
progress.html: Domain-wall fermions: chiral fermions appear bound to a defect in one extra dimension, now standard for lattice QCD with chiral symmetry.

progress.what: Constructed anomaly-free abelian chiral gauge theories on the lattice with exact gauge invariance, using the Ginsparg–Wilson relation.
progress.html: Constructed anomaly-free abelian chiral gauge theories on the lattice with exact gauge invariance, using the Ginsparg–Wilson relation.

progress.what: Argued that symmetric-mass-generation schemes replace mirror fermions by propagator zeros that act as ghosts, so gauge invariance survives but unitarity is lost (PRL 2024).
progress.html: Argued that symmetric-mass-generation schemes replace mirror fermions by propagator zeros that act as ghosts, so gauge invariance survives but unitarity is lost (PRL 2024).

progress.what: Proposed that chiral fermions with exact gauge symmetry live on the boundary of a finite higher-dimensional system, local only when gauge anomalies cancel (PRL 2024).
progress.html: Proposed that chiral fermions with exact gauge symmetry live on the boundary of a finite higher-dimensional system, local only when gauge anomalies cancel (PRL 2024).

nodes.html: Nobody knows how to define a chiral gauge theory, such as the electroweak part of the Standard Model, on a lattice beyond perturbation theory: the Nielsen–Ninomiya theorem (1981) forbids the naive route. Lüscher’s construction covers abelian theories (1998), and boundary and mass-generation proposals are disputed; a lattice formulation of a non-abelian chiral gauge theory, tested in simulation, would settle it.
nodes.summary: Nobody knows how to define a chiral gauge theory, such as the electroweak part of the Standard Model, on a lattice beyond perturbation theory: the Nielsen–Ninomiya theorem (1981) forbids the naive route.

nodes.title: Bell Test Experiments
nodes.html: John Clauser and Stuart Freedman made the first Bell test to show a violation in 1972, and in 1982 Alain Aspect narrowed the locality loophole by switching the polarizer settings while the photons were in flight. The inequalities were violated, as quantum mechanics predicts. Loophole-free tests followed in 2015, and Aspect, Clauser and Anton Zeilinger shared the 2022 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: John Clauser and Stuart Freedman made the first Bell test to show a violation in 1972, and in 1982 Alain Aspect narrowed the locality loophole by switching the polarizer settings while the photons were in flight.

nodes.title: Fractional Quantum Hall Effect
nodes.html: Daniel Tsui and Horst Störmer, with crystals grown by Arthur Gossard, found in 1982 Hall plateaus at fractional fillings such as one third in very clean two-dimensional electron gases. Robert Laughlin explained them in 1983 as a new quantum liquid whose quasiparticles carry a fraction of the electron’s charge. Their anyon statistics were observed directly in 2020.
nodes.summary: Daniel Tsui and Horst Störmer, with crystals grown by Arthur Gossard, found in 1982 Hall plateaus at fractional fillings such as one third in very clean two-dimensional electron gases.

nodes.title: Topological Band Invariants (TKNN)
nodes.html: David Thouless, Mahito Kohmoto, Peter Nightingale and Marcel den Nijs showed in 1982 that the quantized Hall conductance of a filled electron band is a topological integer, later identified as the Chern number, unchanged by smooth deformations. It brought topology into condensed matter physics and led to the classification of topological phases. Thouless shared the 2016 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: David Thouless, Mahito Kohmoto, Peter Nightingale and Marcel den Nijs showed in 1982 that the quantized Hall conductance of a filled electron band is a topological integer, later identified as the Chern number, unchanged by smooth deformations.

nodes.title: Haldane Conjecture

progress.what: Proved the half-integer part in the Lieb–Schultz–Mattis sense: such chains have gapless excitations or a degenerate ground state.
progress.html: Proved the half-integer part in the Lieb–Schultz–Mattis sense: such chains have gapless excitations or a degenerate ground state.

progress.what: The AKLT model, a spin-1 chain close to Heisenberg’s, has an exactly known valence-bond ground state and a proven gap.
progress.html: The AKLT model, a spin-1 chain close to Heisenberg’s, has an exactly known valence-bond ground state and a proven gap.

progress.what: Proved that if the spin-1 Heisenberg chain has a unique gapped ground state, that state lies in a nontrivial symmetry-protected topological phase (PRL 2025).
progress.html: Proved that if the spin-1 Heisenberg chain has a unique gapped ground state, that state lies in a nontrivial symmetry-protected topological phase (PRL 2025).

progress.what: Claimed proof that the spin-1 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain on even periodic rings has a spectral gap bounded away from zero uniformly in the length (family 268 of OpenAI’s math release). Not formalized and not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that the spin-1 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain on even periodic rings has a spectral gap bounded away from zero uniformly in the length (family 268 of OpenAI’s math release). Not formalized and not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Haldane (1983) predicted that antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chains of integer spin have an energy gap above a unique ground state, while half-integer chains do not. Affleck and Lieb proved a form of the half-integer side (1986), and experiments since 1986 and numerics confirm the spin-1 gap, but no proof for the spin-1 chain existed before a 2026 claim, which awaits independent review.
nodes.summary: Haldane (1983) predicted that antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chains of integer spin have an energy gap above a unique ground state, while half-integer chains do not.

nodes.title: Superstring Anomaly Cancellation
nodes.html: Michael Green and John Schwarz showed in 1984 that the gauge and gravitational anomalies of ten-dimensional superstring theory cancel only for the gauge groups SO(32) and E8×E8, the latter realized by the heterotic string of 1985. This made the theory consistent and led to rapid growth of research on string theory as a candidate theory of quantum gravity, which remains untested.
nodes.summary: Michael Green and John Schwarz showed in 1984 that the gauge and gravitational anomalies of ten-dimensional superstring theory cancel only for the gauge groups SO(32) and E8×E8, the latter realized by the heterotic string of 1985.

nodes.title: Berry Phase
nodes.html: Michael Berry showed in 1984 that when a quantum system is carried slowly around a loop in parameter space, its state acquires, besides the usual dynamical phase, a geometric phase that depends only on the path. Shivaramakrishnan Pancharatnam had found an optical analogue in 1956. Berry phases appear in molecules, electron bands and topological matter.
nodes.summary: Michael Berry showed in 1984 that when a quantum system is carried slowly around a loop in parameter space, its state acquires, besides the usual dynamical phase, a geometric phase that depends only on the path.

nodes.title: Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit Conjecture

progress.what: Semiclassical theory of spectral rigidity: periodic orbits reproduce the random-matrix spectral form factor at short times (the diagonal approximation).
progress.html: Semiclassical theory of spectral rigidity: periodic orbits reproduce the random-matrix spectral form factor at short times (the diagonal approximation).

progress.what: Summed correlated pairs of periodic orbits to all orders, recovering the full random-matrix form factor semiclassically; the argument is not rigorous.
progress.html: Summed correlated pairs of periodic orbits to all orders, recovering the full random-matrix form factor semiclassically; the argument is not rigorous.

progress.what: First exact random-matrix spectral form factor in a chaotic many-body system, the self-dual kicked Ising chain, in the limit of large system size.
progress.html: First exact random-matrix spectral form factor in a chaotic many-body system, the self-dual kicked Ising chain, in the limit of large system size.

progress.what: For random hyperbolic surfaces of large genus, the variance of a smoothed eigenvalue count matches the GOE prediction on average over moduli space (GAFA 2023).
progress.html: For random hyperbolic surfaces of large genus, the variance of a smoothed eigenvalue count matches the GOE prediction on average over moduli space (GAFA 2023).

nodes.html: Bohigas, Giannoni and Schmit (1984) conjectured that quantum systems whose classical motion is chaotic, such as the Sinai billiard, have energy levels with the statistics of random matrices. Numerics support it overwhelmingly and periodic-orbit theory explains it, but there is no proof for any single chaotic billiard or surface; rigorous results cover random ensembles and special many-body models.
nodes.summary: Bohigas, Giannoni and Schmit (1984) conjectured that quantum systems whose classical motion is chaotic, such as the Sinai billiard, have energy levels with the statistics of random matrices.

nodes.title: Crystallization Conjecture

progress.what: Ground states of ‘sticky disks’ in the plane are pieces of the triangular lattice, an early rigorous crystallization result.
progress.html: Ground states of ‘sticky disks’ in the plane are pieces of the triangular lattice, an early rigorous crystallization result.

progress.what: Crystallization in two dimensions for a class of short-range Lennard-Jones-type potentials: energy minimizers converge to the triangular lattice.
progress.html: Crystallization in two dimensions for a class of short-range Lennard-Jones-type potentials: energy minimizers converge to the triangular lattice.

progress.what: The E8 and Leech lattices are universally optimal: they minimize energy for every completely monotone potential of squared distance in dimensions 8 and 24 (Annals 2022).
progress.html: The E8 and Leech lattices are universally optimal: they minimize energy for every completely monotone potential of squared distance in dimensions 8 and 24 (Annals 2022).

progress.what: Claimed proof that the triangular lattice is universally optimal in the plane, minimizing energy for every completely monotone potential of squared distance (family 090 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that the triangular lattice is universally optimal in the plane, minimizing energy for every completely monotone potential of squared distance (family 090 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Why do crystals exist? The crystallization conjecture asks for a proof that many particles with realistic interactions arrange themselves periodically at low temperature; it is problem 11 on Barry Simon’s 1984 list. Proofs exist only for special interactions, mostly in two dimensions (Theil, 2006) and in dimensions 8 and 24 (2019); periodic ground states for a Lennard-Jones-type potential in three dimensions remain the classic target.
nodes.summary: Why do crystals exist?

nodes.title: Ionization Conjecture

progress.what: A nucleus of charge Z binds fewer than 2Z + 1 electrons, which settles the conjecture for hydrogen.
progress.html: A nucleus of charge Z binds fewer than 2Z + 1 electrons, which settles the conjecture for hydrogen.

progress.what: The maximal number of bound electrons is at most Z + O(Z^(5/7)), still the best asymptotic bound for the Schrödinger atom; Seco, Sigal and Solovej gave another proof the same year.
progress.html: The maximal number of bound electrons is at most Z + O(Z^(5/7)), still the best asymptotic bound for the Schrödinger atom; Seco, Sigal and Solovej gave another proof the same year.

progress.what: Proved the bound Z + C in Hartree–Fock theory, the first version of the conjecture for a realistic many-electron model.
progress.html: Proved the bound Z + C in Hartree–Fock theory, the first version of the conjecture for a realistic many-electron model.

progress.what: Claimed proof that a molecule with M nuclei of total charge Z binds at most Z + CM electrons in the full nonrelativistic Coulomb model, which gives Z + C for atoms (family 263 of OpenAI’s math release). The Lean formalizations cover only companion asymptotic results; not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that a molecule with M nuclei of total charge Z binds at most Z + CM electrons in the full nonrelativistic Coulomb model, which gives Z + C for atoms (family 263 of OpenAI’s math release). The Lean formalizations cover only companion asymptotic results; not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Experiments show that a neutral atom binds at most one or two extra electrons. The ionization conjecture asks for a proof from the many-body Schrödinger equation that a nucleus of charge Z binds at most Z + C electrons, with C universal. Lieb proved fewer than 2Z + 1 (1984) and Solovej proved Z + C in Hartree–Fock theory (2003); a 2026 claim of the full result awaits independent review.
nodes.summary: Experiments show that a neutral atom binds at most one or two extra electrons.

nodes.title: Cold Dark Matter Simulations
nodes.html: Marc Davis, George Efstathiou, Carlos Frenk and Simon White ran N-body simulations in 1985 in which cold dark matter, slow-moving particles that interact only through gravity, grows into the filaments, clusters and voids of the observed galaxy distribution. Navarro, Frenk and White found in 1996 that the resulting halos share a universal density profile.
nodes.summary: Marc Davis, George Efstathiou, Carlos Frenk and Simon White ran N-body simulations in 1985 in which cold dark matter, slow-moving particles that interact only through gravity, grows into the filaments, clusters and voids of the observed galaxy distribution.

nodes.title: Laser Cooling & Trapping
nodes.html: In 1985 Steven Chu and colleagues slowed atoms with laser beams tuned just below an atomic resonance, so that atoms moving against a beam see it Doppler-shifted into resonance, reaching a few hundred microkelvin. Magneto-optical traps (1987) and the work of William Phillips and Claude Cohen-Tannoudji extended the method, which underlies atomic clocks and Bose-Einstein condensates.
nodes.summary: In 1985 Steven Chu and colleagues slowed atoms with laser beams tuned just below an atomic resonance, so that atoms moving against a beam see it Doppler-shifted into resonance, reaching a few hundred microkelvin.

nodes.title: Macroscopic Quantum Tunnelling
nodes.html: John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis showed in 1984-85 that the phase across a superconducting Josephson junction, a variable describing billions of Cooper pairs, tunnels through an energy barrier and has quantized energy levels like a single atom. The experiments underlie superconducting quantum bits, and the three shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics.
nodes.summary: John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis showed in 1984-85 that the phase across a superconducting Josephson junction, a variable describing billions of Cooper pairs, tunnels through an energy barrier and has quantized energy levels like a single atom.

nodes.title: KPZ Exponents Beyond One Dimension

progress.what: Large simulations in 2+1 dimensions gave a roughness exponent of 0.3869(4), ruling out the long-standing conjecture of exactly 2/5.
progress.html: Large simulations in 2+1 dimensions gave a roughness exponent of 0.3869(4), ruling out the long-standing conjecture of exactly 2/5.

progress.what: Constructed the KPZ fixed point, the exact universal scaling limit in one dimension, the benchmark for what solving higher dimensions would mean (Acta Mathematica).
progress.html: Constructed the KPZ fixed point, the exact universal scaling limit in one dimension, the benchmark for what solving higher dimensions would mean (Acta Mathematica).

progress.what: Constructed the critical two-dimensional stochastic heat flow, a rigorous scaling limit at the critical point of KPZ-type growth in two dimensions (Inventiones 2023).
progress.html: Constructed the critical two-dimensional stochastic heat flow, a rigorous scaling limit at the critical point of KPZ-type growth in two dimensions (Inventiones 2023).

progress.what: Conjectured the growth exponents β = 7/(8d + 13) for substrate dimension d, matching the best numerical estimates up to d = 15.
progress.html: Conjectured the growth exponents β = 7/(8d + 13) for substrate dimension d, matching the best numerical estimates up to d = 15.

nodes.html: The Kardar–Parisi–Zhang equation (1986) describes randomly growing interfaces such as burning paper fronts and bacterial colonies. In one dimension its exponents (growth exponent 1/3) and fluctuations are known exactly, but in two or more dimensions they are known only numerically, and whether there is an upper critical dimension is disputed. Exact exponents in 2+1 dimensions, or a proof of a closed formula, would settle it.
nodes.summary: The Kardar–Parisi–Zhang equation (1986) describes randomly growing interfaces such as burning paper fronts and bacterial colonies.

nodes.title: Relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell Regularity

progress.what: Smooth solutions continue as long as particle momenta stay bounded.
progress.html: Smooth solutions continue as long as particle momenta stay bounded.

progress.what: Proved global existence of weak solutions.
progress.html: Proved global existence of weak solutions.

progress.what: Claimed proof of global existence and uniqueness of smooth solutions for arbitrary smooth data with compactly supported particle density, in three dimensions for one species (family 362 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof of global existence and uniqueness of smooth solutions for arbitrary smooth data with compactly supported particle density, in three dimensions for one species (family 362 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: The relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell system models a collisionless plasma moving in its own electromagnetic field. Robert Glassey and Walter Strauss showed in 1986 that smooth solutions persist while particle momenta stay bounded, but large-data global regularity in three dimensions stayed open. OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims it for one species, formalized in Lean but not yet independently reviewed.
nodes.summary: The relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell system models a collisionless plasma moving in its own electromagnetic field.

nodes.title: Atlantic Overturning Tipping Point

progress.what: A sea-surface-temperature fingerprint indicates the AMOC has weakened by about 15% since the mid-twentieth century.
progress.html: A sea-surface-temperature fingerprint indicates the AMOC has weakened by about 15% since the mid-twentieth century.

progress.what: Early-warning statistics in a temperature proxy estimated a collapse between 2025 and 2095, most likely around 2057, under current emissions; other researchers judged the uncertainty too large.
progress.html: Early-warning statistics in a temperature proxy estimated a collapse between 2025 and 2095, most likely around 2057, under current emissions; other researchers judged the uncertainty too large.

progress.what: A physics-based indicator from a model that undergoes a tipping event suggests the present AMOC is on a tipping course.
progress.html: A physics-based indicator from a model that undergoes a tipping event suggests the present AMOC is on a tipping course.

progress.what: Across 34 climate models, Southern Ocean upwelling keeps a weakened AMOC running even under extreme forcing, making collapse this century unlikely.
progress.html: Across 34 climate models, Southern Ocean upwelling keeps a weakened AMOC running even under extreme forcing, making collapse this century unlikely.

nodes.html: Could the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, which carries heat to the North Atlantic, collapse under global warming?
