Stommel’s 1961 box model and a 1988 coupled model have two stable states (Broecker warned of the risk in 1987); statistical early-warning signals suggest a collapse this century, while most climate models weaken it without collapse before 2100. Reconciling the two would settle it.
nodes.summary: Could the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, which carries heat to the North Atlantic, collapse under global warming?

nodes.title: Superconductivity in the Hubbard Model

progress.what: Several independent numerical methods agreed that the underdoped model near 1/8 doping forms stripes (Science 2017).
progress.html: Several independent numerical methods agreed that the underdoped model near 1/8 doping forms stripes (Science 2017).

progress.what: With nearest-neighbour hopping only, the ground state in the relevant regime is striped and not superconducting.
progress.html: With nearest-neighbour hopping only, the ground state in the relevant regime is striped and not superconducting.

progress.what: Adding next-nearest-neighbour hopping t′ gives d-wave superconductivity coexisting with partially filled stripes (Science 2024).
progress.html: Adding next-nearest-neighbour hopping t′ gives d-wave superconductivity coexisting with partially filled stripes (Science 2024).

progress.what: Pfaffian neural quantum states found evidence for uniform d-wave superconductivity at U = 4 even without t′, and a non-superconducting stripe phase at strong coupling and low doping.
progress.html: Pfaffian neural quantum states found evidence for uniform d-wave superconductivity at U = 4 even without t′, and a non-superconducting stripe phase at strong coupling and low doping.

nodes.html: Does the two-dimensional Hubbard model, proposed by Anderson (1987) as the minimal model of the copper-oxide superconductors, have a d-wave superconducting ground state? Large simulations find stripes without superconductivity when electrons hop only to nearest neighbours (2020) and superconductivity once next-nearest hopping is added (2024). Agreement across methods on the doped phase diagram would settle it.
nodes.summary: Does the two-dimensional Hubbard model, proposed by Anderson (1987) as the minimal model of the copper-oxide superconductors, have a d-wave superconducting ground state?

nodes.title: Ice-Core Climate Record
nodes.html: Ice cores drilled at Vostok, Antarctica, and analysed by Claude Lorius, Jean Jouzel, Jean-Marc Barnola and colleagues, showed in 1987 that carbon dioxide and temperature rose and fell together through the last 160,000 years of glacial cycles. The EPICA core extended the record to 800,000 years in 2008. Air trapped in the ice gives direct samples of past atmospheres.
nodes.summary: Ice cores drilled at Vostok, Antarctica, and analysed by Claude Lorius, Jean Jouzel, Jean-Marc Barnola and colleagues, showed in 1987 that carbon dioxide and temperature rose and fell together through the last 160,000 years of glacial cycles.

nodes.title: Quantum Hall Transition Exponent

progress.what: Large network-model simulations gave ν = 2.593, with a confidence interval of 2.587 to 2.598, well above the measured value.
progress.html: Large network-model simulations gave ν = 2.593, with a confidence interval of 2.587 to 2.598, well above the measured value.

progress.what: Network models with random geometry gave ν ≈ 2.37, close to the experimental 2.38, suggesting the regular network misses something (PRB 2017).
progress.html: Network models with random geometry gave ν ≈ 2.37, close to the experimental 2.38, suggesting the regular network misses something (PRB 2017).

progress.what: Proposed that the transition is a GL(r|r) Wess–Zumino–Witten theory at level 4 with a truly marginal deformation, predicting parabolic multifractal exponents (Nucl. Phys. B 2019).
progress.html: Proposed that the transition is a GL(r|r) Wess–Zumino–Witten theory at level 4 with a truly marginal deformation, predicting parabolic multifractal exponents (Nucl. Phys. B 2019).

progress.what: Scaling of the longitudinal conductance in much larger systems gave ν = 2.607(8), confirming the gap with experiment (PRL 2022).
progress.html: Scaling of the longitudinal conductance in much larger systems gave ν = 2.607(8), confirming the gap with experiment (PRL 2022).

nodes.html: At the transition between quantum Hall plateaus the localization length diverges with an exponent ν. Simulations of the Chalker–Coddington network model (1988) give about 2.6, experiments about 2.38, and no accepted field theory explains either. Identifying the critical theory, or showing that interactions or disorder geometry account for the difference, would settle it.
nodes.summary: At the transition between quantum Hall plateaus the localization length diverges with an exponent ν.

nodes.title: CMB Anisotropies
nodes.html: The COBE satellite’s FIRAS instrument (John Mather) showed in 1990 that the cosmic microwave background has a perfect black-body spectrum at about 2.7 K, and its DMR instrument (George Smoot) detected in 1992 temperature ripples of about one part in 100,000. These are the seeds of galaxies and clusters, and they confirmed the Big Bang picture and the growth of structure.
nodes.summary: The COBE satellite’s FIRAS instrument (John Mather) showed in 1990 that the cosmic microwave background has a perfect black-body spectrum at about 2.7 K, and its DMR instrument (George Smoot) detected in 1992 temperature ripples of about one part in 100,000.

nodes.title: Cusp–Core Problem

progress.what: Proposed self-interacting dark matter, whose collisions naturally flatten central cusps into cores.
progress.html: Proposed self-interacting dark matter, whose collisions naturally flatten central cusps into cores.

progress.what: Simulations showed that supernova-driven outflows can turn dark-matter cusps into cores in dwarf galaxies.
progress.html: Simulations showed that supernova-driven outflows can turn dark-matter cusps into cores in dwarf galaxies.

progress.what: Explained how repeated bursts of supernova feedback pump energy into dark matter and turn cusps into cores.
progress.html: Explained how repeated bursts of supernova feedback pump energy into dark matter and turn cusps into cores.

progress.what: Dwarfs that kept forming stars longer have lower central dark-matter densities, as feedback-driven ‘dark matter heating’ predicts.
progress.html: Dwarfs that kept forming stars longer have lower central dark-matter densities, as feedback-driven ‘dark matter heating’ predicts.

nodes.html: Simulations of cold dark matter predict steeply rising ‘cusps’ of density at galaxy centres, but many dwarf galaxies show flat ‘cores’ (Flores and Primack; Moore, 1994). Is the difference caused by supernova feedback, self-interacting dark matter or something else? One model matching the full range of observed dwarf profiles, or data ruling a mechanism out, would settle it.
nodes.summary: Simulations of cold dark matter predict steeply rising ‘cusps’ of density at galaxy centres, but many dwarf galaxies show flat ‘cores’ (Flores and Primack; Moore, 1994).

nodes.title: Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis
nodes.html: Josh Deutsch (1991) and Mark Srednicki (1994) argued that in a chaotic quantum system each individual energy eigenstate already looks thermal for local measurements, with expectation values that depend smoothly on energy. This hypothesis explains how an isolated quantum system can thermalize, and it has been tested numerically and in cold-atom experiments.
nodes.summary: Josh Deutsch (1991) and Mark Srednicki (1994) argued that in a chaotic quantum system each individual energy eigenstate already looks thermal for local measurements, with expectation values that depend smoothly on energy.

nodes.title: Bose–Einstein Condensate
nodes.html: Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman at JILA cooled rubidium atoms to about 170 nanokelvin in June 1995, and Wolfgang Ketterle at MIT did the same with sodium a few months later, producing a gas in which a large fraction of the atoms occupy one quantum state. It realized the state Bose and Einstein predicted 70 years earlier, and the three shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics.
nodes.summary: Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman at JILA cooled rubidium atoms to about 170 nanokelvin in June 1995, and Wolfgang Ketterle at MIT did the same with sodium a few months later, producing a gas in which a large fraction of the atoms occupy one quantum state.

nodes.title: Detection & Attribution of Warming
nodes.html: Klaus Hasselmann developed statistical fingerprint methods in 1979-93 to separate human influence on climate from natural variability, and Benjamin Santer and others applied them to observed temperature patterns. The 1995 IPCC report concluded that the balance of evidence suggests a discernible human influence on global climate. Hasselmann shared the 2021 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Klaus Hasselmann developed statistical fingerprint methods in 1979-93 to separate human influence on climate from natural variability, and Benjamin Santer and others applied them to observed temperature patterns.

nodes.title: Exoplanets
nodes.html: Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail found planets around the pulsar PSR B1257+12 in 1992, and in 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi b, a giant planet orbiting a Sun-like star every four days, from the star’s periodic Doppler shift. Thousands of exoplanets are now known, and planets are common and varied. Mayor and Queloz shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
nodes.summary: Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail found planets around the pulsar PSR B1257+12 in 1992, and in 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi b, a giant planet orbiting a Sun-like star every four days, from the star’s periodic Doppler shift.

nodes.title: Geodynamo Simulation
nodes.html: Gary Glatzmaier and Paul Roberts ran in 1995 a three-dimensional computer simulation of convection and magnetic field generation in Earth’s liquid outer core. It produced a dipole field like Earth’s that reversed polarity spontaneously after tens of thousands of simulated years, showing that the geodynamo and its reversals can be studied by solving the fluid and magnetic equations.
nodes.summary: Gary Glatzmaier and Paul Roberts ran in 1995 a three-dimensional computer simulation of convection and magnetic field generation in Earth’s liquid outer core.

nodes.title: AdS/CFT Correspondence
nodes.html: Juan Maldacena proposed in 1997 that string theory in anti-de Sitter space is equivalent to a quantum field theory without gravity on its boundary, and in 1998 Gubser, Klebanov, Polyakov and Edward Witten made it precise. The conjectured duality has thousands of checks, is a model of quantum gravity, and gives tools for strongly coupled systems such as the quark-gluon plasma.
nodes.summary: Juan Maldacena proposed in 1997 that string theory in anti-de Sitter space is equivalent to a quantum field theory without gravity on its boundary, and in 1998 Gubser, Klebanov, Polyakov and Edward Witten made it precise.

nodes.title: Accelerating Universe
nodes.html: The Supernova Cosmology Project led by Saul Perlmutter and the High-Z Supernova Search Team led by Brian Schmidt, with Adam Riess, found in 1998-99 that distant Type Ia supernovae are fainter than expected, so the expansion of the universe is speeding up. The cause, dark energy, makes up about 68 percent of the cosmic energy budget, and the three shared the 2011 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: The Supernova Cosmology Project led by Saul Perlmutter and the High-Z Supernova Search Team led by Brian Schmidt, with Adam Riess, found in 1998-99 that distant Type Ia supernovae are fainter than expected, so the expansion of the universe is speeding up.

nodes.title: Nature of Dark Energy

progress.what: Anthropic bound: galaxies could form only if the cosmological constant is not much larger than the matter density, roughly the value later observed.
progress.html: Anthropic bound: galaxies could form only if the cosmological constant is not much larger than the matter density, roughly the value later observed.

progress.what: Second-year baryon acoustic oscillation data prefer dark energy that weakens over time at 3.1σ with the CMB, and at 2.8–4.2σ adding supernovae.
progress.html: Second-year baryon acoustic oscillation data prefer dark energy that weakens over time at 3.1σ with the CMB, and at 2.8–4.2σ adding supernovae.

progress.what: Recalibrating the Dark Energy Survey supernovae cut the strongest evolving-dark-energy case from 4.2σ to 3.2σ (MNRAS 2026).
progress.html: Recalibrating the Dark Energy Survey supernovae cut the strongest evolving-dark-energy case from 4.2σ to 3.2σ (MNRAS 2026).

nodes.html: Why is the expansion of the universe accelerating (1998)? A cosmological constant fits the data, but naive quantum estimates of vacuum energy exceed it by up to 120 orders of magnitude, and DESI data (2024–2025) hint that dark energy weakens over time. Showing whether it is constant, and explaining its value, would settle it; DESI finished its five-year survey in April 2026, with full results expected in 2027.
nodes.summary: Why is the expansion of the universe accelerating (1998)?

nodes.title: Neutrino Oscillations
nodes.html: Bruno Pontecorvo proposed neutrino oscillations in 1957. Super-Kamiokande (Takaaki Kajita) saw atmospheric muon neutrinos vanish in 1998, and the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (Arthur McDonald) showed in 2001-02 that solar neutrinos change flavour, solving the problem Raymond Davis and John Bahcall raised. Neutrinos therefore have mass, which the Standard Model lacked.
nodes.summary: Bruno Pontecorvo proposed neutrino oscillations in 1957.

nodes.title: Attosecond Light Pulses
nodes.html: Anne L’Huillier showed in 1987 that intense laser light in a gas produces very high harmonics. In 2001 Pierre Agostini’s group made trains of pulses lasting about 250 attoseconds and Ferenc Krausz’s group isolated single pulses of 650 attoseconds. Such flashes can follow the motion of electrons in atoms and molecules, and the three shared the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics.
nodes.summary: Anne L’Huillier showed in 1987 that intense laser light in a gas produces very high harmonics.

nodes.title: Moon’s Isotopic Crisis

progress.what: Lunar titanium isotopes match Earth’s to a few parts per million, implying lunar material came largely from the proto-Earth.
progress.html: Lunar titanium isotopes match Earth’s to a few parts per million, implying lunar material came largely from the proto-Earth.

progress.what: New impact scenarios, a fast-spinning proto-Earth hit by a small impactor (Ćuk and Stewart) and a collision of two similar-sized bodies (Canup), can each make an Earth-like Moon.
progress.html: New impact scenarios, a fast-spinning proto-Earth hit by a small impactor (Ćuk and Stewart) and a collision of two similar-sized bodies (Canup), can each make an Earth-like Moon.

progress.what: Found no oxygen-isotope difference between Earth and Moon at the sub-ppm level.
progress.html: Found no oxygen-isotope difference between Earth and Moon at the sub-ppm level.

progress.what: Iron isotopes, with chromium, calcium, titanium, molybdenum and zirconium data, suggest Theia formed in the inner Solar System, probably closer to the Sun than Earth.
progress.html: Iron isotopes, with chromium, calcium, titanium, molybdenum and zirconium data, suggest Theia formed in the inner Solar System, probably closer to the Sun than Earth.

nodes.html: Simulations of the canonical giant impact make the Moon mostly from the impactor Theia, yet Earth and Moon have nearly identical oxygen, titanium and tungsten isotopes, a match sharpened since 2001. Which impact, or which Theia, makes such a twin? Candidates include a fast-spinning Earth, equal-mass collisions and synestias; a model that matches both the dynamics and the isotopes would settle it.
nodes.summary: Simulations of the canonical giant impact make the Moon mostly from the impactor Theia, yet Earth and Moon have nearly identical oxygen, titanium and tungsten isotopes, a match sharpened since 2001.

nodes.title: Slow Earthquakes
nodes.html: Herb Dragert, Kelin Wang and Thomas James used GPS in 2001 to detect a silent slip lasting weeks on the fault beneath Cascadia, and Kazushige Obara found tremor in Japan in 2002. Garry Rogers and Dragert tied slip and tremor together in 2003. Slow earthquakes show that faults slip at a wide range of speeds, which changed how subduction zones are studied.
nodes.summary: Herb Dragert, Kelin Wang and Thomas James used GPS in 2001 to detect a silent slip lasting weeks on the fault beneath Cascadia, and Kazushige Obara found tremor in Japan in 2002.

nodes.title: Black Hole at the Milky Way’s Centre
nodes.html: Two teams led by Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez tracked for years the orbits of stars near the centre of the Milky Way, finding by 2002 that the star S2 circles an invisible object of about four million solar masses in 16 years. Only a supermassive black hole fits, and it is the best evidence that such black holes exist. Genzel and Ghez shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics.
nodes.summary: Two teams led by Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez tracked for years the orbits of stars near the centre of the Milky Way, finding by 2002 that the star S2 circles an invisible object of about four million solar masses in 16 years.

nodes.title: ΛCDM Concordance Model
nodes.html: Measurements of the cosmic microwave background by BOOMERanG (2000), WMAP (2003) and Planck (2013-18) confirmed the ΛCDM model and fixed its parameters: a spatially flat universe, 13.8 billion years old, with about 5 percent ordinary matter, 27 percent cold dark matter and 68 percent dark energy. It fits many data sets with six parameters and is the standard model of cosmology.
nodes.summary: Measurements of the cosmic microwave background by BOOMERanG (2000), WMAP (2003) and Planck (2013-18) confirmed the ΛCDM model and fixed its parameters: a spatially flat universe, 13.8 billion years old, with about 5 percent ordinary matter, 27 percent cold dark matter and 68 percent dark energy.

nodes.title: Cosmological Lithium Problem

progress.what: Big Bang nucleosynthesis with the baryon density measured by WMAP predicts about three times more lithium-7 than the halo-star plateau shows.
progress.html: Big Bang nucleosynthesis with the baryon density measured by WMAP predicts about three times more lithium-7 than the halo-star plateau shows.

progress.what: Atomic diffusion in stars of the globular cluster NGC 6397 lowers surface lithium enough to reconcile the plateau with the predicted primordial value.
progress.html: Atomic diffusion in stars of the globular cluster NGC 6397 lowers surface lithium enough to reconcile the plateau with the predicted primordial value.

progress.what: Measured the beryllium-7 (n,α) cross section at CERN over a wide energy range, ruling out this reaction as a nuclear fix.
progress.html: Measured the beryllium-7 (n,α) cross section at CERN over a wide energy range, ruling out this reaction as a nuclear fix.

progress.what: Stellar models with atomic diffusion and parametrized turbulence reproduce the lithium plateau and its depletion from Population II to Population I stars.
progress.html: Stellar models with atomic diffusion and parametrized turbulence reproduce the lithium plateau and its depletion from Population II to Population I stars.

nodes.html: Big Bang nucleosynthesis, using the baryon density measured from the cosmic microwave background (2003), predicts about three times more lithium-7 than old halo stars show. Nuclear-physics fixes have been largely excluded, so either stars destroyed their lithium or new physics is needed. A stellar model that depletes lithium uniformly along the Spite plateau, confirmed by data, would settle it.
nodes.summary: Big Bang nucleosynthesis, using the baryon density measured from the cosmic microwave background (2003), predicts about three times more lithium-7 than old halo stars show.

nodes.title: Deconfined Quantum Criticality

progress.what: Simulations of the J-Q model found an apparently continuous transition between Néel and valence-bond-solid order, as the theory predicts.
progress.html: Simulations of the J-Q model found an apparently continuous transition between Néel and valence-bond-solid order, as the theory predicts.

progress.what: Conformal bootstrap bounds showed the measured exponents are hard to reconcile with a unitary conformal field theory with emergent SO(5) symmetry.
progress.html: Conformal bootstrap bounds showed the measured exponents are hard to reconcile with a unitary conformal field theory with emergent SO(5) symmetry.

progress.what: Fuzzy-sphere simulations found approximate conformal symmetry, explained as pseudo-criticality from nearby complex fixed points (PRX 2024).
progress.html: Fuzzy-sphere simulations found approximate conformal symmetry, explained as pseudo-criticality from nearby complex fixed points (PRX 2024).

progress.what: Extended J-Q models show unambiguous but very weak first-order transitions with emergent SO(5) symmetry, near-critical over a wide range of models.
progress.html: Extended J-Q models show unambiguous but very weak first-order transitions with emergent SO(5) symmetry, near-critical over a wide range of models.

nodes.html: Senthil and co-workers (2004) proposed that a two-dimensional quantum magnet can pass directly between two differently ordered phases through a continuous transition beyond Landau’s theory, with fractionalized excitations at the critical point. Simulations since 2007 show near-critical behaviour, but whether the transition is truly continuous, weakly first order, or governed by complex fixed points is unsettled.
nodes.summary: Senthil and co-workers (2004) proposed that a two-dimensional quantum magnet can pass directly between two differently ordered phases through a continuous transition beyond Landau’s theory, with fractionalized excitations at the critical point.

nodes.title: Solar Abundance Problem

progress.what: Three-dimensional models of the solar atmosphere lowered the oxygen abundance by about a third, breaking the agreement between solar models and helioseismology.
progress.html: Three-dimensional models of the solar atmosphere lowered the oxygen abundance by about a third, breaking the agreement between solar models and helioseismology.

progress.what: Measured iron opacity at solar-interior temperatures at Sandia’s Z machine, finding it 30–400% higher than predicted at many wavelengths, a possible fix through opacities.
progress.html: Measured iron opacity at solar-interior temperatures at Sandia’s Z machine, finding it 30–400% higher than predicted at many wavelengths, a possible fix through opacities.

progress.what: Derived a higher solar metallicity, Z/X = 0.0225, and reported that solar models built with it match helioseismology; other groups dispute the abundances.
progress.html: Derived a higher solar metallicity, Z/X = 0.0225, and reported that solar models built with it match helioseismology; other groups dispute the abundances.

progress.what: Neutrinos from the Sun’s CNO cycle, combined with beryllium-7 and boron-8 fluxes, disfavour the low-metallicity solar model at 3.1σ.
progress.html: Neutrinos from the Sun’s CNO cycle, combined with beryllium-7 and boron-8 fluxes, disfavour the low-metallicity solar model at 3.1σ.

nodes.html: Since 2004, improved spectroscopic analyses have lowered the Sun’s measured abundances of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen, and solar models built with them no longer match the sound speed and convection-zone depth measured by helioseismology. Are the abundances or the interior opacities wrong? Abundance determinations still disagree (2021–2022); a model fitting helioseismology and solar neutrinos together would settle it.
nodes.summary: Since 2004, improved spectroscopic analyses have lowered the Sun’s measured abundances of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen, and solar models built with them no longer match the sound speed and convection-zone depth measured by helioseismology.

nodes.title: Baryon Acoustic Oscillations
nodes.html: In 2005 Daniel Eisenstein’s team using the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, and Shaun Cole’s team using the 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey, found an excess of galaxy pairs about 150 megaparsecs apart, the imprint of sound waves in the early universe. This standard ruler measures cosmic distances and the expansion history, and it is a key probe of dark energy.
nodes.summary: In 2005 Daniel Eisenstein’s team using the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, and Shaun Cole’s team using the 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey, found an excess of galaxy pairs about 150 megaparsecs apart, the imprint of sound waves in the early universe.

nodes.title: Binary Black Hole Simulations
nodes.html: Frans Pretorius in 2005 and, soon after, the groups of Manuela Campanelli and of John Baker achieved stable numerical simulations of two black holes orbiting, merging and settling down, solving Einstein’s equations on supercomputers after decades of attempts. Such waveforms were used to identify and interpret the gravitational waves that LIGO detected in 2015.
nodes.summary: Frans Pretorius in 2005 and, soon after, the groups of Manuela Campanelli and of John Baker achieved stable numerical simulations of two black holes orbiting, merging and settling down, solving Einstein’s equations on supercomputers after decades of attempts.

nodes.title: On-Shell Scattering Amplitudes
nodes.html: Zvi Bern, Lance Dixon, David Dunbar and David Kosower showed in 1994 that unitarity cuts let gauge-theory scattering amplitudes be built from simpler on-shell ones, and in 2004-05 Ruth Britto, Freddy Cachazo, Bo Feng and Edward Witten found and proved a recursion relation that does so without Feynman diagrams. The methods reveal hidden simplicity and speed up collider predictions.
nodes.summary: Zvi Bern, Lance Dixon, David Dunbar and David Kosower showed in 1994 that unitarity cuts let gauge-theory scattering amplitudes be built from simpler on-shell ones, and in 2004-05 Ruth Britto, Freddy Cachazo, Bo Feng and Edward Witten found and proved a recursion relation that does so without Feynman diagrams.

nodes.title: Many-Body Localization
nodes.html: Igor Gornyi, Alexander Mirlin and Dmitry Polyakov (2005) and, independently, Denis Basko, Igor Aleiner and Boris Altshuler (2006) argued that interacting particles in a disordered system can fail to thermalize, staying localized even at finite energy density. Signatures were seen in cold-atom experiments in 2015, and whether the phase survives in large systems is debated.
nodes.summary: Igor Gornyi, Alexander Mirlin and Dmitry Polyakov (2005) and, independently, Denis Basko, Igor Aleiner and Boris Altshuler (2006) argued that interacting particles in a disordered system can fail to thermalize, staying localized even at finite energy density.

nodes.title: Weak Gravity Conjecture

progress.what: Showed that simple forms of the conjecture are not preserved by dimensional reduction and proposed the stronger lattice and sublattice versions (2015–2016).
progress.html: Showed that simple forms of the conjecture are not preserved by dimensional reduction and proposed the stronger lattice and sublattice versions (2015–2016).

progress.what: If higher-derivative corrections increase black-hole entropy, small extremal black holes themselves satisfy the conjecture.
progress.html: If higher-derivative corrections increase black-hole entropy, small extremal black holes themselves satisfy the conjecture.

progress.what: Proved the conjecture, in a strict sublattice form, for perturbative bosonic string theory in six or more dimensions; the superstring is left for future work (JHEP 2025).
progress.html: Proved the conjecture, in a strict sublattice form, for perturbative bosonic string theory in six or more dimensions; the superstring is left for future work (JHEP 2025).

nodes.html: In any consistent theory of quantum gravity, gravity should be the weakest force: some particle must have a charge-to-mass ratio at least that of an extremal black hole (Arkani-Hamed, Motl, Nicolis and Vafa, 2006). It holds in every known string compactification and has black-hole and unitarity arguments behind it; a general proof, starting with superstring theory, or a counterexample would settle it.
nodes.summary: In any consistent theory of quantum gravity, gravity should be the weakest force: some particle must have a charge-to-mass ratio at least that of an extremal black hole (Arkani-Hamed, Motl, Nicolis and Vafa, 2006).

nodes.title: Fast Radio Bursts
nodes.html: Duncan Lorimer and colleagues found in 2007, in archival pulsar survey data from the Parkes telescope, a radio flash lasting about five milliseconds from far outside the Galaxy. Thousands of such fast radio bursts have since been found, some of them repeating, and in 2020 a magnetar in the Milky Way produced one, tying at least some to neutron stars.
nodes.summary: Duncan Lorimer and colleagues found in 2007, in archival pulsar survey data from the Parkes telescope, a radio flash lasting about five milliseconds from far outside the Galaxy.

nodes.title: Galaxy Zoo
nodes.html: Galaxy Zoo, launched in July 2007 by Chris Lintott, Kevin Schawinski and colleagues, asked online volunteers to classify the shapes of nearly a million galaxies imaged by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Volunteers found new kinds of objects, such as Hanny’s Voorwerp, discovered by Hanny van Arkel, and the project became the model for online citizen science.
nodes.summary: Galaxy Zoo, launched in July 2007 by Chris Lintott, Kevin Schawinski and colleagues, asked online volunteers to classify the shapes of nearly a million galaxies imaged by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey.

nodes.title: Topological Insulators
nodes.html: Charles Kane and Eugene Mele (2005), and Andrei Bernevig, Taylor Hughes and Shoucheng Zhang (2006), predicted insulators whose bulk has an energy gap but whose edges or surfaces carry protected conducting states. Laurens Molenkamp’s group observed the edge states in HgTe quantum wells in 2007, and three-dimensional examples followed in 2008-09.
nodes.summary: Charles Kane and Eugene Mele (2005), and Andrei Bernevig, Taylor Hughes and Shoucheng Zhang (2006), predicted insulators whose bulk has an energy gap but whose edges or surfaces carry protected conducting states.

nodes.title: Conformal Bootstrap
nodes.html: Riccardo Rattazzi, Slava Rychkov, Erik Tonni and Alessandro Vichi revived in 2008 the idea that consistency conditions on conformal field theories, such as crossing symmetry and unitarity, can by themselves bound which theories exist. Numerical bootstrap calculations (2012-16) gave the most precise exponents of the three-dimensional Ising universality class.
nodes.summary: Riccardo Rattazzi, Slava Rychkov, Erik Tonni and Alessandro Vichi revived in 2008 the idea that consistency conditions on conformal field theories, such as crossing symmetry and unitarity, can by themselves bound which theories exist.

nodes.title: Onset of Turbulence in Pipe Flow
nodes.html: Osborne Reynolds saw in 1883 that pipe flow turns turbulent at high speed, but the threshold stayed unclear. In 2011 Kerstin Avila, Björn Hof and colleagues measured how turbulent puffs decay and split and found that turbulence becomes sustained at a Reynolds number of about 2,040, where splitting wins. Experiments and modelling in 2024 tied the transition to directed percolation.
nodes.summary: Osborne Reynolds saw in 1883 that pipe flow turns turbulent at high speed, but the threshold stayed unclear.

nodes.title: Higgs Boson
nodes.html: Predicted in 1964 and found at the Large Hadron Collider in 2012. It was the last missing particle of the Standard Model.
nodes.summary: Predicted in 1964 and found at the Large Hadron Collider in 2012.

nodes.title: Age of the Inner Core

progress.what: First-principles calculations gave iron at core conditions a thermal conductivity two to three times earlier estimates, implying a young inner core.
progress.html: First-principles calculations gave iron at core conditions a thermal conductivity two to three times earlier estimates, implying a young inner core.

progress.what: Diamond-anvil measurements supported high conductivity, while a study published alongside by Konôpková and co-workers found it low, leaving the question open.
progress.html: Diamond-anvil measurements supported high conductivity, while a study published alongside by Konôpková and co-workers found it low, leaving the question open.

progress.what: An ultra-low geomagnetic field about 565 million years ago suggests a weakening dynamo just before a young inner core began to grow.
progress.html: An ultra-low geomagnetic field about 565 million years ago suggests a weakening dynamo just before a young inner core began to grow.

progress.what: Simulations of how solid iron nucleates showed that many proposed core compositions need implausible supercooling; an iron–carbon liquid with about 10–15% carbon fits the geophysical constraints.
progress.html: Simulations of how solid iron nucleates showed that many proposed core compositions need implausible supercooling; an iron–carbon liquid with about 10–15% carbon fits the geophysical constraints.

nodes.html: If iron conducts heat as well as calculations (2012) and some experiments suggest, the core loses so much heat by conduction that the inner core must be young, under about a billion years, and the early geodynamo is hard to power: the ‘new core paradox’. Conductivity experiments disagree and age estimates still vary widely; consistent values for iron alloys at core conditions, from experiment and first principles, would settle it.
nodes.summary: If iron conducts heat as well as calculations (2012) and some experiments suggest, the core loses so much heat by conduction that the inner core must be young, under about a billion years, and the early geodynamo is hard to power: the ‘new core paradox’.

nodes.title: High-Energy Cosmic Neutrinos
nodes.html: IceCube, a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice instrumented with light sensors and led by Francis Halzen, reported in 2013 evidence for neutrinos from beyond the solar system: 28 events with energies up to about a petaelectronvolt. Neutrinos were later traced to the blazar TXS 0506+056 (2018) and to the Milky Way, opening neutrino astronomy. Halzen received the 2026 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: IceCube, a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice instrumented with light sensors and led by Francis Halzen, reported in 2013 evidence for neutrinos from beyond the solar system: 28 events with energies up to about a petaelectronvolt.

nodes.title: Hubble Tension

progress.what: Planck’s final analysis gives H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5 km/s/Mpc, assuming the ΛCDM model (A&A 2020).
progress.html: Planck’s final analysis gives H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5 km/s/Mpc, assuming the ΛCDM model (A&A 2020).

progress.what: Cepheid-calibrated supernovae give 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc, a 5σ disagreement with Planck.
progress.html: Cepheid-calibrated supernovae give 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc, a 5σ disagreement with Planck.

progress.what: Red-giant distances from JWST and Hubble give 70.39 ± 1.22 (stat) ± 1.33 (sys) km/s/Mpc, consistent with ΛCDM (ApJ 2025).
progress.html: Red-giant distances from JWST and Hubble give 70.39 ± 1.22 (stat) ± 1.33 (sys) km/s/Mpc, consistent with ΛCDM (ApJ 2025).

progress.what: A community consensus combining 12 kinds of distance indicators gives 73.50 ± 0.81 km/s/Mpc, 7.1σ from ΛCDM fits to Planck, SPT and ACT (A&A 2026).
progress.html: A community consensus combining 12 kinds of distance indicators gives 73.50 ± 0.81 km/s/Mpc, 7.1σ from ΛCDM fits to Planck, SPT and ACT (A&A 2026).

nodes.html: The expansion rate measured locally with Cepheids and supernovae, about 73 km/s/Mpc, disagrees with the 67 to 68 inferred from the cosmic microwave background under ΛCDM, a gap first flagged around 2013 that exceeded 5σ by 2022. Is it a measurement error or new physics? An independent local method reaching 1% precision, or a cosmological model that fits all the data, would decide it.
nodes.summary: The expansion rate measured locally with Cepheids and supernovae, about 73 km/s/Mpc, disagrees with the 67 to 68 inferred from the cosmic microwave background under ΛCDM, a gap first flagged around 2013 that exceeded 5σ by 2022.

nodes.title: Gravitational Waves
nodes.html: On 14 September 2015 LIGO detected ripples in spacetime from two merging black holes. That confirmed a hundred-year-old prediction with mirrors that moved less than a proton’s width.
nodes.summary: On 14 September 2015 LIGO detected ripples in spacetime from two merging black holes.

nodes.title: Neutron-Star Merger GW170817
nodes.html: On 17 August 2017 LIGO and Virgo detected gravitational waves from two merging neutron stars, and about two seconds later telescopes saw a gamma-ray burst from the same place, followed by a kilonova seen across the spectrum. The event showed that gravitational waves travel at the speed of light to about one part in a quadrillion and that mergers forge heavy elements such as gold.
nodes.summary: On 17 August 2017 LIGO and Virgo detected gravitational waves from two merging neutron stars, and about two seconds later telescopes saw a gamma-ray burst from the same place, followed by a kilonova seen across the spectrum.

nodes.title: Stability of Many-Body Localization

progress.what: Proved many-body localization for a disordered quantum spin chain, assuming a limited form of level repulsion that remains unproven.
progress.html: Proved many-body localization for a disordered quantum spin chain, assuming a limited form of level repulsion that remains unproven.

progress.what: Argued that rare thermal regions set off avalanches that destroy localization in two or more dimensions and constrain it in one.
progress.html: Argued that rare thermal regions set off avalanches that destroy localization in two or more dimensions and constrain it in one.

progress.what: Finite-size drifts in exact diagonalization suggested that apparent localization in short chains may be a crossover.
progress.html: Finite-size drifts in exact diagonalization suggested that apparent localization in short chains may be a crossover.

progress.what: Avalanches and many-body resonances push any one-dimensional MBL transition to far stronger disorder than earlier estimates.
progress.html: Avalanches and many-body resonances push any one-dimensional MBL transition to far stronger disorder than earlier estimates.

nodes.html: Is many-body localization, in which a disordered interacting quantum system never thermalizes, a true phase of matter in arbitrarily large systems? Imbrie’s one-dimensional proof (2016) rests on an unproven assumption, rare thermal regions can set off avalanches (2017), and numerics and cold-atom experiments through 2025 show finite-size drifts, so the existence of the phase remains open.
nodes.summary: Is many-body localization, in which a disordered interacting quantum system never thermalizes, a true phase of matter in arbitrarily large systems?

nodes.title: Neural-Network Quantum States
aliases: machine learning for quantum many-body physics
nodes.html: Giuseppe Carleo and Matthias Troyer showed in 2017 that a neural network can represent the wavefunction of an interacting quantum system and be trained by variational Monte Carlo to find its ground state. The same year Juan Carrasquilla and Roger Melko showed that networks can recognize phases of matter from samples, helping to start machine learning in many-body physics.
nodes.summary: Giuseppe Carleo and Matthias Troyer showed in 2017 that a neural network can represent the wavefunction of an interacting quantum system and be trained by variational Monte Carlo to find its ground state.

nodes.title: De Sitter Vacua in String Theory

progress.what: KKLT outlined how flux compactifications with nonperturbative effects and an anti-brane could give metastable de Sitter vacua.
progress.html: KKLT outlined how flux compactifications with nonperturbative effects and an anti-brane could give metastable de Sitter vacua.

progress.what: Conjectured that consistent quantum gravity forbids de Sitter vacua, which would make dark energy evolve.
progress.html: Conjectured that consistent quantum gravity forbids de Sitter vacua, which would make dark energy evolve.

progress.what: Constructed explicit supersymmetric anti-de Sitter vacua with exponentially small vacuum energy in controlled compactifications.
progress.html: Constructed explicit supersymmetric anti-de Sitter vacua with exponentially small vacuum energy in controlled compactifications.

progress.what: Built 30 explicit KKLT-type candidate de Sitter vacua on Calabi–Yau orientifolds, controlled at leading order; whether they survive subleading corrections is open.
progress.html: Built 30 explicit KKLT-type candidate de Sitter vacua on Calabi–Yau orientifolds, controlled at leading order; whether they survive subleading corrections is open.

nodes.html: Does string theory have stable or long-lived vacua with positive vacuum energy, like our accelerating universe? KKLT (2003) argued yes, while swampland conjectures (2018) say perhaps not, which would require evolving dark energy. Explicit candidate de Sitter vacua appeared in 2024, controlled only at leading order; a construction that survives all corrections, or a no-go theorem, would settle it.
nodes.summary: Does string theory have stable or long-lived vacua with positive vacuum energy, like our accelerating universe?

nodes.title: Magic-Angle Twisted Graphene
nodes.html: Pablo Jarillo-Herrero’s group at MIT reported in 2018 that two graphene sheets stacked with a twist of about 1.1 degrees, the magic angle that Rafi Bistritzer and Allan MacDonald had predicted in 2011 to give extremely flat electronic bands, behave as a correlated insulator and, when doped, as a superconductor. The result set off the rapid growth of twistronics.
nodes.summary: Pablo Jarillo-Herrero’s group at MIT reported in 2018 that two graphene sheets stacked with a twist of about 1.1 degrees, the magic angle that Rafi Bistritzer and Allan MacDonald had predicted in 2011 to give extremely flat electronic bands, behave as a correlated insulator and, when doped, as a superconductor.

nodes.title: Black Hole Imaged
nodes.html: The Event Horizon Telescope, an array of radio dishes across Earth linked by very-long-baseline interferometry, published in April 2019 the first image of a black hole, the ring and dark shadow of the 6.5-billion-solar-mass black hole in the galaxy M87. In May 2022 it released an image of Sagittarius A*, the Milky Way’s black hole. Both are consistent with general relativity.
nodes.summary: The Event Horizon Telescope, an array of radio dishes across Earth linked by very-long-baseline interferometry, published in April 2019 the first image of a black hole, the ring and dark shadow of the 6.5-billion-solar-mass black hole in the galaxy M87.

nodes.title: Proton Radius Puzzle
nodes.html: In 2010 Randolf Pohl and colleagues measured the proton’s charge radius with muonic hydrogen and found it about 4 percent smaller than values from hydrogen spectroscopy and electron scattering. In 2019 the PRad experiment and a hydrogen measurement by Bezginov and colleagues favoured the small value, about 0.84 femtometres, now adopted by CODATA. The puzzle is largely resolved.
nodes.summary: In 2010 Randolf Pohl and colleagues measured the proton’s charge radius with muonic hydrogen and found it about 4 percent smaller than values from hydrogen spectroscopy and electron scattering.

nodes.title: Missing Baryons Found
nodes.html: Censuses of stars and gas at low redshift found less than half of the ordinary matter that Big Bang nucleosynthesis requires. In 2020 Jean-Pierre Macquart’s team used fast radio bursts to weigh the gas between galaxies and found the missing baryons there; a 2025 survey by Liam Connor, Vikram Ravi and colleagues put about three quarters of all baryons in it.
nodes.summary: Censuses of stars and gas at low redshift found less than half of the ordinary matter that Big Bang nucleosynthesis requires.

nodes.title: AI Weather Forecasting
nodes.html: Machine-learned models trained on decades of reanalysis data, Huawei’s Pangu-Weather (Kaifeng Bi and colleagues) and Google DeepMind’s GraphCast (Remi Lam and colleagues), matched or beat the best physics-based medium-range forecasts in 2023 at a small fraction of the computing cost. ECMWF began running its own AI forecasting system operationally in 2025.
nodes.summary: Machine-learned models trained on decades of reanalysis data, Huawei’s Pangu-Weather (Kaifeng Bi and colleagues) and Google DeepMind’s GraphCast (Remi Lam and colleagues), matched or beat the best physics-based medium-range forecasts in 2023 at a small fraction of the computing cost.

nodes.title: Fractional Quantum Anomalous Hall Effect
nodes.html: In 2023 groups led by Xiaodong Xu, by Kin Fai Mak and Jie Shan, and by Tingxin Li observed fractional quantum Hall states without an external magnetic field in twisted MoTe2, and in 2024 Long Ju’s group saw them in rhombohedral graphene. Their fractionally charged excitations at zero field offer a possible route to non-abelian anyons and topological qubits.
nodes.summary: In 2023 groups led by Xiaodong Xu, by Kin Fai Mak and Jie Shan, and by Tingxin Li observed fractional quantum Hall states without an external magnetic field in twisted MoTe2, and in 2024 Long Ju’s group saw them in rhombohedral graphene.

nodes.title: Nanohertz Gravitational-Wave Background
nodes.html: In June 2023 the NANOGrav, European (EPTA), Parkes (PPTA) and Chinese (CPTA) pulsar timing array collaborations reported correlated shifts in the arrival times of pulses from millisecond pulsars, with the angular pattern predicted by Hellings and Downs, evidence for a background of nanohertz gravitational waves. The source is probably supermassive black hole binaries.
nodes.summary: In June 2023 the NANOGrav, European (EPTA), Parkes (PPTA) and Chinese (CPTA) pulsar timing array collaborations reported correlated shifts in the arrival times of pulses from millisecond pulsars, with the angular pattern predicted by Hellings and Downs, evidence for a background of nanohertz gravitational waves.

nodes.title: Altermagnetism
nodes.html: Libor Šmejkal, Jairo Sinova, Tomáš Jungwirth and colleagues showed in 2022 by symmetry analysis that a third class of collinear magnets exists, with zero net magnetization like antiferromagnets but spin-split electronic bands like ferromagnets. Photoemission experiments saw the spin splitting in MnTe in 2024. Altermagnets could be used in spintronic devices.
nodes.summary: Libor Šmejkal, Jairo Sinova, Tomáš Jungwirth and colleagues showed in 2022 by symmetry analysis that a third class of collinear magnets exists, with zero net magnetization like antiferromagnets but spin-split electronic bands like ferromagnets.

nodes.title: Thorium-229 Nuclear Clock Transition
nodes.html: In 2024 groups in Vienna and Braunschweig (Thorsten Schumm, Ekkehard Peik) and at JILA (Jun Ye) used lasers to excite the low-energy isomeric state of the thorium-229 nucleus, at about 8.4 electronvolts, the first laser excitation of an atomic nucleus. The transition could serve as a nuclear clock more stable than atomic clocks and test whether constants of nature vary.
nodes.summary: In 2024 groups in Vienna and Braunschweig (Thorsten Schumm, Ekkehard Peik) and at JILA (Jun Ye) used lasers to excite the low-energy isomeric state of the thorium-229 nucleus, at about 8.4 electronvolts, the first laser excitation of an atomic nucleus.

nodes.title: Muon g−2 Anomaly
nodes.html: Brookhaven (2001) and Fermilab (2021-25) measured the muon’s magnetic anomaly and found it above Standard Model predictions based on electron-positron data. Lattice QCD calculations (BMW, 2020) raised the predicted value, and Fermilab’s final result of June 2025, at 127 parts per billion, agrees with the 2025 theory value. The electron-positron data sets still disagree.
nodes.summary: Brookhaven (2001) and Fermilab (2021-25) measured the muon’s magnetic anomaly and found it above Standard Model predictions based on electron-positron data.

nodes.title: Stability of Kerr Black Holes

progress.what: Nonlinear stability of the Schwarzschild family: data near Schwarzschild, within a codimension-3 set, settle down to a nearby Schwarzschild black hole.
progress.html: Nonlinear stability of the Schwarzschild family: data near Schwarzschild, within a codimension-3 set, settle down to a nearby Schwarzschild black hole.

progress.what: Nonlinear stability of slowly rotating Kerr black holes (|a| much smaller than M), completed in a series of papers from 2021 to 2022 and published in 2023 and 2024.
progress.html: Nonlinear stability of slowly rotating Kerr black holes (|a| much smaller than M), completed in a series of papers from 2021 to 2022 and published in 2023 and 2024.

progress.what: Linear stability of Kerr black holes in the full subextremal range |a| < M.
progress.html: Linear stability of Kerr black holes in the full subextremal range |a| < M.

progress.what: Claimed nonlinear stability of every subextremal Kerr black hole in a 339-page preprint using a modified wave map gauge and a Nash–Moser iteration. Not yet refereed as of October 2026.
progress.html: Claimed nonlinear stability of every subextremal Kerr black hole in a 339-page preprint using a modified wave map gauge and a Nash–Moser iteration. Not yet refereed as of October 2026.

nodes.html: Do rotating black holes settle down after a disturbance? The Kerr stability conjecture says that small perturbations of a Kerr black hole decay, leaving a nearby Kerr black hole. Slow rotation was settled by Klainerman, Szeftel and Giorgi (2021–2022); in June 2026 Peter Hintz posted a 339-page proof for every subextremal Kerr black hole, which has not yet been refereed.
nodes.summary: Do rotating black holes settle down after a disturbance?

nodes.title: Earthquake Prediction

progress.what: Predicted a magnitude-6 earthquake at Parkfield, California, by 1993; it came only in 2004, without detected precursors.
progress.html: Predicted a magnitude-6 earthquake at Parkfield, California, by 1993; it came only in 2004, without detected precursors.

progress.what: Machine learning predicted the timing of laboratory earthquakes from the acoustic noise of a sheared fault.
progress.html: Machine learning predicted the timing of laboratory earthquakes from the acoustic noise of a sheared fault.

progress.what: Stacking GPS records before dozens of large earthquakes, claimed accelerating slip in the two hours before rupture; a 2024 tiltmeter study found no such signal before the 2011 Tohoku earthquake.
progress.html: Stacking GPS records before dozens of large earthquakes, claimed accelerating slip in the two hours before rupture; a 2024 tiltmeter study found no such signal before the 2011 Tohoku earthquake.

progress.what: A global detection and alert system using Android phones demonstrated earthquake early warning at planetary scale, which gives seconds of notice after a rupture starts.
progress.html: A global detection and alert system using Android phones demonstrated earthquake early warning at planetary scale, which gives seconds of notice after a rupture starts.

nodes.html: Can the time, place and size of a large earthquake be predicted hours to days ahead? Probabilistic forecasts and early warning, which gives seconds of notice after a rupture begins, work; reliable prediction does not, and claimed precursors have not survived testing, as the Parkfield experiment (1985–2004) showed. A method validated prospectively against a public catalogue would settle it.
nodes.summary: Can the time, place and size of a large earthquake be predicted hours to days ahead?

nodes.title: Glacial CO₂ Problem

progress.what: The Vostok ice core showed atmospheric CO2 rising and falling with temperature over 160,000 years, from about 190 ppm in glacials to 280 ppm in interglacials.
progress.html: The Vostok ice core showed atmospheric CO2 rising and falling with temperature over 160,000 years, from about 190 ppm in glacials to 280 ppm in interglacials.

progress.what: A synthesis argued that the deep ocean, especially around Antarctica, must have stored the missing carbon, and weighed the candidate mechanisms.
progress.html: A synthesis argued that the deep ocean, especially around Antarctica, must have stored the missing carbon, and weighed the candidate mechanisms.

progress.what: Air-sea disequilibrium greatly amplifies the effect of colder water and iron fertilization on glacial ocean carbon storage, while circulation and sea-ice changes contribute relatively little.
progress.html: Air-sea disequilibrium greatly amplifies the effect of colder water and iron fertilization on glacial ocean carbon storage, while circulation and sea-ice changes contribute relatively little.

progress.what: A carbon-isotope mass balance attributes 75 ± 40 ppm of the drawdown to biologically stored ocean carbon, mostly held in disequilibrium with the air.
progress.html: A carbon-isotope mass balance attributes 75 ± 40 ppm of the drawdown to biologically stored ocean carbon, mostly held in disequilibrium with the air.

nodes.html: Ice cores show that atmospheric CO2 fell to about 190 ppm at glacial maxima, roughly 90 ppm below interglacial levels (Vostok record, 1987). The ocean must have stored the missing carbon, but models using known mechanisms struggle to reproduce the full drawdown. A quantitative carbon budget that a physically based model reproduces across a whole glacial cycle would settle it.
nodes.summary: Ice cores show that atmospheric CO2 fell to about 190 ppm at glacial maxima, roughly 90 ppm below interglacial levels (Vostok record, 1987).

nodes.title: Kagome Antiferromagnet Ground State

progress.what: DMRG on wide cylinders found a gapped spin liquid, consistent with Z2 topological order.
progress.html: DMRG on wide cylinders found a gapped spin liquid, consistent with Z2 topological order.

progress.what: DMRG with flux insertion found signatures of Dirac cones, favouring a gapless U(1) Dirac spin liquid.
progress.html: DMRG with flux insertion found signatures of Dirac cones, favouring a gapless U(1) Dirac spin liquid.

progress.what: Tensor-network calculations directly in the infinite plane also found a gapless spin liquid.
progress.html: Tensor-network calculations directly in the infinite plane also found a gapless spin liquid.

progress.what: A machine-learning study claimed a spinon pair-density-wave ground state (PRX 2025); a 2026 comment by Kamal, Kufel, Vu, Laumann and Yao disputes it.
progress.html: A machine-learning study claimed a spinon pair-density-wave ground state (PRX 2025); a 2026 comment by Kamal, Kufel, Vu, Laumann and Yao disputes it.

nodes.html: Is the ground state of the spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the kagome lattice a gapped Z2 spin liquid or a gapless Dirac spin liquid? DMRG first favoured a gap (2011), while later DMRG and tensor-network studies favour Dirac cones (2017). It is a benchmark for numerical methods, including neural networks, and kagome materials such as herbertsmithite let experiments weigh in.
nodes.summary: Is the ground state of the spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the kagome lattice a gapped Z2 spin liquid or a gapless Dirac spin liquid?

nodes.title: Finiteness of N=8 Supergravity

progress.what: Unexpected cancellations found with unitarity methods suggested the theory might be ultraviolet finite.
progress.html: Unexpected cancellations found with unitarity methods suggested the theory might be ultraviolet finite.

progress.what: The four-loop four-graviton amplitude is finite in four dimensions.
progress.html: The four-loop four-graviton amplitude is finite in four dimensions.

progress.what: The theory’s hidden E7(7) symmetry forbids counterterms below seven loops in four dimensions.
progress.html: The theory’s hidden E7(7) symmetry forbids counterterms below seven loops in four dimensions.

progress.what: At five loops the first divergence appears in the critical dimension 24/5, with no cancellations beyond those already understood, leaving the seven-loop question open.
progress.html: At five loops the first divergence appears in the critical dimension 24/5, with no cancellations beyond those already understood, leaving the seven-loop question open.

nodes.html: Is maximal (N = 8) supergravity in four dimensions free of ultraviolet divergences at every loop order? If so, a point-particle quantum theory of gravity would exist without strings. Explicit calculations show finiteness through four loops (2009), symmetry allows the first divergence at seven loops, and a seven-loop calculation, or a symmetry argument forbidding the divergence, would settle it.
nodes.summary: Is maximal (N = 8) supergravity in four dimensions free of ultraviolet divergences at every loop order?

nodes.title: Quantum Gravity
nodes.html: A consistent quantum theory of spacetime. String theory and loop quantum gravity are candidates; no experiment has yet chosen between them.
nodes.summary: A consistent quantum theory of spacetime.

nodes.title: Statistical Theory of Turbulence

progress.what: A hierarchical model of intermittency predicted the anomalous scaling exponents of velocity structure functions in close agreement with experiments.
progress.html: A hierarchical model of intermittency predicted the anomalous scaling exponents of velocity structure functions in close agreement with experiments.

progress.what: First analytic derivation of anomalous scaling, for a passive scalar in Kraichnan’s model of random flow; Chertkov, Falkovich, Kolokolov and Lebedev, and Shraiman and Siggia, found it independently.
progress.html: First analytic derivation of anomalous scaling, for a passive scalar in Kraichnan’s model of random flow; Chertkov, Falkovich, Kolokolov and Lebedev, and Shraiman and Siggia, found it independently.

progress.what: Constructed forced solutions of the 3D Navier–Stokes equations whose energy dissipation stays positive as viscosity goes to zero, a rigorous instance of the zeroth law of turbulence.
progress.html: Constructed forced solutions of the 3D Navier–Stokes equations whose energy dissipation stays positive as viscosity goes to zero, a rigorous instance of the zeroth law of turbulence.

progress.what: Showed that spontaneous stochasticity amplifies even thermal noise to the largest scales of turbulence within a few eddy turnover times.
progress.html: Showed that spontaneous stochasticity amplifies even thermal noise to the largest scales of turbulence within a few eddy turnover times.

nodes.html: Can the statistics of turbulence, its energy cascade, intermittency and anomalous scaling exponents, be derived from the equations of fluid flow? Kolmogorov’s 1941 theory predicts the basic scaling but misses intermittency, and engineering still relies on empirical closure models. A predictive theory of the exponents or a controlled closure would settle it; it is distinct from the Clay regularity problem.
nodes.summary: Can the statistics of turbulence, its energy cascade, intermittency and anomalous scaling exponents, be derived from the equations of fluid flow?

nodes.title: Stone Tools
nodes.html: Flaked stone tools from Lomekwi, Kenya, are about 3.3 million years old, older than the genus Homo. This is the first technology on the tree, and the first prerequisite.
nodes.summary: Flaked stone tools from Lomekwi, Kenya, are about 3.3 million years old, older than the genus Homo.

nodes.title: Hafted Tools
nodes.html: Stone points mounted on wooden shafts at Kathu Pan in South Africa about 500,000 years ago are the earliest known stone-tipped spears. Hafting gave a stone edge more leverage and reach, and it led to axes, knives and later the bow.
nodes.summary: Stone points mounted on wooden shafts at Kathu Pan in South Africa about 500,000 years ago are the earliest known stone-tipped spears.

nodes.title: Bow and Arrow
nodes.html: Stone arrow tips from Sibudu Cave in South Africa show that people used bows about 64,000 years ago. A bow stores muscle energy over the draw and releases it in an instant, which let hunters and warriors strike from a distance, and it stayed the main missile weapon until gunpowder.
nodes.summary: Stone arrow tips from Sibudu Cave in South Africa show that people used bows about 64,000 years ago.

nodes.title: Monumental Stone Architecture
nodes.html: At Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey, people raised carved T-shaped limestone pillars up to about 5.5 metres tall around 9500 BCE, with no clear evidence of farming at the site. It shows that monumental building could come before agriculture, and megalithic building continued for thousands of years, from Malta to Stonehenge.
nodes.summary: At Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey, people raised carved T-shaped limestone pillars up to about 5.5 metres tall around 9500 BCE, with no clear evidence of farming at the site.

nodes.title: Mudbrick Building
nodes.html: Sun-dried bricks of mud mixed with straw were in use by about 9000 BCE, for example in the earliest houses of Jericho. From around 5000 to 4000 BCE builders began firing bricks to make them stronger and more durable. Brick let people build walls, houses and cities where stone was scarce.
nodes.summary: Sun-dried bricks of mud mixed with straw were in use by about 9000 BCE, for example in the earliest houses of Jericho.

nodes.title: Boats
nodes.html: The Pesse canoe, a hollowed pine log found in the Netherlands, was made around 8000 BCE and is the oldest surviving boat. People had crossed open sea to reach Australia more than 50,000 years earlier, so boats are far older than any remains. Watercraft opened coasts, rivers and islands to settlement and trade.
nodes.summary: The Pesse canoe, a hollowed pine log found in the Netherlands, was made around 8000 BCE and is the oldest surviving boat.

nodes.title: Irrigation Canals
nodes.html: Canals built by the Samarra culture around 6000 BCE carried river water to fields in Mesopotamia, which let farmers grow crops where rainfall alone was too low. Irrigation fed the first cities, and irrigated land is about a fifth of the world’s cropland and yields roughly two fifths of its food.
nodes.summary: Canals built by the Samarra culture around 6000 BCE carried river water to fields in Mesopotamia, which let farmers grow crops where rainfall alone was too low.

nodes.title: Sail
nodes.html: Excavations from the Ubaid period in Mesopotamia, around 5000 BCE, give the earliest direct evidence of sailing boats, and Egyptian pottery shows sails by 3200 BCE. A sail turns wind into thrust, which freed boats from paddling and made long voyages and sea trade practical.
nodes.summary: Excavations from the Ubaid period in Mesopotamia, around 5000 BCE, give the earliest direct evidence of sailing boats, and Egyptian pottery shows sails by 3200 BCE.

nodes.title: Loom
nodes.html: A horizontal ground loom is painted on a Badarian dish from Egypt of about 4400 BCE, though woven cloth is thousands of years older. The loom holds warp threads under tension so the weft can be passed through them, and weaving became one of the most widespread crafts and, in the 18th century, the first major industry to be mechanized.
nodes.summary: A horizontal ground loom is painted on a Badarian dish from Egypt of about 4400 BCE, though woven cloth is thousands of years older.

nodes.title: Arch and Vault
nodes.html: Builders in Mesopotamia roofed brick drains with arches, as at Nippur before 3800 BCE, and the Romans later made arches and vaults the basis of their bridges, aqueducts and domes. An arch turns the weight above it into compression along its curve, so stone and brick can span openings without beams.
nodes.summary: Builders in Mesopotamia roofed brick drains with arches, as at Nippur before 3800 BCE, and the Romans later made arches and vaults the basis of their bridges, aqueducts and domes.

nodes.title: Wheel
nodes.html: The potter’s wheel came first; wheeled vehicles appear around 3500 BCE in Mesopotamia and Europe. The axle, a precisely fitted rotating joint, was the hard part.
nodes.summary: The potter’s wheel came first; wheeled vehicles appear around 3500 BCE in Mesopotamia and Europe.

nodes.title: Pyramid Construction
nodes.html: Imhotep is credited with the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara, built around 2670 BCE as one of the first large buildings of cut stone. The Great Pyramid of Giza, finished about 2560 BCE, stayed the tallest structure on Earth for roughly 3,800 years, and the pyramids show what organized labour and surveying could achieve in the third millennium BCE.
nodes.summary: Imhotep is credited with the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara, built around 2670 BCE as one of the first large buildings of cut stone.

nodes.title: Urban Drainage
nodes.html: Indus Valley cities such as Mohenjo-daro had covered brick drains running along their streets and household latrines connected to them by about 2600 BCE. These are among the earliest planned urban sewers, and they show that dense cities could carry waste away from living areas.
nodes.summary: Indus Valley cities such as Mohenjo-daro had covered brick drains running along their streets and household latrines connected to them by about 2600 BCE.

nodes.title: Spoked Wheel
nodes.html: The earliest known spoked wheels are those of the Sintashta culture in the southern Urals, dated to about 2000 BCE. Replacing the solid disc with spokes cut weight sharply and made fast wheeled vehicles possible, and chariots built on them soon spread to the Near East, Egypt, Greece and China.
nodes.summary: The earliest known spoked wheels are those of the Sintashta culture in the southern Urals, dated to about 2000 BCE.

nodes.title: Water Clock
nodes.html: An Egyptian official named Amenemhet is recorded as the inventor of a water clock in the 16th century BCE, and a surviving outflow clock from Karnak dates to about 1400 BCE. Greek engineers such as Ctesibius later added float regulators to keep the flow steady, an early use of feedback. Water clocks told the hours at night and indoors for courts, armies and astronomers.
nodes.summary: An Egyptian official named Amenemhet is recorded as the inventor of a water clock in the 16th century BCE, and a surviving outflow clock from Karnak dates to about 1400 BCE.

nodes.title: Qanat
nodes.html: A qanat is a gently sloping tunnel, reached by a line of vertical shafts, that carries groundwater to the surface by gravity with no pumping. Developed in ancient Iran in the early first millennium BCE, qanats watered farms and towns across Asia and North Africa, and some still flow today.
nodes.summary: A qanat is a gently sloping tunnel, reached by a line of vertical shafts, that carries groundwater to the surface by gravity with no pumping.

nodes.title: Roman Aqueducts
nodes.html: The Aqua Appia, begun in 312 BCE by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, was the first of the eleven aqueducts that brought water to Rome by gravity along underground channels and arcades. Roman engineers surveyed gentle gradients over long distances, and the aqueducts supplied baths, fountains and private houses for centuries.
nodes.summary: The Aqua Appia, begun in 312 BCE by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, was the first of the eleven aqueducts that brought water to Rome by gravity along underground channels and arcades.

nodes.title: Simple Machines
nodes.html: Archimedes gave the law of the lever and built compound pulleys (c. 250 BCE). The gears of the Antikythera mechanism (c. 100 BCE) computed the motions of the sky.
nodes.summary: Archimedes gave the law of the lever and built compound pulleys (c.

nodes.title: Water Wheel
nodes.html: Philo of Byzantium described a water-driven compartmented wheel for irrigation around 250 BCE, and by then wheels were also turning millstones in the Near East. The water wheel gave mills a source of power other than muscle, and for about two thousand years it ground grain and later sawed timber, forged iron and drove textile mills.
nodes.summary: Philo of Byzantium described a water-driven compartmented wheel for irrigation around 250 BCE, and by then wheels were also turning millstones in the Near East.

nodes.title: Roman Concrete
nodes.html: From about 200 BCE Roman builders mixed lime mortar with volcanic ash and rubble into a concrete that sets even under water. It made harbours, bridges and large vaults possible, and the Pantheon’s dome, completed around 125 CE and 43 metres across, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
nodes.summary: From about 200 BCE Roman builders mixed lime mortar with volcanic ash and rubble into a concrete that sets even under water.

nodes.title: Hero’s Automata
nodes.html: Hero of Alexandria, active around 60 CE, described a cart driven by a falling weight and cords that could be set to follow a programmed route, a coin-operated dispenser of holy water, and the aeolipile, a sphere spun by steam jets. They are among the earliest automatic machines on record, though none led to practical engines in his time.
nodes.summary: Hero of Alexandria, active around 60 CE, described a cart driven by a falling weight and cords that could be set to follow a programmed route, a coin-operated dispenser of holy water, and the aeolipile, a sphere spun by steam jets.

nodes.title: Crank and Connecting Rod
nodes.html: A water-powered stone sawmill at Hierapolis in Asia Minor, built in the second half of the third century CE, is the earliest known machine to use a crank and connecting rod to turn rotation into back-and-forth motion. The same linkage later converted the piston’s push into rotation in steam and petrol engines.
nodes.summary: A water-powered stone sawmill at Hierapolis in Asia Minor, built in the second half of the third century CE, is the earliest known machine to use a crank and connecting rod to turn rotation into back-and-forth motion.

nodes.title: Windmill
nodes.html: Windmills with a vertical axis turned millstones in Persia by the ninth century, and windmills with a horizontal axis appeared in northwestern Europe in the 1180s. They ground grain and later drained land, notably in the Netherlands, and the same principle drives today’s wind turbines.
nodes.summary: Windmills with a vertical axis turned millstones in Persia by the ninth century, and windmills with a horizontal axis appeared in northwestern Europe in the 1180s.

nodes.title: Pound Lock
nodes.html: Qiao Weiyue, a Song dynasty transport official, built a pound lock on China’s Grand Canal in 984: a chamber between two gates that lifts or lowers boats between stretches of canal at different levels. Mitre gates, in which two angled leaves meet in a V, came in 15th-century Italy and let canals climb hills with little loss of water.
nodes.summary: Qiao Weiyue, a Song dynasty transport official, built a pound lock on China’s Grand Canal in 984: a chamber between two gates that lifts or lowers boats between stretches of canal at different levels.

nodes.title: Magnetic Compass
nodes.html: Shen Kuo described a magnetized needle that points south in 1088 and noted that it does not point exactly at true south, and Chinese ships were steering by compass by the early twelfth century. The compass spread to the Islamic world and Europe, giving sailors a direction that did not depend on the sun or the stars.
nodes.summary: Shen Kuo described a magnetized needle that points south in 1088 and noted that it does not point exactly at true south, and Chinese ships were steering by compass by the early twelfth century.

nodes.title: Al-Jazari’s Machines
aliases: Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices
nodes.html: Ismail al-Jazari’s Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices (1206) described about fifty machines, among them water-raising pumps driven by cranks, camshafts, segmental gears and programmable automata. It is an illustrated manual that records the state of medieval mechanical engineering.
nodes.summary: Ismail al-Jazari’s Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices (1206) described about fifty machines, among them water-raising pumps driven by cranks, camshafts, segmental gears and programmable automata.

nodes.title: Eyeglasses
nodes.html: Convex reading lenses mounted in frames appeared in Italy around 1286, and a sermon by the friar Giordano da Pisa in 1306 says they had been invented within the previous twenty years. Spectacles extended the working lives of scribes and craftsmen, and the lens makers who spread them later built the first telescopes and microscopes.
nodes.summary: Convex reading lenses mounted in frames appeared in Italy around 1286, and a sermon by the friar Giordano da Pisa in 1306 says they had been invented within the previous twenty years.

nodes.title: Mechanical Clock
nodes.html: Weight-driven clocks regulated by a verge and foliot escapement appeared in European church and town towers around 1300. Su Song’s water-driven astronomical clock tower of the 1090s in China had used an earlier escapement. Mechanical clocks made time a measured quantity in towns and began a tradition of precision instrument making.
nodes.summary: Weight-driven clocks regulated by a verge and foliot escapement appeared in European church and town towers around 1300.

nodes.title: Ocean-Going Sailing Ship
nodes.html: Three-masted carracks with sternpost rudders and mixed square and lateen sails were big enough to carry cargo and crew across oceans. Carracks and their smaller cousins the caravels took Columbus across the Atlantic in 1492 and Vasco da Gama to India in 1498, and Magellan’s expedition sailed around the world from 1519.
nodes.summary: Three-masted carracks with sternpost rudders and mixed square and lateen sails were big enough to carry cargo and crew across oceans.

nodes.title: Flush Toilet
nodes.html: John Harington, a courtier of Elizabeth I, described a valve-operated flushing water closet in 1596, and Alexander Cumming patented the S-shaped trap in 1775, which holds water in its bend to block sewer gas. Connected to sewers, flush toilets carried waste out of houses and became standard in cities during the nineteenth century.
nodes.summary: John Harington, a courtier of Elizabeth I, described a valve-operated flushing water closet in 1596, and Alexander Cumming patented the S-shaped trap in 1775, which holds water in its bend to block sewer gas.

nodes.title: Telescope
nodes.html: Patented in the Netherlands in 1608. Galileo turned one on the sky in 1609–10 and found Jupiter’s moons and the phases of Venus.
nodes.summary: Patented in the Netherlands in 1608.

nodes.title: Micrometer
nodes.html: William Gascoigne, an English astronomer, built a screw micrometer for telescopes around 1640 to measure small angles between stars. Hand-held micrometers for machinists followed in the 19th century, and by turning a fine screw thread into a length reading they made measurement to a thousandth of an inch routine in workshops.
nodes.summary: William Gascoigne, an English astronomer, built a screw micrometer for telescopes around 1640 to measure small angles between stars.

nodes.title: Vacuum Pump
nodes.html: Otto von Guericke, mayor of Magdeburg, built an air pump in 1650 and in 1654 showed that teams of horses could not pull apart two evacuated copper hemispheres pressed together by the air. Vacuum pumps opened experiments on air pressure and the vacuum, and later made light bulbs, electron tubes and chip fabrication workable.
nodes.summary: Otto von Guericke, mayor of Magdeburg, built an air pump in 1650 and in 1654 showed that teams of horses could not pull apart two evacuated copper hemispheres pressed together by the air.

nodes.title: Pendulum Clock
nodes.html: Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656, using a swinging weight to regulate the movement. It cut typical clock error from about fifteen minutes a day to about fifteen seconds, and for nearly three centuries pendulum clocks were the most accurate timekeepers available.
nodes.summary: Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656, using a swinging weight to regulate the movement.

nodes.title: Microscope
nodes.html: Hooke’s Micrographia (1665) named the ‘cell’; van Leeuwenhoek’s single-lens microscopes revealed bacteria (1676).
nodes.summary: Hooke’s Micrographia (1665) named the ‘cell’; van Leeuwenhoek’s single-lens microscopes revealed bacteria (1676).

nodes.title: Reflecting Telescope
nodes.html: Isaac Newton built the first working reflecting telescope in 1668, using a curved mirror in place of a lens so that images lack the coloured fringes of early refractors. Mirrors can be made much larger than lenses, and every major research telescope of the last century has been a reflector.
nodes.summary: Isaac Newton built the first working reflecting telescope in 1668, using a curved mirror in place of a lens so that images lack the coloured fringes of early refractors.

nodes.title: Newton’s Minimal Resistance Problem

progress.what: Studied Newton’s problem among all convex bodies, without assuming rotational symmetry.
progress.html: Studied Newton’s problem among all convex bodies, without assuming rotational symmetry.

progress.what: The minimizer among convex bodies is not radially symmetric, so Newton’s solid is not optimal there.
progress.html: The minimizer among convex bodies is not radially symmetric, so Newton’s solid is not optimal there.

progress.what: Numerical shapes with lower resistance than all theoretically known candidates, showing the minimizers lie outside the classes studied so far.
progress.html: Numerical shapes with lower resistance than all theoretically known candidates, showing the minimizers lie outside the classes studied so far.

nodes.html: Which convex body of given length and width meets the least resistance in Newton’s model, where particles of a rarefied medium bounce off its front surface, a limit relevant to hypersonic flight? Newton solved it in 1687 among bodies of revolution, but the optimum among all convex bodies is not rotationally symmetric (1996) and is still unknown. Solving it means the optimal shape with a proof.
nodes.summary: Which convex body of given length and width meets the least resistance in Newton’s model, where particles of a rarefied medium bounce off its front surface, a limit relevant to hypersonic flight?

nodes.title: Steam Engine
nodes.html: Newcomen’s engine pumped water from mines (1712). Watt’s separate condenser (1769) made steam the power source of the Industrial Revolution.
nodes.summary: Newcomen’s engine pumped water from mines (1712).

nodes.title: Beam Theory
nodes.html: Leonhard Euler and Daniel Bernoulli worked out around 1750 how a beam bends under load, with its curvature proportional to the bending moment, building on Galileo’s 1638 study of the strength of materials. Euler also found the load at which a slender column buckles. The theory let engineers calculate bridges, floors and machine parts instead of relying on rules of thumb.
nodes.summary: Leonhard Euler and Daniel Bernoulli worked out around 1750 how a beam bends under load, with its curvature proportional to the bending moment, building on Galileo’s 1638 study of the strength of materials.

nodes.title: Marine Chronometer
nodes.html: John Harrison’s fourth sea clock, H4, lost only about five seconds during the 81-day voyage to Jamaica in 1761 and 1762, well inside the accuracy that the Longitude Act of 1714 demanded.
