A clock that keeps accurate home time lets a navigator find longitude at sea, and the chronometer made ocean navigation much safer.
nodes.summary: John Harrison’s fourth sea clock, H4, lost only about five seconds during the 81-day voyage to Jamaica in 1761 and 1762, well inside the accuracy that the Longitude Act of 1714 demanded.

nodes.title: Mechanized Spinning
nodes.html: James Hargreaves’s spinning jenny (1764), Richard Arkwright’s water frame (1769) and Samuel Crompton’s mule (1779) multiplied the thread one worker could spin. Arkwright’s water-powered Cromford Mill (1771) was an early factory, and mechanized cotton spinning was the leading industry of the early Industrial Revolution.
nodes.summary: James Hargreaves’s spinning jenny (1764), Richard Arkwright’s water frame (1769) and Samuel Crompton’s mule (1779) multiplied the thread one worker could spin.

nodes.title: Precision Boring Machine
nodes.html: John Wilkinson patented a boring mill in 1774 that machined iron cylinders round enough for pistons to seal, which made James Watt’s steam engines work well. The same method bored cannon, and accurate boring became a basic skill of the engineering industry.
nodes.summary: John Wilkinson patented a boring mill in 1774 that machined iron cylinders round enough for pistons to seal, which made James Watt’s steam engines work well.

nodes.title: Iron Bridge
nodes.html: The Iron Bridge over the River Severn at Coalbrookdale, designed by Thomas Farnolls Pritchard and cast by Abraham Darby III, was completed in 1779. Its cast-iron arch spans about 30 metres, and it was the first major bridge built of iron, showing that iron could replace stone and timber in large structures.
nodes.summary: The Iron Bridge over the River Severn at Coalbrookdale, designed by Thomas Farnolls Pritchard and cast by Abraham Darby III, was completed in 1779.

nodes.title: Balloon Flight
nodes.html: On 21 November 1783 Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d’Arlandes made the first free flight by people, over Paris in a hot-air balloon built by the Montgolfier brothers, and on 1 December Jacques Charles and Nicolas-Louis Robert flew a hydrogen balloon. Balloons gave the first views of the land from the air and led to airships.
nodes.summary: On 21 November 1783 Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d’Arlandes made the first free flight by people, over Paris in a hot-air balloon built by the Montgolfier brothers, and on 1 December Jacques Charles and Nicolas-Louis Robert flew a hydrogen balloon.

nodes.title: Centrifugal Governor
nodes.html: James Watt and Matthew Boulton fitted a centrifugal governor to their steam engines in 1788. Two weighted balls swung outward as the engine sped up and closed the throttle, so the machine held a steady speed without an operator, and it became the standard example of a feedback controller.
nodes.summary: James Watt and Matthew Boulton fitted a centrifugal governor to their steam engines in 1788.

nodes.title: Hydraulic Press
nodes.html: Joseph Bramah patented a hydraulic press in 1795 that used Pascal’s principle, a small pump pushing water against a large piston, to multiply force. Henry Maudslay, who worked for Bramah, solved the sealing problem with a leather cup washer. Hydraulic presses later forged and pressed metal, and hydraulic power still moves cranes and excavators.
nodes.summary: Joseph Bramah patented a hydraulic press in 1795 that used Pascal’s principle, a small pump pushing water against a large piston, to multiply force.

nodes.title: Screw-Cutting Lathe
nodes.html: Henry Maudslay built an all-metal lathe around 1800 with a slide rest and a lead screw that cut screw threads accurately and repeatably. Accurate screws allowed precise measuring instruments and parts that fit, and Maudslay’s workshop trained the engineers who built the first machine tools.
nodes.summary: Henry Maudslay built an all-metal lathe around 1800 with a slide rest and a lead screw that cut screw threads accurately and repeatably.

nodes.title: High-Pressure Steam Engine
nodes.html: Richard Trevithick in Cornwall and Oliver Evans in the United States built steam engines that worked at pressures well above atmospheric around 1801. They were far smaller and lighter than Watt’s low-pressure engines, light enough to move themselves, and Trevithick’s locomotive hauled a train at Penydarren in Wales in 1804.
nodes.summary: Richard Trevithick in Cornwall and Oliver Evans in the United States built steam engines that worked at pressures well above atmospheric around 1801.

nodes.title: Steamboat
nodes.html: Robert Fulton’s North River Steamboat, later known as Clermont, began regular passenger service between New York and Albany in 1807, the first commercially successful steamboat service. Earlier steamboats, such as Jouffroy’s Pyroscaphe on the Saône in 1783, had worked but did not pay. Steamboats opened American rivers to upstream traffic and shortened journeys.
nodes.summary: Robert Fulton’s North River Steamboat, later known as Clermont, began regular passenger service between New York and Albany in 1807, the first commercially successful steamboat service.

nodes.title: Stethoscope
nodes.html: René Laennec, a French physician, first rolled paper into a tube to listen to a patient’s chest in 1816 and then made a wooden tube, the first stethoscope. Listening to the heart and lungs let doctors link sounds to disease, checked against autopsy findings, and began the routine use of instruments in diagnosis.
nodes.summary: René Laennec, a French physician, first rolled paper into a tube to listen to a patient’s chest in 1816 and then made a wooden tube, the first stethoscope.

nodes.title: Bicycle
nodes.html: Karl Drais showed his pedal-less running machine in 1817, and in 1885 John Kemp Starley’s Rover, with two wheels of equal size and a chain drive, set the form of the modern bicycle. Bicycles gave ordinary people cheap, fast personal transport, and bicycle makers supplied skills and parts for early cars and the Wright brothers’ aeroplane.
nodes.summary: Karl Drais showed his pedal-less running machine in 1817, and in 1885 John Kemp Starley’s Rover, with two wheels of equal size and a chain drive, set the form of the modern bicycle.

nodes.title: Interchangeable Parts
nodes.html: Honoré Blanc in France tried in the 1780s to make interchangeable musket parts, though they were still filed by hand. In the 1820s Simeon North’s milling machines and John H. Hall’s gauges in the United States turned out truly interchangeable rifle parts. Guns, then sewing machines, clocks and cars could then be assembled without fitting, which made mass production possible.
nodes.summary: Honoré Blanc in France tried in the 1780s to make interchangeable musket parts, though they were still filed by hand.

nodes.title: Steam Railway
nodes.html: The Stockton and Darlington Railway (1825) was the first public line to use steam locomotives, and the Liverpool and Manchester Railway (1830), whose engine Rocket had won the Rainhill Trials in 1829, ran all its trains by steam between two cities. Designs by George and Robert Stephenson set the pattern, and railways cut journey times and reshaped trade and cities.
nodes.summary: The Stockton and Darlington Railway (1825) was the first public line to use steam locomotives, and the Liverpool and Manchester Railway (1830), whose engine Rocket had won the Rainhill Trials in 1829, ran all its trains by steam between two cities.

nodes.title: Tunnelling Shield
nodes.html: Marc Brunel patented a tunnelling shield in 1818, an iron frame that supported the ground at the working face while miners dug, and used it from 1825 on the Thames Tunnel, the first tunnel under a navigable river. James Henry Greathead’s circular shield of 1869 led to the tunnel boring machines that now dig subway, sewer and road tunnels in soft ground.
nodes.summary: Marc Brunel patented a tunnelling shield in 1818, an iron frame that supported the ground at the working face while miners dug, and used it from 1825 on the Thames Tunnel, the first tunnel under a navigable river.

nodes.title: Suspension Bridge
nodes.html: Thomas Telford’s Menai Suspension Bridge (1826) hung a 176 metre span from wrought-iron chains, the longest in the world when it opened. The Brooklyn Bridge (1883), designed by John A. Roebling, used spun steel-wire cables and set the modern form, and suspension bridges now hold the span records, above two kilometres.
nodes.summary: Thomas Telford’s Menai Suspension Bridge (1826) hung a 176 metre span from wrought-iron chains, the longest in the world when it opened.

nodes.title: Water Turbine
nodes.html: Benoît Fourneyron built a water turbine in 1827 that was more efficient and more compact than any water wheel, and developed it over the following years. James B. Francis’s inward-flow turbine of 1849 and Lester Pelton’s impulse wheel of 1879 are still the main designs in hydroelectric plants.
nodes.summary: Benoît Fourneyron built a water turbine in 1827 that was more efficient and more compact than any water wheel, and developed it over the following years.

nodes.title: Slow Sand Filter
nodes.html: James Simpson built slow sand filters at the Chelsea Waterworks in London in 1829, passing Thames water through beds of sand to clear it. In the cholera epidemic of 1892, filtered Altona had far fewer cases than neighbouring Hamburg, which drew unfiltered river water, and filtration became standard for city supplies.
nodes.summary: James Simpson built slow sand filters at the Chelsea Waterworks in London in 1829, passing Thames water through beds of sand to clear it.

nodes.title: Electric Motor
nodes.html: Michael Faraday showed continuous electromagnetic rotation in 1821, and in 1834 Moritz von Jacobi built a motor that did useful work. Electric motors turn electrical energy into motion with little loss, and they now use close to half of the world’s electricity, driving pumps, fans, tools, trains and vehicles.
nodes.summary: Michael Faraday showed continuous electromagnetic rotation in 1821, and in 1834 Moritz von Jacobi built a motor that did useful work.

nodes.title: Vapour-Compression Refrigeration
nodes.html: Jacob Perkins patented a closed-cycle vapour-compression refrigerating machine in 1834, in which a compressor, condenser and evaporator move heat from a cold space to a warm one. Carl von Linde’s ammonia machines of the 1870s industrialized cold storage and brewing, and refrigerators, air conditioners and heat pumps still run the same cycle.
nodes.summary: Jacob Perkins patented a closed-cycle vapour-compression refrigerating machine in 1834, in which a compressor, condenser and evaporator move heat from a cold space to a warm one.

nodes.title: Electric Telegraph
nodes.html: Messages at the speed of electricity (1837). A transatlantic cable worked for three weeks in 1858 and for good from 1866.
nodes.summary: Messages at the speed of electricity (1837).

nodes.title: Screw-Driven Iron Steamship
nodes.html: Isambard Kingdom Brunel’s SS Great Britain, launched in 1843, was the first large ocean-going ship to combine an iron hull with a screw propeller, and in 1845 the first iron steamer to cross the Atlantic. The propeller had been patented in 1836 by Francis Pettit Smith and John Ericsson, and iron hulls and propellers replaced wooden paddle steamers.
nodes.summary: Isambard Kingdom Brunel’s SS Great Britain, launched in 1843, was the first large ocean-going ship to combine an iron hull with a screw propeller, and in 1845 the first iron steamer to cross the Atlantic.

nodes.title: Safety Elevator
nodes.html: Elisha Otis invented a safety brake for hoists in 1852 and demonstrated it at the New York Crystal Palace in 1854, cutting the rope of a platform he stood on and letting a ratchet catch the fall. With the fear of falling removed, passenger elevators spread from 1857, and they made tall buildings practical to use.
nodes.summary: Elisha Otis invented a safety brake for hoists in 1852 and demonstrated it at the New York Crystal Palace in 1854, cutting the rope of a platform he stood on and letting a ratchet catch the fall.

nodes.title: Hypodermic Syringe
nodes.html: In 1853 Alexander Wood in Edinburgh and Charles Pravaz in Lyon each devised a syringe with a hollow needle for injecting liquids under the skin, and Wood used his to give morphine. Hypodermic injection gave a fast, dosed route for drugs and later underpinned vaccination, anaesthesia and insulin treatment.
nodes.summary: In 1853 Alexander Wood in Edinburgh and Charles Pravaz in Lyon each devised a syringe with a hollow needle for injecting liquids under the skin, and Wood used his to give morphine.

nodes.title: Metal Fatigue
nodes.html: August Wöhler tested railway axles under repeated loading in the 1850s and 1860s and showed that steel can break at stresses far below its static strength if the load is cycled, and that below a certain stress it can last indefinitely. His stress-against-life curve, now called the S-N curve, is the basis of fatigue design for axles, aircraft and bridges.
nodes.summary: August Wöhler tested railway axles under repeated loading in the 1850s and 1860s and showed that steel can break at stresses far below its static strength if the load is cycled, and that below a certain stress it can last indefinitely.

nodes.title: 3D Generic Rigidity

progress.what: Generic rigidity in the plane is characterized by edge counts, a result rediscovered by Laman in 1970.
progress.html: Generic rigidity in the plane is characterized by edge counts, a result rediscovered by Laman in 1970.

progress.what: Generic rigidity depends only on the graph, not on the positions of the joints.
progress.html: Generic rigidity depends only on the graph, not on the positions of the joints.

progress.what: Rigidity matroids, with the conjecture that the generic 3D rigidity matroid is the largest abstract 3-rigidity matroid.
progress.html: Rigidity matroids, with the conjecture that the generic 3D rigidity matroid is the largest abstract 3-rigidity matroid.

progress.what: Proved Whiteley’s maximality conjecture in dimension 3: the C¹₂-cofactor matroid from spline theory is the largest abstract 3-rigidity matroid.
progress.html: Proved Whiteley’s maximality conjecture in dimension 3: the C¹₂-cofactor matroid from spline theory is the largest abstract 3-rigidity matroid.

nodes.html: When is a generic framework of bars and joints in space rigid? In the plane the answer depends only on counting edges in subgraphs (Pollaczek-Geiringer 1927, Laman 1970), but in 3D Maxwell’s 1864 count is not enough and no combinatorial characterization is known; rigidity can only be tested by a matrix rank computation at random coordinates. Solving it means a combinatorial characterization of generic 3D rigidity.
nodes.summary: When is a generic framework of bars and joints in space rigid?

nodes.title: Modern Sewerage
nodes.html: Hamburg began planned sewers in the 1840s to a design by William Lindley, and Joseph Bazalgette’s intercepting sewers carried London’s sewage east of the city from 1865, after the Great Stink of 1858. Sewer networks carried waste away from homes and water supplies, which helped end London’s cholera epidemics, and became the model for city sanitation.
nodes.summary: Hamburg began planned sewers in the 1840s to a design by William Lindley, and Joseph Bazalgette’s intercepting sewers carried London’s sewage east of the city from 1865, after the Great Stink of 1858.

nodes.title: Dynamo
nodes.html: In 1866 and 1867 Werner von Siemens, Charles Wheatstone and others built self-excited dynamos, in which the machine’s own current feeds its magnet, and Zénobe Gramme’s ring dynamo of 1871 gave smooth direct current. Generators turn mechanical power from steam or water into electricity, which became cheap enough for industry, lighting and tramways.
nodes.summary: In 1866 and 1867 Werner von Siemens, Charles Wheatstone and others built self-excited dynamos, in which the machine’s own current feeds its magnet, and Zénobe Gramme’s ring dynamo of 1871 gave smooth direct current.

nodes.title: Reinforced Concrete
nodes.html: Joseph Monier patented iron-reinforced concrete garden tubs in 1867, and François Hennebique’s patented system of 1892 used reinforced beams, columns and slabs to frame whole buildings. Concrete resists compression and steel resists tension, so together they span floors and bridges cheaply, and reinforced concrete is now the most widely used structural material in the world.
nodes.summary: Joseph Monier patented iron-reinforced concrete garden tubs in 1867, and François Hennebique’s patented system of 1892 used reinforced beams, columns and slabs to frame whole buildings.

nodes.title: Feedback Stability Theory
nodes.html: James Clerk Maxwell’s paper On Governors (1868) analysed a steam engine’s speed governor with differential equations and showed that stability depends on the roots of its characteristic equation. Edward Routh (1877) and Adolf Hurwitz (1895) found tests that decide stability from the equation’s coefficients, which began the mathematical theory of feedback control.
nodes.summary: James Clerk Maxwell’s paper On Governors (1868) analysed a steam engine’s speed governor with differential equations and showed that stability depends on the roots of its characteristic equation.

nodes.title: Wind Tunnel
nodes.html: Francis Herbert Wenham designed and ran the first enclosed wind tunnel in 1871 for the Aeronautical Society of Great Britain, blowing air past models to measure lift and drag. Tunnel tests let designers study wings without risking flights, and the Wright brothers’ tunnel experiments in 1901 corrected earlier published data and fixed their wing design.
nodes.summary: Francis Herbert Wenham designed and ran the first enclosed wind tunnel in 1871 for the Aeronautical Society of Great Britain, blowing air past models to measure lift and drag.

nodes.title: Internal Combustion Engine
nodes.html: Otto’s four-stroke engine (1876) and Diesel’s compression-ignition engine (1893) put compact power into cars, ships and aircraft.
nodes.summary: Otto’s four-stroke engine (1876) and Diesel’s compression-ignition engine (1893) put compact power into cars, ships and aircraft.

nodes.title: Telephone
nodes.html: Alexander Graham Bell was granted the first US telephone patent in March 1876, after filing on the same day as Elisha Gray’s caveat for a similar device, and soon spoke to his assistant Thomas Watson over a wire. Telephone networks became the first worldwide switched communication system, and Almon Strowger’s automatic exchange of 1891 removed the operator.
nodes.summary: Alexander Graham Bell was granted the first US telephone patent in March 1876, after filing on the same day as Elisha Gray’s caveat for a similar device, and soon spoke to his assistant Thomas Watson over a wire.

nodes.title: Sound Recording
nodes.html: Thomas Edison recorded and played back sound on a tinfoil-covered cylinder in 1877, and Emile Berliner’s flat-disc gramophone of 1887 led to the mass-produced record. Recorded sound let music, speech and news be stored and copied, and the recording industry grew from these machines.
nodes.summary: Thomas Edison recorded and played back sound on a tinfoil-covered cylinder in 1877, and Emile Berliner’s flat-disc gramophone of 1887 led to the mass-produced record.

nodes.title: Electric Traction
nodes.html: Werner von Siemens showed a small electric railway at the Berlin trade fair in 1879, and Frank Sprague’s streetcar system in Richmond, Virginia, which opened in 1888, was the first large and successful electric tramway. Electric traction led to streetcars and then subways, which were cleaner and quicker than horses or steam in cities.
nodes.summary: Werner von Siemens showed a small electric railway at the Berlin trade fair in 1879, and Frank Sprague’s streetcar system in Richmond, Virginia, which opened in 1888, was the first large and successful electric tramway.

nodes.title: Incandescent Light Bulb
nodes.html: Joseph Swan in Britain and Thomas Edison in the United States made durable carbon-filament lamps in an evacuated glass bulb in 1878 to 1880, and Edison’s bamboo-filament lamp lasted more than a thousand hours. Cheap, safe electric light created the demand for power stations and grids and replaced gas and oil lamps in homes and streets.
nodes.summary: Joseph Swan in Britain and Thomas Edison in the United States made durable carbon-filament lamps in an evacuated glass bulb in 1878 to 1880, and Edison’s bamboo-filament lamp lasted more than a thousand hours.

nodes.title: Arc Welding
nodes.html: Nikolay Benardos and Stanisław Olszewski demonstrated carbon-arc welding in 1881, using an electric arc between a carbon rod and the work to melt and join metal, and patented it in the 1880s. Arc welding with metal electrodes soon followed, and welded steel later built ships, pipelines and skyscrapers.
nodes.summary: Nikolay Benardos and Stanisław Olszewski demonstrated carbon-arc welding in 1881, using an electric arc between a carbon rod and the work to melt and join metal, and patented it in the 1880s.

nodes.title: Electric Power Grid
nodes.html: Edison’s Pearl Street Station (1882) lit lower Manhattan; Tesla and Westinghouse’s alternating current (from 1888) carried power across whole regions.
nodes.summary: Edison’s Pearl Street Station (1882) lit lower Manhattan; Tesla and Westinghouse’s alternating current (from 1888) carried power across whole regions.

nodes.title: Hydroelectric Power
nodes.html: The Vulcan Street Plant at Appleton, Wisconsin, began generating electricity from falling water in September 1882. Hydroelectric stations spread quickly, with Niagara Falls sending alternating current to Buffalo in 1896 and pumped storage plants appearing in the 1890s. Hydropower remains the largest renewable source of electricity.
nodes.summary: The Vulcan Street Plant at Appleton, Wisconsin, began generating electricity from falling water in September 1882.

nodes.title: Steam Turbine
nodes.html: Charles Parsons patented a multistage steam turbine in 1884 and coupled it to a dynamo, and his turbine-driven Turbinia dashed past the Royal Navy fleet at about 34 knots in 1897. Steam turbines drive most of the world’s electric generators and many ships, because they run smoothly at high speed with far better efficiency than piston engines.
nodes.summary: Charles Parsons patented a multistage steam turbine in 1884 and coupled it to a dynamo, and his turbine-driven Turbinia dashed past the Royal Navy fleet at about 34 knots in 1897.

nodes.title: Electrical Transformer
nodes.html: Károly Zipernowsky, Ottó Bláthy and Miksa Déri at the Ganz Works in Budapest built closed-iron-core transformers in 1885, and William Stanley made a practical one for the Westinghouse system in 1886. A transformer steps alternating voltage up for long-distance transmission and down for use, which made high-voltage AC grids possible.
nodes.summary: Károly Zipernowsky, Ottó Bláthy and Miksa Déri at the Ganz Works in Budapest built closed-iron-core transformers in 1885, and William Stanley made a practical one for the Westinghouse system in 1886.

nodes.title: Steel-Frame Skyscraper
nodes.html: William Le Baron Jenney’s ten-storey Home Insurance Building in Chicago, completed in 1885, is often cited as the first skyscraper, with a metal skeleton supporting its floors and walls. Together with the safety elevator, steel frames let buildings rise far higher, and the Burj Khalifa reached 828 metres in 2010.
nodes.summary: William Le Baron Jenney’s ten-storey Home Insurance Building in Chicago, completed in 1885, is often cited as the first skyscraper, with a metal skeleton supporting its floors and walls.

nodes.title: Automobile
nodes.html: Karl Benz patented his three-wheeled Patent-Motorwagen, powered by a one-cylinder petrol engine, in January 1886, and Bertha Benz drove one 106 kilometres in 1888 to show it was practical. Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach built a four-wheeled motor carriage in 1886 as well. Motor vehicles have reshaped cities and trade, and over a billion are now on the road.
nodes.summary: Karl Benz patented his three-wheeled Patent-Motorwagen, powered by a one-cylinder petrol engine, in January 1886, and Bertha Benz drove one 106 kilometres in 1888 to show it was practical.

nodes.title: Wind Turbine
nodes.html: James Blyth in Scotland in 1887 and Charles Brush in Ohio in 1888 each built a windmill that generated electricity, and Poul la Cour in Denmark developed generating turbines in the 1890s. Johannes Juul’s Gedser turbine of 1957 set the three-blade, upwind layout still used today, and wind is now among the cheapest sources of new electricity.
nodes.summary: James Blyth in Scotland in 1887 and Charles Brush in Ohio in 1888 each built a windmill that generated electricity, and Poul la Cour in Denmark developed generating turbines in the 1890s.

nodes.title: Induction Motor
nodes.html: Galileo Ferraris in Italy and Nikola Tesla in the United States independently described rotating magnetic fields and the induction motor in 1888. Alternating current in fixed coils produces a field that drags a simple rotor around, so the motor needs no brushes. Induction motors are rugged and cheap, and they power most of the world’s industrial machinery.
nodes.summary: Galileo Ferraris in Italy and Nikola Tesla in the United States independently described rotating magnetic fields and the induction motor in 1888.

nodes.title: Pneumatic Tyre
nodes.html: Robert William Thomson patented an air-filled tyre in 1845, and John Boyd Dunlop reinvented it and patented it for bicycles in 1888. The air cushion absorbs bumps and lowers rolling resistance, and pneumatic tyres made bicycles and later road vehicles faster and more comfortable.
nodes.summary: Robert William Thomson patented an air-filled tyre in 1845, and John Boyd Dunlop reinvented it and patented it for bicycles in 1888.

nodes.title: Heavier-Than-Air Glider
nodes.html: George Cayley built the first glider to carry a person around 1853, and Otto Lilienthal made some two thousand controlled glides in Germany between 1891 and 1896, dying after a crash in 1896. Lilienthal’s measurements of curved wings and his photographs of flights showed that heavier-than-air flight was possible, and they inspired the Wright brothers.
nodes.summary: George Cayley built the first glider to carry a person around 1853, and Otto Lilienthal made some two thousand controlled glides in Germany between 1891 and 1896, dying after a crash in 1896.

nodes.title: Three-Phase Power
nodes.html: Mikhail Dolivo-Dobrovolsky developed practical three-phase generators and motors at AEG in 1888 and 1889, and in 1891 a three-phase line sent power about 175 km from Lauffen to Frankfurt, in a demonstration organized by Oskar von Miller. Three-phase current gives smooth, constant power to motors and needs less wire than single-phase, and today’s grids all use it.
nodes.summary: Mikhail Dolivo-Dobrovolsky developed practical three-phase generators and motors at AEG in 1888 and 1889, and in 1891 a three-phase line sent power about 175 km from Lauffen to Frankfurt, in a demonstration organized by Oskar von Miller.

nodes.title: Painlevé Paradox

progress.what: For the classic sliding rod, the contact force can grow without bound near singular points while its impulse stays finite, so the motion must jump.
progress.html: For the classic sliding rod, the contact force can grow without bound near singular points while its impulse stays finite, so the motion must jump.

progress.what: A mathematical resolution with measure differential inclusions, in which solutions exist once impulsive contact forces are allowed.
progress.html: A mathematical resolution with measure differential inclusions, in which solutions exist once impulsive contact forces are allowed.

progress.what: A review finds forward evolution unsolved except in restricted planar single-contact cases, with dynamic jam and reverse chatter as ambiguities reachable in finite time.
progress.html: A review finds forward evolution unsolved except in restricted planar single-contact cases, with dynamic jam and reverse chatter as ambiguities reachable in finite time.

nodes.html: With Coulomb friction, the equations of a sliding rigid body can have no solution or several (Painlevé, 1895), so a simulator cannot always say what happens next. Resolutions exist for a single contact in the plane, but no consistent general rule for forward evolution with several contacts or in 3D is known, which affects robot grasping and contact simulation. Solving it means a well-posed, physically justified rule covering these cases.
nodes.summary: With Coulomb friction, the equations of a sliding rigid body can have no solution or several (Painlevé, 1895), so a simulator cannot always say what happens next.

nodes.title: Radio
nodes.html: Hertz produced Maxwell’s waves in the lab (1887); Marconi turned them into wireless telegraphy (1895) and sent a signal across the Atlantic (1901).
nodes.summary: Hertz produced Maxwell’s waves in the lab (1887); Marconi turned them into wireless telegraphy (1895) and sent a signal across the Atlantic (1901).

nodes.title: Medical X-Ray Imaging
nodes.html: Wilhelm Röntgen announced X-rays in December 1895, and within weeks doctors were using them to find fractures, bullets and swallowed objects. For the first time a living body could be seen inside without surgery. Radiography became routine in hospitals and led to fluoroscopy, mammography and CT.
nodes.summary: Wilhelm Röntgen announced X-rays in December 1895, and within weeks doctors were using them to find fractures, bullets and swallowed objects.

nodes.title: Cathode-Ray Tube
nodes.html: Karl Ferdinand Braun built a cathode-ray tube with a fluorescent screen in 1897, in which a beam of electrons steered by magnetic fields draws a trace. The Braun tube became the oscilloscope display, the radar screen, the television picture tube and the monitor of early computers, until flat panels replaced it in the 2000s.
nodes.summary: Karl Ferdinand Braun built a cathode-ray tube with a fluorescent screen in 1897, in which a beam of electrons steered by magnetic fields draws a trace.

nodes.title: Submarine
nodes.html: John Philip Holland’s submarine, launched in 1897 and bought by the US Navy in 1900 as USS Holland, was one of the first practical ones: it ran on a petrol engine at the surface and on batteries underwater, and could dive and be steered while submerged. Submarines changed naval warfare in the First World War and later carried nuclear missiles.
nodes.summary: John Philip Holland’s submarine, launched in 1897 and bought by the US Navy in 1900 as USS Holland, was one of the first practical ones: it ran on a petrol engine at the surface and on batteries underwater, and could dive and be steered while submerged.

nodes.title: Air Conditioning
nodes.html: Willis Carrier designed a system for a Brooklyn printing plant in 1902 that passed air over cold coils to control both temperature and humidity, and patented the apparatus in 1906. Air conditioning made factories, hospitals and data centres workable in heat, and it let cities and industry grow in hot regions.
nodes.summary: Willis Carrier designed a system for a Brooklyn printing plant in 1902 that passed air over cold coils to control both temperature and humidity, and patented the apparatus in 1906.

nodes.title: Electrocardiograph
nodes.html: Willem Einthoven used a string galvanometer to record the electrical activity of the human heart and published his method in 1903, naming the waves of the trace P, Q, R, S and T. The electrocardiogram became the basic tool for diagnosing arrhythmias and heart attacks, and Einthoven received the 1924 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
nodes.summary: Willem Einthoven used a string galvanometer to record the electrical activity of the human heart and published his method in 1903, naming the waves of the trace P, Q, R, S and T.

nodes.title: Powered Flight
nodes.html: Twelve seconds and 37 metres at Kitty Hawk on 17 December 1903. The Moon landing came 66 years later.
nodes.summary: Twelve seconds and 37 metres at Kitty Hawk on 17 December 1903.

nodes.title: Geothermal Power
nodes.html: On 4 July 1904 Prince Piero Ginori Conti lit five light bulbs with a dynamo driven by natural steam at Larderello in Italy, and a commercial geothermal power station began there in 1911. Geothermal plants use the Earth’s heat for steady power in volcanic regions, and the Larderello field still produces electricity.
nodes.summary: On 4 July 1904 Prince Piero Ginori Conti lit five light bulbs with a dynamo driven by natural steam at Larderello in Italy, and a commercial geothermal power station began there in 1911.

nodes.title: Michell’s Three-Forces Problem

progress.what: A large class of exact least-weight solutions, later the basis of three-force layouts.
progress.html: A large class of exact least-weight solutions, later the basis of three-force layouts.

progress.what: Exact solutions of the three forces problem for a class of loads, applied to least-weight symmetric frameworks.
progress.html: Exact solutions of the three forces problem for a class of loads, applied to least-weight symmetric frameworks.

progress.what: Exact layouts when two of the forces are perpendicular, classified by the position of the third, guided by adaptive ground-structure numerics.
progress.html: Exact layouts when two of the forces are perpendicular, classified by the position of the third, guided by adaptive ground-structure numerics.

nodes.html: Find the lightest fully stressed truss that carries three balanced forces applied anywhere in the plane, the basic unsolved case of Michell’s 1904 theory of optimal frame structures. Exact solutions are known only for special configurations, such as two of the forces being perpendicular (Sokół and Lewiński, 2016). Solving it means the optimal layout and weight for every position of the three forces.
nodes.summary: Find the lightest fully stressed truss that carries three balanced forces applied anywhere in the plane, the basic unsolved case of Michell’s 1904 theory of optimal frame structures.

nodes.title: Vacuum Tube
nodes.html: Fleming’s diode (1904) and de Forest’s triode amplifier (1906) started electronics. ENIAC used about 18,000 of them.
nodes.summary: Fleming’s diode (1904) and de Forest’s triode amplifier (1906) started electronics.

nodes.title: Water Chlorination
nodes.html: John Leal, with the engineer George Fuller, began continuous chlorination of Jersey City’s water supply in 1908, the first on this scale in the United States. Together with filtration it sharply cut typhoid and other waterborne disease in the cities that adopted it, and it is credited with much of the fall in urban death rates in the early twentieth century.
nodes.summary: John Leal, with the engineer George Fuller, began continuous chlorination of Jersey City’s water supply in 1908, the first on this scale in the United States.

nodes.title: Autopilot
nodes.html: Lawrence Sperry demonstrated a gyroscopic stabilizer built by his father Elmer Sperry in 1912, and in 1914 flew a biplane past judges near Paris with his hands raised while the device held it level. Gyroscopic autopilots later flew aircraft over long distances, and computer-driven systems now fly and land airliners.
nodes.summary: Lawrence Sperry demonstrated a gyroscopic stabilizer built by his father Elmer Sperry in 1912, and in 1914 flew a biplane past judges near Paris with his hands raised while the device held it level.

nodes.title: Moving Assembly Line
nodes.html: Henry Ford’s engineers, among them Charles Sorensen, introduced a moving assembly line for the Model T at Highland Park, Michigan, in 1913. Chassis assembly time fell from about twelve hours to about ninety minutes, cutting the car’s price until ordinary families could buy it. Mass production then spread to every large industry.
nodes.summary: Henry Ford’s engineers, among them Charles Sorensen, introduced a moving assembly line for the Model T at Highland Park, Michigan, in 1913.

nodes.title: Activated Sludge
nodes.html: Edward Ardern and William Lockett at the Davyhulme works in Manchester found in 1914 that bubbling air through sewage containing a suspended mass of microbes cleared it of organic matter in hours. Activated sludge is still the main biological process for treating city wastewater, and it keeps sewage from polluting rivers and coasts.
nodes.summary: Edward Ardern and William Lockett at the Davyhulme works in Manchester found in 1914 that bubbling air through sewage containing a suspended mass of microbes cleared it of organic matter in hours.

nodes.title: All-Metal Aircraft
nodes.html: Hugo Junkers’s J 1, which first flew in December 1915, was the first all-metal aircraft, a cantilever monoplane of sheet iron with no wing bracing wires. Metal skins carried loads better than fabric over wood, and stressed-skin airliners such as the Douglas DC-3 of 1935 followed, making aircraft stronger, more durable and more economical.
nodes.summary: Hugo Junkers’s J 1, which first flew in December 1915, was the first all-metal aircraft, a cantilever monoplane of sheet iron with no wing bracing wires.

nodes.title: Sonar
nodes.html: Paul Langevin and Constantin Chilowsky used a quartz crystal transducer to send and receive ultrasonic pulses under water, and between 1915 and 1918 detected objects such as submarines from their echoes. Sonar became essential for naval warfare, fishing and mapping the sea floor, and the same pulse-echo idea led to ultrasonic testing and medical ultrasound.
nodes.summary: Paul Langevin and Constantin Chilowsky used a quartz crystal transducer to send and receive ultrasonic pulses under water, and between 1915 and 1918 detected objects such as submarines from their echoes.

nodes.title: Superheterodyne Receiver
nodes.html: Edwin Howard Armstrong devised the superheterodyne receiver in 1918 while serving in France. It mixes the incoming radio signal with a local oscillator to shift it to one fixed intermediate frequency, where it can be filtered and amplified with high gain and selectivity, and nearly every radio, television and mobile phone receiver still works this way.
nodes.summary: Edwin Howard Armstrong devised the superheterodyne receiver in 1918 while serving in France.

nodes.title: PID Controller
nodes.html: Nicolas Minorsky analysed the automatic steering of ships in 1922 and showed that a controller acting on the error, on its accumulated sum and on its rate of change could hold a course. Proportional, integral and derivative terms are simple to tune, and PID loops still run the large majority of industrial control systems, from thermostats to chemical plants.
nodes.summary: Nicolas Minorsky analysed the automatic steering of ships in 1922 and showed that a controller acting on the error, on its accumulated sum and on its rate of change could hold a course.

nodes.title: Electroencephalography
nodes.html: Hans Berger, a German psychiatrist, recorded the first electrical activity from a human brain through the scalp in 1924 and published it in 1929, describing the alpha rhythm. EEG gives a millisecond record of brain activity without surgery, and it is used to diagnose epilepsy and sleep disorders and underlies non-invasive brain-computer interfaces.
nodes.summary: Hans Berger, a German psychiatrist, recorded the first electrical activity from a human brain through the scalp in 1924 and published it in 1929, describing the alpha rhythm.

nodes.title: Statistical Process Control
nodes.html: Walter Shewhart at Bell Telephone Laboratories drew the first control chart in 1924, separating the random variation inherent in a process from variation with an assignable cause. His method tells a manufacturer when to adjust a process and when to leave it alone, and W. Edwards Deming took the ideas to Japan after 1950, where they shaped modern quality management.
nodes.summary: Walter Shewhart at Bell Telephone Laboratories drew the first control chart in 1924, separating the random variation inherent in a process from variation with an assignable cause.

nodes.title: Liquid-Fuel Rocket
nodes.html: Tsiolkovsky’s rocket equation (1903) showed spaceflight was possible in principle; Goddard flew the first liquid-fuelled rocket in 1926.
nodes.summary: Tsiolkovsky’s rocket equation (1903) showed spaceflight was possible in principle; Goddard flew the first liquid-fuelled rocket in 1926.

nodes.title: Television
nodes.html: John Logie Baird demonstrated mechanically scanned television with moving images in London in 1926, and Philo Farnsworth transmitted the first all-electronic picture in 1927, while Vladimir Zworykin developed an electronic camera tube. Regular broadcasting began in the 1930s, and by the late twentieth century television was a leading source of news and entertainment.
nodes.summary: John Logie Baird demonstrated mechanically scanned television with moving images in London in 1926, and Philo Farnsworth transmitted the first all-electronic picture in 1927, while Vladimir Zworykin developed an electronic camera tube.

nodes.title: Negative-Feedback Amplifier
nodes.html: Harold Black conceived the negative-feedback amplifier on the Lackawanna Ferry in New York on 2 August 1927 and developed it at Bell Labs. Feeding part of the output back with opposite sign gives up some gain in exchange for stable, low-distortion amplification, and it made long-distance telephone repeaters work.
nodes.summary: Harold Black conceived the negative-feedback amplifier on the Lackawanna Ferry in New York on 2 August 1927 and developed it at Bell Labs.

nodes.title: Quartz Clock
nodes.html: Warren Marrison and Joseph Horton at Bell Laboratories built the first quartz clock in 1927, using the steady vibration of a quartz crystal as its timekeeper. Quartz clocks beat the best pendulum clocks, and quartz watches, first sold in 1969, later put that accuracy on nearly every wrist.
nodes.summary: Warren Marrison and Joseph Horton at Bell Laboratories built the first quartz clock in 1927, using the steady vibration of a quartz crystal as its timekeeper.

nodes.title: Magnetic Recording
nodes.html: Valdemar Poulsen recorded speech on steel wire with his Telegraphone in 1898, and in 1928 Fritz Pfleumer patented magnetic tape coated with iron oxide. Magnetic recording led to audio and video tape, computer tape and the hard disk, and magnetic media still hold much of the world’s stored data.
nodes.summary: Valdemar Poulsen recorded speech on steel wire with his Telegraphone in 1898, and in 1928 Fritz Pfleumer patented magnetic tape coated with iron oxide.

nodes.title: Mechanical Ventilator
nodes.html: Philip Drinker and Louis Agassiz Shaw built the iron lung in 1928, a chamber that lowered the pressure around the chest to draw air in, and used it for polio patients who could not breathe. In the Copenhagen polio epidemic of 1952, Bjørn Ibsen ventilated patients by pushing air into the lungs through a tube, the start of intensive care.
nodes.summary: Philip Drinker and Louis Agassiz Shaw built the iron lung in 1928, a chamber that lowered the pressure around the chest to draw air in, and used it for polio patients who could not breathe.

nodes.title: Electron Microscope
nodes.html: Electrons have far shorter wavelengths than light. Ruska and Knoll’s 1931 instrument opened the nanometre world; cryo-EM (Nobel Prize 2017) now images single proteins.
nodes.summary: Electrons have far shorter wavelengths than light.

nodes.title: Nyquist Stability Criterion
nodes.html: Harry Nyquist published his stability criterion in 1932 while working on feedback amplifiers at Bell Labs, a test that decides the stability of a feedback loop from a plot of its frequency response. Hendrik Bode’s gain and phase methods of the late 1930s and 1940s made it a design tool, and frequency-domain methods became the standard way to design feedback systems.
nodes.summary: Harry Nyquist published his stability criterion in 1932 while working on feedback amplifiers at Bell Labs, a test that decides the stability of a feedback loop from a plot of its frequency response.

nodes.title: Particle Accelerators
nodes.html: From Lawrence’s palm-sized cyclotron (1932) to CERN’s 27 km Large Hadron Collider (2008).
nodes.summary: From Lawrence’s palm-sized cyclotron (1932) to CERN’s 27 km Large Hadron Collider (2008).

nodes.title: Radar
nodes.html: Robert Watson-Watt and Arnold Wilkins showed in the Daventry experiment of February 1935 that a radio beam reflected from an aircraft could be detected, and Britain built the Chain Home warning network. John Randall and Harry Boot’s cavity magnetron of 1940 made compact microwave radar possible. Radar now guides air traffic, ships and weather forecasting.
nodes.summary: Robert Watson-Watt and Arnold Wilkins showed in the Daventry experiment of February 1935 that a radio beam reflected from an aircraft could be detected, and Britain built the Chain Home warning network.

nodes.title: Helicopter
nodes.html: Henrich Focke’s Fw 61 of 1936 was the first helicopter that could fly under full control, and Igor Sikorsky’s VS-300 of 1939 set the single main rotor and tail rotor layout that most helicopters have used since. Helicopters can hover and land almost anywhere, which made them vital for rescue, medical evacuation, offshore work and military transport.
nodes.summary: Henrich Focke’s Fw 61 of 1936 was the first helicopter that could fly under full control, and Igor Sikorsky’s VS-300 of 1939 set the single main rotor and tail rotor layout that most helicopters have used since.

nodes.title: Printed Circuit Board
nodes.html: Paul Eisler, an Austrian engineer working in Britain, etched a copper foil bonded to an insulating board into the wiring of a radio set in 1936. The method entered mass production for proximity fuzes in 1943, and nearly every electronic device since has been built on a printed circuit board.
nodes.summary: Paul Eisler, an Austrian engineer working in Britain, etched a copper foil bonded to an insulating board into the wiring of a radio set in 1936.

nodes.title: Jet Engine
nodes.html: Frank Whittle’s turbojet first ran on a test bench in Rugby, England, in April 1937, and Hans von Ohain’s engine powered the Heinkel He 178, which flew on 27 August 1939 as the first jet aircraft. Jet engines allow high speeds and altitudes with far less vibration than propellers, and they made long-haul air travel and supersonic flight possible.
nodes.summary: Frank Whittle’s turbojet first ran on a test bench in Rugby, England, in April 1937, and Hans von Ohain’s engine powered the Heinkel He 178, which flew on 27 August 1939 as the first jet aircraft.

nodes.title: Nuclear Reactor
nodes.html: Chicago Pile-1 sustained a chain reaction on 2 December 1942. Fission reactors now supply about a tenth of the world’s electricity.
nodes.summary: Chicago Pile-1 sustained a chain reaction on 2 December 1942.

nodes.title: V-2 Ballistic Missile
nodes.html: The V-2 first flew successfully on 3 October 1942 at Peenemünde under Wernher von Braun and Walter Dornberger, and a test launch in June 1944 was the first human-made object to reach space. This liquid-fuel ballistic missile with gyroscopic guidance was the ancestor of postwar rockets and missiles, and its production killed thousands of forced labourers.
nodes.summary: The V-2 first flew successfully on 3 October 1942 at Peenemünde under Wernher von Braun and Walter Dornberger, and a test launch in June 1944 was the first human-made object to reach space.

nodes.title: Dialysis Machine
nodes.html: Willem Kolff built a rotating-drum artificial kidney from cellophane tubing, a wooden drum and a tank of fluid in occupied Netherlands in 1943, and in 1945 it saved a patient in acute kidney failure. Dialysis replaces kidney function by filtering the blood outside the body, and it now keeps millions of people with kidney failure alive.
nodes.summary: Willem Kolff built a rotating-drum artificial kidney from cellophane tubing, a wooden drum and a tank of fluid in occupied Netherlands in 1943, and in 1945 it saved a patient in acute kidney failure.

nodes.title: Supersonic Flight
nodes.html: Chuck Yeager flew the rocket-powered Bell X-1 faster than sound at Mach 1.06 over California on 14 October 1947, showing that aircraft could pass through the sharp rise in drag near the speed of sound. Supersonic flight became routine for military aircraft, and data from the X-1 programme fed the design of later fast aircraft.
nodes.summary: Chuck Yeager flew the rocket-powered Bell X-1 faster than sound at Mach 1.06 over California on 14 October 1947, showing that aircraft could pass through the sharp rise in drag near the speed of sound.

nodes.title: Transistor
nodes.html: Bell Labs’ point-contact transistor (December 1947) amplified signals with a sliver of germanium. It has since become the most manufactured device in history.
nodes.summary: Bell Labs’ point-contact transistor (December 1947) amplified signals with a sliver of germanium.

nodes.title: Minimal Passive Network Synthesis

progress.what: Every positive-real impedance can be realized with resistors, inductors and capacitors alone, at the cost of many elements.
progress.html: Every positive-real impedance can be realized with resistors, inductors and capacitors alone, at the cost of many elements.

progress.what: The inerter makes networks of springs, dampers and inerters exact analogues of electrical ones, reviving the minimality question for vehicle suspensions.
progress.html: The inerter makes networks of springs, dampers and inerters exact analogues of electrical ones, reviving the minimality question for vehicle suspensions.

progress.what: For biquadratic impedances, Bott–Duffin realizations use the fewest reactive elements among series-parallel networks, and far more than expected are needed.
progress.html: For biquadratic impedances, Bott–Duffin realizations use the fewest reactive elements among series-parallel networks, and far more than expected are needed.

nodes.html: What is the smallest network of resistors, inductors and capacitors that realizes a given impedance without transformers? Bott and Duffin showed in 1949 that every positive-real impedance can be built this way, but their networks are large and minimal ones are unknown even for most biquadratic impedances. Solving it means a method that finds and proves minimal realizations, which since the inerter (2002) also guides suspension design.
nodes.summary: What is the smallest network of resistors, inductors and capacitors that realizes a given impedance without transformers?

nodes.title: Self-Replicating Machine

progress.what: Theory of Self-Reproducing Automata, published posthumously, set out the logic of a universal constructor.
progress.html: Theory of Self-Reproducing Automata, published posthumously, set out the logic of a universal constructor.

progress.what: The Advanced Automation for Space Missions study (summer 1980) designed a self-replicating lunar factory.
progress.html: The Advanced Automation for Space Missions study (summer 1980) designed a self-replicating lunar factory.

progress.what: Modular cube robots that assemble copies of themselves from supplied cubes.
progress.html: Modular cube robots that assemble copies of themselves from supplied cubes.

progress.what: A RepRap Darwin printed a complete set of its own printed parts on 29 May 2008, 48% of all parts excluding fasteners.
progress.html: A RepRap Darwin printed a complete set of its own printed parts on 29 May 2008, 48% of all parts excluding fasteners.

nodes.html: Build a machine that makes a complete working copy of itself from simple raw stock, motors and electronics included: the kinematic replicator von Neumann described in lectures in 1948 and 1949. Self-copying machines so far rely on bought parts; RepRap’s Darwin printed its own plastic parts in 2008, about half the total, but not its motors, chips or rods. Solving it means a replicator whose copies, built only from stock, replicate in turn.
nodes.summary: Build a machine that makes a complete working copy of itself from simple raw stock, motors and electronics included: the kinematic replicator von Neumann described in lectures in 1948 and 1949.

nodes.title: Stellarator
nodes.html: Lyman Spitzer proposed the stellarator in 1951, a fusion device that confines plasma in a twisted magnetic field produced by external coils alone, with no current driven through the plasma. Early machines leaked, but the computer-optimized coils of Germany’s Wendelstein 7-X, first operated in 2015, showed that the design can confine plasma well.
nodes.summary: Lyman Spitzer proposed the stellarator in 1951, a fusion device that confines plasma in a twisted magnetic field produced by external coils alone, with no current driven through the plasma.

nodes.title: Jet Airliner
nodes.html: The de Havilland Comet entered service with BOAC in May 1952 as the first jet airliner. Metal fatigue around its square windows caused two fatal crashes in 1954, which taught the industry to test airframes for fatigue and design for crack growth. The Boeing 707 of 1958 made jets the standard for long-distance travel.
nodes.summary: The de Havilland Comet entered service with BOAC in May 1952 as the first jet airliner.

nodes.title: Numerical Control
nodes.html: John Parsons began applying punched-card coordinate control to the cutting of helicopter rotor blades in the late 1940s, and in 1952 the MIT Servomechanisms Laboratory demonstrated a three-axis milling machine run by punched tape. Numerical control, later driven by computers as CNC, cuts complex shapes from digital instructions and shapes nearly every machined part today.
nodes.summary: John Parsons began applying punched-card coordinate control to the cutting of helicopter rotor blades in the late 1940s, and in 1952 the MIT Servomechanisms Laboratory demonstrated a three-axis milling machine run by punched tape.

nodes.title: Barker Sequences Beyond 13

progress.what: No Barker sequence of odd length exists beyond 13.
progress.html: No Barker sequence of odd length exists beyond 13.

progress.what: The field descent method rules out even lengths between 13 and 10^22.
progress.html: The field descent method rules out even lengths between 13 and 10^22.

progress.what: Any longer Barker sequence has length above 4×10^33, apart from one exceptional value.
progress.html: Any longer Barker sequence has length above 4×10^33, apart from one exceptional value.

progress.what: The anti-field-descent method removes the exceptional value, so none exists for 13 < n ≤ 4×10^33.
progress.html: The anti-field-descent method removes the exceptional value, so none exists for 13 < n ≤ 4×10^33.

progress.what: Claimed proof that no Barker sequence longer than 13 exists, through a proof that circulant Hadamard matrices exist only in orders 1 and 4 (family 179 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.
progress.html: Claimed proof that no Barker sequence longer than 13 exists, through a proof that circulant Hadamard matrices exist only in orders 1 and 4 (family 179 of OpenAI’s math release, formalized in Lean). Not yet independently reviewed.

nodes.html: Is there a Barker sequence longer than 13, a string of ±1 whose off-peak aperiodic autocorrelations are all 0 or ±1? Barker introduced them in 1953; they suit radar pulse compression, and the length-11 code is used in 802.11b Wi-Fi. Odd lengths beyond 13 are impossible (1961) and an even one would need length above 4×10^33; OpenAI’s October 2026 release claims a proof that none exists.
nodes.summary: Is there a Barker sequence longer than 13, a string of ±1 whose off-peak aperiodic autocorrelations are all 0 or ±1?

nodes.title: Optimal Golomb Rulers

progress.what: Proved the optimal 24-mark ruler (length 425) after years of volunteer computing.
progress.html: Proved the optimal 24-mark ruler (length 425) after years of volunteer computing.

progress.what: Proved the optimal 25-mark ruler (length 480).
progress.html: Proved the optimal 25-mark ruler (length 480).

progress.what: Proved the optimal 27-mark ruler (length 553).
progress.html: Proved the optimal 27-mark ruler (length 553).

progress.what: Proved the optimal 28-mark ruler (length 585) on 23 November 2022.
progress.html: Proved the optimal 28-mark ruler (length 585) on 23 November 2022.

nodes.html: Place n marks on a ruler so that no two pairs of marks are the same distance apart, using the shortest possible ruler; such rulers pick interference-free radio channels and sparse antenna arrays (Babcock, 1953). Optimal rulers are proven only up to 28 marks, the last (length 585) by distributed.net volunteers in November 2022. Solving the next case means proving which 29-mark ruler is shortest.
nodes.summary: Place n marks on a ruler so that no two pairs of marks are the same distance apart, using the shortest possible ruler; such rulers pick interference-free radio channels and sparse antenna arrays (Babcock, 1953).

nodes.title: Heart–Lung Machine
nodes.html: On 6 May 1953 John Gibbon used his heart-lung machine in Philadelphia to take over the work of an eighteen-year-old woman’s heart and lungs for 26 minutes while he closed a hole in her heart. It made open-heart surgery possible, and bypass machines are now used in hundreds of thousands of operations a year.
nodes.summary: On 6 May 1953 John Gibbon used his heart-lung machine in Philadelphia to take over the work of an eighteen-year-old woman’s heart and lungs for 26 minutes while he closed a hole in her heart.

nodes.title: HVDC Transmission
nodes.html: Uno Lamm of ASEA led the building of the first commercial HVDC link, a 98 km undersea cable from the Swedish mainland to Gotland that opened in 1954 with mercury-arc valves. Direct current loses less over very long distances and can join grids that are not synchronized, and thyristor and IGBT converters now let HVDC lines carry gigawatts for thousands of kilometres.
nodes.summary: Uno Lamm of ASEA led the building of the first commercial HVDC link, a 98 km undersea cable from the Swedish mainland to Gotland that opened in 1954 with mercury-arc valves.

nodes.title: Nuclear Power Station
nodes.html: The Obninsk plant near Moscow, a 5 megawatt reactor, fed electricity into a grid in June 1954, and Hyman Rickover’s navy programme produced the pressurized-water reactors of USS Nautilus (1955) and the Shippingport plant (1957). Nuclear plants now supply roughly a tenth of the world’s electricity with very low carbon emissions.
nodes.summary: The Obninsk plant near Moscow, a 5 megawatt reactor, fed electricity into a grid in June 1954, and Hyman Rickover’s navy programme produced the pressurized-water reactors of USS Nautilus (1955) and the Shippingport plant (1957).

nodes.title: Silicon Solar Cell
nodes.html: Bell Labs’ silicon cell (1954) turned 6% of sunlight into electricity. Commercial panels now exceed 20% and produce some of the cheapest electricity in history.
nodes.summary: Bell Labs’ silicon cell (1954) turned 6% of sunlight into electricity.

nodes.title: Atomic Clock
nodes.html: A caesium clock at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory (1955) kept time by an atomic transition. Since 1967 the second has been defined that way.
nodes.summary: A caesium clock at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory (1955) kept time by an atomic transition.

nodes.title: Darlington’s RC Conjecture
nodes.html: Can every resistor–capacitor two-port with a common terminal be realized as a series-parallel network? Sidney Darlington conjectured in 1955 that it can; no proof or counterexample is known, and the question belongs to the wider unsolved problem of efficient passive network synthesis. Solving it means a proof, or an RC two-port that provably needs a bridge network.
nodes.summary: Can every resistor–capacitor two-port with a common terminal be realized as a series-parallel network?

nodes.title: Hard Disk Drive
nodes.html: IBM’s 350 disk storage unit, part of the RAMAC computer announced in 1956 and built by a team led by Reynold Johnson, stored five million characters on fifty 24-inch platters and gave random access to the data. Hard disks grew in capacity by many orders of magnitude and became the main bulk storage of computers and data centres.
nodes.summary: IBM’s 350 disk storage unit, part of the RAMAC computer announced in 1956 and built by a team led by Reynold Johnson, stored five million characters on fifty 24-inch platters and gave random access to the data.

nodes.title: Optimal Control Theory
nodes.html: Lev Pontryagin and colleagues stated the maximum principle in 1956, giving conditions that the best control of a dynamical system must satisfy, and Richard Bellman’s dynamic programming (1953 to 1957) solved the same problems by working backward through time. Optimal control theory plans rocket trajectories, robot motions and industrial processes.
nodes.summary: Lev Pontryagin and colleagues stated the maximum principle in 1956, giving conditions that the best control of a dynamical system must satisfy, and Richard Bellman’s dynamic programming (1953 to 1957) solved the same problems by working backward through time.

nodes.title: Shipping Container
nodes.html: Malcom McLean’s converted tanker Ideal X carried 58 steel containers from Newark to Houston on 26 April 1956, and engineer Keith Tantlinger’s corner fittings and twist-locks made the boxes stackable and standard. Containers cut the cost and time of loading cargo and made global supply chains practical, and nearly all non-bulk cargo now travels in them.
nodes.summary: Malcom McLean’s converted tanker Ideal X carried 58 steel containers from Newark to Houston on 26 April 1956, and engineer Keith Tantlinger’s corner fittings and twist-locks made the boxes stackable and standard.

nodes.title: Fibre-Optic Endoscope
nodes.html: Harold Hopkins and Narinder Singh Kapany showed in 1954 that a bundle of glass fibres could carry an image, and in 1957 Basil Hirschowitz used a flexible fibre-optic gastroscope on a patient in Michigan. Doctors could now look inside the stomach and bowel without surgery, which began minimally invasive medicine.
nodes.summary: Harold Hopkins and Narinder Singh Kapany showed in 1954 that a bundle of glass fibres could carry an image, and in 1957 Basil Hirschowitz used a flexible fibre-optic gastroscope on a patient in Michigan.

nodes.title: Photolithography
nodes.html: Jay Lathrop and James Nall at the US Army’s Diamond Ordnance Fuze Laboratories used photographic methods in 1957 to print transistor patterns, and Jean Hoerni’s planar process at Fairchild (1959) formed transistors under a protective oxide layer. Photolithography prints the circuits on every chip with light, and its steady improvement is what shrank transistors for sixty years.
nodes.summary: Jay Lathrop and James Nall at the US Army’s Diamond Ordnance Fuze Laboratories used photographic methods in 1957 to print transistor patterns, and Jean Hoerni’s planar process at Fairchild (1959) formed transistors under a protective oxide layer.

nodes.title: Orbital Spaceflight
nodes.html: Sputnik 1 reached orbit on 4 October 1957; Yuri Gagarin followed on 12 April 1961.
nodes.summary: Sputnik 1 reached orbit on 4 October 1957; Yuri Gagarin followed on 12 April 1961.

nodes.title: Thyristor
nodes.html: General Electric introduced the silicon-controlled rectifier in 1957, a solid-state switch that stays off until a small pulse at its gate turns it on, and then conducts large currents. Thyristors began solid-state power electronics, controlling motors, light dimmers, welders and high-voltage DC links without moving parts.
nodes.summary: General Electric introduced the silicon-controlled rectifier in 1957, a solid-state switch that stays off until a small pulse at its gate turns it on, and then conducts large currents.

nodes.title: Integrated Circuit
nodes.html: Many transistors on one chip: Kilby’s germanium prototype (1958) and Noyce’s planar silicon circuit (1959).
nodes.summary: Many transistors on one chip: Kilby’s germanium prototype (1958) and Noyce’s planar silicon circuit (1959).

nodes.title: Medical Ultrasound
nodes.html: Ian Donald, John MacVicar and the engineer Tom Brown published pulse-echo ultrasound scans of abdominal masses and of the fetus in The Lancet in June 1958, using a machine adapted from an industrial flaw detector. Ultrasound images soft tissue without ionizing radiation, and it is routine in prenatal care.
nodes.summary: Ian Donald, John MacVicar and the engineer Tom Brown published pulse-echo ultrasound scans of abdominal masses and of the fetus in The Lancet in June 1958, using a machine adapted from an industrial flaw detector.

nodes.title: Implantable Pacemaker
nodes.html: Rune Elmqvist built, and Åke Senning implanted, the first pacemaker in Arne Larsson at the Karolinska hospital in Stockholm on 8 October 1958. Larsson outlived both men and received 26 devices. Pacemakers, shrunk by transistors and long-life batteries such as Wilson Greatbatch’s of 1960, now keep millions of hearts in rhythm.
nodes.summary: Rune Elmqvist built, and Åke Senning implanted, the first pacemaker in Arne Larsson at the Karolinska hospital in Stockholm on 8 October 1958.

nodes.title: Tokamak
nodes.html: Soviet physicists Igor Tamm and Andrei Sakharov proposed the tokamak, a doughnut-shaped magnetic bottle with a current driven through the plasma, around 1950, and Lev Artsimovich’s group ran the first machine, T-1, in 1958. T-3 reached a plasma temperature of about 10 million degrees in 1968, and the tokamak became the leading fusion design, from JET to ITER.
nodes.summary: Soviet physicists Igor Tamm and Andrei Sakharov proposed the tokamak, a doughnut-shaped magnetic bottle with a current driven through the plasma, around 1950, and Lev Artsimovich’s group ran the first machine, T-1, in 1958.

nodes.title: Kremer Marathon Prize

progress.what: The Gossamer Albatross crossed the English Channel under human power on 12 June 1979, winning the £100,000 Kremer prize.
progress.html: The Gossamer Albatross crossed the English Channel under human power on 12 June 1979, winning the £100,000 Kremer prize.

progress.what: Daedalus 88 flew 115 km from Crete to Santorini in 3 hours 54 minutes, still the human-powered records for distance and duration, at about half the speed the marathon prize needs.
progress.html: Daedalus 88 flew 115 km from Crete to Santorini in 3 hours 54 minutes, still the human-powered records for distance and duration, at about half the speed the marathon prize needs.

nodes.html: Fly a human-powered aircraft around a 26-mile (42 km) marathon course in under an hour, for the Royal Aeronautical Society’s £50,000 Kremer Marathon Prize, still unclaimed alongside a £100,000 prize for a manoeuvrable sporting aircraft. The first Kremer prizes, offered from 1959, went to the Gossamer Condor (1977) and Gossamer Albatross (1979). Solving it means a winning flight ratified by the Society.
nodes.summary: Fly a human-powered aircraft around a 26-mile (42 km) marathon course in under an hour, for the Royal Aeronautical Society’s £50,000 Kremer Marathon Prize, still unclaimed alongside a £100,000 prize for a manoeuvrable sporting aircraft.

nodes.title: MOSFET
nodes.html: Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng at Bell Labs made the first working MOSFET in 1959, a transistor in which a voltage on an insulated gate controls a channel of current. It could be shrunk far more easily than earlier transistors and is the building block of microprocessors and memory chips; more than 10^22 have been made, more than any other manufactured object.
nodes.summary: Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng at Bell Labs made the first working MOSFET in 1959, a transistor in which a voltage on an insulated gate controls a channel of current.

nodes.title: Vehicle Routing Benchmarks

progress.what: Introduced the 100-instance X benchmark set.
progress.html: Introduced the 100-instance X benchmark set.

progress.what: VRPSolver, a generic branch-cut-and-price exact solver for vehicle routing and related problems.
progress.html: VRPSolver, a generic branch-cut-and-price exact solver for vehicle routing and related problems.

progress.what: An open-source hybrid genetic search with the SWAP* neighbourhood, a state-of-the-art heuristic for the benchmark.
progress.html: An open-source hybrid genetic search with the SWAP* neighbourhood, a state-of-the-art heuristic for the benchmark.

nodes.html: Find, and prove optimal, the shortest set of routes for capacity-limited delivery trucks leaving one depot, the problem Dantzig and Ramser posed in 1959. The standard test is the X set of Uchoa et al. (2017): 100 instances with 100 to 1,000 customers, of which 39 still lack optimality proofs on CVRPLIB (October 2026). Each new proof, or a better best-known solution, counts.
nodes.summary: Find, and prove optimal, the shortest set of routes for capacity-limited delivery trucks leaving one depot, the problem Dantzig and Ramser posed in 1959.

nodes.title: Kalman Filter
nodes.html: Rudolf Kálmán published a recursive method in 1960 for estimating the state of a noisy dynamic system from a stream of measurements, updating the estimate and its uncertainty at each step. Stanley Schmidt adapted it for Apollo navigation, and Kalman filters now run in GPS receivers, aircraft, robots, phones and weather forecasting.
nodes.summary: Rudolf Kálmán published a recursive method in 1960 for estimating the state of a noisy dynamic system from a stream of measurements, updating the estimate and its uncertainty at each step.

nodes.title: Laser
nodes.html: Einstein described stimulated emission in 1917, the maser followed in 1954, and Maiman’s ruby laser in 1960. Coherent light now carries the internet through fibre and measured gravitational waves.
nodes.summary: Einstein described stimulated emission in 1917, the maser followed in 1954, and Maiman’s ruby laser in 1960.

nodes.title: Reverse-Osmosis Desalination
nodes.html: Sidney Loeb and Srinivasa Sourirajan at UCLA made a cellulose acetate membrane in 1960 with a thin dense skin on a porous layer, which passed water at practical rates when salt water was pushed against it under pressure. Reverse osmosis became the main desalination method and now produces most of the world’s desalinated water.
nodes.summary: Sidney Loeb and Srinivasa Sourirajan at UCLA made a cellulose acetate membrane in 1960 with a thin dense skin on a porous layer, which passed water at practical rates when salt water was pushed against it under pressure.

nodes.title: Space Elevator

progress.what: With colleagues, proposed the Sky-Hook: a satellite in geostationary orbit with a cable down to Earth.
progress.html: With colleagues, proposed the Sky-Hook: a satellite in geostationary orbit with a cable down to Earth.

progress.what: A space elevator design study was shelved after finding that no perfectly formed carbon nanotube strand longer than a metre had been made.
progress.html: A space elevator design study was shelved after finding that no perfectly formed carbon nanotube strand longer than a metre had been made.

progress.what: The study report Road to the Space Elevator Era assessed the concept as a future transport infrastructure.
progress.html: The study report Road to the Space Elevator Era assessed the concept as a future transport infrastructure.

nodes.html: Build a cable from the equator to beyond geostationary orbit, so that climbers can reach orbit on electric power without rockets (Artsutanov, 1960, after Tsiolkovsky’s 1895 tower). An Earth elevator needs a tether with a breaking length of about 3,100 to 8,200 km, far beyond any material made at length; carbon nanotubes come close only in short pieces. Solving it means such a tether at scale and a working elevator.
nodes.summary: Build a cable from the equator to beyond geostationary orbit, so that climbers can reach orbit on electric power without rockets (Artsutanov, 1960, after Tsiolkovsky’s 1895 tower).

nodes.title: Industrial Robot
nodes.html: George Devol patented a programmable transfer arm in 1954, and with Joseph Engelberger he built the Unimate, which began lifting hot die-cast parts at a General Motors plant in New Jersey in 1961. Robot arms spread through car factories and electronics assembly, and millions are now in use worldwide.
nodes.summary: George Devol patented a programmable transfer arm in 1954, and with Joseph Engelberger he built the Unimate, which began lifting hot die-cast parts at a General Motors plant in New Jersey in 1961.

nodes.title: Global Optimum of AC Power Flow

progress.what: A semidefinite relaxation is exact on several IEEE test systems, certifying their global optima.
progress.html: A semidefinite relaxation is exact on several IEEE test systems, certifying their global optima.

progress.what: AC feasibility is NP-hard even on tree networks.
progress.html: AC feasibility is NP-hard even on tree networks.

progress.what: AC power flow feasibility is strongly NP-hard.
progress.html: AC power flow feasibility is strongly NP-hard.

nodes.html: Find, and certify, the cheapest operating point of an AC power grid that satisfies the power-flow physics and equipment limits: the optimal power flow problem posed by Carpentier in 1962. It is NP-hard, and on the PGLib-OPF library (v23.07) the gap between the best known solution and the QC convex relaxation exceeds 1% on 134 of 198 cases, up to 55% on an 8,387-bus grid. Solving it at benchmark scale means closing those gaps with proofs.
nodes.summary: Find, and certify, the cheapest operating point of an AC power grid that satisfies the power-flow physics and equipment limits: the optimal power flow problem posed by Carpentier in 1962.

nodes.title: Communications Satellite
nodes.html: Telstar 1, built by Bell Labs under John Pierce’s direction, relayed live television across the Atlantic in July 1962, and Harold Rosen’s Syncom 3 of 1964 reached geostationary orbit, as Arthur C. Clarke had proposed in 1945. Satellites carried broadcasts, telephone calls and later data between continents, and they still serve ships, aircraft and remote regions.
nodes.summary: Telstar 1, built by Bell Labs under John Pierce’s direction, relayed live television across the Atlantic in July 1962, and Harold Rosen’s Syncom 3 of 1964 reached geostationary orbit, as Arthur C.

nodes.title: Interplanetary Probe
nodes.html: NASA’s Mariner 2, built at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, flew past Venus on 14 December 1962, the first successful mission to another planet. Space probes have since visited every planet, and Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012. Probes have supplied most of what is known about the Solar System’s planets and moons.
nodes.summary: NASA’s Mariner 2, built at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, flew past Venus on 14 December 1962, the first successful mission to another planet.

nodes.title: Light-Emitting Diode
nodes.html: Nick Holonyak at General Electric made the first practical visible-light LED in 1962, a red gallium arsenide phosphide diode. Early LEDs served as indicator lights and calculator displays, and as brighter and more efficient colours were developed they came to light homes, screens and vehicles.
nodes.summary: Nick Holonyak at General Electric made the first practical visible-light LED in 1962, a red gallium arsenide phosphide diode.

nodes.title: Semiconductor Laser
nodes.html: Robert Hall at General Electric and three other American groups made the first semiconductor lasers in 1962, gallium arsenide diodes that worked only at very low temperatures. The heterostructures of Zhores Alferov and Herbert Kroemer led to continuous operation at room temperature in 1970. Diode lasers drive fibre-optic links, optical discs, barcode scanners, laser printers and lidar.
nodes.summary: Robert Hall at General Electric and three other American groups made the first semiconductor lasers in 1962, gallium arsenide diodes that worked only at very low temperatures.

nodes.title: CMOS Logic
nodes.html: Frank Wanlass at Fairchild, working with Chih-Tang Sah, combined n-type and p-type MOS transistors into a complementary pair in 1963, a circuit that draws almost no current except while switching. This low power use let millions and later billions of transistors share a chip without overheating, and CMOS became the basis of nearly all digital integrated circuits.
nodes.summary: Frank Wanlass at Fairchild, working with Chih-Tang Sah, combined n-type and p-type MOS transistors into a complementary pair in 1963, a circuit that draws almost no current except while switching.

nodes.title: Fully Closed-Loop Artificial Pancreas

progress.what: An updated UVA/Padova type 1 diabetes simulator for testing control algorithms in silico.
progress.html: An updated UVA/Padova type 1 diabetes simulator for testing control algorithms in silico.

progress.what: FDA approval of the MiniMed 670G, the first hybrid closed loop, which adjusts basal insulin automatically.
progress.html: FDA approval of the MiniMed 670G, the first hybrid closed loop, which adjusts basal insulin automatically.

progress.what: With an international panel, set the time-in-range targets used to judge closed-loop control.
progress.html: With an international panel, set the time-in-range targets used to judge closed-loop control.

progress.what: FDA approval of the iLet Bionic Pancreas for type 1 diabetes, a closed loop that can deliver insulin and glucagon.
progress.html: FDA approval of the iLet Bionic Pancreas for type 1 diabetes, a closed loop that can deliver insulin and glucagon.

nodes.html: Keep glucose in range for people with type 1 diabetes with no meal announcements or carbohydrate counting, meeting the 2019 consensus targets of more than 70% of time in range (70–180 mg/dL) and under 4% below it. Today’s systems, starting with the hybrid MiniMed 670G (2016), still need users to bolus for or announce meals. Algorithms can be tested first in the UVA/Padova simulator; solving it means meeting the targets in clinical use.
nodes.summary: Keep glucose in range for people with type 1 diabetes with no meal announcements or carbohydrate counting, meeting the 2019 consensus targets of more than 70% of time in range (70–180 mg/dL) and under 4% below it.

nodes.title: High-Speed Rail
nodes.html: The Tōkaidō Shinkansen between Tokyo and Osaka opened on 1 October 1964, running at 210 km/h on dedicated standard-gauge track under chief engineer Hideo Shima of Japanese National Railways. High-speed rail competes with air travel on routes of a few hundred kilometres and has spread to China, Europe and elsewhere, with networks now running at 300 km/h or more.
nodes.summary: The Tōkaidō Shinkansen between Tokyo and Osaka opened on 1 October 1964, running at 210 km/h on dedicated standard-gauge track under chief engineer Hideo Shima of Japanese National Railways.

nodes.title: Costas Arrays of Order 32 and 33

progress.what: Algebraic constructions over finite fields, with Lempel, give arrays of order q − 2 for every prime power q.
progress.html: Algebraic constructions over finite fields, with Lempel, give arrays of order q − 2 for every prime power q.

progress.what: Exhaustive search finds all 164 Costas arrays of order 29, completing enumeration up to 29.
progress.html: Exhaustive search finds all 164 Costas arrays of order 29, completing enumeration up to 29.

progress.what: The fraction of permutations of order n that are Costas arrays decays exponentially.
