nodes.summary: Google DeepMind’s RT-2, announced in July 2023, fine-tuned a vision-language model to output robot actions as text tokens, so a robot could follow instructions involving objects and concepts from web data.

nodes.title: Rocket Booster Catch
nodes.html: On 13 October 2024, on the fifth flight test of Starship, SpaceX caught the 70 metre Super Heavy booster in mid-air with two arms on its launch tower in Texas. Catching the booster is meant to remove the need for landing legs and shorten turnaround, a step towards rapid reuse of both stages.
nodes.summary: On 13 October 2024, on the fifth flight test of Starship, SpaceX caught the 70 metre Super Heavy booster in mid-air with two arms on its launch tower in Texas.

nodes.title: Hollow-Core Fibre
nodes.html: In September 2025 researchers at the University of Southampton and Microsoft Azure Fiber reported in Nature Photonics a hollow-core fibre, which guides light through air, with a loss of 0.091 decibels per kilometre. That is below the roughly 0.14 dB/km of the best solid glass fibre, and light travels faster in air than in glass, which cuts delay.
nodes.summary: In September 2025 researchers at the University of Southampton and Microsoft Azure Fiber reported in Nature Photonics a hollow-core fibre, which guides light through air, with a loss of 0.091 decibels per kilometre.

nodes.title: Stellarator Design Benchmark

progress.what: Released the benchmark: a dataset of quasi-isodynamic-like plasma boundaries with ideal-MHD equilibria, three problems of increasing difficulty, evaluation scripts and baselines.
progress.html: Released the benchmark: a dataset of quasi-isodynamic-like plasma boundaries with ideal-MHD equilibria, three problems of increasing difficulty, evaluation scripts and baselines.

nodes.html: ConStellaration (Proxima Fusion, June 2025) poses three open optimization problems for quasi-isodynamic stellarator shapes: a geometric problem, a simple-to-build design, and a multi-objective design trading compactness against coil simplicity while staying ideal-MHD stable. Each comes with public evaluation code and classical-optimization baselines; solving it means designs that beat those baselines under the official evaluators.
nodes.summary: ConStellaration (Proxima Fusion, June 2025) poses three open optimization problems for quasi-isodynamic stellarator shapes: a geometric problem, a simple-to-build design, and a multi-objective design trading compactness against coil simplicity while staying ideal-MHD stable.

nodes.title: Commercial Fusion Power
nodes.html: A fusion plant that sells electricity to the grid. Tokamaks with high-temperature superconducting magnets and laser-driven designs are both racing toward it.
nodes.summary: A fusion plant that sells electricity to the grid.

nodes.title: Self-Sustaining Mars Settlement
nodes.html: A settlement on Mars that could survive if supply ships from Earth stopped coming.
nodes.summary: A settlement on Mars that could survive if supply ships from Earth stopped coming.

nodes.title: Control of Fire
nodes.html: Ash and burnt bone in Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, suggest hominins were using fire about a million years ago; by 400,000 years ago it was routine. Cooking, warmth and light came first. Kilns and smelting came later.
nodes.summary: Ash and burnt bone in Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, suggest hominins were using fire about a million years ago; by 400,000 years ago it was routine.

nodes.title: Birch-Bark Tar
nodes.html: Neanderthals at Campitello Quarry in Italy glued flint flakes to handles with birch-bark tar about 200,000 years ago. Making the tar means heating bark with little oxygen, a simple dry distillation, so this is among the oldest known manufactured materials and an early use of chemistry to make an adhesive.
nodes.summary: Neanderthals at Campitello Quarry in Italy glued flint flakes to handles with birch-bark tar about 200,000 years ago.

nodes.title: Ochre Paint Making
nodes.html: At Blombos Cave in South Africa, people ground ochre and mixed it with heated bone fat, charcoal and other ingredients in abalone shells about 100,000 years ago (reported 2011). It is the oldest known evidence of deliberate paint making and shows a planned, multistep recipe.
nodes.summary: At Blombos Cave in South Africa, people ground ochre and mixed it with heated bone fat, charcoal and other ingredients in abalone shells about 100,000 years ago (reported 2011).

nodes.title: Pottery
nodes.html: Fired clay vessels from Xianrendong Cave in China are about 20,000 years old. Pottery kilns later reached the temperatures needed to smelt metal.
nodes.summary: Fired clay vessels from Xianrendong Cave in China are about 20,000 years old.

nodes.title: Lime Plaster
nodes.html: Burning limestone to quicklime, slaking it with water and letting it set again makes plaster, mortar and whitewash. Lime plaster appears in Late Natufian sites of the Levant by about 10,000 BCE, before pottery, and the technology later led to Roman concrete and to the cements that followed.
nodes.summary: Burning limestone to quicklime, slaking it with water and letting it set again makes plaster, mortar and whitewash.

nodes.title: Metallurgy
nodes.html: Copper smelting by about 5000 BCE, bronze alloys by 3300 BCE, iron by 1200 BCE. Every later machine is built from what metalworkers learned.
nodes.summary: Copper smelting by about 5000 BCE, bronze alloys by 3300 BCE, iron by 1200 BCE.

nodes.title: Indigo and Mordant Dyes
nodes.html: Cotton textiles dyed with indigo about 6,200 years ago were found at Huaca Prieta in Peru. Natural dyeing depended on chemistry such as the fermentation vat for indigo and mordants like alum that fix madder and other colours, and Tyrian purple from sea snails was a luxury product of the ancient Mediterranean.
nodes.summary: Cotton textiles dyed with indigo about 6,200 years ago were found at Huaca Prieta in Peru.

nodes.title: Glazed Faience
nodes.html: Egyptian craftsmen shaped a paste of ground quartz, lime and alkali, coloured with copper, and fired it so that a bright blue-green glaze formed on the surface, making faience beads and amulets by about 4000 BCE. It is among the first glazed ceramics and a step toward the invention of glass.
nodes.summary: Egyptian craftsmen shaped a paste of ground quartz, lime and alkali, coloured with copper, and fired it so that a bright blue-green glaze formed on the surface, making faience beads and amulets by about 4000 BCE.

nodes.title: Egyptian Blue
nodes.html: Egyptians made the first synthetic pigment, Egyptian blue (calcium copper silicate), by firing sand, lime, a copper source and an alkali at about 900 degrees Celsius; the earliest identified example dates to about 3250 BCE and use was widespread from about 2600 BCE. Its strong near-infrared glow is now used to find traces of ancient paint.
nodes.summary: Egyptians made the first synthetic pigment, Egyptian blue (calcium copper silicate), by firing sand, lime, a copper source and an alkali at about 900 degrees Celsius; the earliest identified example dates to about 3250 BCE and use was widespread from about 2600 BCE.

nodes.title: Glass
nodes.html: Glass beads appear in Mesopotamia around 2500 BCE, and glassblowing (1st century BCE) made glass cheap. Clear glass became lenses, and lenses became optics.
nodes.summary: Glass beads appear in Mesopotamia around 2500 BCE, and glassblowing (1st century BCE) made glass cheap.

nodes.title: Soap
nodes.html: A Sumerian clay tablet of about 2500 BCE gives a formula for a soap-like cleanser made by heating oil with wood ash, used for washing wool. Boiling fat with alkali, saponification, has made soap ever since, and Michel Chevreul worked out its chemistry in the 1810s and 1820s.
nodes.summary: A Sumerian clay tablet of about 2500 BCE gives a formula for a soap-like cleanser made by heating oil with wood ash, used for washing wool.

nodes.title: Mesoamerican Rubber
nodes.html: Mesoamericans mixed latex from the rubber tree with the juice of morning glory vines to change its bounce, and made rubber balls by about 1600 BCE, as finds from El Manatí in Mexico and later experiments show. It is deliberate polymer processing three thousand years before vulcanisation.
nodes.summary: Mesoamericans mixed latex from the rubber tree with the juice of morning glory vines to change its bounce, and made rubber balls by about 1600 BCE, as finds from El Manatí in Mexico and later experiments show.

nodes.title: Cast Iron
nodes.html: Chinese ironworkers were casting iron in quantity by the 5th century BCE, about 1,500 years before Europe, using furnaces hot enough to melt it and moulds for tools, weapons and later pots. Blast furnaces are attested by the Han dynasty, and cast iron became the cheap material of ploughshares and, much later, of bridges and machines.
nodes.summary: Chinese ironworkers were casting iron in quantity by the 5th century BCE, about 1,500 years before Europe, using furnaces hot enough to melt it and moulds for tools, weapons and later pots.

nodes.title: Crucible Steel
nodes.html: South Indian smiths melted iron with carbon-bearing material in sealed clay crucibles from about 300 BCE, as excavations at Kodumanal show, to make high-carbon wootz steel. The ingots were traded across Asia and forged into the patterned blades known as Damascus steel.
nodes.summary: South Indian smiths melted iron with carbon-bearing material in sealed clay crucibles from about 300 BCE, as excavations at Kodumanal show, to make high-carbon wootz steel.

nodes.title: Porcelain
nodes.html: Potters in Zhejiang fired porcelain stone and clay above about 1,260 degrees Celsius to make true porcelain by the late Eastern Han (about 150 CE), a hard, white, translucent ceramic. Chinese porcelain became a major export for a thousand years, and Böttger and Tschirnhaus in Saxony reinvented it in Europe in 1708.
nodes.summary: Potters in Zhejiang fired porcelain stone and clay above about 1,260 degrees Celsius to make true porcelain by the late Eastern Han (about 150 CE), a hard, white, translucent ceramic.

nodes.title: Distillation
nodes.html: Alexandrian alchemists, above all Maria the Jewess (1st to 3rd century CE, known through Zosimos), described stills such as the three-armed tribikos and the kerotakis. Their apparatus led to the alembic and later the distillation column, the main way to separate and purify liquids, from perfumes and spirits to petroleum fractions.
nodes.summary: Alexandrian alchemists, above all Maria the Jewess (1st to 3rd century CE, known through Zosimos), described stills such as the three-armed tribikos and the kerotakis.

nodes.title: Alchemy
nodes.html: Greco-Egyptian alchemists such as Zosimos of Panopolis (about 300 CE), and independently Chinese alchemists, tried to transmute base metals into gold and to make elixirs of life. Their apparatus, procedures and substances, including distillation, sublimation and acids, grew into chemistry, though transmutation was never achieved.
nodes.summary: Greco-Egyptian alchemists such as Zosimos of Panopolis (about 300 CE), and independently Chinese alchemists, tried to transmute base metals into gold and to make elixirs of life.

nodes.title: Gunpowder
nodes.html: Chinese alchemical texts of about 850 CE warn that mixing saltpetre, sulfur and charcoal can cause fires, and the Wujing Zongyao of 1044 gives the first military formulas. Gunpowder reached the Islamic world and Europe by the 13th century, made guns and cannon possible, and remained the only widely used explosive until the 19th century.
nodes.summary: Chinese alchemical texts of about 850 CE warn that mixing saltpetre, sulfur and charcoal can cause fires, and the Wujing Zongyao of 1044 gives the first military formulas.

nodes.title: Arabic Laboratory Alchemy
nodes.html: The Jabirian corpus (about 850 to 950 CE) and Abu Bakr al-Razi’s Secret of Secrets (about 900) classified substances and described laboratory apparatus and procedures. Alkali, alembic and elixir are Arabic loanwords, and Latin translations carried the methods to medieval Europe.
nodes.summary: The Jabirian corpus (about 850 to 950 CE) and Abu Bakr al-Razi’s Secret of Secrets (about 900) classified substances and described laboratory apparatus and procedures.

nodes.title: Mineral Acids
nodes.html: Latin treatises written under the name of Geber, now attributed to Pseudo-Geber (about 1310), give the first clear recipes for nitric acid and aqua regia, and sulfuric acid followed. Strong mineral acids could dissolve metals and minerals that nothing else could, and became chemistry’s main solvents and reagents.
nodes.summary: Latin treatises written under the name of Geber, now attributed to Pseudo-Geber (about 1310), give the first clear recipes for nitric acid and aqua regia, and sulfuric acid followed.

nodes.title: Iatrochemistry
nodes.html: From his time in Basel (about 1527) Paracelsus pushed alchemy toward making medicines from minerals and metals and argued that the dose makes the poison. Iatrochemistry, or medical chemistry, started chemical pharmacology and the idea that diseases can be treated with specific chemical substances.
nodes.summary: From his time in Basel (about 1527) Paracelsus pushed alchemy toward making medicines from minerals and metals and argued that the dose makes the poison.

nodes.title: The Concept of Gas
nodes.html: Jan Baptist van Helmont coined the word gas for the spirit given off by burning charcoal and fermenting wine, which he recognised as distinct from air (published posthumously in 1648). The concept let later chemists collect and study individual gases and opened pneumatic chemistry.
nodes.summary: Jan Baptist van Helmont coined the word gas for the spirit given off by burning charcoal and fermenting wine, which he recognised as distinct from air (published posthumously in 1648).

nodes.title: The Sceptical Chymist
nodes.html: Robert Boyle’s The Sceptical Chymist (1661) attacked the four Aristotelian elements and Paracelsus’s three principles and argued that chemical claims should rest on experiment and on a corpuscular picture of matter. He also proposed an early modern definition of an element, and the book helped turn alchemy into chemistry.
nodes.summary: Robert Boyle’s The Sceptical Chymist (1661) attacked the four Aristotelian elements and Paracelsus’s three principles and argued that chemical claims should rest on experiment and on a corpuscular picture of matter.

nodes.title: Discovery of Phosphorus
nodes.html: Hennig Brand, a Hamburg merchant searching for the philosopher’s stone, boiled down large amounts of urine and obtained a white substance that glowed in the dark (1669). It was the first element whose discoverer is known, and phosphorus later became central to matches, fertilizers and biochemistry.
nodes.summary: Hennig Brand, a Hamburg merchant searching for the philosopher’s stone, boiled down large amounts of urine and obtained a white substance that glowed in the dark (1669).

nodes.title: Phlogiston Theory
nodes.html: Johann Becher (1667) and Georg Ernst Stahl (1703) proposed that burning and rusting release a substance called phlogiston. Although wrong, the theory organised combustion, smelting and respiration into one scheme and guided experiments for a century, until Lavoisier’s oxygen theory replaced it.
nodes.summary: Johann Becher (1667) and Georg Ernst Stahl (1703) proposed that burning and rusting release a substance called phlogiston.

nodes.title: Coke Iron Smelting
nodes.html: Abraham Darby fuelled a blast furnace at Coalbrookdale with coke instead of charcoal in 1709, making iron without clearing forests. Coke iron became cheap and abundant over the following decades and supplied the iron for steam engines, bridges and machines of the Industrial Revolution.
nodes.summary: Abraham Darby fuelled a blast furnace at Coalbrookdale with coke instead of charcoal in 1709, making iron without clearing forests.

nodes.title: Pneumatic Trough
nodes.html: Stephen Hales heated substances in a retort and collected the airs they released in a vessel over water (Vegetable Staticks, 1727). The pneumatic trough, refined by Priestley and others, let chemists isolate and compare gases, and was used for most of the gas discoveries of the 18th century.
nodes.summary: Stephen Hales heated substances in a retort and collected the airs they released in a vessel over water (Vegetable Staticks, 1727).

nodes.title: Lead-Chamber Sulfuric Acid
nodes.html: John Roebuck made sulfuric acid in 1746 by burning sulfur with saltpetre in lead-lined chambers at Birmingham, far cheaper than using glass vessels, and it could be supplied by the tonne. Sulfuric acid became the first heavy chemical of industry; the contact process (patented 1831, industrial from 1875) later replaced the lead chamber.
nodes.summary: John Roebuck made sulfuric acid in 1746 by burning sulfur with saltpetre in lead-lined chambers at Birmingham, far cheaper than using glass vessels, and it could be supplied by the tonne.

nodes.title: Carbon Dioxide (Fixed Air)
nodes.html: Joseph Black heated magnesia alba (magnesium carbonate) and showed by weighing in 1754 that the fixed air it lost is a distinct gas, now called carbon dioxide, that is also produced by fermentation and breathing. It was the first gas characterised by quantitative experiment and began the chemistry of airs.
nodes.summary: Joseph Black heated magnesia alba (magnesium carbonate) and showed by weighing in 1754 that the fixed air it lost is a distinct gas, now called carbon dioxide, that is also produced by fermentation and breathing.

nodes.title: Hydrogen
nodes.html: Henry Cavendish collected the inflammable air released when metals dissolve in acids and measured its properties in 1766, and in 1781 showed that burning it produces water. Lavoisier named it hydrogen in 1783, and its discovery helped show that water is a compound of two gases.
nodes.summary: Henry Cavendish collected the inflammable air released when metals dissolve in acids and measured its properties in 1766, and in 1781 showed that burning it produces water.

nodes.title: Oxygen
nodes.html: Carl Wilhelm Scheele (about 1771, published 1777) and Joseph Priestley (1774) isolated a gas that made candles burn brightly and kept mice alive. Antoine Lavoisier recognised it as the element that combines in burning and named it oxygen, overturning phlogiston theory and starting the chemical revolution.
nodes.summary: Carl Wilhelm Scheele (about 1771, published 1777) and Joseph Priestley (1774) isolated a gas that made candles burn brightly and kept mice alive.

nodes.title: Modern Chemistry
nodes.html: Lavoisier’s Traité élémentaire de chimie (1789): conservation of mass, the role of oxygen, and a list of elements that replaced earth, air, fire and water.
nodes.summary: Lavoisier’s Traité élémentaire de chimie (1789): conservation of mass, the role of oxygen, and a list of elements that replaced earth, air, fire and water.

nodes.title: Leblanc Soda Process
nodes.html: Nicolas Leblanc patented a way to make soda ash (sodium carbonate) from salt, sulfuric acid, chalk and coal in 1791. It supplied glass, soap, paper and textile makers for much of the 19th century, and its hydrogen chloride fumes led to Britain’s Alkali Act of 1863. Solvay’s ammonia-soda process (1861) eventually replaced it.
nodes.summary: Nicolas Leblanc patented a way to make soda ash (sodium carbonate) from salt, sulfuric acid, chalk and coal in 1791.

nodes.title: Stoichiometry
nodes.html: Jeremias Richter measured the fixed weights in which acids and bases neutralise one another and named the quantitative study of chemical proportions stoichiometry (1792). His tables of equivalent weights showed that reactions obey exact numerical rules, a result Dalton’s atomic theory later explained.
nodes.summary: Jeremias Richter measured the fixed weights in which acids and bases neutralise one another and named the quantitative study of chemical proportions stoichiometry (1792).

nodes.title: Law of Definite Proportions
nodes.html: Joseph Proust showed that a pure compound always contains its elements in the same proportions by mass, however it is made (experiments c. 1794 to 1804). His long debate with Claude Berthollet, who held that composition varies, ended in his favour and prepared the ground for Dalton’s atomic theory.
nodes.summary: Joseph Proust showed that a pure compound always contains its elements in the same proportions by mass, however it is made (experiments c.

nodes.title: Electric Battery
nodes.html: Volta’s pile of zinc and copper discs (1800) gave the first steady electric current. Electrochemistry followed at once: Davy used it to isolate sodium and potassium in 1807.
nodes.summary: Volta’s pile of zinc and copper discs (1800) gave the first steady electric current.

nodes.title: Isolation of Alkaloids
nodes.html: Friedrich Sertürner isolated morphine from opium around 1805, the first pure active principle extracted from a plant. Pelletier and Caventou then isolated strychnine (1818) and quinine (1820). Purifying single compounds with known doses began the shift from herbal remedies to modern drugs.
nodes.summary: Friedrich Sertürner isolated morphine from opium around 1805, the first pure active principle extracted from a plant.

nodes.title: Atomic Theory
nodes.html: Each element is made of atoms with a characteristic weight, and compounds combine them in fixed ratios (Dalton, 1808).
nodes.summary: Each element is made of atoms with a characteristic weight, and compounds combine them in fixed ratios (Dalton, 1808).

nodes.title: Avogadro’s Hypothesis
nodes.html: Amedeo Avogadro proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, which explained Gay-Lussac’s simple volume ratios of 1808. Chemists ignored the idea for about fifty years until Cannizzaro revived it in 1860; it fixes molecular weights and underlies the mole.
nodes.summary: Amedeo Avogadro proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, which explained Gay-Lussac’s simple volume ratios of 1808.

nodes.title: Chemical Symbols and Formulas
nodes.html: Jöns Jacob Berzelius replaced alchemical signs and Dalton’s circles with one- or two-letter symbols taken from Latin names (1813 to 1814), and measured accurate atomic weights for most known elements. Formulas such as H2O became the written language of chemistry.
nodes.summary: Jöns Jacob Berzelius replaced alchemical signs and Dalton’s circles with one- or two-letter symbols taken from Latin names (1813 to 1814), and measured accurate atomic weights for most known elements.

nodes.title: Portland Cement
nodes.html: Joseph Aspdin patented a cement made by burning limestone and clay in 1824 and named it after Portland stone. Isaac Johnson’s hotter firing to a hard clinker in the 1840s gave the modern product. Mixed with sand, gravel and water it makes concrete, and about four billion tonnes of cement are now made each year.
nodes.summary: Joseph Aspdin patented a cement made by burning limestone and clay in 1824 and named it after Portland stone.

nodes.title: Isomerism
nodes.html: Liebig’s silver fulminate and Wöhler’s silver cyanate had the same formula but different properties (1824). Berzelius named such compounds isomers in 1830, and the realisation that the arrangement of atoms matters as well as their number led to structural formulas.
nodes.summary: Liebig’s silver fulminate and Wöhler’s silver cyanate had the same formula but different properties (1824).

nodes.title: Combustion Analysis
nodes.html: Justus von Liebig’s five-bulb Kaliapparat trapped the carbon dioxide from a burned sample in potash solution (1831), so that carbon and hydrogen in an organic compound could be weighed accurately within hours. Routine elemental analysis supplied the data on which structural organic chemistry was built.
nodes.summary: Justus von Liebig’s five-bulb Kaliapparat trapped the carbon dioxide from a burned sample in potash solution (1831), so that carbon and hydrogen in an organic compound could be weighed accurately within hours.

nodes.title: Laws of Electrolysis
nodes.html: Michael Faraday showed in 1833 and 1834 that the mass deposited at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed, and that equal charges liberate equivalent amounts of different elements. With William Whewell he coined electrode, anode, cathode, ion and electrolyte. The laws underpin electroplating and industrial electrolysis.
nodes.summary: Michael Faraday showed in 1833 and 1834 that the mass deposited at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed, and that equal charges liberate equivalent amounts of different elements.

nodes.title: Catalysis
nodes.html: After Döbereiner’s platinum lighter (1823) and similar cases, Berzelius proposed in 1835 that some substances provoke reactions by their presence alone and named the effect catalysis. Catalysts now speed up most industrial chemical processes, from fertilizer and fuel production to exhaust cleanup.
nodes.summary: After Döbereiner’s platinum lighter (1823) and similar cases, Berzelius proposed in 1835 that some substances provoke reactions by their presence alone and named the effect catalysis.

nodes.title: Fuel Cell
nodes.html: William Grove combined hydrogen and oxygen over platinum electrodes to produce an electric current in 1839, after Christian Schönbein had reported the effect in 1838. Alkaline fuel cells powered the Apollo spacecraft, and proton-exchange membrane cells now drive hydrogen vehicles and provide backup power.
nodes.summary: William Grove combined hydrogen and oxygen over platinum electrodes to produce an electric current in 1839, after Christian Schönbein had reported the effect in 1838.

nodes.title: Vulcanized Rubber
nodes.html: Heating natural rubber with sulfur cross-links its chains, so it stays elastic instead of turning sticky in summer and brittle in winter. Charles Goodyear found the effect in 1839 and patented it in 1844; Thomas Hancock patented a similar process in Britain in 1843. Vulcanized rubber made tyres, belts, hoses and seals practical.
nodes.summary: Heating natural rubber with sulfur cross-links its chains, so it stays elastic instead of turning sticky in summer and brittle in winter.

nodes.title: Chemical Fertilizers
nodes.html: Justus von Liebig argued in 1840 that plants take their nutrients from mineral salts in the soil, and John Bennet Lawes patented superphosphate, made by treating phosphate rock with sulfuric acid, in 1842. A manufactured fertilizer industry followed and raised crop yields through the rest of the 19th century.
nodes.summary: Justus von Liebig argued in 1840 that plants take their nutrients from mineral salts in the soil, and John Bennet Lawes patented superphosphate, made by treating phosphate rock with sulfuric acid, in 1842.

nodes.title: Molecular Chirality
nodes.html: Louis Pasteur sorted two mirror-image crystal forms of sodium ammonium tartrate by hand in 1848 and found that their solutions rotate polarised light in opposite directions. He concluded that the molecules themselves can be left- or right-handed, the starting point of stereochemistry and of chiral drug design.
nodes.summary: Louis Pasteur sorted two mirror-image crystal forms of sodium ammonium tartrate by hand in 1848 and found that their solutions rotate polarised light in opposite directions.

nodes.title: Reaction Rates
nodes.html: Ludwig Wilhelmy followed the acid-catalysed breakdown of sucrose with a polarimeter and wrote its rate as a differential equation (1850), the first quantitative study of how fast a chemical reaction goes. His work was overlooked for decades but is now counted as the start of chemical kinetics.
nodes.summary: Ludwig Wilhelmy followed the acid-catalysed breakdown of sucrose with a polarimeter and wrote its rate as a differential equation (1850), the first quantitative study of how fast a chemical reaction goes.

nodes.title: Beer–Lambert Law
nodes.html: The absorbance of light by a solution grows in proportion to the concentration of the absorbing substance and the length of the light path. August Beer stated the concentration law in 1852, extending work by Bouguer (1729) and Lambert (1760); it underlies colorimeters, UV-visible spectrometers and much of clinical chemistry.
nodes.summary: The absorbance of light by a solution grows in proportion to the concentration of the absorbing substance and the length of the light path.

nodes.title: Valence
nodes.html: Edward Frankland noticed in 1852 that each element combines with a fixed number of other atoms, its combining power. Kekulé and Couper turned this idea of valence into structural formulas in 1858, giving organic chemists a way to draw and predict molecules.
nodes.summary: Edward Frankland noticed in 1852 that each element combines with a fixed number of other atoms, its combining power.

nodes.title: Kerosene and Oil Refining
nodes.html: Abraham Gesner distilled kerosene from coal in 1846, and Ignacy Łukasiewicz refined it from crude oil and used it to light a hospital operating room in Lviv in 1853. Kerosene lamps replaced whale oil, and after Drake’s well of 1859 refining grew into the industry that supplies fuels and chemical feedstocks.
nodes.summary: Abraham Gesner distilled kerosene from coal in 1846, and Ignacy Łukasiewicz refined it from crude oil and used it to light a hospital operating room in Lviv in 1853.

nodes.title: Bessemer Process
nodes.html: Henry Bessemer blew air through molten pig iron to burn out carbon and silicon, making steel in under half an hour (1856); William Kelly in the United States had found the same effect earlier. The Siemens-Martin open hearth (1865) and the Thomas-Gilchrist basic lining (1878) extended it, and cheap steel built railways, ships and skyscrapers.
nodes.summary: Henry Bessemer blew air through molten pig iron to burn out carbon and silicon, making steel in under half an hour (1856); William Kelly in the United States had found the same effect earlier.

nodes.title: Synthetic Dyes
nodes.html: While trying to make quinine from coal-tar aniline, eighteen-year-old William Perkin obtained the purple dye mauveine (1856). Synthetic alizarin (1868) and indigo (1880, industrial in 1897) followed, and dye makers grew into the modern chemical and pharmaceutical industry.
nodes.summary: While trying to make quinine from coal-tar aniline, eighteen-year-old William Perkin obtained the purple dye mauveine (1856).

nodes.title: Organic Chemistry
nodes.html: Wöhler made urea from inorganic salts (1828), and Kekulé’s theory of carbon valence (1858) made molecules into structures you could draw and design.
nodes.summary: Wöhler made urea from inorganic salts (1828), and Kekulé’s theory of carbon valence (1858) made molecules into structures you could draw and design.

nodes.title: Lead–Acid Battery
nodes.html: Gaston Planté built the first rechargeable battery in 1859 from lead plates in sulfuric acid. Camille Faure’s pasted plates (1881) made it practical, and lead-acid batteries still start most of the world’s cars and back up telecom and power systems.
nodes.summary: Gaston Planté built the first rechargeable battery in 1859 from lead plates in sulfuric acid.

nodes.title: Consistent Atomic Weights
nodes.html: At the first international chemistry congress, held in Karlsruhe in 1860, Stanislao Cannizzaro revived Avogadro’s hypothesis and showed that it gives one consistent set of atomic and molecular weights. Mendeleev and Lothar Meyer attended, and the agreed weights made the periodic table of 1869 possible.
nodes.summary: At the first international chemistry congress, held in Karlsruhe in 1860, Stanislao Cannizzaro revived Avogadro’s hypothesis and showed that it gives one consistent set of atomic and molecular weights.

nodes.title: Colloid Chemistry
nodes.html: Thomas Graham separated dissolved substances by how fast they diffuse through parchment and named colloids and dialysis in 1861. Faraday’s ruby-red gold sols (1857) were an early scientific study of nanoparticles, and colloid science grew into the study of gels, emulsions and nanomaterials.
nodes.summary: Thomas Graham separated dissolved substances by how fast they diffuse through parchment and named colloids and dialysis in 1861.

nodes.title: Semi-Synthetic Plastics
nodes.html: Alexander Parkes moulded nitrocellulose into Parkesine, shown at the 1862 London exhibition. John Wesley Hyatt’s celluloid, nitrocellulose plasticised with camphor (1870), replaced ivory and tortoiseshell and later became photographic and cinema film.
nodes.summary: Alexander Parkes moulded nitrocellulose into Parkesine, shown at the 1862 London exhibition.

nodes.title: Metallography
nodes.html: Henry Clifton Sorby polished and etched sections of steel and examined them under a microscope in 1863, seeing its crystalline grains and distinct phases. Linking microstructure to a metal’s strength and heat treatment, metallography became the basic method for inspecting and understanding metals.
nodes.summary: Henry Clifton Sorby polished and etched sections of steel and examined them under a microscope in 1863, seeing its crystalline grains and distinct phases.

nodes.title: Law of Mass Action
nodes.html: Cato Guldberg and Peter Waage proposed in 1864 that the rate of a reaction is proportional to the concentrations of the reacting substances, and that equilibrium is reached when forward and backward rates are equal. This gave the equilibrium constant, a central quantity of solution and industrial chemistry.
nodes.summary: Cato Guldberg and Peter Waage proposed in 1864 that the rate of a reaction is proportional to the concentrations of the reacting substances, and that equilibrium is reached when forward and backward rates are equal.

nodes.title: Nitroglycerin and Dynamite
nodes.html: Ascanio Sobrero made nitroglycerin in 1847 but found it too dangerous to handle. Alfred Nobel soaked it into porous kieselguhr and added a blasting cap, patenting dynamite in 1867. It made mining, tunnelling and canal building far faster, and its profits endowed the Nobel Prizes.
nodes.summary: Ascanio Sobrero made nitroglycerin in 1847 but found it too dangerous to handle.

nodes.title: Periodic Table
nodes.html: Mendeleev ordered the elements by weight and chemical behaviour (1869) and left gaps for elements nobody had found yet. Gallium, scandium and germanium turned up to fill them.
nodes.summary: Mendeleev ordered the elements by weight and chemical behaviour (1869) and left gaps for elements nobody had found yet.

nodes.title: Tetrahedral Carbon
nodes.html: Jacobus van ‘t Hoff and Joseph Le Bel proposed independently in 1874 that the four bonds of a carbon atom point to the corners of a tetrahedron. A carbon bearing four different groups then comes in two mirror-image forms, which explained Pasteur’s optical isomers and founded stereochemistry. Van ‘t Hoff won the first Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1901).
nodes.summary: Jacobus van ‘t Hoff and Joseph Le Bel proposed independently in 1874 that the four bonds of a carbon atom point to the corners of a tetrahedron.

nodes.title: Gibbs Free Energy and Phase Rule
nodes.html: Josiah Willard Gibbs’s paper ‘On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances’ (1876 to 1878) introduced free energy, chemical potential and the phase rule. It showed how to calculate from thermodynamic data whether a reaction proceeds and where it stops, and became the foundation of physical chemistry and materials science.
nodes.summary: Josiah Willard Gibbs’s paper ‘On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances’ (1876 to 1878) introduced free energy, chemical potential and the phase rule.

nodes.title: Le Chatelier’s Principle
nodes.html: Henry Louis Le Chatelier stated in 1884 that a system at equilibrium shifts in the direction that counteracts an imposed change in temperature, pressure or concentration. Chemists use it to predict how to push a reaction toward more product; Haber applied it to raise ammonia yields at high pressure.
nodes.summary: Henry Louis Le Chatelier stated in 1884 that a system at equilibrium shifts in the direction that counteracts an imposed change in temperature, pressure or concentration.

nodes.title: Hall–Héroult Process
nodes.html: Charles Martin Hall in Ohio and Paul Héroult in France discovered in 1886, independently, that alumina dissolved in molten cryolite can be electrolysed to aluminium. With Bayer’s process for refining bauxite (1888) it still produces essentially all primary aluminium, which went from a precious metal to a commodity.
nodes.summary: Charles Martin Hall in Ohio and Paul Héroult in France discovered in 1886, independently, that alumina dissolved in molten cryolite can be electrolysed to aluminium.

nodes.title: Ionic Dissociation
nodes.html: Svante Arrhenius proposed in his 1884 thesis and a paper of 1887 that salts, acids and bases split into charged ions in water even without a current. The theory explained electrical conductivity, osmotic pressure and the lowering of freezing points, and won him the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
nodes.summary: Svante Arrhenius proposed in his 1884 thesis and a paper of 1887 that salts, acids and bases split into charged ions in water even without a current.

nodes.title: Explaining the Hofmeister Series

progress.what: Proposed that ions of similar charge density pair strongly in water, the ‘law of matching water affinities’, to account for many specific-ion effects.
progress.html: Proposed that ions of similar charge density pair strongly in water, the ‘law of matching water affinities’, to account for many specific-ion effects.

progress.what: Simulations with polarizable ions showed large, soft anions such as bromide and iodide enriched at the air–water interface, overturning the picture of ion-free water surfaces.
progress.html: Simulations with polarizable ions showed large, soft anions such as bromide and iodide enriched at the air–water interface, overturning the picture of ion-free water surfaces.

progress.what: Argued that DLVO theory fails to explain specific-ion effects because it leaves out the dispersion forces acting on ions.
progress.html: Argued that DLVO theory fails to explain specific-ion effects because it leaves out the dispersion forces acting on ions.

progress.what: Showed that anions’ radial charge densities, computed quantum-chemically, correlate with many specific-ion effects and quantify the anion series; cations correlate only weakly.
progress.html: Showed that anions’ radial charge densities, computed quantum-chemically, correlate with many specific-ion effects and quantify the anion series; cations correlate only weakly.

nodes.html: Why do ions change protein solubility, surface tension and colloid stability in the consistent order Franz Hofmeister reported in 1888, when classical electrostatics treats ions of equal charge alike? Hydration, dispersion forces and ion–surface binding have all been invoked, but a 2022 perspective found no general predictive theory. A solution predicts the size and order of specific-ion effects, including reversals, for new ions and surfaces.
nodes.summary: Why do ions change protein solubility, surface tension and colloid stability in the consistent order Franz Hofmeister reported in 1888, when classical electrostatics treats ions of equal charge alike?

nodes.title: Liquid Crystals
nodes.html: Friedrich Reinitzer found in 1888 that cholesteryl benzoate seems to melt twice, first to a cloudy fluid and then to a clear liquid. Otto Lehmann studied it in polarised light and recognised a state between crystal and liquid, the basis of liquid-crystal displays in watches, computers, phones and televisions.
nodes.summary: Friedrich Reinitzer found in 1888 that cholesteryl benzoate seems to melt twice, first to a cloudy fluid and then to a clear liquid.

nodes.title: Arrhenius Equation
nodes.html: Building on van ‘t Hoff’s earlier relation, Svante Arrhenius showed in 1889 that reaction rates rise exponentially with temperature, k = A exp(-Ea/RT), where Ea is an activation energy barrier. It is still the first formula of chemical kinetics, used from drug shelf-life testing to combustion modelling.
nodes.summary: Building on van ‘t Hoff’s earlier relation, Svante Arrhenius showed in 1889 that reaction rates rise exponentially with temperature, k = A exp(-Ea/RT), where Ea is an activation energy barrier.

nodes.title: Nernst Equation
nodes.html: Walther Nernst derived in 1889 how an electrode’s potential depends on the logarithm of the concentrations of the ions involved, linking electrochemistry to thermodynamics. It gives battery and cell voltages, sets the readings of pH and ion-selective electrodes and describes membrane potentials in nerve cells.
nodes.summary: Walther Nernst derived in 1889 how an electrode’s potential depends on the logarithm of the concentrations of the ions involved, linking electrochemistry to thermodynamics.

nodes.title: Chlor-Alkali Electrolysis
nodes.html: Electrolysing brine yields chlorine, caustic soda and hydrogen together. Hamilton Castner’s mercury cell and Karl Kellner’s similar one, both patented in 1892, made it a large industry. Chlorine feeds PVC, solvents, bleach and water disinfection, and caustic soda feeds paper, soap and aluminium refining.
nodes.summary: Electrolysing brine yields chlorine, caustic soda and hydrogen together.

nodes.title: Coordination Chemistry
nodes.html: In 1893 Alfred Werner explained cobalt-ammonia salts as a central metal ion surrounded by six ligands at the corners of an octahedron. His coordination theory, which won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, accounts for the structure, colour and reactivity of transition-metal compounds.
nodes.summary: In 1893 Alfred Werner explained cobalt-ammonia salts as a central metal ion surrounded by six ligands at the corners of an octahedron.

nodes.title: Noble Gases
nodes.html: William Ramsay and Lord Rayleigh isolated argon from air in 1894, after finding that nitrogen from air is denser than nitrogen made from chemicals. Ramsay then found helium on Earth (1895) and, with Morris Travers, neon, krypton and xenon (1898), adding a whole new group to the periodic table. Rayleigh and Ramsay won Nobel Prizes in 1904.
nodes.summary: William Ramsay and Lord Rayleigh isolated argon from air in 1894, after finding that nitrogen from air is denser than nitrogen made from chemicals.

nodes.title: Catalytic Hydrogenation
nodes.html: Paul Sabatier and Jean-Baptiste Senderens showed in 1897 that finely divided nickel adds hydrogen to unsaturated organic compounds. Sabatier shared the 1912 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Hydrogenation hardens fats for margarine and makes fuels and fine chemicals, and the Sabatier reaction turns carbon dioxide and hydrogen into methane.
nodes.summary: Paul Sabatier and Jean-Baptiste Senderens showed in 1897 that finely divided nickel adds hydrogen to unsaturated organic compounds.

nodes.title: Polonium and Radium
nodes.html: Marie and Pierre Curie followed radioactivity through chemical separations of pitchblende and announced polonium and radium in 1898, then isolated radium salts from tonnes of ore. They founded radiochemistry; Marie Curie received the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics (shared) and the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and radium became a cancer treatment and a research tool.
nodes.summary: Marie and Pierre Curie followed radioactivity through chemical separations of pitchblende and announced polonium and radium in 1898, then isolated radium salts from tonnes of ore.

nodes.title: Grignard Reaction
nodes.html: Victor Grignard showed in 1900 that magnesium metal inserts into carbon-halogen bonds to give organomagnesium reagents, which add carbon chains to carbonyl compounds. It gave chemists a general and convenient way to form carbon-carbon bonds, won Grignard the 1912 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and is still used in laboratories and industry.
nodes.summary: Victor Grignard showed in 1900 that magnesium metal inserts into carbon-halogen bonds to give organomagnesium reagents, which add carbon chains to carbonyl compounds.

nodes.title: Iron–Carbon Phase Diagram
nodes.html: William Chandler Roberts-Austen drew an iron-carbon diagram in 1897, and Hendrik Roozeboom interpreted it with Gibbs’s phase rule in 1900. It maps where ferrite, austenite and cementite form at each temperature and carbon content, and turned the heat treatment of steel from craft into science.
nodes.summary: William Chandler Roberts-Austen drew an iron-carbon diagram in 1897, and Hendrik Roozeboom interpreted it with Gibbs’s phase rule in 1900.

nodes.title: Ostwald Process
nodes.html: Wilhelm Ostwald patented in 1902 the oxidation of ammonia to nitric oxide over a platinum gauze, with the oxide then converted to nitric acid. Combined with Haber-Bosch ammonia, it makes the nitric acid for fertilizers and explosives from air and natural gas. Ostwald won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on catalysis.
nodes.summary: Wilhelm Ostwald patented in 1902 the oxidation of ammonia to nitric oxide over a platinum gauze, with the oxide then converted to nitric acid.

nodes.title: Infrared Spectroscopy
nodes.html: William Coblentz recorded the infrared spectra of more than a hundred compounds in 1905 and showed that chemical groups such as OH and C=O absorb at characteristic frequencies. Infrared spectra became fingerprints for identifying compounds and functional groups, and infrared spectrometers are standard equipment in chemical and forensic laboratories.
nodes.summary: William Coblentz recorded the infrared spectra of more than a hundred compounds in 1905 and showed that chemical groups such as OH and C=O absorb at characteristic frequencies.

nodes.title: Age-Hardened Aluminium
nodes.html: Alfred Wilm found in 1906 that an aluminium alloy with copper and magnesium, quenched from a high temperature, keeps hardening for days at room temperature. Sold as Duralumin from 1909, it was the first high-strength aluminium alloy and went into Zeppelins and then all-metal aircraft; fine precipitates inside the metal cause the hardening.
nodes.summary: Alfred Wilm found in 1906 that an aluminium alloy with copper and magnesium, quenched from a high temperature, keeps hardening for days at room temperature.

nodes.title: Chromatography
nodes.html: Mikhail Tsvet separated plant pigments into coloured bands as they moved down a chalk-filled column and named the method chromatography (1903 to 1906). Martin and Synge’s partition chromatography (1941; Nobel Prize 1952) made it general, and chromatography is now the standard way to separate and purify mixtures in chemistry, biology and medicine.
nodes.summary: Mikhail Tsvet separated plant pigments into coloured bands as they moved down a chalk-filled column and named the method chromatography (1903 to 1906).

nodes.title: Bakelite
nodes.html: Leo Baekeland combined phenol and formaldehyde under heat and pressure to make a hard resin that no longer softens when reheated (1907, patented 1909), the first fully synthetic plastic. Bakelite insulated electrical parts and moulded radios, telephones and appliances, and opened the era of plastics made entirely from chemicals.
nodes.summary: Leo Baekeland combined phenol and formaldehyde under heat and pressure to make a hard resin that no longer softens when reheated (1907, patented 1909), the first fully synthetic plastic.

nodes.title: Haber–Bosch Process
nodes.html: Ammonia from the nitrogen in air (Haber 1909; industrial scale at BASF under Bosch, 1913). Fertilizer made this way feeds roughly half of humanity.
nodes.summary: Ammonia from the nitrogen in air (Haber 1909; industrial scale at BASF under Bosch, 1913).

nodes.title: pH Scale
nodes.html: Søren Sørensen, working at the Carlsberg Laboratory on brewing and enzymes, defined pH as the negative logarithm of the hydrogen-ion concentration in 1909. The scale made acidity a number that could be measured and controlled in laboratories, industry, medicine and agriculture; glass electrodes later turned it into a meter reading.
nodes.summary: Søren Sørensen, working at the Carlsberg Laboratory on brewing and enzymes, defined pH as the negative logarithm of the hydrogen-ion concentration in 1909.

nodes.title: Synthetic Rubber
nodes.html: Fritz Hofmann’s team at Bayer patented the process for methyl rubber, an early synthetic rubber, in 1909. German Buna rubbers (1929) and DuPont’s neoprene (1930) followed, and wartime shortages of natural rubber made synthetic rubber a very large industry in the 1940s. It now supplies about half of the world’s rubber.
nodes.summary: Fritz Hofmann’s team at Bayer patented the process for methyl rubber, an early synthetic rubber, in 1909.

nodes.title: Artificial Photosynthesis

progress.what: A monolithic device combining a photovoltaic junction with a photoelectrochemical cell split water at 12.4% efficiency.
progress.html: A monolithic device combining a photovoltaic junction with a photoelectrochemical cell split water at 12.4% efficiency.

progress.what: A 100 m² array of photocatalyst panels ran for months and recovered hydrogen safely, at a maximum solar-to-hydrogen efficiency of 0.76%.
progress.html: A 100 m² array of photocatalyst panels ran for months and recovered hydrogen safely, at a maximum solar-to-hydrogen efficiency of 0.76%.

progress.what: InGaN/GaN nanowire photocatalysts reached 9.2% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency from pure water under concentrated simulated sunlight, and 6.2% in a larger outdoor prototype.
progress.html: InGaN/GaN nanowire photocatalysts reached 9.2% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency from pure water under concentrated simulated sunlight, and 6.2% in a larger outdoor prototype.

nodes.html: Make fuels such as hydrogen or methanol directly from sunlight, water and CO2 with efficient, durable and cheap devices, as Giacomo Ciamician urged in 1912. Devices built from costly III–V semiconductors have exceeded 10% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency since 1998, while a 100 m² photocatalyst array reached 0.76% in 2021. A solution is a scalable system that stores over 10% of sunlight as fuel for years at a cost competitive with fossil fuels.
nodes.summary: Make fuels such as hydrogen or methanol directly from sunlight, water and CO2 with efficient, durable and cheap devices, as Giacomo Ciamician urged in 1912.

nodes.title: X-ray Crystallography
nodes.html: Crystals diffract X-rays (von Laue, 1912), and the pattern reveals where every atom sits (the Braggs, 1913). It later solved salt, penicillin, DNA and proteins.
nodes.summary: Crystals diffract X-rays (von Laue, 1912), and the pattern reveals where every atom sits (the Braggs, 1913).

nodes.title: Chain Reactions
nodes.html: Max Bodenstein explained the reaction of hydrogen and chlorine under light in 1913 as a chain of steps in which each reactive intermediate produces another. Nikolay Semenov and Cyril Hinshelwood extended the idea to branching chains that explain flames and explosions, and shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
nodes.summary: Max Bodenstein explained the reaction of hydrogen and chlorine under light in 1913 as a chain of steps in which each reactive intermediate produces another.

nodes.title: Stainless Steel
nodes.html: Harry Brearley, looking for a better gun-barrel steel in Sheffield, found in 1913 that steel with about 12 percent chromium resisted corrosion and staining. Chromium forms a thin, self-repairing oxide film, and stainless steels went on to cutlery, kitchens, chemical plants, medical instruments and buildings. Krupp’s chromium-nickel grades appeared at about the same time.
nodes.summary: Harry Brearley, looking for a better gun-barrel steel in Sheffield, found in 1913 that steel with about 12 percent chromium resisted corrosion and staining.

nodes.title: Czochralski Crystal Growth
nodes.html: Jan Czochralski pulled a thin metal crystal from a melt in 1916 while measuring crystallisation rates. Gordon Teal and John Little revived the method at Bell Labs in 1950 to grow single-crystal germanium and then silicon, and it now grows nearly all the silicon wafers used for chips and solar cells.
nodes.summary: Jan Czochralski pulled a thin metal crystal from a melt in 1916 while measuring crystallisation rates.

nodes.title: Langmuir Adsorption
nodes.html: Irving Langmuir modelled adsorption in 1916 to 1918 as molecules sticking to a fixed number of identical sites on a surface, forming at most one layer. His isotherm and picture of surface reactions founded surface chemistry and the kinetics of heterogeneous catalysis, and he received the 1932 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
nodes.summary: Irving Langmuir modelled adsorption in 1916 to 1918 as molecules sticking to a fixed number of identical sites on a surface, forming at most one layer.

nodes.title: Electron-Pair Bond
nodes.html: Gilbert N. Lewis proposed in 1916 that a covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms, and drew atoms with dots for their outer electrons. Irving Langmuir’s octet rule (1919) extended the idea, and Lewis dot structures remain the first way chemists draw and reason about bonding.
nodes.summary: Gilbert N.

nodes.title: Powder X-ray Diffraction
nodes.html: Peter Debye and Paul Scherrer in Göttingen (1916) and Albert Hull in the United States (1917) recorded X-ray diffraction rings from powdered samples, so that no single crystal was needed. Powder patterns act as fingerprints of crystalline phases and are the routine tool for identifying minerals, drugs, catalysts and battery materials.
nodes.summary: Peter Debye and Paul Scherrer in Göttingen (1916) and Albert Hull in the United States (1917) recorded X-ray diffraction rings from powdered samples, so that no single crystal was needed.

nodes.title: Mass Spectrometry
nodes.html: Francis Aston’s mass spectrograph (1919) sorted ions by mass and showed that most elements are mixtures of isotopes (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1922), building on J. J. Thomson’s ion-beam parabolas of 1912 to 1913. Mass spectrometry grew into one of the most sensitive and general analytical tools in chemistry, used from proteomics to drug testing, forensics and space missions.
nodes.summary: Francis Aston’s mass spectrograph (1919) sorted ions by mass and showed that most elements are mixtures of isotopes (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1922), building on J.

nodes.title: Polymers
nodes.html: Staudinger argued that rubber and plastics are giant chain molecules (1920); Carothers’s nylon (1935) showed they could be designed on purpose.
nodes.summary: Staudinger argued that rubber and plastics are giant chain molecules (1920); Carothers’s nylon (1935) showed they could be designed on purpose.

nodes.title: Diffuse Interstellar Bands

progress.what: Laboratory spectra of cold C60+ ions matched two near-infrared bands at 963.2 and 957.7 nm, the first identified carrier.
progress.html: Laboratory spectra of cold C60+ ions matched two near-infrared bands at 963.2 and 957.7 nm, the first identified carrier.

progress.what: Hubble Space Telescope spectra, free of telluric water lines, confirmed the weaker C60+ bands predicted by the laboratory work.
progress.html: Hubble Space Telescope spectra, free of telluric water lines, confirmed the weaker C60+ bands predicted by the laboratory work.

progress.what: Helium-tagging spectra of cyclic C4+ matched the broad band at 503.9 nm, a proposed second carrier awaiting confirmation.
progress.html: Helium-tagging spectra of cyclic C4+ matched the broad band at 503.9 nm, a proposed second carrier awaiting confirmation.

nodes.html: More than 550 absorption bands imprinted on starlight by interstellar gas, first noted by Mary Lea Heger in 1922, still lack known carriers; only ionized buckminsterfullerene, C60+, is confirmed (2015–2019), accounting for five of them. A solution assigns further bands to specific molecules by matching laboratory or computed spectra in wavelength, width and relative strength, confirmed by independent groups.
nodes.summary: More than 550 absorption bands imprinted on starlight by interstellar gas, first noted by Mary Lea Heger in 1922, still lack known carriers; only ionized buckminsterfullerene, C60+, is confirmed (2015–2019), accounting for five of them.

nodes.title: Acid–Base Theory
nodes.html: In 1923 Johannes Brønsted and Thomas Lowry independently defined an acid as a proton donor and a base as a proton acceptor, while Gilbert Lewis defined acids as electron-pair acceptors and bases as electron-pair donors. The first is the working definition in water chemistry and biochemistry, and the second extends to catalysis and coordination chemistry.
nodes.summary: In 1923 Johannes Brønsted and Thomas Lowry independently defined an acid as a proton donor and a base as a proton acceptor, while Gilbert Lewis defined acids as electron-pair acceptors and bases as electron-pair donors.

nodes.title: Debye–Hückel Theory
nodes.html: Peter Debye and Erich Hückel showed in 1923 that each ion in a dilute electrolyte is surrounded by a cloud of opposite charge that screens it. Their theory gives the activity coefficients and conductivities of dilute salt solutions, and its screening length, the Debye length, is used throughout colloid science and plasma physics.
nodes.summary: Peter Debye and Erich Hückel showed in 1923 that each ion in a dilute electrolyte is surrounded by a cloud of opposite charge that screens it.

nodes.title: Fischer–Tropsch Synthesis
nodes.html: Franz Fischer and Hans Tropsch at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Coal Research found in 1925 that carbon monoxide and hydrogen over iron or cobalt catalysts form liquid hydrocarbons. The process makes synthetic fuels from coal, natural gas, biomass or captured carbon dioxide; Germany made fuel this way in the Second World War, and South Africa still does.
nodes.summary: Franz Fischer and Hans Tropsch at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Coal Research found in 1925 that carbon monoxide and hydrogen over iron or cobalt catalysts form liquid hydrocarbons.

nodes.title: Quantum Chemistry
nodes.html: Heitler and London explained the hydrogen molecule with quantum mechanics (1927). Pauling’s The Nature of the Chemical Bond (1939) turned the result into working chemistry.
nodes.summary: Heitler and London explained the hydrogen molecule with quantum mechanics (1927).

nodes.title: Chlorofluorocarbons
nodes.html: Thomas Midgley and his team at General Motors made chlorofluorocarbons in 1928 as non-toxic, non-flammable refrigerants and sold them as Freon from 1930. They replaced ammonia and sulfur dioxide in refrigerators and air conditioners and served as aerosol propellants; their stability later let them reach the stratosphere and destroy ozone.
nodes.summary: Thomas Midgley and his team at General Motors made chlorofluorocarbons in 1928 as non-toxic, non-flammable refrigerants and sold them as Freon from 1930.

nodes.title: Diels–Alder Reaction
nodes.html: Otto Diels and Kurt Alder reported in 1928 that a diene and an alkene join in one step to form a six-membered ring, with predictable stereochemistry. The Diels-Alder reaction became one of the most reliable ring-forming reactions in synthesis, used for steroids, vitamins and polymers, and won them the 1950 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
nodes.summary: Otto Diels and Kurt Alder reported in 1928 that a diene and an alkene join in one step to form a six-membered ring, with predictable stereochemistry.

nodes.title: Molecular Orbital Theory
nodes.html: Friedrich Hund and Robert Mulliken described electrons in molecules as occupying orbitals spread over the whole molecule (1927 to 1928), and John Lennard-Jones’s linear combination of atomic orbitals (1929) made the idea computable. Mulliken named the orbital in 1932 and won the 1966 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; molecular orbital theory underlies most computational chemistry.
nodes.summary: Friedrich Hund and Robert Mulliken described electrons in molecules as occupying orbitals spread over the whole molecule (1927 to 1928), and John Lennard-Jones’s linear combination of atomic orbitals (1929) made the idea computable.

nodes.title: Crystal Field Theory
nodes.html: Hans Bethe showed in 1929 that the electric field of the surrounding ions splits the energy levels of a metal ion’s d electrons, and John Van Vleck developed the idea for chemistry in the 1930s. Later refined as ligand field theory, it explains the colours, magnetism and spectra of transition-metal compounds.
nodes.summary: Hans Bethe showed in 1929 that the electric field of the surrounding ions splits the energy levels of a metal ion’s d electrons, and John Van Vleck developed the idea for chemistry in the 1930s.

nodes.title: Pauling’s Rules
nodes.html: Linus Pauling proposed five rules in 1929 for how ions pack into ionic crystals: the coordination polyhedron around each ion follows from the ratio of ion radii, the charges around each ion should balance, and sharing of polyhedron edges and faces is unfavourable. They guided the interpretation of oxide and silicate structures for decades.
nodes.summary: Linus Pauling proposed five rules in 1929 for how ions pack into ionic crystals: the coordination polyhedron around each ion follows from the ratio of ion radii, the charges around each ion should balance, and sharing of polyhedron edges and faces is unfavourable.

nodes.title: Hartree–Fock Method
nodes.html: Douglas Hartree introduced the self-consistent field method in 1928, and Vladimir Fock and John Slater added electron exchange and antisymmetry in 1930. Each electron moves in the average field of all the others, and the method is the starting point of nearly every later quantum-chemistry method.
nodes.summary: Douglas Hartree introduced the self-consistent field method in 1928, and Vladimir Fock and John Slater added electron exchange and antisymmetry in 1930.

nodes.title: Hückel Theory
nodes.html: Erich Hückel’s simple orbital model of pi electrons (1931) explained why planar rings with 4n+2 pi electrons, such as benzene, are unusually stable. Despite its crudeness it still guides chemists’ thinking about aromaticity, conjugated molecules, dyes and organic electronics.
nodes.summary: Erich Hückel’s simple orbital model of pi electrons (1931) explained why planar rings with 4n+2 pi electrons, such as benzene, are unusually stable.

nodes.title: Electronegativity
nodes.html: Linus Pauling put numbers on how strongly an atom attracts the electrons it shares in a bond (1932), starting from bond energies. His electronegativity scale explains bond polarity and acidity and helps predict reactivity across the periodic table; Mulliken (1934) and Allred and Rochow (1958) proposed other scales.
nodes.summary: Linus Pauling put numbers on how strongly an atom attracts the electrons it shares in a bond (1932), starting from bond energies.

nodes.title: Polyethylene
nodes.html: ICI chemists Eric Fawcett and Reginald Gibson obtained a waxy white solid from ethylene gas at about 1,400 atmospheres in March 1933, in an experiment on high-pressure reactions. The polymer, polyethylene, insulated radar cables in the Second World War and is now the most-produced plastic, used in bags, bottles, pipes and films.
nodes.summary: ICI chemists Eric Fawcett and Reginald Gibson obtained a waxy white solid from ethylene gas at about 1,400 atmospheres in March 1933, in an experiment on high-pressure reactions.

nodes.title: Dislocation Theory
nodes.html: Three papers of 1934 by G. I. Taylor, Egon Orowan and Michael Polanyi independently proposed line defects in crystals, called dislocations, to explain why metals yield at a tiny fraction of their theoretical strength. The theory of how dislocations glide, tangle and pin one another is the basis of metal strengthening, alloy design and work hardening.
nodes.summary: Three papers of 1934 by G.

nodes.title: Reaction Mechanisms (SN1/SN2)
nodes.html: Christopher Ingold and Edward Hughes showed from rate laws and stereochemistry in 1935 that nucleophilic substitution proceeds by two routes: SN2, in one concerted step with inversion of configuration, and SN1, through a carbocation intermediate. Their work founded physical organic chemistry, the study of how and why reactions happen.
nodes.summary: Christopher Ingold and Edward Hughes showed from rate laws and stereochemistry in 1935 that nucleophilic substitution proceeds by two routes: SN2, in one concerted step with inversion of configuration, and SN1, through a carbocation intermediate.

nodes.title: Transition State Theory
nodes.html: Henry Eyring, and independently Meredith Evans with Michael Polanyi, derived reaction rates in 1935 from the properties of a short-lived activated complex at the top of the energy barrier. The Eyring equation links the rate to the free energy of activation, and transition state theory remains the main framework for understanding and computing reaction rates.
nodes.summary: Henry Eyring, and independently Meredith Evans with Michael Polanyi, derived reaction rates in 1935 from the properties of a short-lived activated complex at the top of the energy barrier.

nodes.title: Catalytic Cracking
nodes.html: Eugene Houdry’s process passed heated heavy oil over a clay catalyst, splitting large molecules into high-octane gasoline in commercial units from 1936 to 1937. It supplied aviation fuel to the Allied air forces in the Second World War; fluid catalytic cracking, and zeolite catalysts from the 1960s, later took over and remain central to gasoline production.
nodes.summary: Eugene Houdry’s process passed heated heavy oil over a clay catalyst, splitting large molecules into high-octane gasoline in commercial units from 1936 to 1937.

nodes.title: BET Surface Area
nodes.html: Stephen Brunauer, Paul Emmett and Edward Teller extended Langmuir’s adsorption model to multiple layers in 1938. The BET method, which measures how much nitrogen gas a powder adsorbs, is the standard way to determine the surface area of catalysts, pharmaceuticals, cements and porous materials such as zeolites and metal-organic frameworks.
nodes.summary: Stephen Brunauer, Paul Emmett and Edward Teller extended Langmuir’s adsorption model to multiple layers in 1938.

nodes.title: Teflon (PTFE)
nodes.html: Roy Plunkett at DuPont found in 1938 that a cylinder of tetrafluoroethylene gas had polymerised by itself into a slippery white solid. Polytetrafluoroethylene, sold as Teflon, resists heat and nearly all chemicals; it sealed uranium hexafluoride equipment in the Manhattan Project before it coated cookware and lined chemical plant.
nodes.summary: Roy Plunkett at DuPont found in 1938 that a cylinder of tetrafluoroethylene gas had polymerised by itself into a slippery white solid.

nodes.title: Kroll Process
nodes.html: William Kroll showed in 1940 that titanium tetrachloride reduced with molten magnesium gives titanium metal. The Kroll process, run commercially from the late 1940s, still supplies most titanium metal for jet engines, airframes, chemical plant and medical implants, although it is slow and costly.
nodes.summary: William Kroll showed in 1940 that titanium tetrachloride reduced with molten magnesium gives titanium metal.

nodes.title: Silicones
nodes.html: Frederic Kipping studied organosilicon compounds for decades. Eugene Rochow at General Electric found in 1940, and Richard Müller in Germany independently soon after, that methyl chloride passed over heated silicon and copper gives methylchlorosilanes. This direct process makes silicone oils, rubbers, resins and sealants cheaply, for uses from medical implants to building construction.
nodes.summary: Frederic Kipping studied organosilicon compounds for decades.

nodes.title: Transuranium Elements
nodes.html: Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson made neptunium, element 93, in 1940, and Glenn Seaborg’s group made plutonium, element 94, in 1940 to 1941 at Berkeley. Seaborg’s actinide concept (1944) redrew the periodic table, and McMillan and Seaborg shared the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; elements up to 118 had been made by 2010.
nodes.summary: Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson made neptunium, element 93, in 1940, and Glenn Seaborg’s group made plutonium, element 94, in 1940 to 1941 at Berkeley.

nodes.title: Polyester (PET)
nodes.html: John Rex Whinfield and James Tennant Dickson at the Calico Printers’ Association in Manchester made polyethylene terephthalate in 1941, building on Wallace Carothers’s work on polyesters. As Terylene and Dacron it became a major textile fibre, and as PET it is the plastic of drinks bottles and food packaging.
nodes.summary: John Rex Whinfield and James Tennant Dickson at the Calico Printers’ Association in Manchester made polyethylene terephthalate in 1941, building on Wallace Carothers’s work on polyesters.

nodes.title: Flory–Huggins Theory
nodes.html: Paul Flory and Maurice Huggins independently developed in 1941 and 1942 a lattice model of polymer solutions that predicts when a polymer dissolves, swells or separates from its solvent. Flory-Huggins theory remains the basic thermodynamic model for polymer solutions and blends, and Flory received the 1974 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on polymers.
nodes.summary: Paul Flory and Maurice Huggins independently developed in 1941 and 1942 a lattice model of polymer solutions that predicts when a polymer dissolves, swells or separates from its solvent.

nodes.title: Synthetic Zeolites
nodes.html: Richard Barrer made synthetic zeolites by hydrothermal methods from 1948, and Robert Milton at Union Carbide produced zeolites A and X from 1949 and developed them as molecular sieves for drying and separating gases. Zeolite catalysts transformed oil refining from the 1960s, and zeolites are also used in detergents and water softening.
nodes.summary: Richard Barrer made synthetic zeolites by hydrothermal methods from 1948, and Robert Milton at Union Carbide produced zeolites A and X from 1949 and developed them as molecular sieves for drying and separating gases.

nodes.title: Ferrocene
nodes.html: Peter Pauson and Thomas Kealy made an unexpectedly stable orange iron compound in 1951. Geoffrey Wilkinson and Ernst Otto Fischer independently worked out in 1952 that it is an iron atom sandwiched between two cyclopentadienyl rings. Ferrocene launched modern organometallic chemistry, and Wilkinson and Fischer shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
nodes.summary: Peter Pauson and Thomas Kealy made an unexpectedly stable orange iron compound in 1951.

nodes.title: NMR Spectroscopy
nodes.html: After Felix Bloch and Edward Purcell detected nuclear magnetic resonance in 1946, chemists found that a nucleus’s resonance frequency depends on its chemical surroundings (1950). The three-peak ethanol spectrum of Arnold, Dharmatti and Packard (1951) made the point, and NMR became the main method for working out molecular structures. Its imaging offspring is MRI.
nodes.summary: After Felix Bloch and Edward Purcell detected nuclear magnetic resonance in 1946, chemists found that a nucleus’s resonance frequency depends on its chemical surroundings (1950).

nodes.title: Roothaan–Hall Equations
nodes.html: Clemens Roothaan and George Hall independently showed in 1951 that expanding molecular orbitals in a finite set of basis functions turns the Hartree-Fock equations into matrix equations that a computer can solve. Frank Boys’s use of Gaussian functions (1950) made the integrals fast to compute, and the approach underlies nearly every ab initio program.
nodes.summary: Clemens Roothaan and George Hall independently showed in 1951 that expanding molecular orbitals in a finite set of basis functions turns the Hartree-Fock equations into matrix equations that a computer can solve.

nodes.title: Basic Oxygen Steelmaking
nodes.html: At Linz and Donawitz in Austria in 1952, a process developed by Robert Durrer and colleagues blew pure oxygen onto molten iron in a converter, refining a heat of steel in under an hour. The basic oxygen furnace replaced the open hearth, cut costs, and now produces about 70 percent of the world’s steel.
nodes.summary: At Linz and Donawitz in Austria in 1952, a process developed by Robert Durrer and colleagues blew pure oxygen onto molten iron in a converter, refining a heat of steel in under an hour.

nodes.title: Gas Chromatography
nodes.html: Archer Martin and Anthony James separated volatile compounds carried by a gas through a heated column in 1952. Connected to mass spectrometers from the late 1950s, gas chromatography finds trace contaminants, drugs and flavours in complex mixtures. Martin shared the 1952 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for partition chromatography.
nodes.summary: Archer Martin and Anthony James separated volatile compounds carried by a gas through a heated column in 1952.

nodes.title: III–V Semiconductors
nodes.html: Heinrich Welker at Siemens showed in 1952 that compounds of group III and group V elements, such as gallium arsenide and indium antimonide, are semiconductors with useful electronic properties. Direct-gap III-V materials went on to make LEDs, laser diodes, space solar cells and fast radio-frequency chips.
nodes.summary: Heinrich Welker at Siemens showed in 1952 that compounds of group III and group V elements, such as gallium arsenide and indium antimonide, are semiconductors with useful electronic properties.

nodes.title: Piezoelectric Ceramics (PZT)
nodes.html: After barium titanate was found to be ferroelectric in the 1940s, Gen Shirane, Etsuro Sawaguchi and Bernard Jaffe showed in 1952 to 1954 that lead zirconate titanate (PZT) is a strongly piezoelectric ferroelectric ceramic. PZT became the standard material in ultrasound probes, sonar, sensors, actuators and fuel injectors.
nodes.summary: After barium titanate was found to be ferroelectric in the 1940s, Gen Shirane, Etsuro Sawaguchi and Bernard Jaffe showed in 1952 to 1954 that lead zirconate titanate (PZT) is a strongly piezoelectric ferroelectric ceramic.

nodes.title: Zone Refining
nodes.html: William Pfann showed in 1952 that sweeping a narrow molten zone along a solid bar carries impurities with it to one end, purifying the material with each pass. Zone refining gave the germanium and silicon, pure to parts per billion, that early transistors needed, and it is still used for ultrapure metals and semiconductors.
nodes.summary: William Pfann showed in 1952 that sweeping a narrow molten zone along a solid bar carries impurities with it to one end, purifying the material with each pass.

nodes.title: Glass-Ceramics
nodes.html: Don Stookey at Corning overheated a photosensitive lithium silicate glass in 1953 and found that it had crystallised into a strong, opaque ceramic instead of melting. Controlled crystallisation of glass gave Pyroceram for missile nose cones and CorningWare cookware, and glass-ceramics are now used for stovetops and telescope mirror blanks.
nodes.summary: Don Stookey at Corning overheated a photosensitive lithium silicate glass in 1953 and found that it had crystallised into a strong, opaque ceramic instead of melting.

nodes.title: Ziegler–Natta Catalysts
nodes.html: Karl Ziegler found in 1953 that titanium and aluminium compounds polymerise ethylene at low pressure into linear polyethylene, and Giulio Natta used related catalysts in 1954 to make stereoregular polypropylene. Ziegler-Natta catalysts gave the polyolefin industry its main plastics and won the two chemists the 1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
nodes.summary: Karl Ziegler found in 1953 that titanium and aluminium compounds polymerise ethylene at low pressure into linear polyethylene, and Giulio Natta used related catalysts in 1954 to make stereoregular polypropylene.

nodes.title: Synthetic Diamond
nodes.html: General Electric researchers, using H. Tracy Hall’s belt press, made the first reproducible synthetic diamonds from graphite at about 100,000 atmospheres and 2,000 °C in December 1954; ASEA in Sweden (Baltzar von Platen) had made diamonds in 1953 without publishing. Synthetic diamond now supplies most industrial abrasives, and vapour deposition (1980s) makes gem and electronic grades.
nodes.summary: General Electric researchers, using H.

nodes.title: Wittig Reaction
nodes.html: Georg Wittig showed in 1954 that a phosphorus ylide converts a ketone or aldehyde into an alkene, placing the new carbon-carbon double bond exactly where the carbonyl group was. The Wittig reaction is a standard tool for making alkenes, used industrially for vitamin A, and brought Wittig a share of the 1979 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
nodes.summary: Georg Wittig showed in 1954 that a phosphorus ylide converts a ketone or aldehyde into an alkene, placing the new carbon-carbon double bond exactly where the carbonyl group was.

nodes.title: Living Polymerization
nodes.html: Michael Szwarc showed in 1956 that anionic polymerisation of styrene started with sodium naphthalene has no termination step, so the chains keep growing whenever more monomer is added. Living polymerisation gives polymers of uniform chain length and lets chemists build block copolymers; it is the model for later controlled radical methods.
nodes.summary: Michael Szwarc showed in 1956 that anionic polymerisation of styrene started with sodium naphthalene has no termination step, so the chains keep growing whenever more monomer is added.

nodes.title: Marcus Theory
nodes.html: Rudolph Marcus showed in 1956 that the rate of electron transfer between molecules depends on how much the solvent must rearrange, and predicted an inverted region in which a larger driving force slows the reaction. Experiments confirmed this in 1984. The theory underlies electrochemistry and photosynthesis research and won the 1992 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
nodes.summary: Rudolph Marcus showed in 1956 that the rate of electron transfer between molecules depends on how much the solvent must rearrange, and predicted an inverted region in which a larger driving force slows the reaction.

nodes.title: Molecular Dynamics Simulation
nodes.html: Berni Alder and Thomas Wainwright used a computer in 1957 to follow hard spheres colliding and found that they form a solid at high density. Aneesur Rahman simulated liquid argon with realistic forces in 1964, and molecular dynamics became the standard way to simulate liquids, proteins and materials atom by atom.
nodes.summary: Berni Alder and Thomas Wainwright used a computer in 1957 to follow hard spheres colliding and found that they form a solid at high density.

nodes.title: Silicon Oxide Passivation
nodes.html: Carl Frosch and Lincoln Derick at Bell Labs found in 1957 that a thermally grown silicon dioxide layer masks silicon against dopants, and Mohamed Atalla showed in 1957 to 1959 that it also passivates the surface. These findings made the planar process and the MOSFET possible, and with them the integrated circuit industry.
nodes.summary: Carl Frosch and Lincoln Derick at Bell Labs found in 1957 that a thermally grown silicon dioxide layer masks silicon against dopants, and Mohamed Atalla showed in 1957 to 1959 that it also passivates the surface.

nodes.title: Molecular Manufacturing
nodes.html: Building materials and machines atom by atom, as Feynman imagined in ‘There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom’ (1959) and Drexler elaborated (1986). Cells do it every second; we cannot yet do it in general.
nodes.summary: Building materials and machines atom by atom, as Feynman imagined in ‘There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom’ (1959) and Drexler elaborated (1986).

nodes.title: Metallic Glass
nodes.html: Pol Duwez’s group at Caltech cooled a gold-silicon melt at about a million degrees per second in 1960 and froze it into a disordered, glass-like metal.
