nodes.html: Using Golgi’s silver stain, Cajal showed that the nervous system is made of separate cells, neurons, which communicate across tiny gaps (1888).
nodes.summary: Using Golgi’s silver stain, Cajal showed that the nervous system is made of separate cells, neurons, which communicate across tiny gaps (1888).

nodes.title: Antibodies
nodes.html: Emil von Behring and Shibasaburo Kitasato showed in 1890 that serum from animals immunised against diphtheria or tetanus toxin protected other animals, and Paul Ehrlich standardised the antitoxin. Serum therapy was the first effective treatment for diphtheria, and Behring received the first Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1901.
nodes.summary: Emil von Behring and Shibasaburo Kitasato showed in 1890 that serum from animals immunised against diphtheria or tetanus toxin protected other animals, and Paul Ehrlich standardised the antitoxin.

nodes.title: Meiosis
nodes.html: Oscar Hertwig first saw meiosis in sea urchin eggs in 1876, and in 1883 Edouard Van Beneden showed in roundworm eggs that gametes carry half the usual number of chromosomes. By 1890 August Weismann had explained why two divisions are needed and Theodor Boveri had traced its course. Meiosis keeps chromosome number constant across generations and mixes parental chromosomes.
nodes.summary: Oscar Hertwig first saw meiosis in sea urchin eggs in 1876, and in 1883 Edouard Van Beneden showed in roundworm eggs that gametes carry half the usual number of chromosomes.

nodes.title: Discovery of Viruses
nodes.html: Dmitri Ivanovsky showed in 1892 that sap from diseased tobacco plants stayed infectious after passing through a filter fine enough to hold back all bacteria. In 1898 Martinus Beijerinck concluded that the agent was a contagious living fluid, and the field of virology grew from these experiments.
nodes.summary: Dmitri Ivanovsky showed in 1892 that sap from diseased tobacco plants stayed infectious after passing through a filter fine enough to hold back all bacteria.

nodes.title: Weismann Barrier
nodes.html: In Das Keimplasma (1892) August Weismann argued that heredity passes only through the germ line, and that changes acquired by the body, such as the effects of use or injury, do not travel back to the eggs and sperm. His experiment of cutting the tails off mice for many generations supported the case against Lamarckian inheritance.
nodes.summary: In Das Keimplasma (1892) August Weismann argued that heredity passes only through the germ line, and that changes acquired by the body, such as the effects of use or injury, do not travel back to the eggs and sperm.

nodes.title: Aspirin
nodes.html: Felix Hoffmann and Arthur Eichengrün at Bayer made pure, well-tolerated acetylsalicylic acid in 1897 from salicylic acid, the pain-relieving compound derived from willow bark. Marketed from 1899, aspirin became the first mass-market synthetic drug. John Vane showed in 1971 that it works by blocking prostaglandin synthesis.
nodes.summary: Felix Hoffmann and Arthur Eichengrün at Bayer made pure, well-tolerated acetylsalicylic acid in 1897 from salicylic acid, the pain-relieving compound derived from willow bark.

nodes.title: Enzymes
nodes.html: Eduard Buchner showed in 1897 that juice pressed from ground yeast, with no living cells in it, still fermented sugar. Fermentation was therefore chemistry done by molecules, which came to be called enzymes, and the finding opened biochemistry. Buchner won the 1907 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
nodes.summary: Eduard Buchner showed in 1897 that juice pressed from ground yeast, with no living cells in it, still fermented sugar.

nodes.title: ABO Blood Groups
nodes.html: Karl Landsteiner found in 1901 that mixing the blood of one person with the serum of another sometimes makes it clump, and sorted human blood into the groups A, B and O (AB followed in 1902). The groups explained why transfusions had so often failed and made safe transfusion possible. He won the 1930 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Karl Landsteiner found in 1901 that mixing the blood of one person with the serum of another sometimes makes it clump, and sorted human blood into the groups A, B and O (AB followed in 1902).

nodes.title: Chromosome Theory of Heredity
nodes.html: Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri noted independently in 1902 that chromosomes pair and separate in meiosis exactly as Mendel’s hereditary factors do. They concluded that the factors are carried on chromosomes, which gave heredity a physical location and led to the fly work of Thomas Hunt Morgan.
nodes.summary: Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri noted independently in 1902 that chromosomes pair and separate in meiosis exactly as Mendel’s hereditary factors do.

nodes.title: Hormones
nodes.html: William Bayliss and Ernest Starling showed in 1902 that secretin, released by the intestine, travels in the blood to make the pancreas secrete, which proved that organs can signal chemically through the circulation. In 1905 Starling named such substances hormones, and endocrinology followed.
nodes.summary: William Bayliss and Ernest Starling showed in 1902 that secretin, released by the intestine, travels in the blood to make the pancreas secrete, which proved that organs can signal chemically through the circulation.

nodes.title: Drug Receptors
nodes.html: John Newport Langley proposed in 1905, from the actions of nicotine and curare on muscle, that cells carry receptive substances that drugs combine with. Paul Ehrlich’s earlier side-chain theory had suggested binding sites for toxins and dyes. The receptor idea became the basis of pharmacology and of drug design.
nodes.summary: John Newport Langley proposed in 1905, from the actions of nicotine and curare on muscle, that cells carry receptive substances that drugs combine with.

nodes.title: Integrative Action of the Nerves
nodes.html: Charles Sherrington’s The Integrative Action of the Nervous System (1906) described how reflexes combine excitation and inhibition, and how nerve cells communicate across junctions that he had named synapses. His work established the reflex arc as the unit of nervous integration and earned him the 1932 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Charles Sherrington’s The Integrative Action of the Nervous System (1906) described how reflexes combine excitation and inhibition, and how nerve cells communicate across junctions that he had named synapses.

nodes.title: Hardy–Weinberg Principle
nodes.html: G. H. Hardy and Wilhelm Weinberg showed independently in 1908 that in a large randomly mating population, allele and genotype frequencies stay constant from generation to generation unless something acts on them. It answered the objection that dominant alleles must spread, and serves as the baseline model of population genetics.
nodes.summary: G.

nodes.title: Hybrid Corn
nodes.html: George Shull and Edward East showed around 1908 that crossing two inbred maize lines produces plants that outyield either parent, an effect called hybrid vigour. Hybrid seed spread through the US Corn Belt from the 1930s and, with fertiliser, helped more than double American maize yields by 1960. It also created the commercial seed industry.
nodes.summary: George Shull and Edward East showed around 1908 that crossing two inbred maize lines produces plants that outyield either parent, an effect called hybrid vigour.

nodes.title: Chemotherapy and Salvarsan
nodes.html: Paul Ehrlich and Sahachiro Hata found in 1909 that compound 606, an arsenic compound later named arsphenamine, cleared syphilis spirochaetes from infected rabbits, and it was sold as Salvarsan from 1910. It was the first synthetic drug to treat an infection effectively, and Ehrlich coined the word chemotherapy.
nodes.summary: Paul Ehrlich and Sahachiro Hata found in 1909 that compound 606, an arsenic compound later named arsphenamine, cleared syphilis spirochaetes from infected rabbits, and it was sold as Salvarsan from 1910.

nodes.title: Model Organisms
nodes.html: In 1910 Thomas Hunt Morgan found a white-eyed fruit fly at Columbia University, and his laboratory used Drosophila to show that genes sit on chromosomes. Its quick breeding and cheap upkeep made the fly the first widely shared genetic model organism, followed by E. coli, yeast, the worm, zebrafish and the mouse.
nodes.summary: In 1910 Thomas Hunt Morgan found a white-eyed fruit fly at Columbia University, and his laboratory used Drosophila to show that genes sit on chromosomes.

nodes.title: Vitamins
nodes.html: Christiaan Eijkman showed in the 1890s that beriberi comes from a diet of polished rice, and Frederick Gowland Hopkins found that animals need small amounts of accessory food factors. Casimir Funk coined ‘vitamine’ in 1912. Scurvy, beriberi, rickets and pellagra became preventable by diet.
nodes.summary: Christiaan Eijkman showed in the 1890s that beriberi comes from a diet of polished rice, and Frederick Gowland Hopkins found that animals need small amounts of accessory food factors.

nodes.title: Genetic Linkage Maps
nodes.html: Alfred Sturtevant, then an undergraduate in Thomas Hunt Morgan’s laboratory, used how often genes are separated by crossing over to place six fly genes in a line on the X chromosome (published 1913). It was the first genetic map and showed that genes are arranged linearly on chromosomes.
nodes.summary: Alfred Sturtevant, then an undergraduate in Thomas Hunt Morgan’s laboratory, used how often genes are separated by crossing over to place six fly genes in a line on the X chromosome (published 1913).

nodes.title: Michaelis–Menten Kinetics
nodes.html: Leonor Michaelis and Maud Menten published in 1913 an equation for how the rate of an enzyme reaction rises with substrate concentration and levels off at a maximum. Its constants Km and Vmax became the standard language of enzyme kinetics and of drug action.
nodes.summary: Leonor Michaelis and Maud Menten published in 1913 an equation for how the rate of an enzyme reaction rises with substrate concentration and levels off at a maximum.

nodes.title: Blood Transfusion
nodes.html: In 1914 Albert Hustin in Brussels and Luis Agote in Buenos Aires used sodium citrate to stop donated blood clotting, and Richard Lewisohn in New York soon refined it. Blood could then be stored and carried to the patient, which made transfusion routine in surgery and, in the First World War, on the battlefield.
nodes.summary: In 1914 Albert Hustin in Brussels and Luis Agote in Buenos Aires used sodium citrate to stop donated blood clotting, and Richard Lewisohn in New York soon refined it.

nodes.title: Bacteriophage
nodes.html: Félix d’Hérelle reported in 1917 that an invisible agent in filtrates could dissolve bacterial cultures, and named it bacteriophage (‘bacteria eater’). Frederick Twort had seen the effect in 1915. Phages were tried as therapy, then neglected after antibiotics, and became the main experimental system of early molecular biology.
nodes.summary: Félix d’Hérelle reported in 1917 that an invisible agent in filtrates could dissolve bacterial cultures, and named it bacteriophage (‘bacteria eater’).

nodes.title: Insulin
nodes.html: In 1921 Frederick Banting and Charles Best, in J. J. R. Macleod’s laboratory at Toronto, extracted insulin from dog pancreas, and James Collip purified it. In January 1922 it was given to Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old dying of diabetes. Type 1 diabetes changed from a fatal illness to a manageable one.
nodes.summary: In 1921 Frederick Banting and Charles Best, in J.

nodes.title: Chemical Synaptic Transmission
nodes.html: Otto Loewi showed in 1921 that fluid from a stimulated frog heart slowed a second heart, so nerves signal by releasing a chemical, which Henry Dale identified as acetylcholine. The two shared the 1936 Nobel Prize. It settled the long debate over whether most synapses work by chemicals or by electricity.
nodes.summary: Otto Loewi showed in 1921 that fluid from a stimulated frog heart slowed a second heart, so nerves signal by releasing a chemical, which Henry Dale identified as acetylcholine.

nodes.title: Origin of Life

progress.what: Sparking a reducing mixture of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water produced amino acids, showing that the building blocks of life form without life.
progress.html: Sparking a reducing mixture of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water produced amino acids, showing that the building blocks of life form without life.

progress.what: A polymerase ribozyme with improved copying fidelity propagated a second functional RNA through repeated rounds of replication and selection, so Darwinian evolution ran with RNA as both the information and the catalyst.
progress.html: A polymerase ribozyme with improved copying fidelity propagated a second functional RNA through repeated rounds of replication and selection, so Darwinian evolution ran with RNA as both the information and the catalyst.

progress.what: Thioesters aminoacylated RNA selectively at its 2’,3’-diol in water and went on to peptidyl-RNA, a prebiotic route to the chemistry that precedes coded protein synthesis.
progress.html: Thioesters aminoacylated RNA selectively at its 2’,3’-diol in water and went on to peptidyl-RNA, a prebiotic route to the chemistry that precedes coded protein synthesis.

progress.what: QT45, a 45-nucleotide polymerase ribozyme found in random sequence pools, copied its own complementary strand in alkaline eutectic ice at 94.1% fidelity per nucleotide, in about 0.2% yield over 72 days.
progress.html: QT45, a 45-nucleotide polymerase ribozyme found in random sequence pools, copied its own complementary strand in alkaline eutectic ice at 94.1% fidelity per nucleotide, in about 0.2% yield over 72 days.

nodes.html: Build an unbroken chemical route from plausible prebiotic conditions to a self-replicating, evolving system, the problem Oparin posed in 1924. Every step demonstrated so far has been staged by a chemist. A solution is one set of conditions under which the whole sequence runs by itself and ends in a replicator that copies itself and evolves.
nodes.summary: Build an unbroken chemical route from plausible prebiotic conditions to a self-replicating, evolving system, the problem Oparin posed in 1924.

nodes.title: The Spemann Organizer
nodes.html: Hans Spemann and Hilde Mangold grafted the dorsal lip of one newt gastrula onto the side of another and found that the host grew a second body axis (1924). Some embryonic cells, the organizer, instruct neighbouring cells what to become. Spemann received the 1935 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Hans Spemann and Hilde Mangold grafted the dorsal lip of one newt gastrula onto the side of another and found that the host grew a second body axis (1924).

nodes.title: Predator–Prey Equations
nodes.html: Alfred Lotka (1925) and Vito Volterra (1926) wrote down coupled equations for a predator and its prey that give regular oscillations in both populations. Volterra was prompted by Umberto D’Ancona’s Adriatic fish catches, which showed more predators when fishing stopped in the First World War. The equations opened mathematical ecology.
nodes.summary: Alfred Lotka (1925) and Vito Volterra (1926) wrote down coupled equations for a predator and its prey that give regular oscillations in both populations.

nodes.title: Food Webs and Trophic Levels
nodes.html: Charles Elton’s Animal Ecology (1927) set out food chains, food webs and the pyramid of numbers, and the idea that each species has a niche, a role in the community. Raymond Lindeman added energy flow between trophic levels in 1942, which made ecology the study of how matter and energy pass through living systems.
nodes.summary: Charles Elton’s Animal Ecology (1927) set out food chains, food webs and the pyramid of numbers, and the idea that each species has a niche, a role in the community.

nodes.title: The SIR Epidemic Model
nodes.html: William Kermack and Anderson McKendrick published equations in 1927 for how a population moves from susceptible to infected to recovered. They showed that an epidemic takes off only when susceptibles exceed a threshold, and that it ends before everyone is infected. Later work on the reproduction number and herd immunity builds on it.
nodes.summary: William Kermack and Anderson McKendrick published equations in 1927 for how a population moves from susceptible to infected to recovered.

nodes.title: Antibiotics
nodes.html: Fleming noticed a mould killing bacteria (1928); Florey and Chain turned penicillin into a mass-produced drug in the 1940s.
nodes.summary: Fleming noticed a mould killing bacteria (1928); Florey and Chain turned penicillin into a mass-produced drug in the 1940s.

nodes.title: Modern Synthesis
nodes.html: Population genetics reconciled Darwin with Mendel (Fisher 1930, Haldane, Wright). Much of modern statistics was invented along the way.
nodes.summary: Population genetics reconciled Darwin with Mendel (Fisher 1930, Haldane, Wright).

nodes.title: The Metabolic Scaling Exponent

progress.what: Reanalysed the mammal and bird data sets of Kleiber and others and found little evidence for rejecting an exponent of 2/3 in favour of 3/4.
progress.html: Reanalysed the mammal and bird data sets of Kleiber and others and found little evidence for rejecting an exponent of 2/3 in favour of 3/4.

progress.what: Across 619 mammal species, after correcting for body temperature, digestive state and phylogeny, basal metabolic rate scaled as mass to the 2/3.
progress.html: Across 619 mammal species, after correcting for body temperature, digestive state and phylogeny, basal metabolic rate scaled as mass to the 2/3.

progress.what: Showed that mammalian metabolic rate curves upward against mass on a log-log plot, so it is not a pure power law, a test the fractal-network model fails as published.
progress.html: Showed that mammalian metabolic rate curves upward against mass on a log-log plot, so it is not a pure power law, a test the fractal-network model fails as published.

progress.what: Derived metabolic scaling from the joint optimization of metabolism, growth and reproduction, which reproduces the observed allometries of animal life.
progress.html: Derived metabolic scaling from the joint optimization of metabolism, growth and reproduction, which reproduces the observed allometries of animal life.

nodes.html: Basal metabolic rate rises roughly as body mass to the power 3/4, as Max Kleiber reported in 1932, but whether the exponent is really 3/4, 2/3 or variable, and why, is unresolved. West, Brown and Enquist’s fractal-network derivation (1997) is disputed, and mammal data curve on log-log axes. Solving it means a mechanistic theory that predicts measured exponents, their curvature and their variation across taxa without fitted constants.
nodes.summary: Basal metabolic rate rises roughly as body mass to the power 3/4, as Max Kleiber reported in 1932, but whether the exponent is really 3/4, 2/3 or variable, and why, is unresolved.

nodes.title: Competitive Exclusion Principle
nodes.html: In The Struggle for Existence (1934) Georgy Gause grew two species of Paramecium together on a limited food supply and found that one always died out. Two species competing for the same limiting resource cannot coexist indefinitely, a principle that became the foundation of niche theory.
nodes.summary: In The Struggle for Existence (1934) Georgy Gause grew two species of Paramecium together on a limited food supply and found that one always died out.

nodes.title: The Ecosystem
nodes.html: Arthur Tansley coined the word ecosystem in 1935 for a community of organisms together with its physical environment, treated as one system of matter and energy. The concept let ecologists measure flows of energy and nutrients and became a basis of environmental science and conservation.
nodes.summary: Arthur Tansley coined the word ecosystem in 1935 for a community of organisms together with its physical environment, treated as one system of matter and energy.

nodes.title: Isotopic Tracers in Metabolism
nodes.html: Rudolf Schoenheimer and David Rittenberg fed animals compounds labelled with heavy hydrogen from 1935, and later heavy nitrogen, and followed the atoms through the body. They found that fats and proteins are constantly broken down and rebuilt, so that body constituents are in a dynamic state. Isotope labelling became a basic tool of biochemistry.
nodes.summary: Rudolf Schoenheimer and David Rittenberg fed animals compounds labelled with heavy hydrogen from 1935, and later heavy nitrogen, and followed the atoms through the body.

nodes.title: Sulfa Drugs
nodes.html: Gerhard Domagk at Bayer showed in 1932 that the red dye Prontosil cured streptococcal infection in mice, and published in 1935 after successful clinical use. A Pasteur Institute team found that the active part is sulfanilamide. Sulfa drugs were the first broadly effective antibacterial medicines, and Domagk won the 1939 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Gerhard Domagk at Bayer showed in 1932 that the red dye Prontosil cured streptococcal infection in mice, and published in 1935 after successful clinical use.

nodes.title: Citric Acid Cycle
nodes.html: Hans Krebs proposed in 1937 that cells oxidise the fragments of food molecules through a closed cycle of reactions that starts and ends with the same compound and releases carbon dioxide and energy-rich electrons. This citric acid cycle is the central pathway of energy metabolism in aerobic life. Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize with Fritz Lipmann.
nodes.summary: Hans Krebs proposed in 1937 that cells oxidise the fragments of food molecules through a closed cycle of reactions that starts and ends with the same compound and releases carbon dioxide and energy-rich electrons.

nodes.title: Glycolysis
nodes.html: Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and Jakub Parnas and their co-workers pieced together the ten steps by which a cell converts glucose to pyruvate and gains ATP, a pathway complete by about 1940. It is shared by almost all living cells and is a central route of energy metabolism.
nodes.summary: Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and Jakub Parnas and their co-workers pieced together the ten steps by which a cell converts glucose to pyruvate and gains ATP, a pathway complete by about 1940.

nodes.title: ATP as Energy Currency
nodes.html: Fritz Lipmann proposed in 1941 that cells carry energy in the phosphate bonds of ATP, which is made in energy-yielding reactions and spent in energy-demanding ones. Karl Lohmann had isolated ATP in 1929. ATP came to be recognised as the universal energy currency of life.
nodes.summary: Fritz Lipmann proposed in 1941 that cells carry energy in the phosphate bonds of ATP, which is made in energy-yielding reactions and spent in energy-demanding ones.

nodes.title: One Gene, One Enzyme
nodes.html: George Beadle and Edward Tatum exposed the bread mould Neurospora to X-rays in 1941 and found mutants that each lacked one enzyme of a metabolic pathway. They concluded that each gene directs the making of one enzyme, which linked genetics to biochemistry and earned them the 1958 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: George Beadle and Edward Tatum exposed the bread mould Neurospora to X-rays in 1941 and found mutants that each lacked one enzyme of a metabolic pathway.

nodes.title: DNA Carries Heredity
nodes.html: Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty showed in 1944 that the substance that transformed harmless pneumococci into a virulent type is DNA. Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase confirmed in 1952, with radioactively labelled phage, that DNA carries heredity. The result pointed biology toward the nucleic acids and led to the double helix.
nodes.summary: Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty showed in 1944 that the substance that transformed harmless pneumococci into a virulent type is DNA.

nodes.title: Cancer Chemotherapy
nodes.html: Sidney Farber gave the folate antagonist aminopterin to children with acute leukaemia in 1948 and produced the first temporary remissions. His work followed wartime studies of nitrogen mustard by Louis Goodman and Alfred Gilman, who treated a lymphoma patient in 1942. Drug treatment of cancer began with these results.
nodes.summary: Sidney Farber gave the folate antagonist aminopterin to children with acute leukaemia in 1948 and produced the first temporary remissions.

nodes.title: Cohort Studies
nodes.html: The Framingham Heart Study, begun in 1948 under Thomas Dawber, enrolled 5,209 healthy adults in a Massachusetts town and followed them for decades. It identified high blood pressure, high cholesterol and smoking as risk factors for heart disease, and gave the term risk factor to medicine.
nodes.summary: The Framingham Heart Study, begun in 1948 under Thomas Dawber, enrolled 5,209 healthy adults in a Massachusetts town and followed them for decades.

nodes.title: The Randomized Controlled Trial
nodes.html: The Medical Research Council trial of streptomycin for tuberculosis, designed by Austin Bradford Hill and reported in 1948, allocated patients to treatment or bed rest by sealed envelopes drawn from a random sequence, so that neither doctors nor patients chose. It became the model for the randomised controlled trial, now the standard test of whether a treatment works.
nodes.summary: The Medical Research Council trial of streptomycin for tuberculosis, designed by Austin Bradford Hill and reported in 1948, allocated patients to treatment or bed rest by sealed envelopes drawn from a random sequence, so that neither doctors nor patients chose.

nodes.title: Hebbian Plasticity
nodes.html: In The Organization of Behavior (1949) Donald Hebb proposed that when one cell repeatedly helps to fire another, the connection between them strengthens. The postulate, often summarised as cells that fire together wire together, guided later work on learning and memory and is an ancestor of learning rules in artificial neural networks.
nodes.summary: In The Organization of Behavior (1949) Donald Hebb proposed that when one cell repeatedly helps to fire another, the connection between them strengthens.

nodes.title: The Calvin Cycle
nodes.html: Melvin Calvin, Andrew Benson and James Bassham fed plants radioactive carbon dioxide and used paper chromatography to identify the compounds that formed within seconds, working out from 1946 how plants build sugar from carbon dioxide. The cycle was published in the early 1950s and won Calvin the 1961 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Melvin Calvin, Andrew Benson and James Bassham fed plants radioactive carbon dioxide and used paper chromatography to identify the compounds that formed within seconds, working out from 1946 how plants build sugar from carbon dioxide.

nodes.title: Smoking Causes Lung Cancer
nodes.html: In 1950 Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill, and independently Ernest Wynder and Evarts Graham, found in case-control studies that lung cancer patients were far more often heavy smokers. Doll and Hill’s British doctors cohort, begun in 1951, confirmed the link. These studies changed what epidemiology could establish and led to tobacco control.
nodes.summary: In 1950 Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill, and independently Ernest Wynder and Evarts Graham, found in case-control studies that lung cancer patients were far more often heavy smokers.

nodes.title: Transposable Elements
nodes.html: Barbara McClintock found in maize in the late 1940s that some genetic elements move from place to place on chromosomes and switch neighbouring genes on and off, and described them in 1950. Her results met scepticism for decades. Transposable elements are now known to make up nearly half of the human genome, and she won the 1983 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Barbara McClintock found in maize in the late 1940s that some genetic elements move from place to place on chromosomes and switch neighbouring genes on and off, and described them in 1950.

nodes.title: Cell Culture and HeLa
nodes.html: George Gey’s laboratory at Johns Hopkins grew cells from the cervical tumour of Henrietta Lacks, taken without her knowledge in 1951, and they proved to divide without limit. HeLa cells became the standard human cell line, used for the polio vaccine, cancer research and countless other studies, and their history shaped debate on consent.
nodes.summary: George Gey’s laboratory at Johns Hopkins grew cells from the cervical tumour of Henrietta Lacks, taken without her knowledge in 1951, and they proved to divide without limit.

nodes.title: Protein Sequencing
nodes.html: Frederick Sanger worked out the complete amino acid sequence of insulin between 1951 and 1955, using a chemical label for the end of each chain and partial digestion into fragments. It showed that a protein has a precise, unique sequence, and it paved the way for the study of how genes specify proteins. He received the 1958 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
nodes.summary: Frederick Sanger worked out the complete amino acid sequence of insulin between 1951 and 1955, using a chemical label for the end of each chain and partial digestion into fragments.

nodes.title: Hodgkin–Huxley Model
nodes.html: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley recorded currents in the squid giant axon with a voltage clamp and in 1952 fitted four differential equations that reproduce the action potential from the opening and closing of sodium and potassium conductances. It was the first quantitative model of a neuron and won them the 1963 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley recorded currents in the squid giant axon with a voltage clamp and in 1952 fitted four differential equations that reproduce the action potential from the opening and closing of sodium and potassium conductances.

nodes.title: Reaction–Diffusion Patterning
nodes.html: Alan Turing showed in 1952 that two chemicals that react and diffuse at different rates can turn a uniform mixture into stable stripes or spots. The paper The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis proposed that such reaction-diffusion patterns might shape animal markings and tissues, and experiments have since found Turing patterns in several living systems.
nodes.summary: Alan Turing showed in 1952 that two chemicals that react and diffuse at different rates can turn a uniform mixture into stable stripes or spots.

nodes.title: DNA Double Helix

quote.text: It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.

nodes.html: Watson and Crick’s model (1953), built on Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray data, showed how genetic information is stored and copied.
nodes.summary: Watson and Crick’s model (1953), built on Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray data, showed how genetic information is stored and copied.

nodes.title: Open-Heart Surgery
nodes.html: On 6 May 1953 John Gibbon closed a hole in the heart of 18-year-old Cecelia Bavolek in Philadelphia while a heart-lung machine he had developed over twenty years carried her circulation. C. Walton Lillehei in Minneapolis used cross-circulation between patients and parent donors from 1954. Surgery inside the stopped heart became possible.
nodes.summary: On 6 May 1953 John Gibbon closed a hole in the heart of 18-year-old Cecelia Bavolek in Philadelphia while a heart-lung machine he had developed over twenty years carried her circulation.

nodes.title: Organ Transplantation
nodes.html: On 23 December 1954 at the Peter Bent Brigham Hospital in Boston, Joseph Murray transplanted a kidney from Ronald Herrick into his identical twin Richard, who lived for eight more years. Because the donor was a twin, no rejection occurred. The operation showed that organ transplantation could work, and Murray shared the 1990 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: On 23 December 1954 at the Peter Bent Brigham Hospital in Boston, Joseph Murray transplanted a kidney from Ronald Herrick into his identical twin Richard, who lived for eight more years.

nodes.title: Cell Organelles
nodes.html: Albert Claude, Christian de Duve and George Palade spun broken cells in the ultracentrifuge and examined the fractions by electron microscopy between about 1945 and 1955. They characterised mitochondria, lysosomes, ribosomes and the endoplasmic reticulum and traced how proteins move through the secretory pathway. The three shared the 1974 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Albert Claude, Christian de Duve and George Palade spun broken cells in the ultracentrifuge and examined the fractions by electron microscopy between about 1945 and 1955.

nodes.title: Malaria Eradication

progress.what: The Global Malaria Eradication Programme, launched in 1955 on DDT house spraying, was abandoned after mosquito and parasite resistance and funding gaps. It had cleared malaria from Europe, North America and much of the Caribbean, but was never attempted across most of tropical Africa.
progress.html: The Global Malaria Eradication Programme, launched in 1955 on DDT house spraying, was abandoned after mosquito and parasite resistance and funding gaps. It had cleared malaria from Europe, North America and much of the Caribbean, but was never attempted across most of tropical Africa.

progress.what: On 6 October 2021 the WHO recommended RTS,S/AS01 for broad use in children in areas of moderate to high transmission, the first vaccine ever recommended against a human parasite.
progress.html: On 6 October 2021 the WHO recommended RTS,S/AS01 for broad use in children in areas of moderate to high transmission, the first vaccine ever recommended against a human parasite.

progress.what: A second and cheaper vaccine, R21/Matrix-M, was recommended on 2 October 2023, with trial efficacy of 75% in children aged 5 to 17 months at sites with seasonal transmission.
progress.html: A second and cheaper vaccine, R21/Matrix-M, was recommended on 2 October 2023, with trial efficacy of 75% in children aged 5 to 17 months at sites with seasonal transmission.

progress.what: The World Malaria Report of 4 December 2025 estimated 282 million cases and 610,000 deaths in 2024, about 9 million more cases than the year before, with artemisinin partial resistance confirmed or suspected in at least eight African countries. 47 countries and one territory are certified malaria-free.
progress.html: The World Malaria Report of 4 December 2025 estimated 282 million cases and 610,000 deaths in 2024, about 9 million more cases than the year before, with artemisinin partial resistance confirmed or suspected in at least eight African countries. 47 countries and one territory are certified malaria-free.

nodes.html: The WHO launched a global malaria eradication programme in 1955 and gave it up in 1969. Malaria still caused an estimated 282 million cases and 610,000 deaths in 2024, most of them children, and the parasite is becoming partly resistant to artemisinin in Africa. Eradication means certified zero indigenous transmission worldwide, as was achieved for smallpox in 1980.
nodes.summary: The WHO launched a global malaria eradication programme in 1955 and gave it up in 1969.

nodes.title: Polio Vaccine
nodes.html: Jonas Salk’s inactivated poliovirus vaccine was declared safe and effective on 12 April 1955 after a field trial of about 1.8 million American children. Oral live vaccines, tested first by Hilary Koprowski and licensed in Albert Sabin’s form in 1961, followed. Together they drove polio from nearly the whole world.
nodes.summary: Jonas Salk’s inactivated poliovirus vaccine was declared safe and effective on 12 April 1955 after a field trial of about 1.8 million American children.

nodes.title: Protein Phosphorylation
nodes.html: Edmond Fischer and Edwin Krebs showed in 1955 that the enzyme glycogen phosphorylase is switched from an inactive to an active form by the addition of a phosphate group, and later that this is controlled by a kinase responding to hormones. Reversible phosphorylation became the main way cells regulate proteins and relay signals, and they won the 1992 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Edmond Fischer and Edwin Krebs showed in 1955 that the enzyme glycogen phosphorylase is switched from an inactive to an active form by the addition of a phosphate group, and later that this is controlled by a kinase responding to hormones.

nodes.title: Clonal Selection Theory
nodes.html: Frank Macfarlane Burnet, building on ideas of Niels Jerne and David Talmage, proposed in 1957 that each lymphocyte carries receptors for one antigen and that exposure selects and multiplies the cells that fit. The theory explained antibody diversity, immune memory and tolerance, and organised modern immunology.
nodes.summary: Frank Macfarlane Burnet, building on ideas of Niels Jerne and David Talmage, proposed in 1957 that each lymphocyte carries receptors for one antigen and that exposure selects and multiplies the cells that fit.

nodes.title: Memory Systems and H.M.
nodes.html: After William Scoville removed the medial temporal lobes of Henry Molaison in 1953 to treat his epilepsy, Brenda Milner showed in 1957 that he could no longer form new memories of events, though he could still learn new motor skills. The case showed that the brain has separate memory systems and that the hippocampus is central to making lasting memories.
nodes.summary: After William Scoville removed the medial temporal lobes of Henry Molaison in 1953 to treat his epilepsy, Brenda Milner showed in 1957 that he could no longer form new memories of events, though he could still learn new motor skills.

nodes.title: Dopamine and Parkinson’s
nodes.html: Arvid Carlsson showed in 1957-58 that dopamine is a neurotransmitter in its own right, found mainly in the basal ganglia. Oleh Hornykiewicz found in 1960 that it is depleted in the brains of people with Parkinson’s disease, and L-DOPA, which the brain converts to dopamine, then relieved their rigidity and slowness. Carlsson shared the 2000 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Arvid Carlsson showed in 1957-58 that dopamine is a neurotransmitter in its own right, found mainly in the basal ganglia.

nodes.title: Protein Structure
nodes.html: The first atomic models of proteins, myoglobin (1958) and haemoglobin (1959), each took years of crystallography. Anfinsen then showed that a protein’s sequence determines its shape.
nodes.summary: The first atomic models of proteins, myoglobin (1958) and haemoglobin (1959), each took years of crystallography.

nodes.title: Horizontal Gene Transfer
nodes.html: Japanese researchers including Tomoichiro Akiba and Kunitaro Ochiai reported in 1959 and 1960 that resistance to several antibiotics passed together from one species of gut bacteria to another, carried on transferable plasmids. Bacteria exchange genes sideways as well as by descent, which explains how antibiotic resistance spreads so quickly.
nodes.summary: Japanese researchers including Tomoichiro Akiba and Kunitaro Ochiai reported in 1959 and 1960 that resistance to several antibiotics passed together from one species of gut bacteria to another, carried on transferable plasmids.

nodes.title: Receptive Fields in Visual Cortex
nodes.html: David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel recorded from single neurons in cat visual cortex from 1959 and found that cells respond to bars of light at a particular orientation, with simple cells feeding complex ones in stages. Their hierarchy of feature detectors inspired convolutional neural networks, and they shared the 1981 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel recorded from single neurons in cat visual cortex from 1959 and found that cells respond to bars of light at a particular orientation, with simple cells feeding complex ones in stages.

nodes.title: Chemiosmotic Theory
nodes.html: Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 that respiration pumps protons across a membrane and that the resulting gradient drives the making of ATP. Biochemists had been searching for a high-energy chemical intermediate, and his theory met strong resistance before experiments confirmed it. He won the 1978 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 that respiration pumps protons across a membrane and that the resulting gradient drives the making of ATP.

nodes.title: Efficient Coding Hypothesis
nodes.html: Horace Barlow proposed in 1961 that sensory neurons are adapted to recode their input to remove redundancy, so that the brain represents the natural world with few spikes. The hypothesis connected neuroscience to information theory and still predicts the shape of receptive fields in vision and hearing.
nodes.summary: Horace Barlow proposed in 1961 that sensory neurons are adapted to recode their input to remove redundancy, so that the brain represents the natural world with few spikes.

nodes.title: Genetic Code
nodes.html: Three-letter codons map DNA to amino acids. Nirenberg and Matthaei read the first word, UUU = phenylalanine (1961), and the full code was known by 1966.
nodes.summary: Three-letter codons map DNA to amino acids.

nodes.title: Green Revolution
nodes.html: Plant breeders led by Norman Borlaug in Mexico, with M. S. Swaminathan and others in India, developed short-strawed wheat and rice that gave high yields with fertiliser and irrigation. Adopted across Mexico, India, Pakistan and the Philippines in the 1960s, they roughly doubled cereal yields in much of Asia and Latin America. Borlaug won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize.
nodes.summary: Plant breeders led by Norman Borlaug in Mexico, with M.

nodes.title: Stem Cells
nodes.html: James Till and Ernest McCulloch injected bone marrow cells into irradiated mice in 1961 and counted colonies of blood cells that grew in the spleen. Each colony came from a single cell that could both renew itself and give rise to several kinds of blood cell, which demonstrated the existence of stem cells.
nodes.summary: James Till and Ernest McCulloch injected bone marrow cells into irradiated mice in 1961 and counted colonies of blood cells that grew in the spleen.

nodes.title: Gene Regulation and the Operon
nodes.html: François Jacob and Jacques Monod proposed in 1961 that genes are switched on and off by repressor proteins that bind DNA near them, using the lac operon of E. coli, which makes lactose-digesting enzymes only when lactose is present. It introduced gene regulation and the idea of messenger RNA, and they shared the 1965 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: François Jacob and Jacques Monod proposed in 1961 that genes are switched on and off by repressor proteins that bind DNA near them, using the lac operon of E.

nodes.title: The Paradox of the Plankton

progress.what: Showed that competition for three or more resources can drive species abundances into oscillations and chaos, letting many species coexist on a handful of resources.
progress.html: Showed that competition for three or more resources can drive species abundances into oscillations and chaos, letting many species coexist on a handful of resources.

progress.what: Two Baltic Sea picocyanobacteria, one red and one blue-green, coexisted stably in competition experiments by using different parts of the light spectrum.
progress.html: Two Baltic Sea picocyanobacteria, one red and one blue-green, coexisted stably in competition experiments by using different parts of the light spectrum.

progress.what: A Baltic Sea plankton food web kept under constant laboratory conditions for more than 2,300 days fluctuated chaotically, with positive Lyapunov exponents and a predictability horizon of 15 to 30 days.
progress.html: A Baltic Sea plankton food web kept under constant laboratory conditions for more than 2,300 days fluctuated chaotically, with positive Lyapunov exponents and a predictability horizon of 15 to 30 days.

progress.what: Metatranscriptomes from the Sargasso Sea showed heterotrophic bacteria, eukaryotic phytoplankton and cyanobacteria expressing phosphorus-uptake genes in the morning, day and dusk respectively: temporal niche partitioning in the open ocean.
progress.html: Metatranscriptomes from the Sargasso Sea showed heterotrophic bacteria, eukaryotic phytoplankton and cyanobacteria expressing phosphorus-uptake genes in the morning, day and dusk respectively: temporal niche partitioning in the open ocean.

nodes.html: G. Evelyn Hutchinson asked in 1961 how dozens of phytoplankton species coexist in well-mixed water while competing for a few nutrients and light, when competition theory allows no more species at equilibrium than limiting resources. Chaos, fluctuating environments, grazing, viruses and niche partitioning each suffice in models. Solving it means measuring which of these actually maintains the diversity of a real community, and by how much.
nodes.summary: G.

nodes.title: The Molecular Clock
nodes.html: Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling compared haemoglobins of different species and found in 1962 that amino acid differences grow roughly in step with time since divergence. Molecules could therefore date evolutionary branch points, and the molecular clock became a main tool for reconstructing the history of life.
nodes.summary: Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling compared haemoglobins of different species and found in 1962 that amino acid differences grow roughly in step with time since divergence.

nodes.title: Silent Spring
nodes.html: Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring (1962) documented how DDT and other pesticides moved up food chains, thinned the eggshells of raptors and poisoned wildlife. The book drew public attention to the ecological side effects of chemicals, helped lead to the US ban on DDT in 1972, and is widely credited with launching the environmental movement.
nodes.summary: Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring (1962) documented how DDT and other pesticides moved up food chains, thinned the eggshells of raptors and poisoned wildlife.

nodes.title: Kin Selection
nodes.html: W. D. Hamilton showed in 1964 that a gene for helping can spread if the cost to the helper is less than the benefit to the recipient weighted by relatedness (rb > c). The rule explains sterile worker insects, alarm calls and other altruism toward relatives, and gave evolutionary biology the idea of inclusive fitness.
nodes.summary: W.

nodes.title: Allosteric Regulation
nodes.html: Jacques Monod, Jeffries Wyman and Jean-Pierre Changeux proposed in 1965 that a protein built of subunits can flip between two shapes and that binding of a molecule at one site shifts the balance, changing activity at another site. The model explains haemoglobin and the feedback control of many enzymes and is a basis of drug design.
nodes.summary: Jacques Monod, Jeffries Wyman and Jean-Pierre Changeux proposed in 1965 that a protein built of subunits can flip between two shapes and that binding of a molecule at one site shifts the balance, changing activity at another site.

nodes.title: Bradford Hill Criteria
nodes.html: In a 1965 address Austin Bradford Hill listed nine considerations for judging whether an association between a factor and a disease is causal: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment and analogy. They remain a standard guide for epidemiologists weighing evidence.
nodes.summary: In a 1965 address Austin Bradford Hill listed nine considerations for judging whether an association between a factor and a disease is causal: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment and analogy.

nodes.title: Endosymbiotic Theory
nodes.html: Lynn Margulis (then Lynn Sagan) argued in 1967 that mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by an ancestral cell and stayed. The idea was rejected for about a decade, then confirmed when the organelles’ own DNA and ribosomes were found to resemble those of bacteria.
nodes.summary: Lynn Margulis (then Lynn Sagan) argued in 1967 that mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by an ancestral cell and stayed.

nodes.title: Theory of Island Biogeography
nodes.html: Robert MacArthur and E. O. Wilson proposed in 1967 that the number of species on an island settles at a balance between immigration of new species and extinction of those present, which depends on the island’s size and distance from the mainland. The theory shaped conservation biology and the design of nature reserves.
nodes.summary: Robert MacArthur and E.

nodes.title: Why This Genetic Code?

progress.what: Weighting mistranslation and transition bias realistically, only about one in a million random alternative codes limits the damage from errors better than the standard code.
progress.html: Weighting mistranslation and transition bias realistically, only about one in a million random alternative codes limits the damage from errors better than the standard code.

progress.what: Simulated codon-series swaps put the standard code about half way from a random code to the top of its local fitness peak, so error minimisation is at best partial and the landscape is rugged.
progress.html: Simulated codon-series swaps put the standard code about half way from a random code to the top of its local fitness peak, so error minimisation is at best partial and the landscape is rugged.

progress.what: Syn61, an E. coli with a four-megabase synthetic genome, replaced all 18,214 occurrences of two sense codons and a stop codon, showing that the code’s redundancy can be removed in a living cell.
progress.html: Syn61, an E. coli with a four-megabase synthetic genome, replaced all 18,214 occurrences of two sense codons and a stop codon, showing that the code’s redundancy can be removed in a living cell.

progress.what: Syn57 replaced every known occurrence of six sense codons and a stop codon, about 100,000 in all, leaving an E. coli that uses 55 codons for the 20 amino acids.
progress.html: Syn57 replaced every known occurrence of six sense codons and a stop codon, about 100,000 in all, leaving an E. coli that uses 55 codons for the 20 amino acids.

nodes.html: The standard genetic code assigns 64 codons to 20 amino acids, and it limits the damage from mutation and mistranslation better than all but about one random alternative in a million (Freeland and Hurst, 1998). Crick called it a frozen accident in 1968. Solving it means showing which of selection, coevolution with amino acid biosynthesis and direct chemical affinity shaped it, and in what order it was built.
nodes.summary: The standard genetic code assigns 64 codons to 20 amino acids, and it limits the damage from mutation and mistranslation better than all but about one random alternative in a million (Freeland and Hurst, 1998).

nodes.title: Neutral Theory of Evolution
nodes.html: Motoo Kimura argued in 1968, and Jack King and Thomas Jukes in 1969, that most molecular changes between species are neither helped nor hindered by selection and spread by chance drift. The neutral theory gave molecular evolution a null model and an explanation for the steady rate of the molecular clock.
nodes.summary: Motoo Kimura argued in 1968, and Jack King and Thomas Jukes in 1969, that most molecular changes between species are neither helped nor hindered by selection and spread by chance drift.

nodes.title: Oral Rehydration Therapy
nodes.html: Glucose in a salt solution makes the gut absorb sodium and water even during cholera. Robert Cash, David Nalin and colleagues showed this in Dhaka in 1968, and Dilip Mahalanabis used it widely among refugees in 1971. Oral rehydration therapy has saved tens of millions of lives, and The Lancet called it potentially the most important medical advance of the 20th century.
nodes.summary: Glucose in a salt solution makes the gut absorb sodium and water even during cholera.

nodes.title: Keystone Species
nodes.html: Robert Paine removed the predatory starfish Pisaster from a rocky shore in Washington state, and the community of 15 species collapsed to 8 as mussels took over the space. He called such predators keystone species in 1969, a concept central to conservation and to understanding food-web structure.
nodes.summary: Robert Paine removed the predatory starfish Pisaster from a rocky shore in Washington state, and the community of 15 species collapsed to 8 as mussels took over the space.

nodes.title: Metapopulation Theory
nodes.html: Richard Levins introduced the metapopulation in 1969, a population of local populations living in habitat patches, where a species persists because new colonisations balance local extinctions. The idea changed how ecologists think about fragmented habitats and underlies much conservation planning.
nodes.summary: Richard Levins introduced the metapopulation in 1969, a population of local populations living in habitat patches, where a species persists because new colonisations balance local extinctions.

nodes.title: Morphogen Gradients
nodes.html: Lewis Wolpert proposed in 1969 that cells in a developing tissue learn their position from the concentration of a signalling molecule that spreads from a source, and choose a fate according to thresholds, the French flag model. Gradients of Bicoid and other morphogens later confirmed it in fly embryos.
nodes.summary: Lewis Wolpert proposed in 1969 that cells in a developing tissue learn their position from the concentration of a signalling molecule that spreads from a source, and choose a fate according to thresholds, the French flag model.

nodes.title: Restriction Enzymes
nodes.html: Werner Arber described bacterial enzymes that cut invading DNA, and in 1970 Hamilton Smith isolated one, HindII, that cuts DNA at a fixed sequence. Daniel Nathans used such enzymes to map the SV40 virus genome. Restriction enzymes became the scissors of recombinant DNA, and the three shared the 1978 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Werner Arber described bacterial enzymes that cut invading DNA, and in 1970 Hamilton Smith isolated one, HindII, that cuts DNA at a fixed sequence.

nodes.title: Reverse Transcriptase
nodes.html: Howard Temin with Satoshi Mizutani, and David Baltimore independently, found in 1970 that RNA tumour viruses carry an enzyme that copies RNA into DNA. The discovery showed that genetic information can flow from RNA back to DNA, gave molecular biology the cDNA technique and made possible drugs against HIV. Temin and Baltimore shared the 1975 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Howard Temin with Satoshi Mizutani, and David Baltimore independently, found in 1970 that RNA tumour viruses carry an enzyme that copies RNA into DNA.

nodes.title: Sequence Alignment
nodes.html: Saul Needleman and Christian Wunsch published in 1970 a dynamic programming method for finding the best global alignment of two protein sequences, and Temple Smith and Michael Waterman added local alignment in 1981. Comparing sequences is the basis of bioinformatics, used to find related genes and infer function and ancestry.
nodes.summary: Saul Needleman and Christian Wunsch published in 1970 a dynamic programming method for finding the best global alignment of two protein sequences, and Temple Smith and Michael Waterman added local alignment in 1981.

nodes.title: Second Messengers and G Proteins
nodes.html: Earl Sutherland found in 1957 that cyclic AMP carries the message of hormones such as adrenaline inside a cell, the first second messenger. In 1971 Martin Rodbell showed that a GTP-binding step couples the hormone receptor to the enzyme making it, and Alfred Gilman purified the G protein involved. G proteins mediate signalling for many receptors and are targeted by about a third of drugs.
nodes.summary: Earl Sutherland found in 1957 that cyclic AMP carries the message of hormones such as adrenaline inside a cell, the first second messenger.

nodes.title: Place and Grid Cells
nodes.html: John O’Keefe and Jonathan Dostrovsky found in 1971 that some neurons in the rat hippocampus fire only when the animal is in one particular place. In 2005 May-Britt and Edvard Moser found grid cells in the neighbouring entorhinal cortex, firing in a hexagonal lattice. Together these cells form the brain’s map of space, and O’Keefe and the Mosers shared the 2014 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: John O’Keefe and Jonathan Dostrovsky found in 1971 that some neurons in the rat hippocampus fire only when the animal is in one particular place.

nodes.title: Programmed Cell Death
nodes.html: John Kerr, Andrew Wyllie and Alastair Currie described in 1972 a distinct, orderly form of cell death that they named apoptosis. Robert Horvitz later identified the genes that carry it out in the nematode worm. Cells are built to die on cue during development and in defence against disease, and failure of apoptosis contributes to cancer.
nodes.summary: John Kerr, Andrew Wyllie and Alastair Currie described in 1972 a distinct, orderly form of cell death that they named apoptosis.

nodes.title: The Diversity–Stability Debate

progress.what: In a decade-long grassland experiment that set the number of plant species directly, plots with more species had more stable year-to-year productivity.
progress.html: In a decade-long grassland experiment that set the number of plant species directly, plots with more species had more stable year-to-year productivity.

progress.what: Extended May’s criterion to structured networks: predator–prey interactions stabilize large communities, while mutualistic and competitive interactions destabilize them.
progress.html: Extended May’s criterion to structured networks: predator–prey interactions stabilize large communities, while mutualistic and competitive interactions destabilize them.

progress.what: Showed that if population growth scales sublinearly with biomass, competition no longer leads to exclusion and stability increases with diversity.
progress.html: Showed that if population growth scales sublinearly with biomass, competition no longer leads to exclusion and stability increases with diversity.

progress.what: In the generalized Lotka–Volterra model, spatial structure and environmental noise together let arbitrarily many strongly competing species coexist stably; neither alone is enough.
progress.html: In the generalized Lotka–Volterra model, spatial structure and environmental noise together let arbitrarily many strongly competing species coexist stably; neither alone is enough.

nodes.html: Robert May proved in 1972 that a large community with random interactions is almost surely unstable once its richness, connectance and interaction strength pass a threshold, against the older view that diversity begets stability. Field experiments find diverse communities more stable. Solving it means identifying the features of real interaction networks that reconcile the two and confirming them on measured communities.
nodes.summary: Robert May proved in 1972 that a large community with random interactions is almost surely unstable once its richness, connectance and interaction strength pass a threshold, against the older view that diversity begets stability.

nodes.title: Fluid Mosaic Membrane
nodes.html: S. J. Singer and Garth Nicolson proposed in 1972 that a cell membrane is a fluid sheet of lipid in which proteins float and move sideways. The model displaced the older view of a fixed protein-lipid sandwich and explained how membrane proteins can cluster, signal and be recycled.
nodes.summary: S.

nodes.title: Punctuated Equilibria
nodes.html: Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould argued in 1972 that the fossil record shows species staying largely unchanged for long periods, interrupted by brief bursts of change at the time new species form. The proposal started a long debate on the tempo of evolution that reshaped palaeobiology.
nodes.summary: Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould argued in 1972 that the fossil record shows species staying largely unchanged for long periods, interrupted by brief bursts of change at the time new species form.

nodes.title: Evolutionarily Stable Strategies
nodes.html: John Maynard Smith and George Price defined in 1973 an evolutionarily stable strategy as one that, once common in a population, cannot be displaced by any rare alternative. Applying game theory to animal conflict, they showed that ritualised fighting can be stable, and the method became a standard tool for analysing behaviour.
nodes.summary: John Maynard Smith and George Price defined in 1973 an evolutionarily stable strategy as one that, once common in a population, cannot be displaced by any rare alternative.

nodes.title: Long-Term Potentiation
nodes.html: Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo reported in 1973 that a brief high-frequency burst of stimulation strengthens synapses in the rabbit hippocampus for hours or weeks. Long-term potentiation is the best-studied cellular model of learning and memory and a physical realisation of Hebb’s rule.
nodes.summary: Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo reported in 1973 that a brief high-frequency burst of stimulation strengthens synapses in the rabbit hippocampus for hours or weeks.

nodes.title: Recombinant DNA
nodes.html: Cut DNA with restriction enzymes, splice it into bacteria, and they copy it (1973). Genetic engineering followed, and bacteria were making human insulin by 1978.
nodes.summary: Cut DNA with restriction enzymes, splice it into bacteria, and they copy it (1973).

nodes.title: Lewontin’s Paradox of Variation

progress.what: Across 40 obligately sexual species, selection at linked sites removed more neutral diversity in species with larger populations, offered as a possible resolution.
progress.html: Across 40 obligately sexual species, selection at linked sites removed more neutral diversity in species with larger populations, offered as a possible resolution.

progress.what: Combining diversity estimates for 172 animal taxa with new census-size estimates, showed that even strong and abundant linked selection is unlikely to compress diversity this much.
progress.html: Combining diversity estimates for 172 animal taxa with new census-size estimates, showed that even strong and abundant linked selection is unlikely to compress diversity this much.

progress.what: Argued that selection alone is insufficient and that many species may be far below the equilibrium diversity their current census sizes imply, because of past changes in population size.
progress.html: Argued that selection alone is insufficient and that many species may be far below the equilibrium diversity their current census sizes imply, because of past changes in population size.

progress.what: In 98 plant species, population-size proxies scaled about 3 to over 20 times faster with k-mer-based diversity than with SNP-based nucleotide diversity, suggesting that reference-based SNP calling misses part of the variation.
progress.html: In 98 plant species, population-size proxies scaled about 3 to over 20 times faster with k-mer-based diversity than with SNP-based nucleotide diversity, suggesting that reference-based SNP calling misses part of the variation.

nodes.html: Neutral theory says genetic diversity should grow in proportion to population size, yet across animals diversity spans only two to three orders of magnitude while census sizes span many more. Richard Lewontin pointed out the mismatch in 1974. Solving it means a quantitative model of demography, linked selection and measurement bias that predicts each species’ diversity from its census size on taxa it was not fitted to.
nodes.summary: Neutral theory says genetic diversity should grow in proportion to population size, yet across animals diversity spans only two to three orders of magnitude while census sizes span many more.

nodes.title: MHC Restriction
nodes.html: Rolf Zinkernagel and Peter Doherty showed in 1974 that killer T cells recognise virus-infected cells only when the viral fragment is presented on the body’s own MHC molecules. The same molecules provoke rejection of transplants. The discovery explained how T cells distinguish self from non-self, and won the 1996 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Rolf Zinkernagel and Peter Doherty showed in 1974 that killer T cells recognise virus-infected cells only when the viral fragment is presented on the body’s own MHC molecules.

nodes.title: The Nucleosome
nodes.html: Roger Kornberg proposed in 1974, from X-ray and biochemical data, that chromatin is built from repeating units of about 200 base pairs of DNA wound around a core of eight histones. Ada and Donald Olins saw such beads on a string with the electron microscope the same year. How tightly DNA is wrapped, and its chemical marks, controls which genes can be read.
nodes.summary: Roger Kornberg proposed in 1974, from X-ray and biochemical data, that chromatin is built from repeating units of about 200 base pairs of DNA wound around a core of eight histones.

nodes.title: Asilomar and Biosafety
nodes.html: In July 1974 Paul Berg and other leading molecular biologists called for a pause in certain recombinant DNA experiments, and in February 1975 about 140 scientists, lawyers and doctors met at Asilomar, California, to agree safeguards. The meeting led to the NIH biosafety guidelines and is often cited as a model of scientists regulating their own research.
nodes.summary: In July 1974 Paul Berg and other leading molecular biologists called for a pause in certain recombinant DNA experiments, and in February 1975 about 140 scientists, lawyers and doctors met at Asilomar, California, to agree safeguards.

nodes.title: Epigenetic Inheritance
nodes.html: Robin Holliday and John Pugh, and independently Arthur Riggs, proposed in 1975 that methylation of cytosine in DNA can be copied when DNA replicates, so that a pattern of gene silencing is inherited through cell division. The idea of heritable chemical marks beyond the DNA sequence founded the modern study of epigenetics.
nodes.summary: Robin Holliday and John Pugh, and independently Arthur Riggs, proposed in 1975 that methylation of cytosine in DNA can be copied when DNA replicates, so that a pattern of gene silencing is inherited through cell division.

nodes.title: Monoclonal Antibodies
nodes.html: Georges Köhler and César Milstein fused antibody-making B cells with myeloma tumour cells in 1975 to create hybridomas, immortal lines that each make one chosen antibody in unlimited amounts. Monoclonal antibodies became standard reagents and diagnostics and the basis of many of today’s best-selling drugs. They shared the 1984 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Georges Köhler and César Milstein fused antibody-making B cells with myeloma tumour cells in 1975 to create hybridomas, immortal lines that each make one chosen antibody in unlimited amounts.

nodes.title: Patch Clamp
nodes.html: Erwin Neher and Bert Sakmann pressed a fine glass pipette against a cell membrane and recorded the tiny current through a single ion channel in 1976. Improved sealing in 1980-81 gave the gigaohm seal and whole-cell recording. Patch clamping made individual channels measurable and won them the 1991 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Erwin Neher and Bert Sakmann pressed a fine glass pipette against a cell membrane and recorded the tiny current through a single ion channel in 1976.

nodes.title: Statins
nodes.html: Akira Endo isolated mevastatin, a fungal inhibitor of cholesterol synthesis, from the mould Penicillium citrinum in 1976. Merck’s lovastatin, approved in 1987, was the first marketed statin. Trials showed that statins cut heart attacks and strokes, and they became one of the most prescribed classes of medicine in the world.
nodes.summary: Akira Endo isolated mevastatin, a fungal inhibitor of cholesterol synthesis, from the mould Penicillium citrinum in 1976.

nodes.title: V(D)J Recombination
nodes.html: Susumu Tonegawa showed in 1976 that the DNA encoding antibodies is rearranged as B cells develop: gene segments are cut out and joined, so the antibody genes of a mature lymphocyte differ from those in other cells. Combining a few hundred segments produces an enormous number of different antibodies. He won the 1987 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Susumu Tonegawa showed in 1976 that the DNA encoding antibodies is rearranged as B cells develop: gene segments are cut out and joined, so the antibody genes of a mature lymphocyte differ from those in other cells.

nodes.title: DNA Sequencing
nodes.html: Sanger’s chain-termination method (1977) read DNA one letter at a time. Today’s machines read a whole human genome in about a day.
nodes.summary: Sanger’s chain-termination method (1977) read DNA one letter at a time.

nodes.title: Molecular Dynamics of Proteins
nodes.html: J. Andrew McCammon, Bruce Gelin and Martin Karplus simulated the motions of a small protein, bovine pancreatic trypsin inhibitor, for 9.2 picoseconds on a computer in 1977. It showed that proteins constantly flex and fluctuate, and began the computational study of biomolecules honoured by the 2013 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (Karplus, Michael Levitt and Arieh Warshel).
nodes.summary: J.

nodes.title: Peto’s Paradox

progress.what: Estimated elephant cancer mortality at 4.81%, against 11 to 25% for humans, and found at least 20 copies of TP53 in African elephants, whose cells die more readily after DNA damage.
progress.html: Estimated elephant cancer mortality at 4.81%, against 11 to 25% for humans, and found at least 20 copies of TP53 in African elephants, whose cells die more readily after DNA damage.

progress.what: Zoo records of 110,148 adult mammals from 191 species showed cancer mortality largely independent of body mass and adult life expectancy, with carnivores at highest risk.
progress.html: Zoo records of 110,148 adult mammals from 191 species showed cancer mortality largely independent of body mass and adult life expectancy, with carnivores at highest risk.

progress.what: Across amphibians, birds, mammals and squamate reptiles, larger species had somewhat higher cancer prevalence, which the authors read as no evidence for the paradox; critics noted the rise is far smaller than cell numbers would predict.
progress.html: Across amphibians, birds, mammals and squamate reptiles, larger species had somewhat higher cancer prevalence, which the authors read as no evidence for the paradox; critics noted the rise is far smaller than cell numbers would predict.

progress.what: Bowhead whale cells repaired DNA double-strand breaks more accurately and had lower mutation rates than cells of other mammals; the protein CIRBP, abundant in whale cells, boosted repair in human cells.
progress.html: Bowhead whale cells repaired DNA double-strand breaks more accurately and had lower mutation rates than cells of other mammals; the protein CIRBP, abundant in whale cells, boosted repair in human cells.

nodes.html: A whale has vastly more cells than a mouse and lives far longer, yet big, long-lived species do not get proportionally more cancer, as Richard Peto noted in 1977. Zoo studies from 2022 to 2025 disagree on whether risk rises with body mass at all, and a 2025 Bayesian reanalysis found the samples too small to decide. Solving it means settling the scaling and identifying the defences, such as extra TP53 copies in elephants, that explain it.
nodes.summary: A whale has vastly more cells than a mouse and lives far longer, yet big, long-lived species do not get proportionally more cancer, as Richard Peto noted in 1977.

nodes.title: Split Genes and RNA Splicing
nodes.html: Richard Roberts, Phillip Sharp and their colleagues found in 1977 that adenovirus genes are interrupted by stretches of DNA that are transcribed but then cut out of the messenger RNA. Genes in complex organisms are mosaics of exons and introns, and alternative splicing lets one gene make many proteins. They shared the 1993 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Richard Roberts, Phillip Sharp and their colleagues found in 1977 that adenovirus genes are interrupted by stretches of DNA that are transcribed but then cut out of the messenger RNA.

nodes.title: Three Domains of Life
nodes.html: Carl Woese and George Fox compared ribosomal RNA sequences and announced in 1977 that the prokaryotes include two groups as different from each other as either is from eukaryotes. The archaea were recognised as a third domain of life alongside bacteria and eukaryotes, and Woese formalised the three domains in 1990.
nodes.summary: Carl Woese and George Fox compared ribosomal RNA sequences and announced in 1977 that the prokaryotes include two groups as different from each other as either is from eukaryotes.

nodes.title: In Vitro Fertilisation
nodes.html: Louise Brown, the first baby conceived by in vitro fertilisation, was born in Oldham on 25 July 1978 after years of work by the physiologist Robert Edwards, the gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe and the nurse and embryologist Jean Purdy. More than twelve million people have since been born through IVF. Edwards received the 2010 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Louise Brown, the first baby conceived by in vitro fertilisation, was born in Oldham on 25 July 1978 after years of work by the physiologist Robert Edwards, the gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe and the nurse and embryologist Jean Purdy.

nodes.title: Transplant Immunosuppression
nodes.html: Jean-François Borel at Sandoz found in 1972 that ciclosporin, made by a fungus from Norwegian soil, suppresses the immune system, and Roy Calne at Cambridge used it in transplant patients from 1978. It acts selectively on T cells, raised one-year survival of kidney grafts from about 50% to above 80%, and made heart, liver and lung transplants practical.
nodes.summary: Jean-François Borel at Sandoz found in 1972 that ciclosporin, made by a fungus from Norwegian soil, suppresses the immune system, and Roy Calne at Cambridge used it in transplant patients from 1978.

nodes.title: Is There a Limit to Human Lifespan?

progress.what: Gains in survival fall away after age 100 and the age of the world’s oldest person has not risen since the 1990s, which the authors read as evidence of a fixed ceiling.
progress.html: Gains in survival fall away after age 100 and the age of the world’s oldest person has not risen since the 1990s, which the authors read as evidence of a fixed ceiling.

progress.what: Hazard rates for all 3,836 Italians who reached 105 between 2009 and 2015 were essentially constant beyond that age, the clearest evidence yet of a mortality plateau in humans.
progress.html: Hazard rates for all 3,836 Italians who reached 105 between 2009 and 2015 were essentially constant beyond that age, the clearest evidence yet of a mortality plateau in humans.

progress.what: Extreme-value analysis of Italian and French semi-supercentenarians fits a constant force of mortality beyond 108 and makes an upper bound below 130 years implausible.
progress.html: Extreme-value analysis of Italian and French semi-supercentenarians fits a constant force of mortality beyond 108 and makes an upper bound below 130 years implausible.

progress.what: Across the ten longest-lived populations, improvements in life expectancy have slowed since 1990, and survival to 100 is unlikely to exceed 15% for women and 5% for men.
progress.html: Across the ten longest-lived populations, improvements in life expectancy have slowed since 1990, and survival to 100 is unlikely to exceed 15% for women and 5% for men.

nodes.html: James Fries argued in 1980 that human life span is fixed, with an ideal average near 85 years. Death rates appear to stop rising after about 108, which would mean no detectable ceiling. Solving it means settling, on validated extreme-age records, whether the force of mortality plateaus and whether a finite bound exists. Jeanne Calment’s 122 years, reached in 1997, is still the record.
nodes.summary: James Fries argued in 1980 that human life span is fixed, with an ideal average near 85 years.

nodes.title: Smallpox Eradication
nodes.html: The World Health Organization’s intensified campaign from 1967, led by Donald Henderson and built on a proposal by Viktor Zhdanov, used surveillance and ring vaccination of contacts to end transmission. The last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977, and the WHO declared smallpox eradicated on 8 May 1980, the first human disease to be eradicated.
nodes.summary: The World Health Organization’s intensified campaign from 1967, led by Donald Henderson and built on a proposal by Viktor Zhdanov, used surveillance and ring vaccination of contacts to end transmission.

nodes.title: DNA Synthesis
nodes.html: Marvin Caruthers and Serge Beaucage developed phosphoramidite chemistry in 1981, which lets machines build short DNA strands one base at a time, quickly and reliably. Har Gobind Khorana had made the first synthetic gene in 1970. Automated oligonucleotide synthesis supplies primers for PCR and sequencing and underlies gene synthesis.
nodes.summary: Marvin Caruthers and Serge Beaucage developed phosphoramidite chemistry in 1981, which lets machines build short DNA strands one base at a time, quickly and reliably.

nodes.title: Why Influenza Is Seasonal

progress.what: Twenty guinea-pig experiments at 5 to 30 degrees Celsius and 20 to 80% relative humidity showed that aerosol transmission of influenza is favoured by cold and dry air, acting mostly on the virus particle.
progress.html: Twenty guinea-pig experiments at 5 to 30 degrees Celsius and 20 to 80% relative humidity showed that aerosol transmission of influenza is favoured by cold and dry air, acting mostly on the virus particle.

progress.what: Reanalysis showed absolute rather than relative humidity is the controlling variable, explaining 50% of the variability in transmission and 90% in virus survival, against 12% and 36% for relative humidity.
progress.html: Reanalysis showed absolute rather than relative humidity is the controlling variable, explaining 50% of the variability in transmission and 90% in virus survival, against 12% and 36% for relative humidity.

progress.what: Mice housed in dry air suffered worse influenza through impaired mucociliary clearance, weaker interferon responses and poorer tissue repair, independent of viral load, so humidity acts on the host as well as the virus.
progress.html: Mice housed in dry air suffered worse influenza through impaired mucociliary clearance, weaker interferon responses and poorer tissue repair, independent of viral load, so humidity acts on the host as well as the virus.

progress.what: Across eleven years of surveillance in mainland China and Hong Kong, absolute humidity had a U-shaped relation to transmissibility but explained at most 15% of the variance in the reproduction number.
progress.html: Across eleven years of surveillance in mainland China and Hong Kong, absolute humidity had a U-shaped relation to transmissibility but explained at most 15% of the variance in the reproduction number.

nodes.html: Influenza epidemics arrive each winter in temperate countries and behave quite differently in the tropics, a pattern Hope-Simpson set out in 1981. Humidity, cold-impaired airway defences, aerosol chemistry and indoor crowding each explain part of it. A solution is a mechanistic model that predicts epidemic timing and size at temperate and tropical sites from environment and behaviour alone.
nodes.summary: Influenza epidemics arrive each winter in temperate countries and behave quite differently in the tropics, a pattern Hope-Simpson set out in 1981.

nodes.title: Phylogenetic Inference
nodes.html: Joseph Felsenstein published in 1981 an algorithm that computes the likelihood of an evolutionary tree given DNA sequences, making maximum-likelihood tree building practical, and in 1985 introduced the bootstrap to put confidence values on branches. Walter Fitch had earlier built trees by parsimony and distance methods. Statistical methods became standard in phylogenetics.
