nodes.summary: Joseph Felsenstein published in 1981 an algorithm that computes the likelihood of an evolutionary tree given DNA sequences, making maximum-likelihood tree building practical, and in 1985 introduced the bootstrap to put confidence values on branches.

nodes.title: GenBank and Sequence Databases
nodes.html: GenBank, set up by Walter Goad and colleagues at Los Alamos in 1982, was a public archive of every published DNA sequence. As journals and funders began to require deposit of sequences, it became the core of a shared international database and made biological sequence data a commons that anyone could search.
nodes.summary: GenBank, set up by Walter Goad and colleagues at Los Alamos in 1982, was a public archive of every published DNA sequence.

nodes.title: Prions
nodes.html: Stanley Prusiner proposed in 1982 that scrapie, a fatal brain disease of sheep, is caused by a misfolded protein that converts normal copies of itself and contains no nucleic acid. The idea met fierce scepticism and was later accepted, since the same mechanism explains Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and mad cow disease. Prusiner won the 1997 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Stanley Prusiner proposed in 1982 that scrapie, a fatal brain disease of sheep, is caused by a misfolded protein that converts normal copies of itself and contains no nucleic acid.

nodes.title: Recombinant Human Insulin
nodes.html: Genentech scientists, including David Goeddel, made human insulin in E. coli from a synthetic gene in 1978, and Herbert Boyer had cofounded the company. Eli Lilly’s Humulin, approved by the US FDA in October 1982, was the first licensed drug made by recombinant DNA technology and marked the start of the biotechnology drug industry.
nodes.summary: Genentech scientists, including David Goeddel, made human insulin in E.

nodes.title: Catalytic RNA
nodes.html: Thomas Cech found in 1982 that a ribosomal RNA from the ciliate Tetrahymena cuts itself out of a longer transcript with no protein help, and Sidney Altman showed in 1983 that the RNA part of RNase P is the catalyst. RNA can therefore act as an enzyme, which supports the idea that early life ran on RNA. They shared the 1989 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Thomas Cech found in 1982 that a ribosomal RNA from the ciliate Tetrahymena cuts itself out of a longer transcript with no protein help, and Sidney Altman showed in 1983 that the RNA part of RNase P is the catalyst.

nodes.title: The C. elegans Cell Lineage
nodes.html: John Sulston and colleagues traced the divisions of every cell in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans from egg to adult (1983), finding that the lineage of all 959 body cells of the hermaphrodite is the same in every animal. Some cells were found to be programmed to die, and Sulston, Robert Horvitz and Sydney Brenner shared the 2002 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: John Sulston and colleagues traced the divisions of every cell in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans from egg to adult (1983), finding that the lineage of all 959 body cells of the hermaphrodite is the same in every animal.

nodes.title: Cell Cycle Control
nodes.html: Leland Hartwell found cell-division-cycle genes in yeast in the 1970s, Paul Nurse identified the key kinase cdc2 in fission yeast, and Tim Hunt discovered in 1983 cyclin proteins that rise and are destroyed in each cycle of sea urchin eggs. Cyclin-dependent kinases drive the cell through division, and their misregulation is central to cancer. The three shared the 2001 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Leland Hartwell found cell-division-cycle genes in yeast in the 1970s, Paul Nurse identified the key kinase cdc2 in fission yeast, and Tim Hunt discovered in 1983 cyclin proteins that rise and are destroyed in each cycle of sea urchin eggs.

nodes.title: HIV Identified
nodes.html: In 1983 Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier at the Pasteur Institute isolated a retrovirus from a patient with swollen lymph nodes, and Robert Gallo’s laboratory in 1984 showed that such a virus causes AIDS. A blood test followed in 1985. Barré-Sinoussi and Montagnier shared the 2008 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: In 1983 Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier at the Pasteur Institute isolated a retrovirus from a patient with swollen lymph nodes, and Robert Gallo’s laboratory in 1984 showed that such a virus causes AIDS.

nodes.title: Hox Genes and Evo-Devo
nodes.html: Edward Lewis, Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard and Eric Wieschaus identified genes that set the body plan of the fruit fly, and in 1983-84 Walter Gehring’s group found a shared DNA motif, the homeobox, in them and in vertebrate genes. The same clusters of Hox genes lay out the head-to-tail axis in flies and in humans, joining developmental and evolutionary biology.
nodes.summary: Edward Lewis, Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard and Eric Wieschaus identified genes that set the body plan of the fruit fly, and in 1983-84 Walter Gehring’s group found a shared DNA motif, the homeobox, in them and in vertebrate genes.

nodes.title: PCR
nodes.html: Copy a stretch of DNA a billion-fold by cycling the temperature (1983). It became the photocopier of molecular biology.
nodes.summary: Copy a stretch of DNA a billion-fold by cycling the temperature (1983).

nodes.title: Ancient DNA
nodes.html: Russell Higuchi, Allan Wilson and colleagues recovered DNA from a 140-year-old museum skin of the extinct quagga in 1984, and Svante Pääbo extracted DNA from an Egyptian mummy in 1985. PCR then made the study of old DNA practical, and the field grew to whole genomes from fossils tens of thousands of years old.
nodes.summary: Russell Higuchi, Allan Wilson and colleagues recovered DNA from a 140-year-old museum skin of the extinct quagga in 1984, and Svante Pääbo extracted DNA from an Egyptian mummy in 1985.

nodes.title: DNA Fingerprinting
nodes.html: Alec Jeffreys at the University of Leicester saw on an X-ray film in September 1984 that variable repeated DNA sequences give each person a distinctive banding pattern. DNA profiling was used first in an immigration dispute and then to catch the murderer Colin Pitchfork in 1987, and it transformed forensic science and paternity testing.
nodes.summary: Alec Jeffreys at the University of Leicester saw on an X-ray film in September 1984 that variable repeated DNA sequences give each person a distinctive banding pattern.

nodes.title: Origin of the Eukaryotic Cell

progress.what: Lokiarchaeota, assembled from marine sediment metagenomes, grouped with eukaryotes and carried an expanded set of proteins previously thought to be eukaryote-specific.
progress.html: Lokiarchaeota, assembled from marine sediment metagenomes, grouped with eukaryotes and carried an expanded set of proteins previously thought to be eukaryote-specific.

progress.what: A decade of culturing produced the first Asgard archaeon in the laboratory, Prometheoarchaeum syntrophicum, an extremely slow-growing anaerobe with no organelle-like structures but long branching protrusions.
progress.html: A decade of culturing produced the first Asgard archaeon in the laboratory, Prometheoarchaeum syntrophicum, an extremely slow-growing anaerobe with no organelle-like structures but long branching protrusions.

progress.what: Placed eukaryotes as a well-nested clade inside the Asgard archaea, sister to the Hodarchaeales within Heimdallarchaeia, and inferred a mesophilic, heterotrophic ancestor for the eukaryote lineage.
progress.html: Placed eukaryotes as a well-nested clade inside the Asgard archaea, sister to the Hodarchaeales within Heimdallarchaeia, and inferred a mesophilic, heterotrophic ancestor for the eukaryote lineage.

progress.what: 223 new Asgard genomes put eukaryotes outside all sampled Heimdallarchaeia instead, blaming the earlier placement on chimeric Njordarchaeales genomes, and reconstructed the shared ancestor as an anaerobic hydrogen-dependent acetogen.
progress.html: 223 new Asgard genomes put eukaryotes outside all sampled Heimdallarchaeia instead, blaming the earlier placement on chimeric Njordarchaeales genomes, and reconstructed the shared ancestor as an anaerobic hydrogen-dependent acetogen.

nodes.html: Every eukaryote descends from one merger of an archaeal host with the bacterium that became the mitochondrion. Since Lake’s eocyte proposal of 1984 the host has been traced to the Asgard archaea, but its exact sister lineage is disputed and the order in which the nucleus, mitochondrion and endomembranes arrived is unknown. A solution is a stable placement plus a step-by-step account.
nodes.summary: Every eukaryote descends from one merger of an archaeal host with the bacterium that became the mitochondrion.

nodes.title: An HIV Vaccine

progress.what: RV144 in Thailand, with 16,402 volunteers, showed 31.2% efficacy in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. It remains the only efficacy signal from any HIV vaccine trial.
progress.html: RV144 in Thailand, with 16,402 volunteers, showed 31.2% efficacy in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. It remains the only efficacy signal from any HIV vaccine trial.

progress.what: In a phase 1 trial the germline-targeting immunogen eOD-GT8 60mer primed VRC01-class precursors of broadly neutralizing antibodies in 97% of recipients, establishing proof of concept for the priming step.
progress.html: In a phase 1 trial the germline-targeting immunogen eOD-GT8 60mer primed VRC01-class precursors of broadly neutralizing antibodies in 97% of recipients, establishing proof of concept for the priming step.

progress.what: The phase 1 trials IAVI G002 and G003 primed the same precursors with mRNA-encoded nanoparticles and showed that a different booster drives further maturation, in the United States, Rwanda and South Africa.
progress.html: The phase 1 trials IAVI G002 and G003 primed the same precursors with mRNA-encoded nanoparticles and showed that a different booster drives further maturation, in the United States, Rwanda and South Africa.

progress.what: In outbred macaques a germline-targeting protein regimen produced broadly neutralizing antibody lineages in at least half the animals, with up to 67% of the reference antibody’s breadth and serum activity in 44%.
progress.html: In outbred macaques a germline-targeting protein regimen produced broadly neutralizing antibody lineages in at least half the animals, with up to 67% of the reference antibody’s breadth and serum activity in 44%.

nodes.html: No vaccine protects against HIV, more than forty years after one was promised within two years in 1984. Only the Thai RV144 trial has ever shown efficacy, 31.2% in 2009. Solving it means a licensed vaccine with durable efficacy in people; the leading route primes the rare B cells that can mature into broadly neutralizing antibodies, which now works in macaques but has not been tested for efficacy.
nodes.summary: No vaccine protects against HIV, more than forty years after one was promised within two years in 1984.

nodes.title: Cytoskeleton and Motor Proteins
nodes.html: Ronald Vale, Thomas Reese and Michael Sheetz identified kinesin in 1985, a motor protein that walks along microtubules carrying cargo through the cell. Together with myosin and dynein, motors showed that cells contain molecular machines that move, and that the cytoskeleton is a set of tracks for transport.
nodes.summary: Ronald Vale, Thomas Reese and Michael Sheetz identified kinesin in 1985, a motor protein that walks along microtubules carrying cargo through the cell.

nodes.title: Phage Display
nodes.html: George Smith showed in 1985 that a foreign peptide can be fused to a coat protein of filamentous phage and displayed on its surface, and Greg Winter later displayed antibodies the same way. Libraries of billions of variants can be searched for those that bind a target, a method behind drugs such as adalimumab. Smith and Winter shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
nodes.summary: George Smith showed in 1985 that a foreign peptide can be fused to a coat protein of filamentous phage and displayed on its surface, and Greg Winter later displayed antibodies the same way.

nodes.title: Telomeres and Telomerase
nodes.html: Elizabeth Blackburn and Carol Greider discovered telomerase in 1984-85, an enzyme containing an RNA template that rebuilds the repeated DNA sequences capping chromosome ends, and Jack Szostak showed that the caps protect chromosomes. Telomere shortening limits how often normal cells can divide, and telomerase is active in most cancers. The three shared the 2009 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Elizabeth Blackburn and Carol Greider discovered telomerase in 1984-85, an enzyme containing an RNA template that rebuilds the repeated DNA sequences capping chromosome ends, and Jack Szostak showed that the caps protect chromosomes.

nodes.title: Connectomics
nodes.html: The full wiring diagram of the worm C. elegans, 302 neurons, was published in 1986. In 2024 the FlyWire consortium mapped an adult fruit-fly brain: about 140,000 neurons.
nodes.summary: The full wiring diagram of the worm C.

nodes.title: The RNA World
nodes.html: Walter Gilbert coined the term RNA world in 1986 for a stage of early life in which RNA both stored information and catalysed reactions. Carl Woese, Francis Crick and Leslie Orgel had proposed the idea in the 1960s, and the discovery of ribozymes made it plausible. The hypothesis frames much research on the origin of life.
nodes.summary: Walter Gilbert coined the term RNA world in 1986 for a stage of early life in which RNA both stored information and catalysed reactions.

nodes.title: Energy Landscapes of Folding
nodes.html: Joseph Bryngelson and Peter Wolynes proposed in 1987, with later work by José Onuchic and others, that a protein folds by sliding down a funnel-shaped energy landscape in which many routes lead to the native state. This resolved Levinthal’s paradox, the puzzle that a random search of all conformations would take far too long.
nodes.summary: Joseph Bryngelson and Peter Wolynes proposed in 1987, with later work by José Onuchic and others, that a protein folds by sliding down a funnel-shaped energy landscape in which many routes lead to the native state.

nodes.title: Mitochondrial Eve
nodes.html: Rebecca Cann, Mark Stoneking and Allan Wilson compared mitochondrial DNA from 147 people worldwide and reported in 1987 that all lineages trace back to one maternal ancestor who lived in Africa roughly 200,000 years ago. She was one of many women alive then, and hers is the only maternal line that survives in everyone. The result supported a recent African origin of modern humans.
nodes.summary: Rebecca Cann, Mark Stoneking and Allan Wilson compared mitochondrial DNA from 147 people worldwide and reported in 1987 that all lineages trace back to one maternal ancestor who lived in Africa roughly 200,000 years ago.

nodes.title: Gene Targeting in Mice
nodes.html: Mario Capecchi, Oliver Smithies and Martin Evans developed methods in the 1980s to replace a chosen gene in mouse embryonic stem cells by homologous recombination, and the first knockout mice were reported in 1989. Deleting a gene on purpose became the standard way to test its function, and they shared the 2007 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Mario Capecchi, Oliver Smithies and Martin Evans developed methods in the 1980s to replace a chosen gene in mouse embryonic stem cells by homologous recombination, and the first knockout mice were reported in 1989.

nodes.title: The Root of the Tree of Life

progress.what: Rooted the universal tree using elongation factors and ATPase subunits that had duplicated before the last common ancestor, so each copy roots the other. Gogarten’s group reached the same conclusion from the ATPase subunits that year.
progress.html: Rooted the universal tree using elongation factors and ATPase subunits that had duplicated before the last common ancestor, so each copy roots the other. Gogarten’s group reached the same conclusion from the ATPase subunits that year.

progress.what: Screened 286,514 protein clusters from sequenced prokaryotes and found 355 families that trace to the last universal common ancestor, portraying it as an anaerobic, hydrogen-dependent, nitrogen-fixing thermophile.
progress.html: Screened 286,514 protein clusters from sequenced prokaryotes and found 355 families that trace to the last universal common ancestor, portraying it as an anaerobic, hydrogen-dependent, nitrogen-fixing thermophile.

progress.what: Dated the last universal common ancestor to about 4.2 billion years ago and reconstructed a genome of at least 2.5 Mb encoding roughly 2,600 proteins, an acetogen already part of an ecosystem rather than alone.
progress.html: Dated the last universal common ancestor to about 4.2 billion years ago and reconstructed a genome of at least 2.5 Mb encoding roughly 2,600 proteins, an acetogen already part of an ecosystem rather than alone.

nodes.html: Where does the universal tree take root, and what did the last universal common ancestor have? Every possible outgroup sits inside the tree, so since 1989 the root has been inferred from genes that duplicated before that ancestor. A solution is a root and an ancestral gene set that survive models accounting for horizontal transfer, compositional bias and long branches.
nodes.summary: Where does the universal tree take root, and what did the last universal common ancestor have?

nodes.title: BLAST and Sequence Search
nodes.html: Stephen Altschul, Warren Gish, Webb Miller, Eugene Myers and David Lipman published BLAST in 1990, a fast heuristic that finds similar stretches in a sequence database and scores them statistically. It made it routine to ask what a newly sequenced gene resembles and became one of the most cited papers in biology.
nodes.summary: Stephen Altschul, Warren Gish, Webb Miller, Eugene Myers and David Lipman published BLAST in 1990, a fast heuristic that finds similar stretches in a sequence database and scores them statistically.

nodes.title: Neural Correlates of Consciousness

progress.what: Argued that requiring subjects to report what they experience has biased the search, and set out no-report paradigms that study conscious experience in the absence of any report.
progress.html: Argued that requiring subjects to report what they experience has biased the search, and set out no-report paradigms that study conscious experience in the absence of any report.

progress.what: The perturbational complexity index, the complexity of the EEG response to a magnetic pulse, separated conscious from unconscious conditions with 100% sensitivity and specificity in 150 benchmark subjects; 9 of 43 vegetative-state patients scored in the conscious range.
progress.html: The perturbational complexity index, the complexity of the EEG response to a magnetic pulse, separated conscious from unconscious conditions with 100% sensitivity and specificity in 150 benchmark subjects; 9 of 43 vegetative-state patients scored in the conscious range.

progress.what: An adversarial collaboration tested preregistered, conflicting predictions of integrated information theory and global neuronal workspace theory with fMRI, MEG and intracranial EEG in 256 participants; the results contradicted key tenets of both.
progress.html: An adversarial collaboration tested preregistered, conflicting predictions of integrated information theory and global neuronal workspace theory with fMRI, MEG and intracranial EEG in 256 participants; the results contradicted key tenets of both.

progress.what: Cogitate released its multi-site fMRI data from 118 participants in the open BIDS format, with analysis code, for testing other theories of consciousness.
progress.html: Cogitate released its multi-site fMRI data from 118 participants in the open BIDS format, with analysis code, for testing other theories of consciousness.

nodes.html: Which brain activity is minimally sufficient for a specific conscious experience, as distinct from the processing before it or the report after it? Francis Crick and Christof Koch launched the modern search in 1990. Solving it means a theory whose preregistered predictions survive adversarial tests; the first such test (Cogitate, Nature 2025, 256 people) contradicted key claims of both integrated information and global workspace theory.
nodes.summary: Which brain activity is minimally sufficient for a specific conscious experience, as distinct from the processing before it or the report after it?

nodes.title: Gene Therapy
nodes.html: On 14 September 1990 at the US National Institutes of Health, W. French Anderson, Michael Blaese and Kenneth Culver gave four-year-old Ashanthi DeSilva her own T cells carrying a working ADA gene, as a treatment for a severe immune deficiency. Setbacks followed in 1999 and 2002, and gene therapies were approved in Europe from 2012 and in the United States from 2017.
nodes.summary: On 14 September 1990 at the US National Institutes of Health, W.

nodes.title: Two-Photon Calcium Imaging
nodes.html: Winfried Denk, James Strickler and Watt Webb showed in 1990 that a pulsed infrared laser can excite fluorescent dyes only at the focus of a microscope, through the near-simultaneous absorption of two photons. The method images deep into living tissue with little damage, and it later allowed calcium signals of hundreds of neurons to be watched in the brains of living animals.
nodes.summary: Winfried Denk, James Strickler and Watt Webb showed in 1990 that a pulsed infrared laser can excite fluorescent dyes only at the focus of a microscope, through the near-simultaneous absorption of two photons.

nodes.title: Functional MRI
nodes.html: Seiji Ogawa showed in 1990 that blood oxygen level changes the MRI signal, and in 1992 Ogawa’s group, Kenneth Kwong’s group and others used it to map activity in the human visual cortex, as John Belliveau had done with a contrast agent in 1991. Functional MRI turned human cognitive neuroscience into an imaging science.
nodes.summary: Seiji Ogawa showed in 1990 that blood oxygen level changes the MRI signal, and in 1992 Ogawa’s group, Kenneth Kwong’s group and others used it to map activity in the human visual cortex, as John Belliveau had done with a contrast agent in 1991.

nodes.title: Directed Evolution
nodes.html: Frances Arnold applied random mutation and screening to the enzyme subtilisin to make it work in organic solvent (1993), and Willem Stemmer added DNA shuffling in 1994. Repeated rounds of mutation and screening can improve an enzyme without knowing how it works, and the approach now supplies enzymes for industry and medicine. Arnold shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
nodes.summary: Frances Arnold applied random mutation and screening to the enzyme subtilisin to make it work in organic solvent (1993), and Willem Stemmer added DNA shuffling in 1994.

nodes.title: MicroRNAs
nodes.html: Victor Ambros and Rosalind Lee, with Gary Ruvkun’s group, showed in 1993 that lin-4, a gene of the nematode worm, makes a tiny RNA about 22 nucleotides long that silences another gene, lin-14, by pairing with its messenger RNA. MicroRNAs turned out to be a large class that tunes much of the genome in animals and plants. Ambros and Ruvkun won the 2024 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Victor Ambros and Rosalind Lee, with Gary Ruvkun’s group, showed in 1993 that lin-4, a gene of the nematode worm, makes a tiny RNA about 22 nucleotides long that silences another gene, lin-14, by pairing with its messenger RNA.

nodes.title: Vesicle Traffic and SNAREs
nodes.html: Randy Schekman found the yeast genes needed for secretion, James Rothman and colleagues described in 1993 the SNARE proteins that make a vesicle fuse with its target membrane, and Thomas Südhof found how calcium triggers that fusion at synapses. The machinery of vesicle traffic explains hormone release and neurotransmission. The three shared the 2013 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Randy Schekman found the yeast genes needed for secretion, James Rothman and colleagues described in 1993 the SNARE proteins that make a vesicle fuse with its target membrane, and Thomas Südhof found how calcium triggers that fusion at synapses.

nodes.title: Flux Balance Analysis
nodes.html: Amit Varma and Bernhard Palsson showed in 1994 that a cell’s metabolic network, written as a matrix of reactions with a growth objective, can be solved by linear programming to predict growth rates and by-products in E. coli. Flux balance analysis predicts the effect of gene deletions without kinetic parameters and became the basis of genome-scale metabolic models.
nodes.summary: Amit Varma and Bernhard Palsson showed in 1994 that a cell’s metabolic network, written as a matrix of reactions with a growth objective, can be solved by linear programming to predict growth rates and by-products in E.

nodes.title: DNA Microarrays
nodes.html: Mark Schena, Patrick Brown and colleagues printed cDNAs in a grid on a glass slide and measured the activity of many genes at once (1995). By 1997 Brown’s group with David Botstein followed the expression of nearly every yeast gene on one array. Microarrays made expression profiles a basic way to compare tissues, diseases and conditions.
nodes.summary: Mark Schena, Patrick Brown and colleagues printed cDNAs in a grid on a glass slide and measured the activity of many genes at once (1995).

nodes.title: Regulatory T Cells
nodes.html: Shimon Sakaguchi showed in 1995 that a subset of T cells carrying the surface protein CD25 prevents autoimmune disease in mice by suppressing other T cells. Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell found in 2001 that mutations in the gene Foxp3 cause fatal autoimmunity, and Foxp3 was later shown to define regulatory T cells. The three shared the 2025 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Shimon Sakaguchi showed in 1995 that a subset of T cells carrying the surface protein CD25 prevents autoimmune disease in mice by suppressing other T cells.

nodes.title: Whole-Genome Shotgun Assembly
nodes.html: In 1995 a team at The Institute for Genomic Research, led by Craig Venter, Claire Fraser and Hamilton Smith with Robert Fleischmann as first author, broke the 1.8 million bases of Haemophilus influenzae into random fragments, sequenced them and reassembled the genome by computer. It was the first complete genome of a free-living organism and proved the whole-genome shotgun strategy.
nodes.summary: In 1995 a team at The Institute for Genomic Research, led by Craig Venter, Claire Fraser and Hamilton Smith with Robert Fleischmann as first author, broke the 1.8 million bases of Haemophilus influenzae into random fragments, sequenced them and reassembled the genome by computer.

nodes.title: Combination Antiretroviral Therapy
nodes.html: Trials reported at the 1996 International AIDS Conference in Vancouver showed that three drugs taken together, including a protease inhibitor, could suppress HIV to undetectable levels, as David Ho’s work on viral dynamics had suggested. Combination antiretroviral therapy then cut US AIDS deaths by about two thirds between 1995 and 1998 and made HIV a chronic, treatable condition.
nodes.summary: Trials reported at the 1996 International AIDS Conference in Vancouver showed that three drugs taken together, including a protease inhibitor, could suppress HIV to undetectable levels, as David Ho’s work on viral dynamics had suggested.

nodes.title: Immune Checkpoint Blockade
nodes.html: James Allison showed in 1996 that an antibody blocking CTLA-4, a brake on T cells, made mice reject tumours, and Tasuku Honjo’s work on PD-1 led to a second class of checkpoint inhibitors. Ipilimumab, approved in 2011, was the first drug shown to extend survival in metastatic melanoma. Allison and Honjo shared the 2018 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: James Allison showed in 1996 that an antibody blocking CTLA-4, a brake on T cells, made mice reject tumours, and Tasuku Honjo’s work on PD-1 led to a second class of checkpoint inhibitors.

nodes.title: Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer
nodes.html: Ian Wilmut, Keith Campbell and colleagues at the Roslin Institute created Dolly, born on 5 July 1996, by transferring the nucleus of a cell from an adult sheep’s udder into an egg whose own nucleus had been removed (announced 1997). It showed that the nucleus of a specialised adult cell can be reprogrammed to produce a whole animal.
nodes.summary: Ian Wilmut, Keith Campbell and colleagues at the Roslin Institute created Dolly, born on 5 July 1996, by transferring the nucleus of a cell from an adult sheep’s udder into an egg whose own nucleus had been removed (announced 1997).

nodes.title: Genetically Modified Crops
nodes.html: Crops carrying inserted genes reached the market with the Flavr Savr tomato in 1994, and large-scale planting began in 1996 with herbicide-tolerant soybean and insect-resistant Bt maize and cotton. Plant transformation with Agrobacterium was first achieved in 1983. GM crops now cover nearly 200 million hectares, and their use remains contested.
nodes.summary: Crops carrying inserted genes reached the market with the Flavr Savr tomato in 1994, and large-scale planting began in 1996 with herbicide-tolerant soybean and insect-resistant Bt maize and cotton.

nodes.title: Metabolic Scaling Theory
nodes.html: Geoffrey West, James Brown and Brian Enquist proposed in 1997 that the branching, space-filling networks that supply blood or sap to tissues explain why metabolic rate scales with body mass to the power three-quarters, as Max Kleiber had found in 1932. The model is influential and its assumptions and exact exponent are still debated.
nodes.summary: Geoffrey West, James Brown and Brian Enquist proposed in 1997 that the branching, space-filling networks that supply blood or sap to tissues explain why metabolic rate scales with body mass to the power three-quarters, as Max Kleiber had found in 1932.

nodes.title: Simulating C. elegans

progress.what: OpenWorm’s c302 neuron models drive its Sibernetic soft-body simulation through muscle activation, with no sensory feedback yet; the team judged the level of detail still inadequate for biological research.
progress.html: OpenWorm’s c302 neuron models drive its Sibernetic soft-body simulation through muscle activation, with no sensory feedback yet; the team judged the level of detail still inadequate for biological research.

progress.what: A signal propagation atlas measured 23,433 neuron pairs by optogenetic activation and whole-brain calcium imaging, and found that signals spread differently from anatomy-based predictions, partly through extrasynaptic signalling.
progress.html: A signal propagation atlas measured 23,433 neuron pairs by optogenetic activation and whole-brain calcium imaging, and found that signals spread differently from anatomy-based predictions, partly through extrasynaptic signalling.

progress.what: BAAIWorm coupled 136 multi-compartment neuron models to a 96-muscle body in a 3D environment, in closed loop, and reproduced the worm’s zigzag approach to an attractant.
progress.html: BAAIWorm coupled 136 multi-compartment neuron models to a 96-muscle body in a 3D environment, in closed loop, and reproduced the worm’s zigzag approach to an attractant.

progress.what: A connectome-constrained dynamical model fitted to that atlas captured causal interactions between all neuron pairs 82% as well as the data’s own reproducibility, far better than models built on shuffled connectomes (preprint, revised 2026).
progress.html: A connectome-constrained dynamical model fitted to that atlas captured causal interactions between all neuron pairs 82% as well as the data’s own reproducibility, far better than models built on shuffled connectomes (preprint, revised 2026).

nodes.html: Simulate the nematode C. elegans, with its 302 mapped neurons, muscles and body, well enough that it behaves like the real worm. The goal dates from the Perfect C. elegans Project (1998) and OpenWorm (2011); success means a model that predicts held-out whole-brain activity and responses to optogenetic perturbation, and whose behaviour experts cannot tell from a real worm’s. A 2024 closed-loop brain and body model covers 136 of the neurons.
nodes.summary: Simulate the nematode C.

nodes.title: RNA Interference
nodes.html: Andrew Fire and Craig Mello showed in 1998 that double-stranded RNA injected into the nematode worm silences the gene with the matching sequence far more efficiently than single strands. RNA interference became a standard way to switch off any gene, and led to a class of drugs, the first of which was approved in 2018. They won the 2006 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Andrew Fire and Craig Mello showed in 1998 that double-stranded RNA injected into the nematode worm silences the gene with the matching sequence far more efficiently than single strands.

nodes.title: Predictive Coding
nodes.html: Rajesh Rao and Dana Ballard proposed in 1999 that visual cortex works by sending predictions down the hierarchy and passing only prediction errors up, and showed that such a model reproduces effects seen in cortical neurons. Predictive coding became an influential theory of perception and brain function.
nodes.summary: Rajesh Rao and Dana Ballard proposed in 1999 that visual cortex works by sending predictions down the hierarchy and passing only prediction errors up, and showed that such a model reproduces effects seen in cortical neurons.

nodes.title: Synthetic Biology
nodes.html: In 2000 Michael Elowitz and Stanislas Leibler built the repressilator, a ring of three repressor genes that makes E. coli glow in oscillations, and Timothy Gardner, Charles Cantor and James Collins built a genetic toggle switch, a memory element. Designing gene circuits from standard parts started synthetic biology as an engineering discipline.
nodes.summary: In 2000 Michael Elowitz and Stanislas Leibler built the repressilator, a ring of three repressor genes that makes E.

nodes.title: Antibody–Antigen Structure Prediction

progress.what: The first two rounds of CAPRI, the blind docking experiment launched in 2001, drew 19 groups on seven complexes and concluded that scoring functions and conformational change were the limiting problems.
progress.html: The first two rounds of CAPRI, the blind docking experiment launched in 2001, drew 19 groups on seven complexes and concluded that scoring functions and conformational change were the limiting problems.

progress.what: On CASP16’s eight antibody-antigen targets the best group, using FFT-based docking rather than co-folding, reached acceptable accuracy on five. AlphaFold 3 run with 1,000 seeds averaged DockQ about 0.27.
progress.html: On CASP16’s eight antibody-antigen targets the best group, using FFT-based docking rather than co-folding, reached acceptable accuracy on five. AlphaFold 3 run with 1,000 seeds averaged DockQ about 0.27.

progress.what: CASP17 made immune complexes a category of their own, covering antibody-antigen, nanobody-antigen and T-cell receptor complexes, and named them a major failure area for current deep-learning methods.
progress.html: CASP17 made immune complexes a category of their own, covering antibody-antigen, nanobody-antigen and T-cell receptor complexes, and named them a major failure area for current deep-learning methods.

nodes.html: Predict where and how an antibody grips its antigen from the two sequences, the one docking class where no co-folding model has taken over. CASP scores a complex by DockQ, counting 0.23 and above as acceptable; the best CASP16 group managed five of eight antibody-antigen targets in 2024 while AlphaFold 3 averaged about 0.27. CASP17 (2026) made immune complexes their own category.
nodes.summary: Predict where and how an antibody grips its antigen from the two sequences, the one docking class where no co-folding model has taken over.

nodes.title: Targeted Cancer Therapy
nodes.html: Imatinib (Gleevec) blocks BCR-ABL, the overactive fusion kinase produced by the Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukaemia. Brian Druker, Nicholas Lydon and Charles Sawyers led the work that showed its effect in patients, and it was approved in 2001. Most patients now live for many years on a daily pill, and it became the model for targeted cancer therapy.
nodes.summary: Imatinib (Gleevec) blocks BCR-ABL, the overactive fusion kinase produced by the Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukaemia.

nodes.title: Neutral Theory of Biodiversity
nodes.html: Stephen Hubbell’s The Unified Neutral Theory of Biodiversity and Biogeography (2001) assumed that all individuals in a community are ecologically equivalent, so that species abundances arise from random birth, death, dispersal and speciation. It reproduces the abundance patterns of many tropical forests closely and serves as a null model for community ecology.
nodes.summary: Stephen Hubbell’s The Unified Neutral Theory of Biodiversity and Biogeography (2001) assumed that all individuals in a community are ecologically equivalent, so that species abundances arise from random birth, death, dispersal and speciation.

nodes.title: Predicting Protein Complexes

progress.what: AlphaFold-Multimer predicted the interface of a heteromeric complex at DockQ 0.23 or better in 67% of cases and reached high accuracy, DockQ 0.8 or better, in 23%.
progress.html: AlphaFold-Multimer predicted the interface of a heteromeric complex at DockQ 0.23 or better in 67% of cases and reached high accuracy, DockQ 0.8 or better, in 23%.

progress.what: The CASP16 assembly assessment covered 40 blind targets and about 13,600 models from 87 groups. Leading groups reached high accuracy on slightly more than half of the targets, about half of targets stayed below DockQ 0.5 for most groups, and top groups predicted stoichiometry correctly for over 70%.
progress.html: The CASP16 assembly assessment covered 40 blind targets and about 13,600 models from 87 groups. Leading groups reached high accuracy on slightly more than half of the targets, about half of targets stayed below DockQ 0.5 for most groups, and top groups predicted stoichiometry correctly for over 70%.

progress.what: An experimental audit in yeast and human found that high-confidence predictions match experimental quality, but that proteome-wide AI screens underperform at finding genuinely new interactions: the yeast experimental map reported over 40-fold more novel interactions than its AI counterpart.
progress.html: An experimental audit in yeast and human found that high-confidence predictions match experimental quality, but that proteome-wide AI screens underperform at finding genuinely new interactions: the yeast experimental map reported over 40-fold more novel interactions than its AI counterpart.

nodes.html: Given a set of protein sequences, predict whether they assemble, with what stoichiometry, and what the complex looks like. CASP scores blind assembly targets with DockQ, and in CASP16, assessed in 2025, the leading groups reached high accuracy on only slightly more than half of 40 targets. Solving it means high-accuracy models for most blind targets, scored at predictioncenter.org.
nodes.summary: Given a set of protein sequences, predict whether they assemble, with what stoichiometry, and what the complex looks like.

nodes.title: Human Genome
nodes.html: A draft in 2001, declared complete in 2003, and truly gap-free only in 2022, by the Telomere-to-Telomere consortium.
nodes.summary: A draft in 2001, declared complete in 2003, and truly gap-free only in 2022, by the Telomere-to-Telomere consortium.

nodes.title: Protein Design

quote.text: What I cannot create, I do not understand.

nodes.html: Design new proteins from scratch: Top7 (2003), a fold not seen in nature. Generative models such as RFdiffusion (2023) now design binders to order.
nodes.summary: Design new proteins from scratch: Top7 (2003), a fold not seen in nature.

nodes.title: Metagenomics
nodes.html: Jo Handelsman and colleagues named the approach in 1998: sequence the DNA of a whole microbial community without culturing any member. In 2004 Craig Venter’s team shotgun-sequenced Sargasso Sea water and found over a million new genes, and Edward DeLong’s group studied ocean microbes the same way. Metagenomics showed that most microbes have never been grown in a laboratory.
nodes.summary: Jo Handelsman and colleagues named the approach in 1998: sequence the DNA of a whole microbial community without culturing any member.

nodes.title: Next-Generation Sequencing
nodes.html: Machines that read millions of short DNA fragments in parallel began with the 454 sequencer of Jonathan Rothberg’s group (2005) and the Solexa method of Shankar Balasubramanian and David Klenerman, later Illumina’s. The cost of sequencing a human genome fell from about $10 million in 2007 to about $1,000 by 2016, and genomics became a routine tool of biology and medicine.
nodes.summary: Machines that read millions of short DNA fragments in parallel began with the 454 sequencer of Jonathan Rothberg’s group (2005) and the Solexa method of Shankar Balasubramanian and David Klenerman, later Illumina’s.

nodes.title: Optogenetics
nodes.html: Georg Nagel and Peter Hegemann identified channelrhodopsin, a light-gated ion channel from algae, in 2002-03. In 2005 Karl Deisseroth and Edward Boyden expressed it in neurons, so that pulses of light switch them on within milliseconds, and the method was soon used in living animals. Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
nodes.summary: Georg Nagel and Peter Hegemann identified channelrhodopsin, a light-gated ion channel from algae, in 2002-03.

nodes.title: Predicting Visual Cortex Responses

progress.what: A deep network trained only to recognise objects turned out to predict single-site responses of macaque V4 and inferior temporal cortex to natural images.
progress.html: A deep network trained only to recognise objects turned out to predict single-site responses of macaque V4 and inferior temporal cortex to natural images.

progress.what: The Sensorium 2023 benchmark released responses of 78,853 neurons in mouse primary visual cortex to videos; of 22 teams, the winner reached a single-trial correlation of 0.291 against 0.197 for the best baseline.
progress.html: The Sensorium 2023 benchmark released responses of 78,853 neurons in mouse primary visual cortex to videos; of 22 teams, the winner reached a single-trial correlation of 0.291 against 0.197 for the best baseline.

progress.what: A foundation model trained on many mice predicted responses to new natural videos with median normalized correlation 0.58 to 0.76, generalized to new mice and stimulus types, and predicted cell types and connectivity in the MICrONS data.
progress.html: A foundation model trained on many mice predicted responses to new natural videos with median normalized correlation 0.58 to 0.76, generalized to new mice and stimulus types, and predicted cell types and connectivity in the MICrONS data.

nodes.html: Predict how every neuron in visual cortex responds to any natural image or movie, the test Carandini and colleagues set in 2005 for knowing what the early visual system does. Success means reaching the trial-to-trial noise ceiling on new stimuli and new animals. A 2025 mouse model reaches median normalized correlation 0.58 to 0.76, and the Sensorium 2023 winner a single-trial correlation of 0.29; results are posted at sensorium-competition.net.
nodes.summary: Predict how every neuron in visual cortex responds to any natural image or movie, the test Carandini and colleagues set in 2005 for knowing what the early visual system does.

nodes.title: Population Biobanks
nodes.html: UK Biobank, led by Rory Collins, recruited about 500,000 volunteers aged 40 to 69 between 2006 and 2010 and has linked their genomes, scans, blood measurements and health records. Its data are open to approved researchers worldwide, and it set the standard for population biobanks used to study how genes and environment cause disease.
nodes.summary: UK Biobank, led by Rory Collins, recruited about 500,000 volunteers aged 40 to 69 between 2006 and 2010 and has linked their genomes, scans, blood measurements and health records.

nodes.title: HPV Vaccine
nodes.html: Ian Frazer and Jian Zhou made virus-like particles from the HPV capsid protein in 1991, and Douglas Lowy and John Schiller developed them as a vaccine antigen at the US National Cancer Institute, building on Harald zur Hausen’s finding that HPV causes cervical cancer. Gardasil was licensed in 2006 and prevents the infections behind most cervical cancers.
nodes.summary: Ian Frazer and Jian Zhou made virus-like particles from the HPV capsid protein in 1991, and Douglas Lowy and John Schiller developed them as a vaccine antigen at the US National Cancer Institute, building on Harald zur Hausen’s finding that HPV causes cervical cancer.

nodes.title: Cellular Reprogramming
nodes.html: Four transcription factors turn adult cells back into pluripotent stem cells (Yamanaka, 2006). Gurdon had shown in 1962 that a frog cell’s nucleus could be reset.
nodes.summary: Four transcription factors turn adult cells back into pluripotent stem cells (Yamanaka, 2006).

nodes.title: Genome-Wide Association Studies
nodes.html: A genome-wide association study tests hundreds of thousands of common genetic variants for association with a disease or trait across thousands of people. The Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium’s 2007 study of 14,000 cases of seven diseases and 3,000 shared controls set the template, and the method has since linked thousands of genome regions to diseases and traits.
nodes.summary: A genome-wide association study tests hundreds of thousands of common genetic variants for association with a disease or trait across thousands of people.

nodes.title: Sister Group of All Animals

progress.what: Phylogenomics across 21 phyla placed comb jellies, not sponges, as the sister group to all other animals, which would mean nerves and muscles evolved twice or were lost in sponges.
progress.html: Phylogenomics across 21 phyla placed comb jellies, not sponges, as the sister group to all other animals, which would mean nerves and muscles evolved twice or were lost in sponges.

progress.what: Used chromosome-scale gene linkage rather than sequence alignment. Rare, irreversible chromosome fusions shared by sponges, cnidarians and bilaterians but absent in comb jellies again put comb jellies first.
progress.html: Used chromosome-scale gene linkage rather than sequence alignment. Rare, irreversible chromosome fusions shared by sponges, cnidarians and bilaterians but absent in comb jellies again put comb jellies first.

progress.what: Showed that the null model behind the synteny argument shuffled genes as if all species were equally distant, which overstates how significant the shared linkage groups are.
progress.html: Showed that the null model behind the synteny argument shuffled genes as if all species were equally distant, which overstates how significant the shared linkage groups are.

progress.what: Science retracted their November 2025 paper, in which all 490 significant topology tests of 785 had favoured sponges, after the authors found errors in the analysis pipeline.
progress.html: Science retracted their November 2025 paper, in which all 490 significant topology tests of 785 had favoured sponges, after the authors found errors in the analysis pipeline.

nodes.html: Did sponges or comb jellies split off first from the rest of the animals? The answer decides whether nerves and muscles were invented once, twice or lost, and the two camps have traded the lead since 2008. Settling it needs a root that survives changes of model, gene sampling and outgroup; a sponge-first paper in Science was retracted in February 2026.
nodes.summary: Did sponges or comb jellies split off first from the rest of the animals?

nodes.title: Environmental DNA
nodes.html: Gentile Francesco Ficetola, Pierre Taberlet and colleagues showed in 2008 that DNA shed by animals into pond water can reveal which species live there, detecting the invasive American bullfrog in French ponds. Environmental DNA allows biodiversity to be surveyed from a water or soil sample without capturing any animal.
nodes.summary: Gentile Francesco Ficetola, Pierre Taberlet and colleagues showed in 2008 that DNA shed by animals into pond water can reveal which species live there, detecting the invasive American bullfrog in French ponds.

nodes.title: Organoids
nodes.html: Toshiro Sato and Hans Clevers grew single Lgr5-positive intestinal stem cells into self-organising mini-guts in a dish in 2009, and Yoshiki Sasai’s group had grown layered cortical tissue from embryonic stem cells in 2008. Organoids of brain, kidney, liver and tumour tissue followed and are used to model development and disease and to test drugs.
nodes.summary: Toshiro Sato and Hans Clevers grew single Lgr5-positive intestinal stem cells into self-organising mini-guts in a dish in 2009, and Yoshiki Sasai’s group had grown layered cortical tissue from embryonic stem cells in 2008.

nodes.title: Single-Cell RNA Sequencing
nodes.html: Fuchou Tang, Azim Surani and colleagues sequenced the full set of RNA transcripts from a single mouse cell in 2009. Droplet methods such as Drop-seq, developed by Evan Macosko, Steven McCarroll and colleagues, profiled tens of thousands of cells in a single run in 2015. Cell types are now defined by their patterns of gene expression.
nodes.summary: Fuchou Tang, Azim Surani and colleagues sequenced the full set of RNA transcripts from a single mouse cell in 2009.

nodes.title: Proofreading-Free Connectomics

progress.what: Flood-filling networks traced neurons in a zebra finch brain volume with a mean error-free path length of 1.1 mm, an order of magnitude better than earlier methods, at much higher computing cost.
progress.html: Flood-filling networks traced neurons in a zebra finch brain volume with a mean error-free path length of 1.1 mm, an order of magnitude better than earlier methods, at much higher computing cost.

progress.what: The FlyWire connectome of a whole adult fly brain (139,255 neurons, about 50 million synapses) still needed about 33 person-years of manual proofreading on top of automated segmentation.
progress.html: The FlyWire connectome of a whole adult fly brain (139,255 neurons, about 50 million synapses) still needed about 33 person-years of manual proofreading on top of automated segmentation.

progress.what: PATHFINDER, an AI system that assembles neuron fragments and scores whether the resulting shapes are plausible, cut axon reconstruction errors in a mouse cortex volume about tenfold; its authors estimate up to 84 times faster proofreading for a whole mouse brain (preprint).
progress.html: PATHFINDER, an AI system that assembles neuron fragments and scores whether the resulting shapes are plausible, cut axon reconstruction errors in a mouse cortex volume about tenfold; its authors estimate up to 84 times faster proofreading for a whole mouse brain (preprint).

progress.what: ConnectomeBench tested multimodal language models on proofreading tasks from fly and mouse connectomes: they scored 75 to 85% on split-error correction (chance 50%) but generally struggled to identify merge errors, and the best still trail human experts.
progress.html: ConnectomeBench tested multimodal language models on proofreading tasks from fly and mouse connectomes: they scored 75 to 85% on split-error correction (chance 50%) but generally struggled to identify merge errors, and the best still trail human experts.

nodes.html: Reconstruct every neuron and synapse in a brain electron-microscopy volume automatically, with no human proofreading. In 2010 Jain, Seung and Turaga called further cuts in human effort crucial for any connectome larger than the worm’s. Success means automated wiring diagrams as accurate as proofread ones; the fly brain (FlyWire, 2024) took about 33 person-years of proofreading, and brain plus nerve cord (BANC, 2026) about 38.6.
nodes.summary: Reconstruct every neuron and synapse in a brain electron-microscopy volume automatically, with no human proofreading.

nodes.title: Neanderthal Genome
nodes.html: Svante Pääbo, Richard Green and colleagues published a draft Neanderthal genome in 2010, from bones about 40,000 years old, and found that people outside Africa carry 1 to 2% Neanderthal DNA, evidence of interbreeding. The same year Pääbo’s group reported the Denisovans, from DNA in a finger bone found in a Siberian cave. Pääbo received the 2022 Nobel Prize.
nodes.summary: Svante Pääbo, Richard Green and colleagues published a draft Neanderthal genome in 2010, from bones about 40,000 years old, and found that people outside Africa carry 1 to 2% Neanderthal DNA, evidence of interbreeding.

nodes.title: Protein Function Prediction

progress.what: The first CAFA experiment evaluated 54 methods on 866 proteins from 11 organisms and found that the best of them clearly beat first-generation annotation transfer, while leaving much room for improvement.
progress.html: The first CAFA experiment evaluated 54 methods on 866 proteins from 11 organisms and found that the best of them clearly beat first-generation annotation transfer, while leaving much room for improvement.

progress.what: CAFA3 reported slight gains for molecular function and biological process and none for cellular component, and drove experimental screens that produced new annotations for more than 1,000 genes.
progress.html: CAFA3 reported slight gains for molecular function and biological process and none for cellular component, and drove experimental screens that produced new annotations for more than 1,000 genes.

progress.what: ProtBoost, which stacks gradient-boosted models over protein language model embeddings with a graph network over the Gene Ontology, took second place in CAFA5 with 0.58240 on the final leaderboard against 0.57276 for third.
progress.html: ProtBoost, which stacks gradient-boosted models over protein language model embeddings with a graph network over the Gene Ontology, took second place in CAFA5 with 0.58240 on the final leaderboard against 0.57276 for third.

progress.what: The CAFA5 assessment covered 2,850 models from 1,625 teams in 78 countries. Top methods beat every earlier CAFA round, but on proteins already carrying annotations in another ontology the best scores fell 48 to 60% below the no-knowledge setting.
progress.html: The CAFA5 assessment covered 2,850 models from 1,625 teams in 78 countries. Top methods beat every earlier CAFA round, but on proteins already carrying annotations in another ontology the best scores fell 48 to 60% below the no-knowledge setting.

nodes.html: Read a protein sequence and say what it does, in Gene Ontology terms. CAFA scores this as the information-accretion-weighted Fmax averaged over the three ontologies: CAFA5 on Kaggle (2023) drew 1,625 teams and the top entries scored about 0.58, and the 2026 assessment found scores roughly halve on proteins that already carry annotations. Results are posted by the CAFA organisers.
nodes.summary: Read a protein sequence and say what it does, in Gene Ontology terms.

nodes.title: Synthetic Genome
nodes.html: In 2010 Craig Venter, Clyde Hutchison, Daniel Gibson and colleagues chemically synthesised the 1.08 million base genome of Mycoplasma mycoides, put it into a related cell and showed that the cell ran on it. In 2016 the team cut the design down to JCVI-syn3.0, with 473 genes, the smallest genome of any self-replicating cell known.
nodes.summary: In 2010 Craig Venter, Clyde Hutchison, Daniel Gibson and colleagues chemically synthesised the 1.08 million base genome of Mycoplasma mycoides, put it into a related cell and showed that the cell ran on it.

nodes.title: CAR-T Cell Therapy
nodes.html: Zelig Eshhar designed the first chimeric antigen receptors around 1989, and Michel Sadelain and Carl June developed them into engineered T cells that attack cancer cells carrying a chosen antigen. In 2011 June’s team reported remissions in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. The first CAR-T therapies were approved in 2017 for leukaemias that had resisted other treatments.
nodes.summary: Zelig Eshhar designed the first chimeric antigen receptors around 1989, and Michel Sadelain and Carl June developed them into engineered T cells that attack cancer cells carrying a chosen antigen.

nodes.title: Rinderpest Eradication
nodes.html: Rinderpest, a viral disease of cattle that caused famines for thousands of years, was declared eradicated in June 2011, the second disease ever eradicated and the first in animals. Walter Plowright’s tissue-culture vaccine, mass vaccination and surveillance coordinated by the FAO and partners made it possible.
nodes.summary: Rinderpest, a viral disease of cattle that caused famines for thousands of years, was declared eradicated in June 2011, the second disease ever eradicated and the first in animals.

nodes.title: Treating Alzheimer’s Disease

progress.what: In CLARITY-AD, lecanemab cleared amyloid and slowed decline on the 18-point CDR-SB scale by 0.45 points over 18 months. The United States approved it in 2023, the first anti-amyloid antibody shown to slow the disease.
progress.html: In CLARITY-AD, lecanemab cleared amyloid and slowed decline on the 18-point CDR-SB scale by 0.45 points over 18 months. The United States approved it in 2023, the first anti-amyloid antibody shown to slow the disease.

progress.what: In TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2, with 1,736 participants, donanemab slowed decline on the iADRS scale by 3.25 points out of 144 over 76 weeks. It was approved in the United States in 2024.
progress.html: In TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2, with 1,736 participants, donanemab slowed decline on the iADRS scale by 3.25 points out of 144 over 76 weeks. It was approved in the United States in 2024.

progress.what: The evoke and evoke+ trials, with 3,808 participants, found that oral semaglutide improved Alzheimer’s biomarkers but did not slow progression on CDR-SB, announced on 24 November 2025.
progress.html: The evoke and evoke+ trials, with 3,808 participants, found that oral semaglutide improved Alzheimer’s biomarkers but did not slow progression on CDR-SB, announced on 24 November 2025.

progress.what: A Cochrane review of 17 trials and 20,342 participants judged the effect of anti-amyloid antibodies on cognition trivial, while brain swelling rose from 12 to 119 cases per 1,000 treated.
progress.html: A Cochrane review of 17 trials and 20,342 participants judged the effect of anti-amyloid antibodies on cognition trivial, while brain swelling rose from 12 to 119 cases per 1,000 treated.

nodes.html: The United States set itself a national goal in 2012 of preventing and effectively treating Alzheimer’s disease by 2025. Two antibodies now clear amyloid and slow decline slightly, and a 2026 Cochrane review of 17 trials called the cognitive benefit trivial against a tenfold rise in brain swelling. A solution is a treatment that halts or reverses decline rather than delaying it by months.
nodes.summary: The United States set itself a national goal in 2012 of preventing and effectively treating Alzheimer’s disease by 2025.

nodes.title: CRISPR Gene Editing
nodes.html: Bacterial immune machinery repurposed to cut DNA at any chosen sequence (2012). The first CRISPR therapy, for sickle-cell disease, was approved in 2023.
nodes.summary: Bacterial immune machinery repurposed to cut DNA at any chosen sequence (2012).

nodes.title: Whole-Cell Model of E. coli

progress.what: A mechanistic model of 1,219 E. coli genes was used to cross-evaluate decades of measurements, exposing inconsistencies in ribosome and RNA polymerase output and in metabolic parameters, and predicting protein half-lives that were then measured.
progress.html: A mechanistic model of 1,219 E. coli genes was used to cross-evaluate decades of measurements, exposing inconsistencies in ribosome and RNA polymerase output and in metabolic parameters, and predicting protein half-lives that were then measured.

progress.what: Adding 788 polycistronic operons and 1,231 transcription units to the model exposed conflicts with the RNA-seq counts it had been fitted to, including short genes misreported as zero, which were corrected in both model and data.
progress.html: Adding 788 polycistronic operons and 1,231 transcription units to the model exposed conflicts with the RNA-seq counts it had been fitted to, including short genes misreported as zero, which were corrected in both model and data.

progress.what: A machine-learning surrogate trained on model output cut the cost of a run by 95% and was used to design EMine-737, an in silico E. coli keeping 737 of the model’s 1,219 genes.
progress.html: A machine-learning surrogate trained on model output cut the cost of a run by 95% and was used to design EMine-737, an in silico E. coli keeping 737 of the model’s 1,219 genes.

nodes.html: A whole-cell model simulates every gene and molecule of a cell; the first, for Mycoplasma genitalium, appeared in 2012. Escherichia coli is the harder test case, and the public Covert lab model covers 1,219 genes (Science, 2020). Solving it means one parameter set that reproduces growth across media and genetic backgrounds and predicts knockouts it was not fitted to.
nodes.summary: A whole-cell model simulates every gene and molecule of a cell; the first, for Mycoplasma genitalium, appeared in 2012.

nodes.title: Identifying the Dark Metabolome

progress.what: MassSpecGym collected 231,000 labelled spectra covering 29,000 molecules and split them so that no training molecule is within an edge edit distance of 10 of a test molecule, removing the leakage that had inflated earlier scores.
progress.html: MassSpecGym collected 231,000 labelled spectra covering 29,000 molecules and split them so that no training molecule is within an edge edit distance of 10 of a test molecule, removing the leakage that had inflated earlier scores.

progress.what: DiffMS, a graph diffusion decoder restricted by the molecular formula, reached 2.30% top-1 and 4.25% top-10 exact-match accuracy on MassSpecGym, about double the next best method.
progress.html: DiffMS, a graph diffusion decoder restricted by the molecular formula, reached 2.30% top-1 and 4.25% top-10 exact-match accuracy on MassSpecGym, about double the next best method.

progress.what: MSFlow, a flow-matching decoder over formula-restricted spectrum embeddings, reported 32.0% top-1 and 42.5% top-10 on MassSpecGym with formulas taken from SIRIUS. The claim is a preprint and is not in the benchmark’s posted results table.
progress.html: MSFlow, a flow-matching decoder over formula-restricted spectrum embeddings, reported 32.0% top-1 and 42.5% top-10 on MassSpecGym with formulas taken from SIRIUS. The claim is a preprint and is not in the benchmark’s posted results table.

progress.what: A review of the published methods put the state of the art at 4.1% top-10 accuracy once leakage is controlled, and noted that only 2 to 13% of spectra in a typical run can be matched to a library at all.
progress.html: A review of the published methods put the state of the art at 4.1% top-10 accuracy once leakage is controlled, and noted that only 2 to 13% of spectra in a typical run can be matched to a library at all.

nodes.html: Most peaks in an untargeted metabolomics run are molecules that no spectral library can name. The problem is to recover the structure from a tandem mass spectrum alone. MassSpecGym (2024) scores this as top-1 exact-match accuracy under leakage-controlled splits; its posted results table tops out at 2.3%, while 2026 preprints claim up to 32%. Results go to the benchmark repository.
nodes.summary: Most peaks in an untargeted metabolomics run are molecules that no spectral library can name.

nodes.title: The Human Microbiome
nodes.html: The Human Microbiome Project, launched by the US National Institutes of Health in 2007, sequenced the microbes of the gut, mouth, skin and other body sites and published reference catalogues in 2012. Work by Jeffrey Gordon and others tied gut microbial communities to nutrition, obesity, immunity and the metabolism of drugs.
nodes.summary: The Human Microbiome Project, launched by the US National Institutes of Health in 2007, sequenced the microbes of the gut, mouth, skin and other body sites and published reference catalogues in 2012.

nodes.title: RNA 3D Structure Prediction

progress.what: RNA-Puzzles began as a CASP-style blind evaluation of RNA 3D structure prediction, giving the field its first shared yardstick.
progress.html: RNA-Puzzles began as a CASP-style blind evaluation of RNA 3D structure prediction, giving the field its first shared yardstick.

progress.what: The first RNA category in CASP, in CASP15, drew 42 groups on 12 targets. Deep-learning entries scored significantly worse than the top groups, which used no deep learning.
progress.html: The first RNA category in CASP, in CASP15, drew 42 groups on 12 targets. Deep-learning entries scored significantly worse than the top groups, which used no deep learning.

progress.what: The CASP16 assessment found no previously unseen natural RNA predicted above TM-score 0.8 and no appreciable improvement over earlier rounds. The AlphaFold 3 server was outperformed by 8 groups overall.
progress.html: The CASP16 assessment found no previously unseen natural RNA predicted above TM-score 0.8 and no appreciable improvement over earlier rounds. The AlphaFold 3 server was outperformed by 8 groups overall.

progress.what: In the Stanford RNA 3D Folding Kaggle round over 1,700 teams reached scores statistically tied with the CASP16 winners. The top strategy was a 3D template search with no deep learning, and a combined model, RNAPro, averaged TM-align 0.640 on the 20 private targets.
progress.html: In the Stanford RNA 3D Folding Kaggle round over 1,700 teams reached scores statistically tied with the CASP16 winners. The top strategy was a 3D template search with no deep learning, and a combined model, RNAPro, averaged TM-align 0.640 on the 20 private targets.

nodes.html: Predict an RNA’s three-dimensional fold from its sequence as reliably as AlphaFold predicts a protein’s. CASP scores entries by TM-score against the withheld experimental structure; in CASP16 (assessed 2025) no previously unseen natural RNA reached 0.8, and template search still matched deep learning. Solving it means median TM-score above 0.8 on blind, template-free natural RNAs.
nodes.summary: Predict an RNA’s three-dimensional fold from its sequence as reliably as AlphaFold predicts a protein’s.

nodes.title: Cryo-EM Resolution Revolution
nodes.html: Direct electron detectors and better image-processing software, notably Sjors Scheres’s RELION, let cryo-electron microscopy of frozen, unstained molecules reach near-atomic resolution without crystals from about 2013. The methods came from Richard Henderson, Joachim Frank and Jacques Dubochet, who shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Large complexes are now routinely solved this way.
nodes.summary: Direct electron detectors and better image-processing software, notably Sjors Scheres’s RELION, let cryo-electron microscopy of frozen, unstained molecules reach near-atomic resolution without crystals from about 2013.

nodes.title: Genome-Wide CRISPR Screens
nodes.html: In 2014 Ophir Shalem, Neville Sanjana and Feng Zhang, and independently Tim Wang and colleagues in David Sabatini’s and Eric Lander’s laboratories, knocked out essentially every human gene with pooled libraries of guide RNAs and sequenced the surviving cells to see which genes matter for a trait. Genome-wide CRISPR screens became the main route from phenotype to gene.
nodes.summary: In 2014 Ophir Shalem, Neville Sanjana and Feng Zhang, and independently Tim Wang and colleagues in David Sabatini’s and Eric Lander’s laboratories, knocked out essentially every human gene with pooled libraries of guide RNAs and sequenced the surviving cells to see which genes matter for a trait.

nodes.title: Forecasting Influenza Evolution

progress.what: A fitness model for haemagglutinin that scores adaptive epitope changes against deleterious mutations predicted which H3N2 strains would spread the following year, and proposed this as a principled basis for vaccine selection.
progress.html: A fitness model for haemagglutinin that scores adaptive epitope changes against deleterious mutations predicted which H3N2 strains would spread the following year, and proposed this as a principled basis for vaccine selection.

progress.what: Combining laboratory measurements of antigenic drift with sequence-based estimates of functional constraint forecast H3N2 populations a year ahead better than sequence-only fitness models.
progress.html: Combining laboratory measurements of antigenic drift with sequence-based estimates of functional constraint forecast H3N2 populations a year ahead better than sequence-only fitness models.

progress.what: Found individual amino-acid substitutions in H3N2 largely unpredictable: current frequency beat epitope membership and local branching index at predicting fixation, as expected under neutral dynamics.
progress.html: Found individual amino-acid substitutions in H3N2 largely unpredictable: current frequency beat epitope membership and local branching index at predicting fixation, as expected under neutral dynamics.

progress.what: VaxSeer, which predicts both dominance and antigenic match, picked strains with a better match to circulating viruses than the WHO recommendation in 9 of 10 H3N2 seasons and 6 of 10 H1N1 seasons from 2012 to 2021. The test was retrospective.
progress.html: VaxSeer, which predicts both dominance and antigenic match, picked strains with a better match to circulating viruses than the WHO recommendation in 9 of 10 H3N2 seasons and 6 of 10 H1N1 seasons from 2012 to 2021. The test was retrospective.

nodes.html: Twice a year the WHO must choose which influenza strains go into a vaccine made nine months later. Fitness models have tried to predict the winning lineage since Łuksza and Lässig in 2014. The test is beating those choices prospectively on public sequence data, scored by antigenic match to the strains that actually circulate, which no method has yet been shown to do outside a retrospective backtest.
nodes.summary: Twice a year the WHO must choose which influenza strains go into a vaccine made nine months later.

nodes.title: Nanopore Sequencing
nodes.html: David Deamer, Daniel Branton and colleagues showed in 1996 that single DNA strands passing through a protein pore change the ionic current. Hagan Bayley engineered pores for sequencing, and Oxford Nanopore Technologies released the pocket-sized MinION to early users in 2014. Nanopores read very long DNA molecules and allow sequencing in the field.
nodes.summary: David Deamer, Daniel Branton and colleagues showed in 1996 that single DNA strands passing through a protein pore change the ionic current.

nodes.title: Brain-to-Text Decoding

progress.what: Brain-To-Text decoded spoken phrases from electrocorticography in epilepsy patients by modelling phones with speech-recognition methods; the best word error rate was 25%, with a 10-word dictionary.
progress.html: Brain-To-Text decoded spoken phrases from electrocorticography in epilepsy patients by modelling phones with speech-recognition methods; the best word error rate was 25%, with a 10-word dictionary.

progress.what: In a man with ALS, 256 electrodes in the precentral gyrus decoded attempted speech with a 125,000-word vocabulary: 2.5% word error on prompted sentences and 3.7% in conversation, at about 32 words per minute, sustained over 8.4 months.
progress.html: In a man with ALS, 256 electrodes in the precentral gyrus decoded attempted speech with a 125,000-word vocabulary: 2.5% word error on prompted sentences and 3.7% in conversation, at about 32 words per minute, sustained over 8.4 months.

progress.what: The Brain-to-text ‘25 Kaggle benchmark, run by the UC Davis Neuroprosthetics Lab on held-out sentences attempted by a man with ALS, drew more than 460 teams; the winning team reached 1.54% word error on the private test set, against a 6.70% baseline.
progress.html: The Brain-to-text ‘25 Kaggle benchmark, run by the UC Davis Neuroprosthetics Lab on held-out sentences attempted by a man with ALS, drew more than 460 teams; the winning team reached 1.54% word error on the private test set, against a 6.70% baseline.

progress.what: Decoding sentences typed by nine volunteers from noninvasive MEG alone, after 10 hours of recording each, reached an average word error rate of 39%; for the best participant, half the sentences had at most one wrong word.
progress.html: Decoding sentences typed by nine volunteers from noninvasive MEG alone, after 10 hours of recording each, reached an average word error rate of 39%; for the best participant, half the sentences had at most one wrong word.

nodes.html: Decode the words a person is trying to say from recordings of their brain activity. With implanted electrodes this almost works: the winning word error rate in the Brain-to-text ‘25 benchmark on Kaggle, scored on held-out sentences from a man with ALS, was 1.54% (December 2025). Solving it means similar accuracy without surgery; decoding typed sentences from MEG still averages 39% word error (2026).
nodes.summary: Decode the words a person is trying to say from recordings of their brain activity.

nodes.title: Gene Drives
nodes.html: A CRISPR gene drive cuts the matching site on the other chromosome and copies itself there, so nearly all offspring inherit it and it can spread through a wild population against selection. Kevin Esvelt and George Church proposed the idea in 2014, and Valentino Gantz and Ethan Bier demonstrated it in fruit flies in 2015. No gene drive had been released into the wild by 2025.
nodes.summary: A CRISPR gene drive cuts the matching site on the other chromosome and copies itself there, so nearly all offspring inherit it and it can spread through a wild population against selection.

nodes.title: Protein–Ligand Affinity Prediction

progress.what: A thermodynamic perturbation calculation run with molecular dynamics gave the relative binding free energy of two thermolysin inhibitors as 4.21 kcal/mol against an experimental 4.1.
progress.html: A thermodynamic perturbation calculation run with molecular dynamics gave the relative binding free energy of two thermolysin inhibitors as 4.21 kcal/mol against an experimental 4.1.

progress.what: The FEP+ protocol was validated retrospectively on 200 ligands across several target classes and applied prospectively, the first free-energy method accurate enough to guide lead optimization at scale.
progress.html: The FEP+ protocol was validated retrospectively on 200 ligands across several target classes and applied prospectively, the first free-energy method accurate enough to guide lead optimization at scale.

progress.what: Boltz-2 was released with open weights as the first machine-learning model claimed to approach free-energy perturbation accuracy on affinity, at least 1,000 times more cheaply.
progress.html: Boltz-2 was released with open weights as the first machine-learning model claimed to approach free-energy perturbation accuracy on affinity, at least 1,000 times more cheaply.

progress.what: An independent evaluation found only weak to moderate correlations with measured affinities across datasets and no significant correlation on the top 100 compounds, concluding the model lacks the resolution for lead identification.
progress.html: An independent evaluation found only weak to moderate correlations with measured affinities across datasets and no significant correlation on the top 100 compounds, concluding the model lacks the resolution for lead identification.

nodes.html: Predict how tightly a small molecule binds a protein, well enough to rank a congeneric series before anything is synthesised. CASP16 ran the first blind pharmaceutical affinity round over 140 targets, and the 2025 assessment put the best Kendall tau at 0.42 against a ceiling near 0.73 set by experimental error, with ligand molecular weight nearly as predictive. Results are posted at predictioncenter.org.
nodes.summary: Predict how tightly a small molecule binds a protein, well enough to rank a congeneric series before anything is synthesised.

nodes.title: Predicting Smell from Structure

progress.what: In the crowdsourced DREAM Olfaction Prediction Challenge (2015), models built on chemoinformatic features predicted the intensity and pleasantness of molecules and 8 of 19 semantic descriptors; regularized linear models did almost as well as random forests.
progress.html: In the crowdsourced DREAM Olfaction Prediction Challenge (2015), models built on chemoinformatic features predicted the intensity and pleasantness of molecules and 8 of 19 semantic descriptors; regularized linear models did almost as well as random forests.

progress.what: A graph neural network learned a principal odor map. In a prospective test on new odorants rated by 15 trained panellists with a 55-word lexicon, its predicted profile was closer to the panel mean than the median panellist’s for 53% of molecules.
progress.html: A graph neural network learned a principal odor map. In a prospective test on new odorants rated by 15 trained panellists with a 55-word lexicon, its predicted profile was closer to the panel mean than the median panellist’s for 53% of molecules.

progress.what: The third DREAM olfaction challenge asked for 51-descriptor odour profiles of more than 650 mixtures of 2 to 10 molecules. The best entries reached a Pearson correlation of 0.79 with panel ratings, and 0.75 for single molecules at two concentrations.
progress.html: The third DREAM olfaction challenge asked for 51-descriptor odour profiles of more than 650 mixtures of 2 to 10 molecules. The best entries reached a Pearson correlation of 0.79 with panel ratings, and 0.75 for single molecules at two concentrations.

nodes.html: Predict how a molecule, or a mixture, will smell to people from chemical structure alone. A 2023 graph neural network matches a trained panel about as well as a typical panellist on single molecules; solving the problem means the same for mixtures and across concentrations. In the 2025 DREAM Olfaction Challenge, scored on Synapse by Pearson correlation with panel ratings on 51 descriptors, the best mixture models reached r = 0.79.
nodes.summary: Predict how a molecule, or a mixture, will smell to people from chemical structure alone.

nodes.title: Resistance from a Genome

progress.what: A catalogue of 120 resistance-determining and 772 benign mutations predicted 89.2% of drug phenotypes in 1,552 validation genomes at 92.3% sensitivity and 98.4% specificity, and proposed phasing out culture-based testing for tuberculosis.
progress.html: A catalogue of 120 resistance-determining and 772 benign mutations predicted 89.2% of drug phenotypes in 1,552 validation genomes at 92.3% sensitivity and 98.4% specificity, and proposed phasing out culture-based testing for tuberculosis.

progress.what: On 10,209 isolates, sequencing predicted isoniazid and rifampicin resistance with 97.1% and 97.5% sensitivity and 99.0% and 98.8% specificity, but only 91.3% sensitivity for pyrazinamide.
progress.html: On 10,209 isolates, sequencing predicted isoniazid and rifampicin resistance with 97.1% and 97.5% sensitivity and 99.0% and 98.8% specificity, but only 91.3% sensitivity for pyrazinamide.

progress.what: The second edition of the WHO mutation catalogue, published on 15 November 2023, graded more than 30,000 variants against 13 anti-TB drugs using over 52,000 matched isolates from 67 countries.
