progress.html: The second edition of the WHO mutation catalogue, published on 15 November 2023, graded more than 30,000 variants against 13 anti-TB drugs using over 52,000 matched isolates from 67 countries.

progress.what: Across 36,385 isolates and ten drugs the best single tool reached AUC 92.1%, the WHO catalogue had the highest specificity at 97.3% and an ensemble of five tools reached AUC 93.4%. Bedaquiline was left out because too few resistance mutations are known.
progress.html: Across 36,385 isolates and ten drugs the best single tool reached AUC 92.1%, the WHO catalogue had the highest specificity at 97.3% and an ensemble of five tools reached AUC 93.4%. Bedaquiline was left out because too few resistance mutations are known.

nodes.html: Sequence a pathogen and say which drugs will still work, accurately enough to replace culturing it. For tuberculosis, sequencing predicted isoniazid and rifampicin resistance with 97.1% and 97.5% sensitivity in 2018, but across ten drugs the best genotypic tool reached AUC 92.1% on 36,385 isolates in 2025, and bedaquiline has too few known resistance mutations to call.
nodes.summary: Sequence a pathogen and say which drugs will still work, accurately enough to replace culturing it.

nodes.title: Variants of Uncertain Significance

progress.what: Saturation genome editing measured the function of nearly 4,000 single-nucleotide variants in 13 exons of BRCA1, in almost perfect agreement with established pathogenic and benign classifications.
progress.html: Saturation genome editing measured the function of nearly 4,000 single-nucleotide variants in 13 exons of BRCA1, in almost perfect agreement with established pathogenic and benign classifications.

progress.what: AlphaMissense scored every possible human single amino acid substitution and labelled 89% of missense variants likely benign or likely pathogenic.
progress.html: AlphaMissense scored every possible human single amino acid substitution and labelled 89% of missense variants likely benign or likely pathogenic.

progress.what: Saturation genome editing in haploid human cells assigned 6,959 single-nucleotide variants in the BRCA2 DNA-binding domain to pathogenicity categories; combined with ClinGen and ACMG/AMP models, 91% could be classified as pathogenic or benign.
progress.html: Saturation genome editing in haploid human cells assigned 6,959 single-nucleotide variants in the BRCA2 DNA-binding domain to pathogenicity categories; combined with ClinGen and ACMG/AMP models, 91% could be classified as pathogenic or benign.

progress.what: ClinGen’s calibration of AlphaMissense, ESM1b and VARITY found that each supplies at most strong evidence for pathogenicity and moderate evidence for benignity under ACMG/AMP rules, a modest gain over earlier tools.
progress.html: ClinGen’s calibration of AlphaMissense, ESM1b and VARITY found that each supplies at most strong evidence for pathogenicity and moderate evidence for benignity under ACMG/AMP rules, a modest gain over earlier tools.

nodes.html: A variant of uncertain significance (VUS) is a genetic test result too uncertain to guide care; of 1.7 million people given clinical gene panels in 2014–2022, 41% received at least one. Solving it means moving most VUS in a clinical gene panel to benign or pathogenic under the 2015 ACMG/AMP rules; the best zero-shot predictors reach AUC 0.92 on ProteinGym’s clinical benchmark, and ClinGen in 2025 rated AlphaMissense at most strong evidence.
nodes.summary: A variant of uncertain significance (VUS) is a genetic test result too uncertain to guide care; of 1.7 million people given clinical gene panels in 2014–2022, 41% received at least one.

nodes.title: Base Editing
nodes.html: David Liu’s group, with Alexis Komor and Nicole Gaudelli, fused a disabled Cas9 to a deaminase enzyme in 2016 to convert one DNA letter to another at a chosen site without cutting both strands, first C to T and in 2017 A to G. Base editors can correct many disease-causing point mutations, and the related prime editing (2019) makes small insertions and deletions.
nodes.summary: David Liu’s group, with Alexis Komor and Nicole Gaudelli, fused a disabled Cas9 to a deaminase enzyme in 2016 to convert one DNA letter to another at a chosen site without cutting both strands, first C to T and in 2017 A to G.

nodes.title: Human Cell Atlas
nodes.html: The Human Cell Atlas, launched in 2016 by Aviv Regev and Sarah Teichmann, is an international effort to define every human cell type by its molecular profile using single-cell methods. By 2024 it had mapped about 62 million cells, and a November 2024 collection of Nature papers presented a step toward a first draft atlas.
nodes.summary: The Human Cell Atlas, launched in 2016 by Aviv Regev and Sarah Teichmann, is an international effort to define every human cell type by its molecular profile using single-cell methods.

nodes.title: Neoantigen Immunogenicity

progress.what: The Tumor Neoantigen Selection Alliance was announced on 1 December 2016, putting 30 academic and industry groups to work predicting immunogenic epitopes from shared tumour sequencing data.
progress.html: The Tumor Neoantigen Selection Alliance was announced on 1 December 2016, putting 30 academic and industry groups to work predicting immunogenic epitopes from shared tumour sequencing data.

progress.what: TESLA tested 608 predicted epitopes for T-cell binding in patient-matched samples. A model built from presentation and recognition features removed 98% of non-immunogenic peptides at precision above 0.70, and held up on a further 310 epitopes.
progress.html: TESLA tested 608 predicted epitopes for T-cell binding in patient-matched samples. A model built from presentation and recognition features removed 98% of non-immunogenic peptides at precision above 0.70, and held up on a further 310 epitopes.

progress.what: Modelling MHC binding, presentation and T-cell activation in one architecture showed that deep-learning immunogenicity predictors had instead learned a shortcut from HLA label imbalance, a bias the authors quantified and partly corrected.
progress.html: Modelling MHC binding, presentation and T-cell activation in one architecture showed that deep-learning immunogenicity predictors had instead learned a shortcut from HLA label imbalance, a bias the authors quantified and partly corrected.

nodes.html: Of the hundreds of mutant peptides in a tumour, predict the few that a patient’s T cells will attack. The reference set is the 608 epitopes the TESLA consortium tested for immunogenicity (Cell, 2020), where a feature-based filter removed 98% of non-immunogenic peptides at precision above 0.70. Solving it means ranking one patient’s candidates well enough to pick vaccine targets without screening them.
nodes.summary: Of the hundreds of mutant peptides in a tumour, predict the few that a patient’s T cells will attack.

nodes.title: Perturb-seq
nodes.html: Perturb-seq, published in 2016 by Atray Dixit, Britt Adamson and colleagues in the laboratories of Aviv Regev and Jonathan Weissman, pairs a CRISPR perturbation in each cell with sequencing of that cell’s transcriptome. Thousands of genetic perturbations can be tested in one pooled experiment, with the effect of each on the whole expression program read out.
nodes.summary: Perturb-seq, published in 2016 by Atray Dixit, Britt Adamson and colleagues in the laboratories of Aviv Regev and Jonathan Weissman, pairs a CRISPR perturbation in each cell with sequencing of that cell’s transcriptome.

nodes.title: Predicting Phage Host Range

progress.what: WIsH predicted the host genus of 3 kbp phage contigs with 63% mean accuracy among 20 genera, fast enough for metagenomes.
progress.html: WIsH predicted the host genus of 3 kbp phage contigs with 63% mean accuracy among 20 genera, fast enough for metagenomes.

progress.what: A measured matrix of 403 Escherichia strains against 96 phages supported strain-level prediction from genomes alone at AUROC 0.86, and a pipeline that recommended tailored cocktails for 100 pathogenic E. coli isolates.
progress.html: A measured matrix of 403 Escherichia strains against 96 phages supported strain-level prediction from genomes alone at AUROC 0.86, and a pipeline that recommended tailored cocktails for 100 pathogenic E. coli isolates.

progress.what: PhageHostLearn predicted Klebsiella phage-host pairs from receptor-binding proteins and bacterial receptors at a cross-validated ROC AUC of up to 81.8%, and held that accuracy in laboratory validation.
progress.html: PhageHostLearn predicted Klebsiella phage-host pairs from receptor-binding proteins and bacterial receptors at a cross-validated ROC AUC of up to 81.8%, and held that accuracy in laboratory validation.

progress.what: Ranking hosts by cosine similarity of Evo 2 whole-genome embeddings, with no phage-host training labels, gave 19.4% species-level top-1 accuracy against 23.2% for the best alignment baseline; fusing the two reached 26.9%.
progress.html: Ranking hosts by cosine similarity of Evo 2 whole-genome embeddings, with no phage-host training labels, gave 19.4% species-level top-1 accuracy against 23.2% for the best alignment baseline; fusing the two reached 26.9%.

nodes.html: From a phage genome alone, say which bacterial strains it will kill. Solving it means strain-level prediction accurate enough to replace laboratory screening before phage therapy. The best experimentally validated results are AUROC 0.86 within Escherichia and ROC AUC 0.82 for Klebsiella, both 2024, while species-level top-1 accuracy across diverse phages is near 27% (2026).
nodes.summary: From a phage genome alone, say which bacterial strains it will kill.

nodes.title: Spatial Transcriptomics
nodes.html: Patrik Ståhl, Joakim Lundeberg and colleagues published in 2016 a method that captures messenger RNA from a tissue section on a slide of barcoded spots, so that gene expression is measured together with its position in the tissue. Spatially resolved transcriptomics was named Nature Methods’ Method of the Year for 2020 and is used to map cell types in tissues, tumours and brains.
nodes.summary: Patrik Ståhl, Joakim Lundeberg and colleagues published in 2016 a method that captures messenger RNA from a tissue section on a slide of barcoded spots, so that gene expression is measured together with its position in the tissue.

nodes.title: Genes of Unknown Function

progress.what: Combining several in silico annotation methods assigned functions to 66 of the 149 unknown proteins, among them 24 likely transporters. The rest lack orthologues or recognisable domains, or sit in the membrane.
progress.html: Combining several in silico annotation methods assigned functions to 66 of the 149 unknown proteins, among them 24 likely transporters. The rest lack orthologues or recognisable domains, or sit in the membrane.

progress.what: A metabolic reconstruction of the related strain JCVI-syn3A supported 98% of its enzymatic reactions by annotation or experiment and narrowed the gap to 30 essential genes whose function is still unclear.
progress.html: A metabolic reconstruction of the related strain JCVI-syn3A supported 98% of its enzymatic reactions by annotation or experiment and narrowed the gap to 30 essential genes whose function is still unclear.

progress.what: SynWiki gathered the published evidence on every JCVI-syn3A gene, with protein-protein interactions as clues to function; about one third of the 452 protein-coding genes had no known function.
progress.html: SynWiki gathered the published evidence on every JCVI-syn3A gene, with protein-protein interactions as clues to function; about one third of the 452 protein-coding genes had no known function.

progress.what: Remote-homology search with protein language model embeddings found annotated homologs for about 93% of the minimal genome, leaving 15 proteins with no structurally significant match in SwissProt.
progress.html: Remote-homology search with protein language model embeddings found annotated homologs for about 93% of the minimal genome, leaving 15 proteins with no structurally significant match in SwissProt.

nodes.html: JCVI-syn3.0, the smallest genome that supports an autonomously replicating cell, has 473 genes, and 149 of them had no known biological function when it was built in 2016. Solving it means an experimentally supported function for each one. Computational annotation has closed much of the gap, with 66 assigned in 2019 and homologs found for about 93% of the genome by 2025, but those are predictions.
nodes.summary: JCVI-syn3.0, the smallest genome that supports an autonomously replicating cell, has 473 genes, and 149 of them had no known biological function when it was built in 2016.

nodes.title: Disordered Binding Regions

progress.what: The first CAID round, built on DisProt annotations collected from June 2018, scored 43 methods on 646 proteins. Disorder prediction reached Fmax 0.483, but disordered binding regions reached only Fmax 0.231.
progress.html: The first CAID round, built on DisProt annotations collected from June 2018, scored 43 methods on 646 proteins. Disorder prediction reached Fmax 0.483, but disordered binding regions reached only Fmax 0.231.

progress.what: CAID round 2 found that AlphaFold2-derived methods are good disorder predictors but are better at detecting the absence of order than the disorder annotated in DisProt.
progress.html: CAID round 2 found that AlphaFold2-derived methods are good disorder predictors but are better at detecting the absence of order than the disorder annotated in DisProt.

progress.what: In CAID round 3 the best binary disorder predictor reached AUC 0.955 on the Disorder-PDB benchmark, while on the binding benchmark the best average precision was about 0.25 and a plain AlphaFold baseline ranked fourth at AUC 0.772 and APS 0.249.
progress.html: In CAID round 3 the best binary disorder predictor reached AUC 0.955 on the Disorder-PDB benchmark, while on the binding benchmark the best average precision was about 0.25 and a plain AlphaFold baseline ranked fourth at AUC 0.772 and APS 0.249.

nodes.html: Many proteins stay disordered until they meet a partner. Predicting which residues of a disordered region do the binding is the part of disorder prediction that has not moved: CAID, running on DisProt annotations since 2018, scores it by average precision, and in round 3 (2025) the best score was about 0.25 while binary disorder prediction reached AUC 0.955. Results are posted at caid.idpcentral.org.
nodes.summary: Many proteins stay disordered until they meet a partner.

nodes.title: Predicting Perturbation Responses

progress.what: scGen, a variational autoencoder, predicted single-cell responses to stimulation and infection in cell types held out of training, across studies and species.
progress.html: scGen, a variational autoencoder, predicted single-cell responses to stimulation and infection in cell types held out of training, across studies and species.

progress.what: GEARS combined deep learning with a gene-interaction knowledge graph to predict transcriptional outcomes of single and multigene perturbations, including combinations of genes never perturbed in the training data.
progress.html: GEARS combined deep learning with a gene-interaction knowledge graph to predict transcriptional outcomes of single and multigene perturbations, including combinations of genes never perturbed in the training data.

progress.what: Five single-cell foundation models and two other deep-learning models failed to beat deliberately simple baselines, including linear models, at predicting transcriptome changes after single or double gene perturbations.
progress.html: Five single-cell foundation models and two other deep-learning models failed to beat deliberately simple baselines, including linear models, at predicting transcriptome changes after single or double gene perturbations.

progress.what: In the first Virtual Cell Challenge (300 CRISPRi knockdowns in H1 embryonic stem cells; over 1,200 teams), BioMap’s xTrimoSCPerturb won, but models did not consistently beat naive baselines and almost all did worse than the baseline on mean absolute error.
progress.html: In the first Virtual Cell Challenge (300 CRISPRi knockdowns in H1 embryonic stem cells; over 1,200 teams), BioMap’s xTrimoSCPerturb won, but models did not consistently beat naive baselines and almost all did worse than the baseline on mean absolute error.

nodes.html: Predict how a cell’s transcriptome changes when a chosen gene is knocked down, even in cell types never perturbed before. Solving it means beating naive baselines on every metric of Arc Institute’s Virtual Cell Challenge; in 2025 (over 1,200 teams, scored on perturbation discrimination, differential expression and mean absolute error) almost every model lost to the baseline on error, and the zero-shot 2026 round closes on 5 November 2026.
nodes.summary: Predict how a cell’s transcriptome changes when a chosen gene is knocked down, even in cell types never perturbed before.

nodes.title: AlphaFold
nodes.html: Predicts a protein’s 3D shape from its sequence at near-experimental accuracy (CASP14, 2020). Its database covers over 200 million proteins. Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 2024.
nodes.summary: Predicts a protein’s 3D shape from its sequence at near-experimental accuracy (CASP14, 2020).

nodes.title: mRNA Vaccines
nodes.html: Modified nucleosides (Karikó and Weissman, 2005) made mRNA usable as a drug. COVID-19 vaccines went from genome sequence to authorization in under a year (2020).
nodes.summary: Modified nucleosides (Karikó and Weissman, 2005) made mRNA usable as a drug.

nodes.title: Protein Language Models
nodes.html: Alexander Rives and colleagues at Meta AI trained a transformer on 250 million protein sequences (preprint 2019, PNAS 2021) and found that information about structure and function emerges in its internal representations. Such models predict the effects of mutations, and ESMFold (2022) predicts structure from a single sequence. They became a basis for protein design.
nodes.summary: Alexander Rives and colleagues at Meta AI trained a transformer on 250 million protein sequences (preprint 2019, PNAS 2021) and found that information about structure and function emerges in its internal representations.

nodes.title: Protein Conformational Ensembles

progress.what: Subsampling the input alignment made AlphaFold2 produce alternative conformational states of transporters and receptors rather than one structure.
progress.html: Subsampling the input alignment made AlphaFold2 produce alternative conformational states of transporters and receptors rather than one structure.

progress.what: AF-Cluster clustered a protein’s sequence alignment and predicted both states of the KaiB fold switch, which were then confirmed by NMR.
progress.html: AF-Cluster clustered a protein’s sequence alignment and predicted both states of the KaiB fold switch, which were then confirmed by NMR.

progress.what: BioEmu emulated equilibrium ensembles with a generative model, reporting free-energy errors under 1 kcal/mol against millisecond molecular dynamics and measured folding stabilities at four to five orders of magnitude less compute.
progress.html: BioEmu emulated equilibrium ensembles with a generative model, reporting free-energy errors under 1 kcal/mol against millisecond molecular dynamics and measured folding stabilities at four to five orders of magnitude less compute.

progress.what: In CASP16’s flexible-linker target 25 groups submitted 35 predicted conformational distributions, and none closely fit the combined NMR residual dipolar coupling and SAXS data withheld from them.
progress.html: In CASP16’s flexible-linker target 25 groups submitted 35 predicted conformational distributions, and none closely fit the combined NMR residual dipolar coupling and SAXS data withheld from them.

nodes.html: Predict the whole distribution of shapes a protein visits, with the right populations, instead of one structure. CASP16 ran the first blind ensembles experiment in 2024: groups modelled both reference states for 5 of 10 targets, and on the flexible-linker target none of 35 submitted distributions fit the withheld NMR and SAXS data. Solving it means matching those populations on unseen proteins.
nodes.summary: Predict the whole distribution of shapes a protein visits, with the right populations, instead of one structure.

nodes.title: TCR–Epitope Specificity

progress.what: IMMREP22, the first community benchmark for TCR-epitope prediction, fixed the task and the AUC0.1 metric used since.
progress.html: IMMREP22, the first community benchmark for TCR-epitope prediction, fixed the task and the AUC0.1 metric used since.

progress.what: IMMREP23 drew 53 teams and 398 submissions. Methods that did not exploit the test set structure were close to random on unseen peptides, and leakage in the negative set complicated the comparison.
progress.html: IMMREP23 drew 53 teams and 398 submissions. Methods that did not exploit the test set structure were close to random on unseen peptides, and leakage in the negative set complicated the comparison.

progress.what: IMMREP25 scored 126 submissions on 1,000 TCRs against 20 unseen peptides. The best entry, a modified AlphaFold 3 pipeline, reached macro-AUC0.1 0.60 against 0.50 for chance, while the only fully sequence-based method scored 0.518.
progress.html: IMMREP25 scored 126 submissions on 1,000 TCRs against 20 unseen peptides. The best entry, a modified AlphaFold 3 pipeline, reached macro-AUC0.1 0.60 against 0.50 for chance, while the only fully sequence-based method scored 0.518.

nodes.html: Given a T-cell receptor and a peptide-MHC it has never seen, predict whether they bind. The IMMREP benchmarks score this as macro-AUC0.1 over held-out peptides, where 0.50 is chance: no method beat chance on unseen peptides in the 2022 and 2023 rounds, and the best of 126 entries in IMMREP25 reached 0.60 (2026). Solving it means reliable prediction for peptides with no training data.
nodes.summary: Given a T-cell receptor and a peptide-MHC it has never seen, predict whether they bind.

nodes.title: Computational Hit Finding

progress.what: CACHE launched as a public benchmark in which teams nominate catalogue compounds for a target and one laboratory tests every nomination, with all data released without intellectual property restrictions.
progress.html: CACHE launched as a public benchmark in which teams nominate catalogue compounds for a target and one laboratory tests every nomination, with all data released without intellectual property restrictions.

progress.what: In challenge #1, against the ligand-free WDR domain of LRRK2, 23 teams nominated 1,955 compounds and 73 bound below 150 micromolar. Seven series were confirmed in two assays at 18 to 140 micromolar, and machine-learning-accelerated methods did about as well as exhaustive docking.
progress.html: In challenge #1, against the ligand-free WDR domain of LRRK2, 23 teams nominated 1,955 compounds and 73 bound below 150 micromolar. Seven series were confirmed in two assays at 18 to 140 micromolar, and machine-learning-accelerated methods did about as well as exhaustive docking.

progress.what: In challenge #2, against the RNA site of the SARS-CoV-2 helicase Nsp13, 23 teams nominated 1,957 compounds and 0.7% were confirmed as binders. Two scaffolds inhibited helicase unwinding in vitro, the better one at IC50 8.6 micromolar.
progress.html: In challenge #2, against the RNA site of the SARS-CoV-2 helicase Nsp13, 23 teams nominated 1,957 compounds and 0.7% were confirmed as binders. Two scaffolds inhibited helicase unwinding in vitro, the better one at IC50 8.6 micromolar.

progress.what: Results of challenge #5, announced in August 2026 for the GPCR MCHR1, had 24 teams nominate 1,455 compounds, of which 26 gave full dose-response inhibition at Ki 170 nM to 30 micromolar. Nine workflows produced confirmed ligands.
progress.html: Results of challenge #5, announced in August 2026 for the GPCR MCHR1, had 24 teams nominate 1,455 compounds, of which 26 gave full dose-response inhibition at Ki 170 nM to 30 micromolar. Nine workflows produced confirmed ligands.

nodes.html: Nominate compounds from a catalogue that actually bind a protein with no known ligand, instead of screening the catalogue. CACHE tests every nomination in one laboratory and publishes the misses: challenge #1 (LRRK2, 2024) had 73 of 1,955 nominations bind below 150 micromolar, and challenge #2 (Nsp13, 2025) 0.7%. Rounds 7 and 8 run in 2026, with results at cache-challenge.org.
nodes.summary: Nominate compounds from a catalogue that actually bind a protein with no known ligand, instead of screening the catalogue.

nodes.title: Xenotransplantation
nodes.html: On 7 January 2022 surgeons at the University of Maryland, led by Bartley Griffith and Muhammad Mohiuddin, transplanted a pig heart with ten gene edits into David Bennett, who survived for two months. Gene-edited pig kidneys were transplanted into living patients from 2024, with eGenesis and United Therapeutics supplying the animals. Pig organs may relieve the shortage of donor organs.
nodes.summary: On 7 January 2022 surgeons at the University of Maryland, led by Bartley Griffith and Muhammad Mohiuddin, transplanted a pig heart with ten gene edits into David Bennett, who survived for two months.

nodes.title: A Validated Biomarker of Aging

progress.what: The Biomarkers of Aging Consortium set out a shared terminology, a classification of candidate markers and the validation steps a biomarker would have to pass before it could stand in for a clinical outcome.
progress.html: The Biomarkers of Aging Consortium set out a shared terminology, a classification of candidate markers and the validation steps a biomarker would have to pass before it could stand in for a clinical outcome.

progress.what: The consortium ran the first phase of an open competition on held-out DNA methylation profiles from 500 people aged 18 to 99, and reported that the winning models beat the published clocks at predicting chronological age.
progress.html: The consortium ran the first phase of an open competition on held-out DNA methylation profiles from 500 people aged 18 to 99, and reported that the winning models beat the published clocks at predicting chronological age.

progress.what: Results from 152 teams in 28 countries: the best entry predicted chronological age to a mean absolute error of 2.45 years against about 4.8 for the Horvath clock, and the best mortality model reached a C-index of 0.844 against 0.812 for GrimAge version 2.
progress.html: Results from 152 teams in 28 countries: the best entry predicted chronological age to a mean absolute error of 2.45 years against about 4.8 for the Horvath clock, and the best mortality model reached a C-index of 0.844 against 0.812 for GrimAge version 2.

nodes.html: No measure of biological ageing is accepted as a surrogate endpoint, so a trial of an anti-ageing treatment has to wait for deaths or disease. Solving it means a marker whose change under an intervention predicts the change in clinical outcomes. The Biomarkers of Aging Challenge, reported in June 2026, scores age error in years and mortality C-index; the best were 2.45 years and 0.844.
nodes.summary: No measure of biological ageing is accepted as a surrogate endpoint, so a trial of an anti-ageing treatment has to wait for deaths or disease.

nodes.title: AlphaMissense
nodes.html: AlphaMissense (Jun Cheng, Žiga Avsec and colleagues at Google DeepMind, Science, September 2023) adapts AlphaFold, fine-tuned on variant frequencies in humans and primates, to predict the pathogenicity of single amino acid changes. It published predictions for all 71 million possible human missense variants and classified 89% as likely benign or likely pathogenic.
nodes.summary: AlphaMissense (Jun Cheng, Žiga Avsec and colleagues at Google DeepMind, Science, September 2023) adapts AlphaFold, fine-tuned on variant frequencies in humans and primates, to predict the pathogenicity of single amino acid changes.

nodes.title: De Novo Binder Design
nodes.html: RFdiffusion, from David Baker’s laboratory (Joseph Watson and colleagues, Nature 2023), generates new protein backbones around a chosen target site, and BindCraft (Martin Pacesa and colleagues, Nature 2025) designs binders using AlphaFold2. Both produce proteins that bind a given target, and BindCraft reports experimental success rates of 10 to 100% without high-throughput screening.
nodes.summary: RFdiffusion, from David Baker’s laboratory (Joseph Watson and colleagues, Nature 2023), generates new protein backbones around a chosen target site, and BindCraft (Martin Pacesa and colleagues, Nature 2025) designs binders using AlphaFold2.

nodes.title: Predicting Personal Gene Expression

progress.what: Four reference-trained models, Enformer among them, explained little of the expression variation among 421 people in Geuvadis cell-line data: per-gene correlations across individuals centred near zero, and the predicted direction of a variant’s effect was often wrong.
progress.html: Four reference-trained models, Enformer among them, explained little of the expression variation among 421 people in Geuvadis cell-line data: per-gene correlations across individuals centred near zero, and the predicted direction of a variant’s effect was often wrong.

progress.what: With paired genomes and cortex RNA-seq from 839 ROSMAP participants, Enformer often predicted the wrong direction of a variant’s effect on expression, a failure traced to poorly learned sequence-motif grammar.
progress.html: With paired genomes and cortex RNA-seq from 839 ROSMAP participants, Enformer often predicted the wrong direction of a variant’s effect on expression, a failure traced to poorly learned sequence-motif grammar.

progress.what: Fine-tuning a sequence model on personal genomes with matched expression (Variformer) brought predictions for held-out people close to each gene’s cis-heritability, but only for genes seen in training; it did not generalise to unseen genes.
progress.html: Fine-tuning a sequence model on personal genomes with matched expression (Variformer) brought predictions for held-out people close to each gene’s cis-heritability, but only for genes seen in training; it did not generalise to unseen genes.

progress.what: On 500 heritable genes in ROSMAP brain samples, AlphaGenome reached a mean cross-individual Pearson r of 0.151, against 0.058 for Borzoi and 0.670 for a per-gene elastic-net genotype model; for chromatin accessibility it came much closer (0.627 against 0.758).
progress.html: On 500 heritable genes in ROSMAP brain samples, AlphaGenome reached a mean cross-individual Pearson r of 0.151, against 0.058 for Borzoi and 0.670 for a per-gene elastic-net genotype model; for chromatin accessibility it came much closer (0.627 against 0.758).

nodes.html: Predict how one person’s gene expression differs from another’s from their genome sequences alone, for genes the model never saw in training. Solving it means matching a per-gene elastic-net genotype model fitted within the cohort, scored by cross-individual Pearson r on held-out people; on 500 heritable genes in ROSMAP brain data AlphaGenome (Nature, January 2026) reaches 0.151 against the baseline’s 0.670 (Tu et al., bioRxiv, February 2026).
nodes.summary: Predict how one person’s gene expression differs from another’s from their genome sequences alone, for genes the model never saw in training.

nodes.title: AlphaFold 3 and Open Co-Folding
nodes.html: AlphaFold 3, published in Nature in May 2024 by Josh Abramson, John Jumper and colleagues at Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs, uses a diffusion model to predict the joint structure of proteins with DNA, RNA, small-molecule ligands and ions. Open models such as Chai-1 and Boltz-1 reproduced much of its accuracy within months.
nodes.summary: AlphaFold 3, published in Nature in May 2024 by Josh Abramson, John Jumper and colleagues at Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs, uses a diffusion model to predict the joint structure of proteins with DNA, RNA, small-molecule ligands and ions.

nodes.title: Fly Brain Emulation

progress.what: A model of 64 cell types in the fly’s visual motion pathway, given only the connectome and trained to detect motion, predicted neural activity that matched measurements from 26 experimental studies.
progress.html: A model of 64 cell types in the fly’s visual motion pathway, given only the connectome and trained to detect motion, predicted neural activity that matched measurements from 26 experimental studies.

progress.what: A leaky integrate-and-fire model of the whole central brain (over 125,000 neurons and 50 million synapses), built from connectivity and predicted neurotransmitters, picked out feeding and grooming circuit neurons, with predictions confirmed by optogenetic and behavioural tests.
progress.html: A leaky integrate-and-fire model of the whole central brain (over 125,000 neurons and 50 million synapses), built from connectivity and predicted neurotransmitters, picked out feeding and grooming circuit neurons, with predictions confirmed by optogenetic and behavioural tests.

progress.what: Eon Systems wired that brain model to the NeuroMechFly v2 body through a few hand-chosen descending neurons, with no nerve cord, to show grooming, feeding and navigation to food; it conceded that the behaviours lean heavily on the body’s existing controllers and reported no quantitative comparison with real flies.
progress.html: Eon Systems wired that brain model to the NeuroMechFly v2 body through a few hand-chosen descending neurons, with no nerve cord, to show grooming, feeding and navigation to food; it conceded that the behaviours lean heavily on the body’s existing controllers and reported no quantitative comparison with real flies.

progress.what: The BANC connectome mapped an adult fly’s brain and ventral nerve cord in one volume (about 160,000 neurons), supplying the descending and ascending pathways between brain and body that a full emulation needs.
progress.html: The BANC connectome mapped an adult fly’s brain and ventral nerve cord in one volume (about 160,000 neurons), supplying the descending and ascending pathways between brain and body that a full emulation needs.

nodes.html: Run the adult fruit-fly connectome, mapped in 2024, as a working brain. Success means a connectome-based model of brain and nerve cord that predicts held-out neural recordings and responses to new optogenetic perturbations, and drives a simulated body to behave as real flies do. A 2024 model of the whole central brain predicts feeding and grooming circuits; a connectome of brain and nerve cord together followed in 2026.
nodes.summary: Run the adult fruit-fly connectome, mapped in 2024, as a working brain.

nodes.title: Fly Brain Connectome
nodes.html: The FlyWire consortium, led by Sebastian Seung and Mala Murthy at Princeton, reconstructed and proofread the wiring of a whole adult female fruit fly brain from electron microscope images: 139,255 neurons and about 50 million synapses (Nature, October 2024). It is a complete connectome of a brain with more than 100,000 neurons and a resource for linking circuit structure to behaviour.
nodes.summary: The FlyWire consortium, led by Sebastian Seung and Mala Murthy at Princeton, reconstructed and proofread the wiring of a whole adult female fruit fly brain from electron microscope images: 139,255 neurons and about 50 million synapses (Nature, October 2024).

nodes.title: Reliable De Novo Binder Design

progress.what: The first open EGFR binder competition, run from July to October 2024, tested 201 submitted designs in one laboratory. 2.5% bound the target and the best affinity was 491 nM.
progress.html: The first open EGFR binder competition, run from July to October 2024, tested 201 submitted designs in one laboratory. 2.5% bound the target and the best affinity was 491 nM.

progress.what: The second EGFR round, judged in January 2025, tested 400 designs with a 14% hit rate and a best affinity of 1.21 nM. Across both rounds the strongest entries optimized known binders; the best fully de novo design reached 82 nM.
progress.html: The second EGFR round, judged in January 2025, tested 400 designs with a 14% hit rate and a best affinity of 1.21 nM. Across both rounds the strongest entries optimized known binders; the best fully de novo design reached 82 nM.

progress.what: The Nipah virus glycoprotein G round, judged in January 2026, tested about 1,200 designs with a 9.3% hit rate and a best affinity of 0.37 nM.
progress.html: The Nipah virus glycoprotein G round, judged in January 2026, tested about 1,200 designs with a 9.3% hit rate and a best affinity of 0.37 nM.

progress.what: The RBX1 round, run from February to April 2026 with GEM, tested 322 designs on a harder target: the hit rate fell back to 2.8% and the best affinity was 23.7 nM.
progress.html: The RBX1 round, run from February to April 2026 with GEM, tested 322 designs on a harder target: the hit rate fell back to 2.8% and the best affinity was 23.7 nM.

nodes.html: Design a protein that binds a named target at nanomolar affinity on the first try, most of the time. Adaptyv’s open competitions test every entry in one laboratory and publish the misses: the first EGFR round (2024) had 2.5% of 201 designs bind, best 491 nM, and the Nipah round (January 2026) 9.3% of about 1,200, best 0.37 nM. Rates per round are posted at proteinbase.com/competitions.
nodes.summary: Design a protein that binds a named target at nanomolar affinity on the first try, most of the time.

nodes.title: AI-Designed Antibiotics
nodes.html: Jonathan Stokes, James Collins and colleagues used a graph neural network to pick the antibiotic halicin out of a chemical library (Cell, 2020). In 2025 Aarti Krishnan and colleagues used generative models to design new compounds from scratch, NG1 against gonorrhoea and DN1 against MRSA, which reduced bacterial load in mouse infection models (Cell, 2025).
nodes.summary: Jonathan Stokes, James Collins and colleagues used a graph neural network to pick the antibiotic halicin out of a chemical library (Cell, 2020).

nodes.title: AI-Designed Drug in the Clinic
nodes.html: Insilico Medicine’s rentosertib (ISM001-055), a TNIK inhibitor whose target and molecule were both found with generative AI, was tested in a randomised, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial of 71 patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Nature Medicine, June 2025). Forced vital capacity rose by 98 mL at the highest dose and fell by 20 mL on placebo over 12 weeks, and larger trials are needed.
nodes.summary: Insilico Medicine’s rentosertib (ISM001-055), a TNIK inhibitor whose target and molecule were both found with generative AI, was tested in a randomised, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial of 71 patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Nature Medicine, June 2025).

nodes.title: De Novo Antibody Design
nodes.html: RFantibody, from David Baker’s laboratory (Nathaniel Bennett, Joseph Watson and colleagues, Nature, November 2025), uses a fine-tuned RFdiffusion network and yeast display to generate single-domain antibodies and scFvs against chosen epitopes. Cryo-EM confirmed designed binding poses for influenza haemagglutinin and C. difficile toxin B, and affinity maturation reached nanomolar binding.
nodes.summary: RFantibody, from David Baker’s laboratory (Nathaniel Bennett, Joseph Watson and colleagues, Nature, November 2025), uses a fine-tuned RFdiffusion network and yeast display to generate single-domain antibodies and scFvs against chosen epitopes.

nodes.title: Designed Enzymes at Natural Rates
nodes.html: In 2025 Sarel Fleishman’s group (Listov, Lipsh-Sokolik and colleagues) designed Kemp eliminases by a fully computational workflow, without mutant-library screening, reaching efficiencies above 100,000 per molar per second. David Baker’s group (Anna Lauko and colleagues) used RFdiffusion to design serine hydrolases reaching 220,000. Earlier designs needed laboratory optimisation.
nodes.summary: In 2025 Sarel Fleishman’s group (Listov, Lipsh-Sokolik and colleagues) designed Kemp eliminases by a fully computational workflow, without mutant-library screening, reaching efficiencies above 100,000 per molar per second.

nodes.title: MICrONS Cortical Atlas
nodes.html: The MICrONS consortium, including Andreas Tolias, Sebastian Seung and R. Clay Reid, published in Nature in April 2025 a cubic millimetre of mouse visual cortex reconstructed from electron microscopy, with more than 200,000 cells and 0.5 billion synapses, matched to calcium imaging of about 75,000 neurons. It links the wiring of a cortical circuit to what its neurons did.
nodes.summary: The MICrONS consortium, including Andreas Tolias, Sebastian Seung and R.

nodes.title: Missing Heritability Resolved
nodes.html: Twin and family studies long gave higher heritability estimates than genome scans could explain. Pierrick Wainschtein, Loic Yengo, Peter Visscher and colleagues analysed whole genomes of 347,630 UK Biobank participants and found that sequencing captured about 88% of pedigree-based heritability across 34 traits (Nature, November 2025). For 15 traits no significant gap remained.
nodes.summary: Twin and family studies long gave higher heritability estimates than genome scans could explain.

nodes.title: Bespoke Gene-Editing Therapy
nodes.html: Kiran Musunuru and Rebecca Ahrens-Nicklas’s teams designed a base-editing therapy, delivered in lipid nanoparticles, to correct the CPS1 mutation in KJ Muldoon, a newborn with a severe urea cycle disorder. Dosing began about six months after diagnosis in 2025, and the case appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine. It showed that a gene-editing therapy can be built for one patient.
nodes.summary: Kiran Musunuru and Rebecca Ahrens-Nicklas’s teams designed a base-editing therapy, delivered in lipid nanoparticles, to correct the CPS1 mutation in KJ Muldoon, a newborn with a severe urea cycle disorder.

nodes.title: AI Co-Scientists
nodes.html: Google’s Co-Scientist (Juraj Gottweis and colleagues) and FutureHouse’s Robin (Ali Ghareeb and colleagues) are multi-agent systems that generate hypotheses and plan experiments, and both were published in Nature on 19 May 2026. Co-Scientist proposed leukaemia drug-repurposing candidates validated in vitro, and Robin identified ripasudil as a candidate for dry macular degeneration.
nodes.summary: Google’s Co-Scientist (Juraj Gottweis and colleagues) and FutureHouse’s Robin (Ali Ghareeb and colleagues) are multi-agent systems that generate hypotheses and plan experiments, and both were published in Nature on 19 May 2026.

nodes.title: AI-Designed Bacteriophages
nodes.html: Samuel King, Brian Hie and colleagues at the Arc Institute fine-tuned the Evo genome language models to generate complete genomes of phages resembling phiX174 (Science, August 2026). Sixteen of the generated genomes gave viable viruses, and a cocktail of them overcame E. coli strains resistant to phiX174. The authors describe it as the first generative design of complete phage genomes.
nodes.summary: Samuel King, Brian Hie and colleagues at the Arc Institute fine-tuned the Evo genome language models to generate complete genomes of phages resembling phiX174 (Science, August 2026).

nodes.title: AlphaGenome
nodes.html: AlphaGenome, from Google DeepMind (Žiga Avsec and colleagues, Nature, January 2026), takes up to one million DNA bases and predicts thousands of functional genomic tracks at single-base resolution, including gene expression, splicing, chromatin accessibility and contacts. It matched or exceeded the best external models in 25 of 26 variant effect evaluations.
nodes.summary: AlphaGenome, from Google DeepMind (Žiga Avsec and colleagues, Nature, January 2026), takes up to one million DNA bases and predicts thousands of functional genomic tracks at single-base resolution, including gene expression, splicing, chromatin accessibility and contacts.

nodes.title: Genome Language Models
nodes.html: Evo 2, from the Arc Institute and collaborators (Garyk Brixi, Brian Hie, Patrick Hsu and colleagues; Nature, March 2026), is trained on 9 trillion DNA bases from all domains of life. It predicts variant effects, such as in BRCA1, without task-specific training and generates genome-scale mitochondrial, bacterial and eukaryotic sequences. Its code and data are open.
nodes.summary: Evo 2, from the Arc Institute and collaborators (Garyk Brixi, Brian Hie, Patrick Hsu and colleagues; Nature, March 2026), is trained on 9 trillion DNA bases from all domains of life.

nodes.title: 4D Minimal Cell Simulation
nodes.html: Zane Thornburg, Zaida Luthey-Schulten and colleagues simulated a complete cell cycle of about 100 minutes of the genetically minimal bacterium JCVI-syn3A in space and time (Cell, March 2026), covering metabolism, gene expression, growth, chromosome replication and segregation, and division. The model recovers measured doubling time, mRNA half-lives and ribosome counts.
nodes.summary: Zane Thornburg, Zaida Luthey-Schulten and colleagues simulated a complete cell cycle of about 100 minutes of the genetically minimal bacterium JCVI-syn3A in space and time (Cell, March 2026), covering metabolism, gene expression, growth, chromosome replication and segregation, and division.

nodes.title: Rejuvenation Therapy

progress.what: First human dosed in a Phase 1 trial of ER-100, a partial epigenetic reprogramming therapy (three Yamanaka factors) for optic neuropathies; the primary endpoint is safety.
progress.html: First human dosed in a Phase 1 trial of ER-100, a partial epigenetic reprogramming therapy (three Yamanaka factors) for optic neuropathies; the primary endpoint is safety.

nodes.html: Reverse biological ageing in people, for example by partial reprogramming of cells. It works in some mouse studies. In June 2026 the first person was dosed in a trial of partial reprogramming for optic nerve disease; no benefit in humans has been shown yet.
nodes.summary: Reverse biological ageing in people, for example by partial reprogramming of cells.

nodes.title: Virtual Cell
nodes.html: A simulation that predicts how a living cell responds to any genetic or chemical change. Whole-cell models now exist for the minimal bacterium JCVI-syn3A, including a 4D simulation published in Cell in 2026, but not yet for human cells.
nodes.summary: A simulation that predicts how a living cell responds to any genetic or chemical change.

nodes.title: Whole-Brain Emulation
nodes.html: Scan a brain at synaptic resolution and simulate it faithfully enough to behave like the original. A fly will probably come first; a mouse would be the next milestone.
nodes.summary: Scan a brain at synaptic resolution and simulate it faithfully enough to behave like the original.
